This tragic incident cannot be described as anything other than a cold-blooded murder carried out by a dangerous individual who should not have been out on the streets to begin with.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: this week is Police Week, and I think our law enforcement officers would agree that public safety should not be a partisan issue. What we have seen around the country are leftist judges and DAs who are pushing policies that put criminals back on the streets and take tools away from law enforcement. One of the ways that happens is through cashless bail. I was an attorney for 30 years, and I practiced all levels of court, including criminal practice.

gaps: The bill requires quarterly publication of the list but specifies no format, accessibility standard, or enforcement mechanism for failure to publish or update.

The bill covers release on personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds but does not address other low- or no-cash release mechanisms — property bonds, electronic monitoring conditions, or supervised release programs — that are not captured by the reporting requirement.

added: Requirement for Attorney General to publicly list all states and local governments permitting pretrial release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond, published within 30 days and updated quarterly

New "covered offense" definition: a crime the Attorney General finds poses a clear threat to public safety, including violent/sexual acts (murder, rape, sexual assault, carjacking, robbery, burglary, assault) and public-disorder offenses (looting, vandalism, destruction of property, rioting/inciting to riot, fleeing a law enforcement officer)
modified: Publication deadline lengthened from "not later than 30 days" to "not later than one year" after enactment
Update frequency changed from quarterly to annually
List scope narrowed from jurisdictions that release any person "charged with an offense" to only those charged with a "covered offense"

bills.title: Monitor Accountability Act
bills.official_title: To provide for conditions on the appointment of monitors by courts, and for other purposes.
bills.summary: Federal courts must follow new rules when appointing monitors to oversee state and local governments under consent decrees — including fee caps, a 5-year term limit, a one-monitorship-at-a-time restriction, and mandatory public notice before appointment. The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts must issue rules within 90 days, and active monitorships already running 6 or more years must get a new monitor within 180 days and be transferred to a new judge within 1 year.
bills.brief: Sets term limits, fee caps, and public accountability rules for court-appointed monitors overseeing state and local governments under consent decrees.

top_lines.headline: Monitor Term and Appointment Limits
subs: 5-year term limit per court order; no reappointment under the same order after term expires
Monitor may not hold more than one monitorship at a time
Successor monitor may not be employed by the same firm as the prior monitor

top_lines.headline: Fee Caps and Public Accountability
subs: Fees capped at rates set by the Administrative Office of U.S. Courts; pro bono and reduced-rate services explicitly authorized
Annual public accounting of services, fees, and any pro bono work required from each monitor
Court must provide public notice and comment opportunity before appointing any monitor

top_lines.headline: Case Transfer and Retroactivity
subs: Case transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order
Existing monitorships of 6+ years: new monitor appointed within 180 days of enactment, case transferred within 1 year

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 219-204 with only 5 crossover votes — a near party-line result indicating minimal Democratic support. Sponsor Rep. Biggs (R-AZ) had only 2 cosponsors. Consent decree reform is sharply partisan: term limits and fee caps would disrupt ongoing civil rights oversight of police departments, and Democratic senators are expected to oppose unanimously. The Senate 60-vote threshold is not within reach under current conditions.

items.main: Names the Act the “Monitor Accountability Act of 2026”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: The Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts must establish rules within 90 days imposing fee caps, a single-monitorship-at-a-time limit, a 5-year term limit with no reappointment under the same court order, and a prohibition on successive monitors sharing employers.
items.detail: Conditions apply to any person appointed by a district court to monitor the conduct of a state or unit of local government. Fee rules must explicitly authorize pro bono and reduced-rate services. Courts must provide public notice and an opportunity for comment before any monitor appointment.

items.main: Cases are transferred to a new judge in the same district 6 years after the court order imposing the monitorship; monitors must submit annual public accountings of services, fees, and pro bono work to the court.
items.detail: For monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years on the date of enactment, a new monitor must be appointed within 180 days and the case transferred within 1 year. The transfer trigger is purely time-based with no assessment of compliance status required.

underreported.summary: The retroactivity clause requires all monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years to appoint a new monitor within 180 days and transfer the case to a new judge within 1 year, regardless of whether the monitored entity is making progress toward compliance.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed around appointment conditions for future monitorships, but Section 2(d) immediately disrupts currently active consent decree oversight arrangements — including ongoing policing reform monitorships — without any compliance-status prerequisite.

underreported.summary: Cases transfer to a new judge automatically at exactly 6 years after the court order on a time-based trigger with no assessment of case status, compliance progress, or complexity.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill purpose covers appointment conditions, but the judge-transfer provision operates as a mandatory procedural reset on a fixed schedule independent of whether the monitorship is progressing toward its stated goals.

criticisms.why: I do rise today in opposition to H.R. 8365, the Monitor Accountability Act. This bill addresses the work of Federal monitors who are appointed by a court to oversee the progress a State or a unit of local government is making after violating Federal law. Often monitors are put in place after there is a finding of serious misconduct, including violations of constitutional rights or actions that jeopardize people's public health, safety, and well-being.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. McBath
featured_quotes.text: I do rise today in opposition to H.R. 8365, the Monitor Accountability Act. This bill addresses the work of Federal monitors who are appointed by a court to oversee the progress a State or a unit of local government is making after violating Federal law. Often monitors are put in place after there is a finding of serious misconduct, including violations of constitutional rights or actions that jeopardize people's public health, safety, and well-being.

gaps: The bill sets a 5-year term limit for monitors but specifies no continuity procedure if no compliant replacement monitor can be identified or appointed before the prior monitor's term expires.

The bill scope covers monitors appointed to oversee state and local governments but does not address monitors appointed in deferred prosecution agreements with private entities or federal contractors, which operate under the same district court rules.

added: Mandatory conditions on federal court appointment of monitors for state and local government oversight (fee caps, 5-year term limit, single-monitorship limit)
Prohibition on successive monitors under the same court order sharing the same employer
Public notice and comment requirement before any monitor appointment
Annual public accounting of monitor fees and services
Mandatory case transfer to a new judge 6 years after the court order
Retroactivity for all monitorships already in effect for 6 or more years: new monitor within 180 days, new judge within 1 year

modified: Rulemaking authority shifted from the Administrator of the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts to the Judicial Conference of the United States (including the maximum-fee-rate authority)
Rulemaking deadline lengthened from "not later than 90 days" to "not later than 180 days" after the section's effective date
Short title shortened from "Monitor Accountability Act of 2026" to "Monitor Accountability Act"

bills.title: Keeping Violent Offenders Off Our Streets Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend title 18, United States Code, to prohibit fraud in connection with posting bail.
bills.summary: This bill adds the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds to the federal definition of the "business of insurance" under 18 U.S.C. 1033 — making organizations that post bail, including charitable bail funds, subject to the federal criminal fraud and embezzlement provisions that apply to the business of insurance.
bills.brief: Expands the federal definition of "business of insurance" to include bail-posting activity, subjecting charitable bail funds and bail bond companies to federal insurance fraud law.

top_lines.headline: Bail Redefined as Insurance Activity
subs: Adds posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds to the federal definition of "business of insurance"
Subjects bail-posting entities — including charitable bail organizations — to federal criminal fraud and embezzlement provisions that apply to insurance companies

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 243-179 with 33 crossover votes — some bipartisan support, but the mechanism (reclassifying bail-posting entities as insurance companies) remains a partisan flash point. In the Senate, 60 votes are needed to clear a filibuster. Most Democratic senators are expected to oppose a provision that would subject charitable bail funds to federal criminal liability, and no Senate companion bill has been identified.

items.main: Names the Act the “Keeping Violent Offenders Off Our Streets Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Fraud in Connection with Posting Bail

items.main: Amends 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) to add "the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and Federal immigration bail bonds" to the existing definition of the business of insurance.
items.detail: Under 18 U.S.C. 1033, persons engaged in the business of insurance are subject to federal criminal penalties for embezzlement, false statements, and related fraud. After this amendment, entities that post bail — including charitable bail organizations — are subject to those federal criminal provisions.

underreported.summary: The amendment to 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) extends the federal insurance fraud criminal statute to bail-posting entities. Officers, directors, and employees of organizations that post bail could face federal criminal liability for embezzlement or false statements under 1033 — not limited to bail posted for violent offenders.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title references violent offenders, but the operative amendment applies to all bail posting without any offense-type limitation. The mechanism operates through the insurance fraud statute, making the primary legal effect a reclassification that triggers criminal exposure rather than a direct restriction on bail practices.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Menefee
featured_quotes.text: I was proud to defend that consent decree. Let's be clear about what this is. If somebody is a threat to the community, they should be in jail, regardless of whether they have a billion dollars or a thousand dollars. If they are not a threat to the community, they should not be left to languish in jail, potentially lose their livelihood, their family, all so we can make cash bail companies more rich. We should be about protecting the community, not protecting industry.

gaps: The bill amends the "business of insurance" definition but specifies no threshold — in frequency, dollar amount, or organizational structure — at which a bail-posting entity crosses into engaging in the "business" of insurance versus making an occasional bail payment.

The amendment covers criminal bail bonds and federal immigration bail bonds but does not address civil immigration bonds maintained under a separate regulatory regime, which are not referenced in the amendment text.

modified: 18 U.S.C. 1033(f)(1)(A) — definition of "business of insurance" expanded to include the posting of monetary bail, criminal bail bonds, and federal immigration bail bonds
Short title expanded to "Keeping Violent Offenders Off Our Streets Act of 2025" (added "of 2025")

bills.title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025
bills.summary: For decades, families of Holocaust victims have tried to recover artwork stolen by Nazi Germany, only to have American courts dismiss their cases on procedural grounds — time delays, deference to foreign governments, or doctrines unrelated to who actually owned the art. This law permanently removes those barriers. It prohibits courts from dismissing Holocaust art claims based on the passage of time or other procedural defenses, strips foreign governments of a key immunity argument regardless of the victim's nationality, removes the December 31, 2026 filing deadline entirely, and applies all of those changes retroactively to cases currently in court.
bills.brief: Permanently bars courts from dismissing Nazi-looted art claims on procedural grounds, overriding multiple appellate and Supreme Court rulings that had blocked recovery.

top_lines.headline: Procedural Defenses Eliminated
subs: Laches, adverse possession, international comity, forum non conveniens, and act of state doctrine may no longer be used to dismiss Holocaust art claims
Applies retroactively to cases currently pending, including those on appeal

top_lines.headline: Foreign Sovereign Immunity Overridden
subs: Claims against foreign governments proceed regardless of victim nationality — overrides the 2021 Supreme Court ruling in Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp
Nationwide service of process added, allowing courts to reach defendants in any U.S. district

top_lines.headline: Filing Deadline Removed
subs: December 31, 2026 filing deadline eliminated — claims may be filed at any time
Six-year discovery period from the date the claimant learns of the artwork's location still applies

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 13, 2026 as Public Law 119-82.

items.main: Names the Act the “Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Adds new Section 5(f) to the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016, barring all time-based defenses and all non-merits discretionary bases for dismissal against otherwise timely Holocaust art claims.
items.detail: Prohibited time-based defenses include laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, and usucapion. Prohibited non-merits defenses include the act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, and prudential exhaustion. The bill adds findings naming specific court decisions that frustrated the original Act's intent, including Zuckerman v. Metropolitan Museum of Art (2d Cir. 2019), Cassirer v. Thyssen-Bornemisza Foundation (9th Cir. 2024), and Von Saher v. Norton Simon Museum of Art (9th Cir. 2018).

items.main: New Section 5(b) deems Holocaust art claims to constitute actions involving violations of international law for purposes of the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3)), regardless of the nationality or citizenship of the alleged victim.
items.detail: This directly overrides Federal Republic of Germany v. Philipp, 592 U.S. 169 (2021), in which the Supreme Court held that the "domestic takings" rule barred FSIA jurisdiction over property seized from a country's own nationals. Nationwide service of process is added for all civil actions under the Act. All amendments apply to claims pending on the date of enactment — including cases pending on appeal or within the appeal filing window — and to cases filed after enactment.

items.main: Removes the December 31, 2026 deadline for filing claims and replaces it with a perpetual filing window subject to a six-year discovery period.
items.detail: Under prior law, all claims had to be filed by December 31, 2026 regardless of when the claimant discovered the property's location. This deadline is eliminated. Claims must still be filed within six years of the claimant's discovery of the property in question.

underreported.summary: The law applies to any civil claim pending in any court on the date of enactment, including claims pending on appeal and claims for which the time to file an appeal has not yet expired.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is the permanent removal of procedural barriers to future claims. The retroactive reach to cases already dismissed and currently on appeal means courts that previously dismissed Holocaust art claims on laches or international comity grounds could have those dismissals challenged or reversed under the new law, affecting outcomes in litigation already underway.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Raskin
featured_quotes.text: This bill, which has already passed the Senate by unanimous consent, amends the Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016 in a number of key ways to ensure that Holocaust survivors and their heirs have a fair opportunity in court to recover all of the artwork that was stolen by the Nazi regime or what is left of it. In doing so, this bill will provide these victims the chance to obtain some small measure of justice for the horrors and the injustices and indignities their families have endured.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: it is just for Holocaust survivors and their heirs to continue to have their claims relating to art stolen from them  by the Nazis heard in court. These claims should be decided on the merits, not dismissed due to technical defenses. The Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2025 will ensure just that.

gaps: The law bars procedural defenses but does not address the evidentiary standard for establishing provenance or Nazi-era confiscation in the underlying merits of a claim.

The law covers artwork lost "because, or as a result, of Nazi persecution" but does not address property transferred through forced sales under economic duress rather than outright confiscation, a category that has faced definitional challenges in prior litigation.

added: Section 5(b) of the HEAR Act — foreign sovereign immunity exception: Holocaust art claims deemed violations of international law under 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(3) regardless of victim nationality

Section 5(f) — prohibition on all time-based defenses (laches, adverse possession, acquisitive prescription, usucapion) and non-merits discretionary defenses (act of state doctrine, international comity, forum non conveniens, prudential exhaustion)
Section 5(g) — nationwide service of process for Holocaust art civil actions
Section 6 — severability provision
modified: HEAR Act of 2016 findings — expanded to name specific court decisions that frustrated the Act's intent and to state that non-merits defenses must be precluded
HEAR Act Section 3(2) — definition of covered defenses expanded to include "other non-merits defenses" alongside statutes of limitation
removed: December 31, 2026 filing deadline for Holocaust art recovery claims

referencedSources.label: S 2763 (114th Congress) — Holocaust Expropriated Art Recovery Act of 2016 (introduced)

bills.title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
bills.official_title: Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act
bills.summary: The SBIR and STTR programs are the federal government's primary mechanism for funding early-stage technology research at small businesses — agencies with large R&D budgets must set aside a percentage for competitive grants to startups, covering everything from initial feasibility through full development and commercialization. This law extends those programs through fiscal year 2031 and adds a significant national security layer: agencies must now screen all applicants against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary connections, can deny grants based on classified intelligence, and must notify rejected applicants of the basis for denial when doing so won't compromise national security.
bills.brief: Extends SBIR and STTR small-business research grants through FY2031 and adds mandatory screening against eight federal watchlists for foreign adversary ties.

top_lines.headline: Extended Through FY2031
subs: SBIR and STTR programs reauthorized through fiscal year 2031
New strategic breakthrough allocations added — Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching funds

top_lines.headline: Eight-Watchlist Security Screen
subs: Applicants checked against UFLPA, OFAC Chinese Military-Industrial Complex, Section 889, Chinese Military Companies, Military End User, Entity, FCC Equipment, and CBP Withhold Release Orders lists
Classified security risks are also a basis for denial; rejected applicants must be notified of the basis unless doing so would compromise national security

top_lines.headline: Caps and Commercialization
subs: Maximum number of proposals per small business per fiscal year established for Phase I and Phase II
Expanded Phase III commercialization training required for agency contracting officers

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law by the President on April 13, 2026 as Public Law 119-83.

items.main: Names the Act the “Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Requires federal agencies administering SBIR and STTR programs to evaluate whether applicants present security risks, including through coordination with the intelligence community, law enforcement, and other counterintelligence capabilities.
items.detail: Agencies must deny applications from small businesses with a security risk connecting them to entities or individuals on any of eight federal watchlists: the UFLPA Entity List (DHS), the OFAC Non-SDN Chinese Military-Industrial Complex Companies List (Treasury), the Section 889 Prohibition List (DoD), the Chinese Military Companies List (DoD), the Military End User List (Commerce), the Entity List (Commerce), the FCC Equipment and Services List, or the CBP Withhold Release Orders and Findings List. Classified security risks and agency-determined security risks are also grounds for denial. Upon denying an application on security grounds, the agency must notify the small business of the determination and its basis, to the extent doing so does not compromise national security. Denial on security grounds does not bar the business from applying in a subsequent award cycle.

sections.label: Section 3 — Phase II Strategic Breakthrough Funding

items.main: Creates a strategic breakthrough allocation letting agencies (with an SBIR expenditure above $100M) award up to $30M in Phase II funds per small business, drawn from up to 0.50 percent of the agency's extramural R&D budget.
items.detail: Amends Section 9 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 638) subsections (aa) and (ff). Recipients must hold a prior Phase II award, demonstrate at least 100 percent matching funds, and show an effective technology. Total period of performance capped at 48 months; agencies must complete awards within 90 days of receiving a proposal. Briefings to the Small Business and Science committees required within 60 days of enactment. Under subsection (d), this section and its amendments cease to have effect September 30, 2031.

items.main: Requires each agency's SBIR/STTR program director to set, equally for all small businesses, a cap on the number of Phase I and Phase II proposals a business may submit per fiscal year (by fiscal year, solicitation, or topic basis).
items.detail: Adds new subsection (aaa) to 15 U.S.C. 638, effective for fiscal year 2027 and after. Topic-by-topic waivers allowed only for time-sensitive, urgent topics, capped at 5 percent of an agency's topics per fiscal year, with written justification and 15-day approval. Limit must be set no later than 90 days before the start of each fiscal year.

items.main: Directs the SBA Administrator, with the Secretary of Defense and GSA Administrator, to establish training for contracting officers and the agency acquisition workforce on Phase III SBIR/STTR awards.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (e), (r), and (mm). Training covers SBIR/STTR missions and authorities, use of Phase III agreements, Phase III data rights, and Phase III sole source award contracts. Adds a definition of “agency acquisition workforce.”

items.main: Directs procurement center representatives to advocate for maximum practicable use and transition of SBIR/STTR products to Phase III, and requires simplified, standardized procedures and model contracts for Phase I, II, and III awards.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(j)(4) and (r)(4). The SBA Administrator must modify the relevant policy directives within 1 year of enactment. Agencies must also issue standardized solicitation provisions and contract clauses on Phase III eligibility.

sections.label: Section 7 — Technical and Business Assistance Improvements

items.main: Lets SBIR/STTR award recipients choose their technical and business assistance (adding cybersecurity assistance and foreign-involvement screening), and lets businesses use the funds to hire or augment staff.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(q). Sets per-project assistance amounts of not more than $6,500 for Phase I and not more than $50,000 for Phase II. Adds new subsection (bbb) requiring agencies with an I-Corps program to offer participation in I-Corps teams courses or bootcamps to SBIR/STTR recipients.

sections.label: Section 8 — Improving SBIR and STTR Data Collection

items.main: Adds award-type fields to the SBIR database and requires GSA to update the Federal Procurement Data System to flag award designations (direct-to-Phase II, subsequent Phase II, strategic breakthrough, Phase III prime/subcontract).
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638(k)(1) and section 1122(a)(4) of title 41. Also requires reporting on whether non-SBIR contracts use SBIR/STTR-funded technology and that contracting officers reference an SBIR/STTR contract ID number for prior relevant work.

sections.label: Section 9 — Extending SBIR and STTR Authorization

items.main: Extends SBIR and STTR program authorization from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2031 and lets agencies carry over unspent fiscal year 2026 SBIR/STTR funds into fiscal year 2027.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (m) and (n)(1)(A), striking “September 30, 2025”/“2025” and inserting “September 30, 2031”/“2031.”

sections.label: Section 10 — Extension of SBIR and STTR Programs and Activities

items.main: Extends numerous SBIR/STTR pilot programs and activities through September 30, 2031 (or fiscal year 2031), and repeals the GAO mandate in section 5142 of the FY2012 NDAA.
items.detail: Amends 15 U.S.C. 638 subsections (cc), (gg)(7), (hh)(2)(C), (jj)(7), (mm)(1), (qq)(3)(I), (uu)(3), (vv)(3)(C), (yy)(2), (zz)(3), plus section 851(e) of the FY2020 NDAA. Phase Flexibility (cc) is also expanded to add the Department of Energy and NASA and to cover the STTR program. Strikes section 5142 (15 U.S.C. 638a) of Public Law 112-81.

underreported.summary: Agencies may deny SBIR/STTR applications based on a security risk whose primary source is classified, without being required to disclose the basis for denial.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's security screening is presented as a watchlist-based transparency mechanism. The classified-source denial pathway allows rejection without any meaningful notification — the agency's only obligation is to tell the applicant a determination was made, not why, leaving the small business with no basis to challenge or cure the disqualification.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Van Duyne
featured_quotes.text: we must pass S. 3971 to ensure that Federal investment yields results for our country.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lofgren
featured_quotes.text: For more than 40 years, and Small Business Innovation Research Program (SBIR), and later its companion program the Small Business Technology Transfer Program (STTR), have been contributing to U.S. leadership in technological innovation through support for small business research and development. I have had a front-row seat to the explosive growth of entrepreneurship in Silicon Valley over my lifetime. I understand well the importance of innovative small businesses to our local economy and to the U.S. economy.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Houlahan
featured_quotes.text: For years, I proudly led the bipartisan RAMP for Innovators Act, a bill that gives our small businesses the tools they need to turn great ideas into market-ready products. Today, I am thrilled that a significant portion of that work is included in the Small Business Innovation and Economic Security Act. Thanks to this bill, these very important provisions and improvements will soon be law. Today's passage is a testament to what bipartisan and bicameral collaboration can achieve.

gaps: The bill requires agencies to notify denied applicants of the basis for security-related rejections but provides no appeal or reconsideration process for small businesses that dispute a watchlist-based determination.

Strategic breakthrough allocations target "critical technology areas" but the bill does not define or enumerate those areas, leaving the scope of the new allocation category entirely to agency discretion.

added: Requirement for SBIR and STTR agencies to evaluate security risks of applicants through watchlist screening, intelligence community coordination, and classified risk assessment
Eight-watchlist disqualification framework for SBIR and STTR applicants with foreign adversary connections
Notification requirement for security-based denials, to the extent consistent with national security
Maximum proposal cap per small business per fiscal year for Phase I and Phase II solicitations
Strategic breakthrough allocations — additional Phase II awards for critical technology areas requiring matching private funds
modified: SBIR and STTR program authorization extended through fiscal year 2031
Phase III commercialization training requirements for agency contracting officers expanded

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
bills.official_title: Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act
bills.summary: Federal tax law normally requires casualty losses to exceed 10% of your income before you can deduct them — but Congress has repeatedly carved out exceptions for federally declared disaster areas, letting affected taxpayers deduct unreimbursed losses above $500 per incident even without itemizing. This bill applies those disaster-specific deduction rules to disasters with incident periods beginning after July 4, 2025 and before January 1, 2027, and extends the exclusion of wildfire relief payments from taxable income — for forest or range fires federally declared a disaster after 2014 — to payments received in tax years 2026 through 2030.
bills.brief: Extends the federal tax deduction for disaster property losses and the wildfire relief payment exclusion to disasters occurring before January 1, 2027.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Loss Deductions
subs: Applies to disasters with incident periods beginning after July 4, 2025 and before January 1, 2027
Deductible without itemizing; exempt from the alternative minimum tax

top_lines.headline: Wildfire Relief Payments
subs: Relief payments for forest or range fires federally declared a disaster after 2014 excluded from gross income
Exclusion now covers payments received in tax years 2026 through 2030; prior law covered payments received in tax years 2020 through 2025

bills.likelihoodReason: Disaster tax relief has consistent bipartisan support and 14 cosponsors. Extension bills of this type routinely pass the Senate, often attached to larger tax packages. The geographic scope — covering presidentially declared disasters nationwide — limits targeted opposition.

items.main: Names the Act the “Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Adds Section 165(h)(6) to the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, creating a special deduction category for qualified net disaster losses that bypasses the 10% adjusted gross income limitation.
items.detail: A qualified net disaster loss is the excess of qualified disaster-related personal casualty losses over personal casualty gains. A qualified disaster area covers any area with a presidential major disaster declaration under section 401 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act where the incident period begins after July 4, 2025, and before January 1, 2027. Disaster losses may be deducted as part of the standard deduction under new Section 63(c)(1)(C) and are exempt from the alternative minimum tax under Section 56(b)(1)(D).

items.main: Creates new Section 139M of the Internal Revenue Code, excluding qualified wildfire relief payments from gross income.
items.detail: The exclusion applies to payments for forest or range fires federally declared a disaster after December 31, 2014, and covers payments received in taxable years after December 31, 2025 and before January 1, 2031. Under prior law, the exclusion applied only to qualifying payments received in taxable years after December 31, 2019 and before January 1, 2026.

underreported.summary: The bill explicitly exempts the disaster loss deduction from the alternative minimum tax by amending Section 56(b)(1)(D) of the Internal Revenue Code.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is extension of the disaster deduction window. The AMT exception means taxpayers who would otherwise owe AMT — typically higher earners — retain the full value of the deduction, a consequence not apparent from the disaster relief framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: When hurricanes, wildfires, floods, tornadoes, and other disasters strike, American families are left to rebuild their homes, their businesses, their communities, and their lives. When these moments arise, the last thing they need is the Federal Government making their recovery harder by taxing relief payments or denying fair treatment for disaster losses, nor should the government be creating uncertainty in the tax code.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Panetta
featured_quotes.text: I support the Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act. I am a proud cosponsor, co-lead of this bill with Representatives Greg Steube and Mike Thompson, a bill that would build on the Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act which we passed last Congress, thanks to the leadership of Representative Steube, a bill that would ensure that those impacted by disasters nationwide have continued access to tax relief.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fong
featured_quotes.text: In California, we are all too familiar with the devastation caused by wildfires. After these disasters strike in our community, survivors shouldn't have to worry about burdensome Federal taxes as they work to recover and rebuild. Today, we have an opportunity to address that while honoring my friend the late Doug LaMalfa, who was a tireless champion of rural California and an advocate for those rebuilding after wildfires.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Tokuda
featured_quotes.text: I rise today, like so many of my colleagues on both sides of the aisle, to honor our friend Doug LaMalfa. He understood that the disaster after the disaster happens when families cannot recover and return to their hometowns because the funding and resources they receive just don't stretch far enough or, worse, are taxed and taken away from people who need absolutely every single dollar to be able to rebuild. On Saturday, I stood above Lahaina, and for a moment--the briefest of moments--in the darkness, the town almost looked normal.

gaps: The bill covers disasters with incident periods beginning before January 1, 2027, but does not address losses sustained within a qualified disaster area where the damage is discovered or claims are settled after January 1, 2027.

The wildfire relief exclusion applies only to fires paired with a federal disaster declaration and does not address relief payments from state programs for fires that did not receive a federal declaration.

added: Section 165(h)(6) of the Internal Revenue Code — qualified net disaster loss deduction bypassing the 10% AGI limitation
Section 63(c)(1)(C) — disaster loss deduction available as part of the standard deduction

Section 139M — exclusion from gross income for qualified wildfire relief payments for forest or range fires federally declared a disaster after December 31, 2014 (for payments received in taxable years 2026 through 2030)
modified: Section 56(b)(1)(D) of the Internal Revenue Code — disaster loss deduction exempted from the alternative minimum tax
Definition of qualified disaster area extended to incident periods beginning after July 4, 2025, and before January 1, 2027

added: Coordination rule added — section 304(b) of the Taxpayer Certainty and Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2020 and section 70438 of Public Law 119-21 shall not apply to any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024
Wildfire-disaster window now has an end date — "declared after December 31, 2014, and before January 1, 2027" (previously open-ended after Dec. 31, 2014)
modified: Renamed from "Federal Disaster Tax Relief Act of 2025" to "Doug LaMalfa Federal Disaster Tax Relief Certainty Act"
Qualified-disaster-area incident period broadened — now covers disasters beginning on or after December 28, 2019 (was only after July 4, 2025)

Disaster-loss benefit restructured — now an above-the-line deduction for non-itemizers under section 63(b)(8), replacing the introduced standard-deduction add-on (section 63(c)) and AMT treatment (section 56(b)(1)(D))
removed: Dropped the standalone "disaster loss deduction" definition added to section 63(c) and its alternative-minimum-tax carve-out under section 56(b)(1)(D)
Removed section 139M(d) limitation confining the wildfire exclusion to payments received in taxable years after December 31, 2025 and before January 1, 2031

bills.title: Clergy Act
bills.official_title: Clergy Act
bills.summary: Ordained ministers and Christian Science practitioners can apply to permanently opt out of Social Security and Medicare taxes on their ministerial earnings — but that exemption is currently irrevocable. This bill creates a one-time window for those who previously opted out to reverse that decision and re-enter the Social Security system, with coverage beginning for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027. Once revoked, they cannot opt out again.
bills.brief: Creates a one-time window for clergy who opted out of Social Security to reverse that decision and begin accruing retirement benefits.

top_lines.headline: One-Time Re-entry Window
subs: Clergy may revoke their Social Security exemption by filing through the deadline for their second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027
Coverage begins for taxable years starting after December 31, 2027 — cannot opt out again after revoking

top_lines.headline: IRS Outreach Required
subs: Commissioner of Internal Revenue must submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their eligibility within 90 days of enactment

bills.likelihoodReason: The bill has 21 cosponsors and bipartisan backing — sponsors include Fong (R-CA), Thompson (D-CA), and Kelly (R-PA). Providing clergy a window to undo a permanent decision is unlikely to draw opposition. The narrow scope and sympathetic affected population make Senate passage plausible, though floor scheduling is uncertain.

items.main: Names the Act the “Clergy Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Revocation of Social Security Exemption

items.main: Notwithstanding Section 1402(e)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code (which makes the Social Security exemption irrevocable), clergy whose exemption is in effect for the taxable year of enactment may revoke it by filing an application with the IRS.
items.detail: The application must be filed no later than the due date for the second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027. Revocation takes effect for the first or second taxable year beginning after December 31, 2027, as specified by the applicant, and covers both chapter 2 of the IRC (self-employment tax) and title II of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 401 et seq.). If the application is filed retroactively for a year already in effect, the applicant must pay in full all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for that year. After revoking, the applicant may not again file for an exemption under Section 1402(e)(1).

items.main: The Commissioner of Internal Revenue, in consultation with the Commissioner of Social Security, must develop and submit a plan to inform eligible clergy of their revocation eligibility within 90 days of enactment.
items.detail: The plan must be submitted to the Ways and Means Committee of the House and the Finance Committee of the Senate. No minimum outreach activities, funding level, or success metrics are specified in the bill.

underreported.summary: If a clergy member files a revocation application after the due date for a taxable year and elects to have it take effect for that year, they must immediately pay all self-employment taxes that would have been owed for the entire year.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's headline is a window to opt back in. The catch-up payment requirement means that choosing early retroactive coverage triggers a lump-sum tax obligation for the full year of retroactive coverage — a condition not apparent from the bill's title or the primary revocation provision.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, if we are serious about strengthening Social Security, we can't stop at incremental fixes. We must also protect the program from efforts that would weaken this great program. We have heard calls for so-called reforms or tough choices. Let's be clear about what that means: cutting benefits, raising retirement age, or moving toward privatization--steps that undermine the guaranteed security Americans rely on. Democrats reject that approach. We believe Social Security is a promise, not a bargaining chip.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, if we are serious about strengthening Social Security, we can't stop at incremental fixes. We must also protect the program from efforts that would weaken this great program. We have heard calls for so-called reforms or tough choices. Let's be clear about what that means: cutting benefits, raising retirement age, or moving toward privatization--steps that undermine the guaranteed security Americans rely on. Democrats reject that approach. We believe Social Security is a promise, not a bargaining chip.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fong
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan legislation, cosponsored by my fellow California Congressman Mike Thompson, would create a one-time re- enrollment window for pastors and other clergy members who have previously opted out of Social Security, many in their youth, to voluntarily opt back in. For decades, members of the clergy have made the permanent decision of opting out of Social Security. While this choice was made with good intentions, many faith leaders experience significant financial hardship as they approach retirement.

gaps: The bill allows revocation effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027 but does not address Social Security credits for prior years during which the exemption was in effect — those years generate no credits regardless of revocation.
The 90-day outreach plan requirement specifies no minimum outreach activities, distribution channels, or funding, leaving the scope of IRS notification entirely to agency discretion.

added: One-time window for clergy and Christian Science practitioners to revoke their irrevocable Social Security exemption under Section 1402(e)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027
Requirement for the Commissioner of Internal Revenue to submit an outreach plan to inform eligible clergy within 90 days of enactment

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

modified: Revocation timeline pushed back one year — all references to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027 changed to December 31, 2028 (filing deadline, revocation effective dates, and the effective-date provision)

bills.title: Taxpayer Experience Improvement Act
bills.official_title: Taxpayer Experience Improvement Act
bills.summary: This bill requires the IRS to publish real-time data on its public website about phone wait times, call volumes, and processing backlogs for every public phone line it operates, and to make that data available through a public API so third-party apps can display it. It also requires the IRS to give taxpayers online or mobile access to their own tax returns, notices, and refund status including an estimated delivery date.
bills.brief: Requires the IRS to publish live phone wait times and backlog data, and give taxpayers digital access to their own returns and refund status.

top_lines.headline: Real-Time IRS Dashboard
subs: IRS must publish live caller counts, wait times, and callback availability per phone line on its public website
Public API required so any person or app can access the live call data

top_lines.headline: Digital Tax Record Access
subs: Taxpayers can view all returns, notices, and IRS letters via website or mobile app
IRS must provide estimated refund receipt date

top_lines.headline: Monthly Accountability Metrics
subs: IRS must publish monthly averages for call length, hold time, disconnection rate, and percent of callers who got help
Sense of Congress: callback offered within 5 minutes on any unanswered call by 2028

bills.likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor despite bipartisan sponsorship (Schweikert R-AZ and Beyer D-VA). IRS modernization bills often pass the House but stall in the Senate amid disagreements over IRS funding and IT capacity. The real-time dashboard and public API requirements may face resistance from the Treasury Department over implementation feasibility.

items.main: Names the Act the “Taxpayer Experience Improvement Act”, defines “Secretary” as the Secretary of the Treasury or delegate, and lists the Act's table of contents.
items.detail: Short-title/definitions/table-of-contents section — citation name, the “Secretary” reference, and a navigational contents list; no substantive effect.

items.main: Requires the IRS to publish in real time on its public website call volume, wait time, and callback availability for each applicable phone number extension.
items.detail: For each phone line, the IRS must display the number of callers connected to representatives, connected to automated systems, and waiting; the longest current wait time; and whether callback service is available. A public API must be provided for automated access to the data. The IRS must also detect and screen automated calls, and publish processing delay information weekly when significant backlogs occur.

items.main: Requires monthly summary statistics for each phone line, including caller satisfaction data.
items.detail: Monthly metrics must include average and median call lengths and hold times; the percent of calls disconnected or directed to automation; the number of callers transferred; and the number and percent of callers who indicated they received the help they were seeking. The last metric requires the IRS to actively collect caller satisfaction data before calls end.

sections.label: Section 3 — Expansion of Electronic Access to Information About Returns and Refunds

items.main: Requires the Secretary, via website and mobile application, to give taxpayers individualized, up-to-date status on their returns and amended returns — receipt, completed processing (with refund date and estimated receipt date), or suspension with the reason and any requested information.
items.detail: Deadline: not later than January 1 of the first calendar year beginning more than 12 months after enactment. For electronic refunds, must show the partial/full account number plus the institution's name and routing number; for paper checks, the mailing address.

items.main: Expresses the sense of Congress that taxpayers should be able to request a callback, and that by calendar year 2028 the IRS should offer a callback for any call to an applicable phone number extension not answered within 5 minutes.
items.detail: Sense-of-Congress provision (non-binding); applies to any taxpayer, including those residing outside the United States.

items.main: Requires the Secretary to make available a website or mobile application letting any taxpayer view returns, documents, notices and letters from the prior 6-year period, respond to IRS notices online, and authorize representatives, preparers, or qualified reporting agents to access them.
items.detail: Deadline: not later than January 1 of the first calendar year beginning more than 18 months after enactment. Consistent with section 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code. Also requires a program to investigate unauthorized access by designated persons (with annual public reporting) and taxpayer/tax-professional focus groups before launch.

underreported.summary: The monthly statistics requirement includes the number and percent of callers who indicated they received the answers or service they were seeking — a customer satisfaction data point embedded in a call-volume reporting requirement.
underreported.why_unreported: Collecting this metric requires the IRS to actively ask callers before they hang up whether their issue was resolved, effectively mandating a caller survey process. This is a new operational requirement distinct from passively logging call volume and wait times, not apparent from the bill's IRS dashboard framing.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Schweikert
featured_quotes.text: I ask the chairman whether it is tireless or annoying. It is one or the other. Look, I have an absolute fixation, and I have got to thank my Democratic colleague and a number of the team here for tolerating my fixation on the fact that one of the ways you work within the IRS budget to make things more efficient is the adoption of technology. Imagine a world--because it is the one we live in--where some of the number one calls we get to my district office are IRS questions: Where is my refund? Do I owe money?

gaps: The bill requires real-time call data but does not specify a minimum uptime requirement for the dashboard or what disclosures are required if the live data is unavailable.
The digital access requirement does not specify an implementation timeline for the mobile application option, nor minimum device or accessibility standards for the application.

added: Requirement for real-time IRS public dashboard with per-phone-line call volume, wait times, and callback availability, plus public API access
Monthly IRS reporting requirement including caller satisfaction metrics, disconnection rates, and hold times per phone extension
Requirement for IRS to provide taxpayers with online or mobile access to returns, notices, refund status, and estimated refund date
Requirement for IRS to use technology to detect and screen automated calls

bills.title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
bills.official_title: Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act
bills.summary: When the IRS wants information about you from a third party like your employer or bank, current law requires it to notify you in advance — but not what specific information it's seeking. This bill requires the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to collect from the third party, and give you at least 45 days to provide it yourself, whenever the IRS hasn't already asked you for it and you could reasonably provide it. Two exceptions apply: the rule doesn't cover tax collection proceedings, and the Secretary can waive it when third-party contact is deemed necessary.
bills.brief: Requires the IRS to tell taxpayers exactly what information it plans to collect from third parties and give them 45 days to provide it first.

top_lines.headline: Specific Notice Required
subs: IRS must identify each item sought from a third party when the taxpayer hasn't been asked before and could provide it
Taxpayers get at least 45 days to respond — more if they request it with reasonable cause

top_lines.headline: Exceptions
subs: Specificity requirement waived for tax collection proceedings or when Secretary determines third-party contact is necessary regardless

bills.likelihoodReason: Only 1 cosponsor and a narrow taxpayer privacy focus. The IRS exemption allowing the Secretary to waive specificity requirements whenever deemed necessary limits the bill's practical effect, which may reduce the urgency Senate sponsors attach to it. IRS procedural reform bills without broad coalition backing rarely advance quickly in the Senate.

items.main: Names the Act the “Taxpayer Notification and Privacy Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Specificity of Third-Party Contact Notices

items.main: Amends Section 7602(c)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to require the IRS to identify each specific item of information it intends to seek from a third party when that information has not been previously requested from the taxpayer and could reasonably be provided by the taxpayer.
items.detail: The advance notice must provide the taxpayer with a period of not less than 45 days — or more if the taxpayer requests additional time and shows reasonable cause — to respond, including by providing the information themselves, before the IRS contacts the third party. The exception in Section 7602(c)(3)(B) provides that the specificity and waiting period requirements do not apply if the information is sought for collection of a tax liability, or if the Secretary determines the third-party information is necessary regardless of whether the taxpayer could provide it. Effective date: 12 months after enactment.

underreported.summary: The bill's specificity and 45-day notice requirements do not apply whenever the Secretary determines that the third-party information is necessary, without any standard for what constitutes necessity or any procedural check on that determination.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is framed as expanding taxpayer notification rights. The necessity exception allows the IRS to bypass both the itemized notice and the 45-day waiting period entirely based on the Secretary's own judgment, with no defined standard, independent review, or notification to the taxpayer that the exception has been invoked.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steube
featured_quotes.text: At its core, this commonsense legislation is a simple due process idea: Before the IRS goes to your bank, your employer, your vendor, or another third party for information about you, when you can reasonably provide that information yourself, you should be told what they are looking for and given a fair chance to respond. Under current law, taxpayers can receive a general third-party contact notice, but too often those notices aren't specific enough to let a person meaningfully respond.

gaps: The bill requires the IRS to give the taxpayer 45 days to respond but does not specify whether the IRS is barred from contacting the third party if the taxpayer provides the requested information within the window.

The bill does not address the taxpayer's right to receive notice that the Secretary has invoked the necessity exception, leaving taxpayers without information about why the standard procedure was not followed.

added: Section 7602(c)(1)(B) of the Internal Revenue Code — requirement for IRS to identify each specific item of information sought from a third party when not previously requested from the taxpayer
Section 7602(c)(1)(C) amendment — 45-day minimum response period before third-party contact, with extensions available on reasonable cause

modified: New specificity duty narrowed — the IRS must itemize info sought from third parties only when it "is related to determining tax liability" (plus the existing not-previously-requested and taxpayer-could-provide tests)

Exception for the Secretary simplified — the specificity rule now does not apply whenever "the Secretary determines that such information is necessary," replacing the two-prong carve-out (collection of a tax liability, or necessity notwithstanding taxpayer availability)
removed: Dropped the phrase letting taxpayers respond "including by providing the information described in subparagraph (B)" from the 45-day response window
Removed the standalone exception for information sought "with respect to the collection of a tax liability"

bills.title: New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act
bills.official_title: New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act
bills.summary: Self-Employment Assistance programs let unemployed workers collect an allowance in place of their regular unemployment benefits — paid in the same amount and at the same intervals — while they start a business, exempt from the usual work-search requirements. This bill doubles the cap on program participation from 5% to 10% of unemployment recipients per state, removes the requirement that participants be on track to exhaust their benefits, adds a weekly self-certification requirement, and creates an alternative qualification pathway through a state-approved business plan rather than requiring formal entrepreneurial training.
bills.brief: Doubles state SEA program participation to 10%, drops the exhaustion-of-benefits eligibility requirement, and adds a business-plan qualification pathway.

top_lines.headline: Expanded Access
subs: Removes the requirement that participants be likely to exhaust unemployment benefits — opens programs to more applicants
Business plan + market feasibility study now qualifies as an alternative to formal entrepreneurial training

top_lines.headline: Larger Programs, Weekly Accountability
subs: State participation cap raised from 5% to 10% of unemployment benefit recipients
Participants must certify their self-employment activities on at least a weekly basis

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan sponsorship (Carey R-OH and Landsman D-OH among others) and 6 cosponsors. Small business and entrepreneurship provisions attract broad support, but the 2-year implementation delay and required Labor Department rulemaking introduce uncertainty. Senate floor time for unemployment program reforms is limited.

items.main: Names the Act the “New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 3306(t) of the Internal Revenue Code to remove the requirement that SEA participants be identified as likely to exhaust regular unemployment compensation benefits, expanding the eligible population.
items.detail: Subparagraph (B) of Section 3306(t)(3), which required participants to be identified as likely to exhaust benefits, is stricken. Eligible self-employment activities may now qualify through either (i) the existing path of entrepreneurial training, business counseling, and technical assistance approved by the state, or (ii) a new path through a business plan and market feasibility study submitted by the individual and approved by the state or a designated agency. Participants must certify their activities at least weekly to a state-designated agency.

items.main: Raises the state SEA program participation cap from 5% to 10% of individuals receiving regular unemployment compensation.
items.detail: The change to Section 3306(t)(4) doubles the maximum share of unemployment benefit recipients a state may enroll in its SEA program. Changes take effect 2 years after enactment; states may amend their laws before then. The Secretary of Labor must adopt implementing regulations through public notice and comment, subject to OMB approval.

underreported.summary: The bill's changes do not take effect until 2 years after enactment, and states must amend their own laws within that window to be compliant.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's operative changes — expanded eligibility, the business-plan pathway, and the higher participation cap — are the headline. The 2-year gap before any of those changes can be used, combined with the requirement for state-level legislative action, means the bill's benefits may not materialize in states that fail to update their laws in time.

gaps: The bill doubles participation caps and expands eligibility but does not address the funding source for increased SEA allowances, which are paid from state unemployment trust funds that vary significantly in reserves across states.
The bill adds a weekly certification requirement but does not specify consequences for participants who miss certifications or the process for removing a non-compliant participant.

added: Business plan and market feasibility study as an alternative qualifying pathway for SEA program activities under Section 3306(t)(3)
Weekly self-certification requirement for SEA program participants
modified: Section 3306(t)(3) of the Internal Revenue Code — eliminated the requirement that participants be identified as likely to exhaust regular unemployment compensation benefits
Section 3306(t)(4) — state SEA program participation cap raised from 5% to 10% of unemployment benefit recipients
removed: Section 3306(t)(3)(B) — requirement that SEA participants be likely to exhaust unemployment benefits

added: New subsection (g) directs the Secretary of Labor to issue guidance to State workforce agencies — a model list of qualifying self-employment assistance activities and best practices for verifying their completion

bills.title: Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions Act of 2025
bills.official_title: Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions Act of 2025
bills.summary: K-12 teachers can deduct a capped amount of unreimbursed classroom expenses each year directly from their gross income without itemizing ($250 statutory base under 26 U.S.C. 62, indexed for inflation) — but pre-K and early childhood educators are currently excluded. This bill extends that deduction to early childhood educators and adds a statutory definition of the qualifying "school" or childcare facility. Applies to expenses paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.
bills.brief: Extends the above-the-line educator expense deduction ($250 statutory base under 26 U.S.C. 62, inflation-indexed) to early childhood educators, and defines "school" to include childcare facilities serving more than 2 children under age 6 that receive public expense, fees, payments, or grants. Effective for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025.

top_lines.headline: Expanded Educator Deduction
subs: Early childhood educators added to the above-the-line deduction for unreimbursed classroom expenses ($250 statutory base under 26 U.S.C. 62, indexed for inflation)
Applies to expenses paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025

top_lines.headline: Statutory Definition of "School"
subs: Section 62(d)(1)(B) rewritten to define "school" — for early childhood, any school or childcare facility serving more than 2 non-resident children under age 6 that operates at public expense OR receives a fee, payment, or grant (regardless of for-profit status)
For elementary/secondary, any school providing that education as determined under State law

bills.likelihoodReason: Strong bipartisan support with 23 cosponsors. Expanding educator tax benefits is a consistently popular, low-controversy issue in both chambers. The narrow, targeted nature of the change — adding early childhood educators to an existing deduction without raising the $250 cap — limits points of opposition, but the effective date only reaches expenses paid in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, so there is no retroactive-relief pressure driving Senate scheduling.

items.main: Names the Act the "Supporting Early-childhood Educators' Deductions Act" (the "SEED Act").
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Educator Expense Deduction to Include Early Childhood Educators

items.main: Amends Section 62(d)(1) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to add early childhood educators to the above-the-line deduction and to define the qualifying "school" or childcare facility.
items.detail: Section 62(d)(1)(A) is amended by striking "a kindergarten through grade 12 teacher" and inserting "an early childhood or kindergarten through grade 12 teacher." Section 62(d)(1)(B) is rewritten in full to define "school": for early childhood, any school or childcare facility that (I) provides educational or childcare services to more than 2 non-resident individuals who have not attained age 6, AND (II) operates at the public expense or receives a fee, payment, or grant for providing such services (whether or not for profit); for elementary or secondary education (K-12), any school providing such education as determined under State law. Section 62(a)(2)(D) heading is amended to add "early childhood" alongside elementary and secondary school teachers. Effective for expenses paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025.

underreported.section: Section 2 — Public-Expense / Fee Test for Early Childhood Facilities
underreported.summary: The new "school" definition qualifies an early childhood facility only if it operates at public expense OR receives a fee, payment, or grant for the services (whether or not for profit).
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's framing is expansion of the deduction, but this two-prong test decides which providers qualify — home daycares, private preschools, Head Start centers, or school-district pre-K classrooms all get in via the fee-or-grant leg, but a purely volunteer or gift-funded arrangement may not. The scope is defined by the statute itself rather than left to the IRS.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, in Pennsylvania, more than 68,000 early-childhood educators support our youngest learners every single day. The first 5 years of a child's life lay down the foundation for how they learn, how they grow, and how they succeed. These educators are central to that process. They do far more than teach. They create safe, engaging environments where children can thrive.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Panetta
featured_quotes.text: By expanding eligibility for the educator expense deduction to early-childhood educators, the bill will finally recognize the incredible dedication and work of these pre-K educators. This is one step toward supporting those who extend themselves day in and day out to help grow and educate all of our children.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: when it comes to supporting teachers who go the extra mile to provide for their students, including paying out of pocket for supplies and other educational materials, we need to ensure we are acknowledging and rewarding the contributions of all of our educators. That includes the early-childhood teachers, who are charged with instilling in our youth a love of learning and curiosity from the youngest age.

gaps: The bill does not define "early childhood education" itself — only defines the qualifying school/facility by size (more than 2 children under age 6) and funding structure (public expense or fee/payment/grant).
The $250 statutory base and inflation-indexing rules that apply to the deduction are set by the existing 26 U.S.C. 62 provisions; the bill does not modify the cap.

added: Section 62(d)(1)(B) — new statutory definition of "school" that qualifies an early childhood facility by size (more than 2 non-resident children under age 6) and funding structure (public expense or fee/payment/grant, whether or not for profit)
modified: Section 62(d)(1)(A) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 — inserts "an early childhood or kindergarten through grade 12 teacher" in place of "a kindergarten through grade 12 teacher"
Section 62(a)(2)(D) heading — updated to "Certain expenses of early childhood, elementary, and secondary school teachers" (was "Certain expenses of elementary and secondary school teachers")

bills.title: BARCODE Efficiency Act
bills.official_title: Barcode Automation for Revenue Collection to Organize Disbursement and Enhance Efficiency Act
bills.summary: When taxpayers prepare their returns electronically but print and mail them, the IRS currently re-enters all that data by hand. This bill requires those returns to include a scannable barcode so the IRS can convert them to electronic format automatically. For returns prepared entirely by hand and for paper correspondence, the IRS must use optical character recognition software. The technology requirement can be waived if the IRS finds it slower or less reliable than manual processing — but any waiver must be reported to Congress within 30 days.
bills.brief: Mandates barcodes on electronically-prepared paper returns and OCR scanning for handwritten returns and correspondence, with a performance-based waiver.

top_lines.headline: Barcode Mandate
subs: Electronically-prepared paper returns must include a scannable barcode — IRS must scan rather than manually re-enter the data
Applies to individual income tax returns 180 days after enactment

top_lines.headline: OCR for Everything Else
subs: Hand-prepared returns and all paper IRS correspondence must be transcribed using optical character recognition
Estate and gift returns: 24 months; all other returns and correspondence: 12 months after enactment

top_lines.headline: Performance Waiver
subs: IRS may skip the technology if it's slower or less reliable than manual processing — but must report to Congress within 30 days

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan sponsorship (Schneider D-IL and Yakym R-IN) and the efficiency framing make opposition difficult to articulate, but only 1 cosponsor. IRS technology mandate bills often face implementation feasibility questions in the Senate, particularly when they include performance-based exceptions that give the agency discretion to delay compliance.

items.main: Names the Act the “Barcode Automation for Revenue Collection to Organize Disbursement and Enhance Efficiency Act” (the “BARCODE Efficiency Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Scanning and Digitization of Tax Returns and Correspondence

items.main: Requires that any federal tax return prepared electronically and filed on paper must include a scannable code, and that the IRS must use barcode scanning technology to convert such returns to electronic format.
items.detail: If the barcode data cannot be accurately converted, the IRS must use optical character recognition or functionally similar technology. For paper returns not prepared electronically and all paper correspondence (except correspondence originally received electronically), the IRS must use OCR technology to transcribe the document. Effective dates: individual income tax returns within 180 days; all other returns and correspondence within 12 months; estate and gift tax returns within 24 months of enactment.

items.main: The technology requirement is waived if the Secretary determines it is slower or less reliable than manual transcription or any other IRS process — but a waiver report must be submitted to Congress within 30 days.
items.detail: The waiver determination is made entirely by the Secretary without independent oversight or minimum performance benchmarks. The reporting obligation to the Ways and Means Committee and Senate Finance Committee is the sole check on waiver use.

underreported.summary: The IRS determines whether its own technology is slower or less reliable than manual processing. If it makes that finding, it may waive the barcode and OCR requirements with no congressional approval required — only a 30-day report.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's mandate reads as a firm requirement. The waiver mechanism allows the IRS to indefinitely delay compliance through its own performance assessment, with a notification-only check. No minimum performance threshold, time limit on the waiver, or independent evaluation is specified.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Yakym
featured_quotes.text: I am proud to co-lead this act with my friend from Illinois (Mr. Schneider). This is a simple but powerful bill that will make tax return processing faster, more accurate, and more efficient. E-filing taxes is becoming even more common. In 2009, two-thirds of taxpayers e-filed their returns. By 2015, it was up to 85 percent. Last year, 94 percent of taxpayers e-filed their returns. That remaining 6 percent still accounts for 10 million tax returns. There are good reasons to file a paper return.

gaps: The bill requires OCR for paper correspondence but does not address accuracy standards for the OCR process or what happens when digitized data contains errors that affect tax calculations or processing.

The bill does not specify what recourse taxpayers have if their paper-filed barcode return is misread or if the OCR transcription of their correspondence contains errors that affect their tax account.

added: Requirement for scannable barcodes on electronically-prepared federal tax returns filed in paper format
Requirement for IRS to use barcode scanning technology to convert electronically-prepared paper returns to electronic format
Requirement for IRS to use optical character recognition technology for hand-prepared paper returns and paper correspondence
Performance-based waiver with 30-day congressional reporting requirement

modified: Paper-printed e-prepared returns no longer must "bear a code which, when scanned" converts data — instead must be "formatted in a manner that is compatible with the scanning technology"
IRS conversion requirement generalized from "barcode scanning technology" to plain "scanning technology"
Effective date for other returns and correspondence delayed — now received on or after the first calendar year beginning more than 18 months after enactment (was 12 months)

bills.title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to authorize the increase of the retirement age in the United States Capitol Police.
bills.official_title: To amend title 5, United States Code, to authorize the increase of the retirement age in the United States Capitol Police.
bills.summary: Capitol Police officers currently face mandatory retirement at age 60. This bill replaces that fixed age with a range, letting the Capitol Police Board set the mandatory retirement age at any point between 57 and 65 — giving it more flexibility to retain experienced officers beyond the current 60-year cap.
bills.brief: Raises the Capitol Police Board's maximum retirement age waiver from 60 to 65, letting the Board keep experienced officers working longer.

top_lines.headline: Retirement Age Flexibility
subs: Capitol Police Board can now set mandatory retirement at any age between 57 and 65 — replacing the current fixed age of 60
Applies to officers under both the Civil Service Retirement System and the Federal Employees' Retirement System

bills.likelihoodReason: Bipartisan support (Steil R-WI and Morelle D-NY) on a narrow workforce management bill affecting a single law enforcement agency. Capitol security legislation typically advances with little controversy. The limited scope and lack of broader policy implications make Senate passage plausible if floor time is available.

items.main: Amends Sections 8335(c) and 8425(c) of title 5, United States Code to expand the Capitol Police Board's authority over mandatory retirement age from a fixed ceiling of 60 to a range of 57 to 65.
items.detail: Both the Civil Service Retirement System (Section 8335(c)) and Federal Employees' Retirement System (Section 8425(c)) provisions are amended by replacing "becomes 60 years of age" with "attains an age determined by the Board that shall be not less than 57 years of age and not more than 65 years of age." Prior law fixed mandatory retirement at age 60; under the amended text the Board sets a mandatory retirement age anywhere within the 57–65 range for individual officers or as a general policy.

gaps: The bill grants the Board discretion to set retirement age between 57 and 65 but specifies no criteria the Board must use in making that determination for individual officers or as a department-wide policy.

modified: Section 8335(c) of title 5, United States Code (CSRS) — Capitol Police mandatory retirement age ceiling raised from 60 to 65, at the Board's discretion
Section 8425(c) of title 5, United States Code (FERS) — Capitol Police mandatory retirement age ceiling raised from 60 to 65, at the Board's discretion

bills.title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
bills.official_title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
bills.summary: When customs agents suspect imported goods are counterfeit or pirated, they can already ask brand owners to help identify violations — but only certain information can be shared. This bill expands that program to let CBP share nonpublic data generated by online marketplaces, freight forwarders, and shipping operators with brand owners and any other party the Commissioner determines has an interest in the merchandise. It also broadens the physical evidence that can be shared to include packing materials and shipping containers.
bills.brief: Expands what counterfeit-goods intelligence CBP can share with brand owners — adding marketplace and freight data, packing materials, and a broader circle of eligible recipients.

top_lines.headline: Counterfeit Goods Detection
subs: CBP can now share nonpublic data from online marketplaces, freight forwarders, and express consignment operators with brand owners
Packing materials and shipping containers added to physical evidence that can be shared

top_lines.headline: Broader Access
