It excludes VA service-connected disability compensation but does not address other disability benefits such as Social Security disability.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. De La Cruz
featured_quotes.text: Veterans, particularly disabled veterans, have made extraordinary sacrifices for our Nation, and it is simply unacceptable that those who selflessly defended our freedoms are met with bureaucratic red tape when they return home. Government overregulation should never stand in the way of veterans' ability to receive the help they need. That is what this legislation will fix.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Sherman
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I join with the gentleman in his comments about how we need to protect our veterans from the ill-considered actions of President Trump and, I was about to say Secretary Musk, whatever he is. I, of course, join with Mr. Vargas in welcoming our new chair of the Financial Services Committee. I want to focus on the bill at hand, actually two bills at hand. We are dealing with this bill now and about four other bills will go by, and then we will deal with the companion legislation.

added: GAO report within one year on HUD program treatment of service-connected disability compensation
modified: Low/moderate income determinations under the Housing and Community Development Act (42 U.S.C. 5302(a)(20)) must now exclude VA service-connected disability compensation

bills.title: Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to make the postponement of certain deadlines by reason of disasters applicable to the limitation on credit or refund, and to take postponements into account for purposes of sending collection notices.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-64 on December 26, 2025. Passed the House on March 31-April 1, 2025 and the Senate on December 11, 2025.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

bills.summary: When the IRS postpones tax deadlines because of a disaster, this makes that extra time also count toward the deadline for claiming a tax refund, and requires collection notices to reflect the postponement.
bills.brief: Counts IRS disaster-related deadline postponements toward the refund-claim limitation period and in collection notices.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Deadline Postponements
subs: Disaster postponement periods count toward the refund-claim window
Collection notices must reflect disaster postponements
Applies to claims filed and notices issued after enactment

items.main: Names the Act the “Disaster Related Extension of Deadlines Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Postponement of Certain Deadlines by Reason of Disasters Made Applicable to Limitation on Credit or Refund

items.main: Treats IRS disaster-related deadline postponements as filing extensions for purposes of the time limit on tax credits or refunds.
items.detail: Adds subsection (f) to Section 7508A of the Internal Revenue Code so any period disregarded for filing a return is treated as an extension of time for filing under the refund-limitation rule (Section 6511(b)(2)(A)). It also amends Section 6303(b) so the last date for payment shown in a collection notice accounts for any period disregarded under Section 7508A. The changes apply to claims filed and notices issued after enactment.

gaps: The bill aligns disaster postponements with the refund-claim window but does not change the underlying disaster-postponement authority itself.
It applies to claims and notices going forward but does not address refunds already denied for filing outside the prior window.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Murphy
featured_quotes.text: I am blessed to live in eastern North Carolina, which is all too familiar with the devastation caused by natural disasters. For coastal Carolina, it is not a question of if but rather a question of when a hurricane will hit my district. We stick out far in the ocean and have a big bull's-eye target on us. We are still recovering from Hurricane Florence, which occurred in 2018. Despite being 7 years ago, there are still homes and businesses shuttered from the damage of that powerful hurricane.

modified: IRS disaster deadline postponements (Section 7508A) now count as filing extensions for the refund-claim limitation (Section 6511(b)(2)(A))
Collection notices (Section 6303(b)) must account for disaster-related postponement periods

bills.title: Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to amend title 38, United States Code, to require the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to periodically review the automatic maximum coverage under the Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance program and the Veterans' Group Life Insurance program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-54 on December 12, 2025. Passed the House on April 7, 2025 and the Senate on November 20, 2025.
bills.summary: Requires the VA to review every five years whether the maximum automatic coverage under military and veterans' group life insurance has kept pace with inflation, and report to Congress.
bills.brief: Requires the VA to review SGLI and VGLI maximum coverage against inflation every five years and report to Congress.

top_lines.headline: Group Life Insurance Coverage Review
subs: VA must review SGLI and VGLI maximum coverage every 5 years
Benchmark: $500,000 adjusted by average CPI change over 5 years
Results reported to the Veterans' Affairs Committees

items.main: Names the Act the “Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Periodic Review of Automatic Maximum Coverage Under Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance and Veterans' Group Life Insurance

items.main: Requires the VA to review, every five years starting January 1, 2026, the automatic maximum coverage under SGLI and VGLI.
items.detail: Adds Section 1980B to title 38. The Secretary compares the maximum coverage amount in Section 1967(a)(3)(A)(i) to a benchmark equal to $500,000 adjusted by the average percentage change in the Consumer Price Index over the preceding five fiscal years, and reports the results to the House and Senate Committees on Veterans' Affairs as a guide for possible coverage increases.

gaps: The bill requires a review against an inflation benchmark but does not itself raise the maximum coverage amount.
It directs the review to serve as a guide for increases but does not require the VA to act on the findings.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Strickland
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I rise to express my support for my bill, H.R. 970, the Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act of 2025. I first thank Chairmen Bost and Luttrell and Ranking Members Takano and McGarvey for working with me to get this bill to the floor. The Fairness for Servicemembers and their Families Act will help ensure that life insurance benefits for servicemembers and veterans account for changes in the economy.

added: VA 5-year review of SGLI and VGLI maximum automatic coverage against a $500,000 CPI-adjusted benchmark, reported to Congress (new Section 1980B of title 38)

bills.title: MERICA Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to make that Act applicable to hardrock minerals.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Fallon (R-TX) with 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Expanding domestic hardrock-mineral leasing has bipartisan appeal on supply-chain grounds, though it still needs Senate floor time.
bills.summary: Extends the federal leasing system for minerals on government-acquired lands to hardrock minerals such as base, precious, and industrial metals and gemstones.
bills.brief: Makes the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands apply to hardrock minerals.

top_lines.headline: Hardrock Minerals on Acquired Lands
subs: Hardrock minerals added to the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands
Covers base, precious, and industrial metals and gemstones
Excludes coal, oil, gas, sulfur, sodium, potassium, and Materials Act minerals

items.main: Names the Act the “Mineral Extraction for Renewable Industry and Critical Applications Act of 2025” (the “MERICA Act of 2025”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Application of Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to Hardrock Minerals

items.main: Makes hardrock minerals leasable under the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (30 U.S.C. 351 et seq.).
items.detail: Restructures the definitions in Section 2 (30 U.S.C. 351) and adds a definition of 'hardrock mineral' covering minerals found in sedimentary or other rocks, base metals, precious metals, industrial metals, and precious and semi-precious gemstones — but not coal, oil, oil shale, gas, sodium, potassium, sulfur, or materials under the Materials Act of 1947 (30 U.S.C. 601 et seq.). Section 3 (30 U.S.C. 352) is amended to add hardrock minerals to the minerals the Act covers.

gaps: The bill makes hardrock minerals leasable on acquired lands but does not set royalty rates or lease terms specific to them.
It applies only to lands acquired by the United States and does not change leasing on the broader public domain.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fallon
featured_quotes.text: if critical minerals like lithium are essential to our military and to our national security, if that is the case, then why are we still relying on our number one global adversary to supply them? China is mining about 18 percent of all the lithium in the world. With the United States, that percentage is less than 1. As far as refining, China is about 67 percent, some estimates up to 80 percent, where the United States is at 2 percent. For years now, the United States has been overly reliant on the communists in Beijing.

modified: Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (30 U.S.C. 351, 352) now applies to hardrock minerals (base/precious/industrial metals and gemstones), excluding coal, oil, gas, sulfur, sodium, potassium, and Materials Act minerals
"Hardrock mineral" definition: clause (iv) changed from "industrial metals" to "industrial minerals"
removed: Short title section dropped — the "Mineral Extraction for Renewable Industry and Critical Applications Act of 2025" / "MERICA Act of 2025" citation is gone; the hardrock-minerals provision is now the bill's only operative section

bills.title: Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to modify the rules for postponing certain deadlines by reason of disaster.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-29 on July 24, 2025. Passed the House on March 31, 2025 and the Senate on July 10, 2025.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

bills.summary: Lets the IRS postpone federal tax deadlines after a state-declared disaster (not just a federal one) at a governor's request, and doubles the automatic extension period from 60 to 120 days.
bills.brief: Allows IRS tax-deadline postponements for state-declared disasters and extends the mandatory extension from 60 to 120 days.

top_lines.headline: State-Declared Disaster Tax Relief
subs: IRS may postpone tax deadlines for state-declared disasters
Triggered by written request of a Governor (or D.C. Mayor)
Mandatory extension period doubled from 60 to 120 days

items.main: Names the Act the “Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Modification of Rules for Postponing Certain Deadlines by Reason of Disaster

items.main: Authorizes the IRS to postpone federal tax deadlines for state-declared disasters and lengthens the mandatory extension period.
items.detail: Adds subsection (c) to Section 7508A of the Internal Revenue Code: on the written request of a Governor (or the Mayor of D.C.), after consulting FEMA, the IRS may apply its disaster-postponement rules to a 'qualified State declared disaster' (natural catastrophes, or any fire, flood, or explosion of sufficient severity). 'State' includes D.C., Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands. The mandatory extension period is increased from 60 days to 120 days. The changes apply to declarations made after enactment.

gaps: The bill lets governors request federal tax postponements but does not require the IRS to grant a request.
It covers state-declared disasters but does not otherwise change the rules for federally declared disasters beyond the longer extension period.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Kustoff
featured_quotes.text: This bill, the Filing Relief for Natural Disasters Act, H.R. 517, is a bipartisan bill and a commonsense bill. It  will provide relief to Americans who have been impacted by natural disasters and emergencies. Just about every Member of this body at some point has seen their State, their district, or their constituents impacted by a natural disaster or an emergency. Mr. Speaker, just last month, Obion County, which is in my district in Tennessee, was devastated by severe flooding following a levee failure.

added: IRS authority to postpone federal tax deadlines for state-declared disasters on a Governor's request (new Section 7508A(c))
modified: Mandatory disaster extension period increased from 60 days to 120 days (Section 7508A(e))

added: State-declared disaster postponements now require the Secretary to consult the Administrator of the Federal Emergency Management Agency before acting on a Governor's request
modified: On a state-declared disaster, the Secretary now applies the rules of subsections (a) and (b) — not just subsection (a) — to the qualified disaster

bills.title: Veteran Fraud Reimbursement Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to amend title 38, United States Code, to improve the repayment by the Secretary of Veterans Affairs of benefits misused by a fiduciary, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-56 on December 12, 2025. Passed the House on May 5, 2025 and the Senate on November 20, 2025.
bills.summary: Requires the VA to repay veterans the full amount of any benefits stolen or misused by their appointed fiduciary, and to try to recover the money from the fiduciary.
bills.brief: Requires the VA to reissue the full amount of benefits misused by a fiduciary and recoup it from the fiduciary.

top_lines.headline: Reimbursing Misused Veteran Benefits
subs: VA must repay the full amount a fiduciary misused
VA must seek recoupment from the fiduciary
Reissuance not delayed by a pending VA-negligence review

items.main: Names the Act the “Veteran Fraud Reimbursement Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Improvement to Repayment by Secretary of Veterans Affairs of Certain Misused Benefits

items.main: Requires the VA to pay a beneficiary (or successor fiduciary) the full amount of benefits a fiduciary misused.
items.detail: Rewrites Section 6107 of title 38. When a fiduciary misuses a beneficiary's benefits, the Secretary must reissue an equal amount, make a good-faith effort to recoup it from the fiduciary, and promptly remit any recouped funds. For a beneficiary who has died, payment follows Section 5121 (but not to the fiduciary who misused the benefits). Total payments may not exceed the amount misused. The Secretary must set methods and timing for determining whether misuse resulted from VA negligence, but may not withhold reissuance pending that determination and need not make a determination for every instance.

gaps: The bill guarantees repayment of misused benefits but does not set a deadline for the VA to reissue the funds.
It requires good-faith recoupment from fiduciaries but does not specify penalties for fiduciaries who misuse benefits.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Connolly
featured_quotes.text: As a Nation, we have a solemn obligation to ensure that the men and women who have served in our Armed Forces and their families receive the benefits they have rightfully earned through their sacrifice and unwavering dedication. Unfortunately, an unintended consequence of the Johnny Isakson and David P. Roe, M.D. Veterans Health Care and Benefits Improvement Act of 2020 has hindered this mission.

modified: VA reissuance of fiduciary-misused benefits (Section 6107 of title 38): now requires paying the full misused amount and may not be withheld pending a VA-negligence determination

bills.title: Gerald E. Connolly Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to require the Government Accountability Office to produce a report on esophageal cancer, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-96 on June 9, 2026. Passed the House on June 3, 2025 and the Senate on May 20, 2026.
bills.summary: Directs the GAO to report on esophageal cancer costs and screening among federal employees and retirees, and records congressional findings about the disease.
bills.brief: Requires a GAO report on esophageal cancer spending and screening under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program.

top_lines.headline: Esophageal Cancer GAO Report
subs: GAO report within 1 year on esophageal cancer under FEHB
Reviews cancer-related spending for federal employees and retirees
Reviews how often high-risk enrollees are screened

top_lines.headline: Congressional Findings
subs: Bill cites a rise of more than 700% in recent decades
Cites about 1 in 5 patients surviving 5 years

items.main: Names the Act the “Gerald E. Connolly Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Records congressional findings on esophageal cancer.
items.detail: The findings state that esophageal cancer is among the fastest-increasing cancers (cited as up more than 700 percent in recent decades), that about 1 in 5 patients survive five years, and that early detection of its precursor, Barrett's esophagus, sharply improves survival (cited as high as 49 percent at an early stage).

items.main: Requires a GAO report within one year on esophageal cancer under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program.
items.detail: The Comptroller General must evaluate total esophageal-cancer-related health care spending under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program for federal employees and retirees diagnosed with the disease, and how often FEHB enrollees whose records indicate high risk are screened according to established guidelines.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, I strongly support this bill, which of course, supports our fight against cancer and to improve healthcare for all Federal workers. This is such an important way to honor the legacy of our colleague, our Ranking Member Gerry Connolly. Gerry was a dedicated public servant, a fighter, and a mentor to all of us on the Oversight Committee. Gerry worked to hold our government accountable for over 30 years and was dedicated to improving the lives of all Americans.

gaps: The bill orders a report on FEHB esophageal cancer screening but does not require any screening coverage or program changes.
Its findings emphasize early detection, but the bill creates no awareness or screening program — only a report.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I strongly support this bill, which of course, supports our fight against cancer and to improve healthcare for all Federal workers. This is such an important way to honor the legacy of our colleague, our Ranking Member Gerry Connolly. Gerry was a dedicated public servant, a fighter, and a mentor to all of us on the Oversight Committee. Gerry worked to hold our government accountable for over 30 years and was dedicated to improving the lives of all Americans.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: I hope that this legislation can shed some light on the impact of esophageal cancer on Federal Government public servants.

added: GAO report within one year on esophageal cancer spending and screening under the Federal Employees Health Benefits Program

modified: Short title renamed from "Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act" to "Gerald E. Connolly Esophageal Cancer Awareness Act of 2025"

bills.title: Pregnant Students' Rights Act
bills.official_title: To require institutions of higher education to disseminate information on the rights of, and accommodations and resources for, pregnant students, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Hinson (R-IA) with 3 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. As an information-disclosure mandate touching abortion-adjacent politics, it is likely to draw Democratic opposition in the Senate, where 60 votes would be needed.
bills.summary: Requires colleges to tell students each year about the rights, accommodations, and resources available to pregnant students who choose to carry a pregnancy to term.
bills.brief: Requires colleges to disseminate information on pregnant students' rights, accommodations, and resources.

top_lines.headline: Pregnant Student Information
subs: Colleges must share pregnant-student rights and resources yearly
Includes campus and community resources and accommodations
Includes how to file a Title IX complaint

items.main: Names the Act the “Pregnant Students' Rights Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Notice of Pregnant Student Rights, Accommodations, and Resources

items.main: Requires colleges in federal student-aid programs to inform students about resources and accommodations for pregnant students carrying a baby to term.
items.detail: Adds subsection (n) to Section 485 of the Higher Education Act of 1965 (20 U.S.C. 1092). Institutions must give prospective and enrolled students a list of campus and community resources, information on available accommodations, and instructions for filing a Title IX complaint with the Department of Education or the institution. Dissemination must include an annual email, student handbooks, orientations, health or counseling centers, and the institution's website. The subsection does not authorize the Secretary to require additional information or create additional rights.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, I oppose this bill because, among other reasons, the information that is required is incomplete and biased. As written, the Pregnant Students' Rights Act is unfairly limited regarding the information it requires colleges to provide to students and the students it chooses to support. It does not include information about comprehensive family planning resources, and it only supports pregnant students who carry a baby to term. Simply put, the bill fails to support any student with a different pregnancy-related outcome.

gaps: The bill requires distributing information about existing rights but does not create any new accommodations or rights for pregnant students.
It mandates dissemination but specifies no penalty or enforcement mechanism for institutions that fail to comply.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Bonamici
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I oppose this bill because, among other reasons, the information that is required is incomplete and biased. As written, the Pregnant Students' Rights Act is unfairly limited regarding the information it requires colleges to provide to students and the students it chooses to support. It does not include information about comprehensive family planning resources, and it only supports pregnant students who carry a baby to term. Simply put, the bill fails to support any student with a different pregnancy-related outcome.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Miller
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, college can be a challenging environment, especially for pregnant women. Many feel forced to choose between motherhood and their education. Nearly 30 percent of all abortions in the United States are performed on women in college. Title IX already protects the right of pregnant women to stay in school. However, many of them face a lack of resources and support. Some even fear punishment and a loss of scholarships simply for carrying their baby to full term while taking classes.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walberg
featured_quotes.text: to my dear friend and colleague from Georgia, as she has discussed that tragic story with me before, my heart does break. Having experienced that in my own personal family, as well, I understand what she is saying. I am just not capable, I guess, of communicating that this bill is affording all the questions to be answered and all of the issue to be addressed. It also gives pregnant women, who are blessed to be able to continue carrying to completion, the opportunity to also know that their academic opportunity will continue, as well.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Randall
featured_quotes.text: If the sponsor of this bill and the majority party actually believed in supporting student parents, then they would take real action, not just grandstand on the House floor because the March for Life is this weekend. The bill before us today requires the dissemination of incomplete information, but it also comes after House Republicans have worked alongside the Trump regime to dismantle and weaken the Department of Education and protections for students who file complaints around Title IX violations, among other things.

added: Annual college disclosure of pregnant students' rights, accommodations, and resources (new subsection (n) of Higher Education Act Section 485)

bills.title: Snow Water Supply Forecasting Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program Authorization Act.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Hurd (R-CO) with Rep. Neguse (D-CO) and 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. A bipartisan reauthorization of an existing water-data program tends to clear the Senate when floor time allows.
bills.summary: Renews and updates the federal Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program through 2031, shifting its focus toward advanced snowpack measurement and modeling technologies.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program for fiscal years 2027-2031 and refocuses it on integrated snowpack measurement and modeling.

top_lines.headline: Program Reauthorization
subs: Reauthorizes appropriations for fiscal years 2027-2031
Replaces the prior aggregate fiscal year 2022-2026 authorization

top_lines.headline: Technology Focus
subs: Emphasis on integrated snowpack measurement and modeling
Names airborne laser altimetry and imaging spectroscopy
Removes a prior interim report requirement

items.main: Names the Act the “Snow Water Supply Forecasting Reauthorization Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program

items.main: Reauthorizes and updates the Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program (43 U.S.C. 1477) through fiscal year 2031.
items.detail: Reauthorizes appropriations for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031, replacing the prior aggregate authorization for fiscal years 2022 through 2026. Refocuses the program on deploying commercially available technologies that integrate snowpack measurement and modeling — including airborne laser altimetry, airborne imaging spectroscopy, and integrated physics-based snowpack and hydrologic modeling — and on real-time integration with water supply forecasts, including for interstate water management. Removes a prior interim report requirement.

gaps: The bill reauthorizes the program through 2031, but the annual funding amount is set in the underlying statute and is not changed here.
It emphasizes new measurement technologies but does not require the resulting data to be made publicly available.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hurd
featured_quotes.text: this bill reauthorizes a vital program that helps water managers promptly and effectively plan for and respond to drought.

modified: Snow Water Supply Forecasting Program (43 U.S.C. 1477) reauthorized for fiscal years 2027-2031 and refocused on integrated snowpack measurement and modeling technologies
removed: A prior interim report requirement under the program

added: Added requirement that the technologies data paragraph reference "other Federal agencies" including the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the Natural Resources Conservation Service
modified: Authorized appropriation set at $3,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 (introduced version named no dollar figure, only the FY2027-2031 window)
Dropped "commercially available" qualifier — technologies now just "technologies that provide complete integration of" snowpack measurements and models
Snowpack technology list now reads "imaging spectroscopy" instead of "airborne imaging spectroscopy"

bills.title: Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Fair Credit Reporting Act to prevent consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports under certain circumstances, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-36 on September 5, 2025. Passed the House on June 23, 2025 and the Senate on August 2, 2025.
bills.summary: Cracks down on mortgage 'trigger leads' by barring credit bureaus from selling a homebuyer's information to other lenders when the buyer applies for a mortgage, unless the buyer agreed or the lender already works with them.
bills.brief: Restricts credit bureaus from selling mortgage 'trigger leads' unless the consumer consented or the recipient already has a relationship with them.

top_lines.headline: Mortgage Trigger Leads
subs: Limits selling a mortgage applicant's credit data to other lenders
Allowed only with consumer consent or an existing relationship
Must be a firm offer of credit or insurance

top_lines.headline: GAO Study
subs: GAO study on text-message trigger leads within 1 year

items.main: Names the Act the “Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Treatment of Prescreening Report Requests

items.main: Restricts when credit bureaus may sell a mortgage applicant's information as a 'trigger lead.'
items.detail: Amends Section 604(c) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. 1681b(c)). When someone requests a consumer report for a residential mortgage credit transaction, the credit bureau may not furnish that consumer's report to another person based on that request unless it is a firm offer of credit or insurance and the recipient either has the consumer's authorization or already has a relationship with them — having originated the consumer's current mortgage, servicing it, or being an insured depository institution or credit union holding a current account. Takes effect 180 days after enactment.

items.main: Sets the Act and its amendments to take effect 180 days after enactment.
items.detail: Effective-date section — timing only; no substantive effect (15 U.S.C. 1681b note).

items.main: Requires a GAO study on the value of trigger leads received by text message.
items.detail: The Comptroller General must study the value of text-message trigger leads with input from state regulators, mortgage lenders, depository institutions, consumer reporting agencies, and consumers, and report to Congress within 12 months.

criticisms.why: As I have discussed, H.R. 2808 is an important positive step to strengthen data privacy for consumers and curb the harmful practice of trigger leads, protecting consumers from entities that they didn't want to do business with, never sought to do business with, finding out that they are applying for a mortgage and then harassing them with a host of texts and calls, et cetera.

gaps: The bill restricts trigger leads for residential mortgages but does not address trigger leads for other credit products such as auto loans.
It allows trigger leads with consumer authorization but does not specify how that authorization must be obtained or documented.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Sherman
featured_quotes.text: As I have discussed, H.R. 2808 is an important positive step to strengthen data privacy for consumers and curb the harmful practice of trigger leads, protecting consumers from entities that they didn't want to do business with, never sought to do business with, finding out that they are applying for a mortgage and then harassing them with a host of texts and calls, et cetera.

added: GAO study within one year on the value of text-message mortgage trigger leads
modified: Fair Credit Reporting Act (Section 604(c), 15 U.S.C. 1681b(c)) now bars mortgage trigger leads unless the consumer consented or the recipient has an existing relationship

added: New SEC. 4 GAO Study — the Comptroller General must study the value of trigger leads received by text message, with input from state regulators, lenders, depositories, consumer reporting agencies, and consumers
GAO must report findings to Congress within the 12-month period beginning on the date of enactment

bills.title: Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act
bills.official_title: An Act to amend the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Act to require hygienic handling of breast milk and baby formula by security screening personnel of the Transportation Security Administration and personnel of private security companies providing security screening, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-41 on November 25, 2025. Passed the Senate on May 14, 2025 and the House on November 17, 2025.
bills.summary: Requires the TSA to issue guidance for the hygienic handling of breast milk, baby formula, and related items during airport security re-screening, and orders an audit of how well it is followed.
bills.brief: Requires TSA guidance on hygienic handling of breast milk and baby formula during airport screening, plus an Inspector General audit.

top_lines.headline: Hygienic Screening of Infant Items
subs: TSA must issue hygienic-handling guidance within 90 days
Covers breast milk, baby formula, infant water, and juice
Applies to TSA and private screening personnel

top_lines.headline: Compliance Audit
subs: DHS Inspector General audit of compliance within 1 year

items.main: Names the Act the “Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Enhancement Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect (49 U.S.C. 40101 note).

sections.label: Section 2 — Hygienic Handling of Breast Milk and Baby Formula During Aviation Security Screening

items.main: Amends the Bottles and Breastfeeding Equipment Screening Act (Public Law 114-293) to add two new sections requiring hygienic handling of infant items during TSA screening and an Inspector General audit.
items.detail: Adds new SEC. 3 and SEC. 4 to the Act (49 U.S.C. 44901 note). New SEC. 3: within 90 days of enactment, and every five years thereafter if appropriate, the TSA Administrator must issue or update guidance — developed with nationally recognized maternal health organizations — to minimize contamination risk for breast milk, baby formula, purified deionized water for infants, and juice (plus the ice packs, freezer packs, and gel packs used to cool them) subject to re-screening or additional screening; the guidance applies to TSA screeners and private screening company personnel under section 44920 of title 49. New SEC. 4: within one year of enactment, the DHS Inspector General must report to the House Homeland Security Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee an audit of compliance with sections 2 and 3, including the effect of screening technologies such as bottled liquid scanners and the rate at which such items are denied entry into the sterile area.

gaps: The bill requires hygienic-handling guidance but leaves the specific contamination standards to the TSA rather than setting them in law.
It mandates an audit of compliance but specifies no consequence if screeners fail to follow the guidance.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Swalwell
featured_quotes.text: Air travel with children is a nightmare, and I am just talking for the nonparents who have to deal with them at an airport. For parents, it is hell. It is like an Olympic sport. It is like going through a gauntlet dragging little kids who just want to be attached to tablets or anything but the directions that you are giving to them to hopefully get them from the entrance of the airport to the plane. Oftentimes with little kids, you have, in transit with them, a mother who is breastfeeding.

added: TSA hygienic-handling guidance for breast milk, baby formula, infant water, and juice during screening (new Section 3 of Public Law 114-293)
DHS Inspector General audit of compliance within one year (new Section 4)

bills.title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Visit America Act to promote music tourism, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Harshbarger (R-TN) with Rep. Barragan (D-CA) and 10 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. A low-cost, bipartisan addition to existing tourism-promotion duties has a reasonable path to Senate passage.
bills.summary: Adds promoting 'music tourism' to the duties of the Commerce Department's travel and tourism office, directing it to identify and promote U.S. music destinations and events.
bills.brief: Amends the Visit America Act to make promoting music tourism a duty of the Commerce travel and tourism office.

top_lines.headline: Music Tourism Promotion
subs: Commerce must identify and promote U.S. music destinations
Covers both domestic and international travel promotion
Defines 'music tourism' in law

top_lines.headline: Reporting
subs: New report to Congress every 2 years on travel goals

items.main: Names the Act the “American Music Tourism Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Responsibilities of the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism

items.main: Adds promoting music tourism to the duties of the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Travel and Tourism.
items.detail: Amends the Visit America Act (15 U.S.C. 9803, 9801). The Assistant Secretary must identify U.S. locations and events important to music tourism and promote both domestic and international travel to them, alongside existing duties for meetings, conferences, and rural and cultural destinations. Adds a report to the Senate Commerce and House Energy and Commerce Committees within one year and every two years thereafter, and defines 'music tourism' as traveling to visit music-related attractions such as museums, studios, and venues, or to attend music festivals, concerts, or other live musical events.

gaps: The bill directs promotion of music tourism but provides no dedicated funding for the new activities.
It defines music tourism and requires reports but sets no measurable target for increasing it.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Harshbarger
featured_quotes.text: We have the opportunity today to vote on legislation centered around something that brings us all together, and that is music. Today, we will take the American Music Tourism Act under consideration. It is a bipartisan piece of legislation that I am proud to have led through the House alongside my co-lead, Representative Nanette Barragan.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pallone
featured_quotes.text: this bill, as I said, was part of that bipartisan package that we had hoped would be passed last December but for Elon Musk. This bill is important. I know that back in Asbury Park, in particular, they will be very happy to know that our Congress is paying so much attention to American music tourism.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bilirakis
featured_quotes.text: let me tell you, the speaker on the floor of the House of Representatives in the great State of Florida used to begin his speeches by saying, ``I am fired up.'' I am fired up, Mr. Speaker, because we are going to pass a great bill that promotes America. With the previous bill honoring the 1980 USA Gold Medal hockey team, this is a great day in D.C. and all over the United States of America.

added: 'Music tourism' promotion added to the Assistant Secretary of Commerce's travel duties; biennial report to Congress; statutory definition of 'music tourism' (Visit America Act, 15 U.S.C. 9803, 9801)

bills.title: Requesting the Secretary of the Interior to authorize unique and one-time arrangements for displays on the National Mall and the Washington Monument during the period beginning on December 31, 2025, and ending on January 5, 2026
bills.official_title: Requesting the Secretary of the Interior to authorize unique and one-time arrangements for displays on the National Mall and the Washington Monument during the period beginning on December 31, 2025, and ending on January 5, 2026.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-46 on December 2, 2025. Passed the House on November 18, 2025 and the Senate on November 20, 2025.
bills.summary: Asks the Interior Department to allow special one-time displays of 250th-anniversary materials on the National Mall — including projections on the Washington Monument for five nights — around New Year's 2025-2026.
bills.brief: Requests the Interior Secretary authorize one-time 250th-anniversary displays on the National Mall and Washington Monument, December 31, 2025 to January 5, 2026.

subs: Requests Interior to allow National Mall displays
Includes 5 nights of projection on the Washington Monument
For the period December 31, 2025 to January 5, 2026

sections.label: Request to the Secretary of the Interior

items.main: Requests the Interior Secretary authorize unique, one-time displays of 250th-anniversary materials on and around the National Mall.
items.detail: Congress requests that the Secretary of the Interior authorize one-time arrangements to display United States semiquincentennial materials, artifacts, digital content, and film footage in and around the National Mall — including projection onto the surface of the Washington Monument for five nights of public display — during the period December 31, 2025 to January 5, 2026, and requests that an enrolled copy be transmitted to the Secretary and the Chair of the United States Semiquincentennial Commission.

gaps: The resolution requests the displays but does not require the Interior Secretary to grant the request.
It authorizes a one-time event window but provides no funding for the displays.

bills.title: Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To amend title 46, United States Code, with respect to the types of vessels that may enter or operate in navigable waters of the United States or transfer cargo in any port or place under the jurisdiction of the United States, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Pfluger (R-TX) with a bipartisan group of cosponsors (including Reps. Carbajal and Sewell); passed the House. A targeted maritime measure aimed at protecting U.S.-owned port property has bipartisan support, though it has not yet received a Senate vote.
bills.summary: Lets the President restrict ships from entering U.S. ports if they used a port in a Western Hemisphere free-trade partner country that seized port property owned by a U.S. company.
bills.brief: Allows the President to bar from U.S. ports vessels that used a Western Hemisphere free-trade-partner port expropriated from a U.S. owner.

top_lines.headline: Port Entry Restrictions
subs: President may designate expropriated foreign ports
Targets Western Hemisphere free-trade-partner countries
Vessels using designated ports restricted from U.S. ports

top_lines.headline: Removal of Designation
subs: Designation lifted if the property is returned or compensated

items.main: Names the Act the “Defending American Property Abroad Act of 2026”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Condition for Entry into Ports in the United States

items.main: Lets the President designate foreign ports that expropriated U.S.-owned port property, restricting vessels that used them from entering U.S. ports.
items.detail: Amends Section 70022 of title 46. The President may designate a port, harbor, or marine terminal in a Western Hemisphere country with a U.S. free trade agreement if that country nationalized or expropriated port property owned or controlled by a U.S. person and the port is accessible only through U.S.-person-controlled land. Vessels that transited a designated port become subject to the title's port-entry restriction. The President must remove a designation if the property is returned, adequate compensation is paid, the conditions no longer apply, or the dispute is otherwise resolved. Emergencies and owner-authorized transits are excepted.

criticisms.why: the question is: Do we support President Trump with this authority? Absolutely, we do. This legislation makes it clear: The United States will not stand for unlawful harassment campaigns against American companies and American workers. For over 35 years, Vulcan Materials Company, based in Alabama, has lawfully owned and operated a limestone quarry in Mexico. Yet, since 2018, the Mexican Government has unlawfully restricted Vulcan's operations and wrongfully targeted them through coercion and intimidation.

This legislation codifies the commonsense principle that foreign nations should not profit from properties stolen from Americans. This bill is needed because for years the Mexican Government has engaged in a deliberate campaign against an American company, Vulcan Materials, headquartered in my district. In 2022, Mexican authorities used military force to shut down Vulcan's lawful operations. Then, in 2024, they took the dramatic step of declaring Vulcan's private property a protected natural area.

gaps: The bill targets Western Hemisphere free-trade partners but does not address expropriated port property elsewhere in the world.
It excludes matters in pending free-trade-agreement arbitration but sets no deadline for resolving such disputes.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Strong
featured_quotes.text: the question is: Do we support President Trump with this authority? Absolutely, we do. This legislation makes it clear: The United States will not stand for unlawful harassment campaigns against American companies and American workers. For over 35 years, Vulcan Materials Company, based in Alabama, has lawfully owned and operated a limestone quarry in Mexico. Yet, since 2018, the Mexican Government has unlawfully restricted Vulcan's operations and wrongfully targeted them through coercion and intimidation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Palmer
featured_quotes.text: This legislation codifies the commonsense principle that foreign nations should not profit from properties stolen from Americans. This bill is needed because for years the Mexican Government has engaged in a deliberate campaign against an American company, Vulcan Materials, headquartered in my district. In 2022, Mexican authorities used military force to shut down Vulcan's lawful operations. Then, in 2024, they took the dramatic step of declaring Vulcan's private property a protected natural area.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pfluger
featured_quotes.text: Let's be clear, American companies operating abroad should not have to fear arbitrary government actions that undermine their property rights, but right now, that is exactly what is happening. When countries violate trade agreements and illegally seize assets from U.S. companies, it puts American job security, economic security, and, quite frankly, our national security at risk. H.R. 7084 ensures there are enforceable consequences for those actions. Specifically, it strengthens U.S. maritime security law to address these unlawful seizures.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: what we have seen happen to Alabama's own Vulcan Materials Company should concern every Member of this body. A foreign government shut down an American company's operations, moved to seize its property, and ignored the rule of law. If it can happen to one American company, it can happen to any of them. We must protect American jobs and American investments and stand on the principles that the United States will stand for its people and its companies wherever they operate.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to voice my strong opposition to this bill. First of all, this bill and the substance of the bill, this dispute, is undergoing consideration by the international bodies established by the U.S.-Mexico-Canada trade agreement. We really should wait until a decision is arrived at with respect to that mechanism, but there are other considerations. First, let's consider other far-reaching implications.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Aderholt
featured_quotes.text: today, the U.S. House of Representatives is acting in response to a situation in which a foreign government shut down an American company's operations, seized its property, and ignored the rule of law. When an American business is targeted in this way, it is not just an attack on one company, it is an attack on American workers, American jobs, and American interests. Vulcan Materials, an Alabama company, has lawfully operated for 35 years in Mexico. Yet the Mexican government illegally seized its assets.

removed: Dropped the technical amendment inserting "the" before "Federal Register" in subsection (b)(1)

bills.title: Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act
bills.official_title: To direct the Secretary of Labor to train certain employees of Department of Labor how to effectively detect and assist law enforcement in preventing human trafficking during the course of their official duties, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Walberg (R-MI) with Rep. McBath (D-GA) and 3 cosponsors; passed the House. A bipartisan, low-cost training mandate on human-trafficking detection has a reasonable path through the Senate, though it has not yet received a vote there.
bills.summary: Directs the Labor Department to train relevant employees to spot human trafficking during their work and refer cases to law enforcement, and to report yearly to Congress.
bills.brief: Directs the Secretary of Labor to train relevant employees to detect human trafficking and refer cases, with annual reports to Congress.

top_lines.headline: Trafficking Detection Training
subs: Labor Department training program within 180 days
Targets employees whose duties relate to detection
Wage and Hour staff in high child-labor states prioritized

top_lines.headline: Reporting
subs: Annual report on training and trafficking cases referred

items.main: Names the Act the “Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines “human trafficking” for the Act by reference to paragraph (11) of section 103 of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 (22 U.S.C. 7102).
items.detail: Definitions apply throughout; the term adopts the existing statutory definition rather than creating a new one.

sections.label: Section 3 — Training for Department Personnel to Identify Human Trafficking

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Labor to train relevant employees to detect human trafficking and refer cases.
items.detail: Within 180 days of enactment, the Secretary of Labor must implement training and periodic continuing education for Department of Labor employees whose official duties warrant it. For Wage and Hour Division staff, the Secretary must consider employees in states with a significant increase in oppressive child labor (as defined in the Fair Labor Standards Act). Training covers detecting trafficking, identifying suspected victims and traffickers, and a clear path for referring cases to the Department of Justice and other authorities while protecting victims' rights. 'Human trafficking' is defined by reference to the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 (22 U.S.C. 7102).

items.main: Requires annual reports to Congress on the training and trafficking referrals.
items.detail: Within one year of first implementing the program and annually after, the Secretary must report to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the training provided (including its effectiveness and the number of employees trained) and the number of trafficking-detection cases referred to the Department of Justice and other authorities.

gaps: The bill mandates trafficking-detection training but provides no dedicated funding for the program.
It requires referral of suspected cases to the Department of Justice but does not address what happens to workers identified as potential victims.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moylan
featured_quotes.text: I am very happy and pleased to be a cosponsor of this measure. As we know, human trafficking is modern-day slavery, Mr. Speaker, and traffickers abuse and exploit millions of victims, especially children, girls, and women, all for commercial gain. This is a serious problem around the globe, Mr. Speaker, and even here at home. We must do more to raise awareness of this crime. The U.S. Department of Labor is on the front lines of detecting human trafficking.

added: Department of Labor program to train relevant employees to detect human trafficking and refer cases (within 180 days)
Annual reports to Congress on the training and trafficking cases referred to the Department of Justice

bills.title: Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to amend title 36, United States Code, to revise the Federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-57 on December 12, 2025. Passed the Senate on April 30, 2025 and the House on December 1, 2025.
bills.summary: Modernizes the federal charter for the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association, moving governance details to its bylaws and updating standard nonprofit restrictions.
bills.brief: Revises the Title 36 federal charter of the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association.

top_lines.headline: Charter Modernization
subs: Governance and membership rules moved to the bylaws
Standard nonprofit restrictions updated
Principal office no longer fixed in D.C.

items.main: Names the Act the “Foundation of the Federal Bar Association Charter Amendments Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 70501 of title 36 by striking subsection (b) and redesignating subsection (c) as subsection (b).
items.detail: Streamlines the corporation's organization provisions in 36 U.S.C. 70501.

items.main: Rewrites Section 70503 so eligibility for membership and the rights and privileges of members are as provided in the bylaws.
items.detail: Strikes the prior subsections (a) and (b) and redesignates subsection (c) as subsection (b); membership terms move to the bylaws except as provided in the chapter.

items.main: Makes the board of directors the governing body, with most details set in the bylaws.
items.detail: Rewrites Section 70504 so the board of directors governs the corporation and may exercise its powers, with the board's responsibilities and the officers' election left to the bylaws. Related amendments move membership eligibility (Section 70503) to the bylaws, allow the principal office to be any U.S. location set by the board (Section 70508, previously the District of Columbia), and update the service-of-process and dissolution rules.

items.main: Updates the restrictions on the Foundation, barring stock, dividends, political activity, lobbying, private inurement, and insider loans.
items.detail: Rewrites Section 70507 of title 36. The corporation may not issue stock or pay dividends; may not use its funds or property for political activity or to influence legislation; may not let income or assets benefit a director, officer, or member (except reasonable compensation and expense reimbursement); may not make loans to insiders; members and individuals are not liable for its obligations; and it may not claim U.S. government approval or authority for its activities.

items.main: Amends Section 70508 so the principal office may be any United States location decided by the board and specified in the bylaws, instead of the District of Columbia.
items.detail: Strikes “the District of Columbia,” and inserts the board-chosen-location language in 36 U.S.C. 70508.

items.main: Rewrites Section 70510 so the corporation must comply with the service-of-process law of the State or District in which it is incorporated.
items.detail: 36 U.S.C. 70510, retitled with a compliance note.

sections.label: Section 8 — Deposit of Assets on Dissolution or Final Liquidation

items.main: Rewrites Section 70512 so on dissolution any remaining assets, after discharging liabilities, are distributed as provided by the board and in compliance with the charter and bylaws.
Provides that the Act's budgetary effects are determined by reference to the latest “Budgetary Effects of PAYGO Legislation” statement for the Statutory Pay-As-You-Go Act of 2010.
items.detail: Standard PAYGO bookkeeping provision — no substantive effect.

gaps: The bill modernizes the Foundation's charter but does not change its purpose or activities.
It moves governance details from federal law into the Foundation's bylaws, reducing what is fixed in statute.

modified: Federal charter of the Foundation of the Federal Bar Association (title 36, chapter 705) revised — governance and membership moved to bylaws, nonprofit restrictions updated, principal office no longer fixed in D.C.

bills.title: Stop Illegal Entry Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Immigration and Nationality Act to increase penalties for individuals who illegally enter and reenter the United States after being removed, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Bice (R-OK) with 5 cosponsors; passed the Republican-majority House. New mandatory-minimum immigration penalties would need 60 votes in the Senate and are likely to draw unified Democratic opposition, making passage unlikely.
bills.summary: Raises criminal penalties for illegally entering the U.S. and adds mandatory minimum prison terms for people who reenter after being removed, especially those with prior crimes.
bills.brief: Increases penalties for illegal entry and adds mandatory minimums for reentry after removal.

top_lines.headline: Illegal Entry Penalties
subs: Maximum prison term for illegal entry raised from 2 to 5 years
New 5-year mandatory minimum for entry plus a later serious crime

top_lines.headline: Reentry After Removal
subs: Base reentry penalty up to 10 years
Up to 15 years for those with 3+ prior misdemeanors
10-year-to-life mandatory minimum for serious prior offenses

items.main: Names the Act the “Stop Illegal Entry Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Commission of Crimes by Aliens Unlawfully Present

items.main: Raises the maximum penalty for illegal entry and adds a mandatory minimum when entry is followed by a serious crime.
items.detail: Amends Section 275 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1325). The maximum prison term for illegal entry rises from 2 years to 5 years. A new provision imposes a mandatory minimum of 5 years (up to life) on someone who illegally enters, eludes inspection, or enters by misrepresentation and is later convicted of any crime punishable by more than one year.

sections.label: Section 3 — Increased Penalties for Reentry of Removed Alien

items.main: Restructures the penalties for reentering the U.S. after removal, adding mandatory minimums.
items.detail: Amends Section 276 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1326). The base penalty for reentry after removal is up to 10 years; up to 15 years applies for those previously convicted of 3 or more drug or violent misdemeanors; and a 10-year-to-life mandatory minimum applies to those previously convicted of an aggravated felony, another felony, or any crime punishable by more than one year, or convicted of reentry at least twice before. Authority shifts from the Attorney General to the Secretary of Homeland Security.

gaps: The bill raises penalties but does not address the immigration court backlog that affects how quickly removal cases are resolved.
It adds mandatory minimums but provides no additional funding for detention or prosecution.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Harris
featured_quotes.text: I applaud my colleague, Representative Knott, for bringing forth this important legislation. Mr. Speaker, if we reward illegals for breaking our laws, we cannot be surprised when it continues to happen. We all know under the Biden administration, illegal immigrants were welcomed with open arms. They were given hotel rooms, cell phones, plane tickets, and work authorization. I am glad to report those days are over.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Jayapal
featured_quotes.text: This bill is Republicans' latest attempt to scapegoat and fearmonger about immigrants. With President Trump's poll numbers tanking on immigration due to his kidnapping and disappearing of immigrants and U.S. citizens off our streets, House Republicans are, once again, looking to turn the conversation back to immigration and the border.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Correa
featured_quotes.text: there are many marines right now whose parents are undocumented who are ready to lay down their lives for this country. My colleagues on the other side of the aisle, let's work on immigration reform. This does nothing to strengthen our country or our national defense. It hurts our economy. Why are we going down this path? Let's get serious about immigration reform. Let's pass some laws that enable workers to work legally and let employers hire these workers legally, as well.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Bice
featured_quotes.text: Let me first start by saying I think it is rich that we stand here on the House floor and are lectured by the other side of the aisle about immigration issues when they had the last 4 years to actually address this problem. They want to deflect, as my colleague from Kansas mentioned. Let's talk about all the other things that have been happening in the country instead of the actual issue at hand. Under the Biden administration, over 10 million illegal immigrants entered this country.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Kennedy
featured_quotes.text: For too long, open-border policies have left American families at risk. Under the Biden administration, the vast majority of those charged with illegal reentry already had criminal records. In Utah, we have seen the consequences firsthand. This July in Salt Lake County, a 43-year-old Mexican national was sentenced for drug trafficking and illegal reentry. He had been deported three times before. When he was arrested, he carried an illegal firearm and more than 9,000 fentanyl pills.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: I had some prepared remarks, but as I have talked about this and looked at it even more, this is probably one of the most commonsense bills that will come before this Congress. This bill simply says if someone reenters or if someone commits a felony, that this law applies. These comments from the other side to try to confuse this issue, to misrepresent the issue, make no sense.

added: Mandatory minimums for illegal entry followed by a serious crime (5 years to life) and for reentry after removal with serious priors (10 years to life)
modified: Maximum penalty for illegal entry (8 U.S.C. 1325) raised from 2 years to 5 years; reentry penalties (8 U.S.C. 1326) restructured
Short title changed to "Stop Illegal Entry Act of 2025" (was "Stop Illegal Entry Act")
removed: Dropped a second trigger for the 10-year mandatory-minimum reentry penalty — an alien "convicted under this section at least 2 times before such removal or departure" no longer qualifies on that basis (the prior-conviction-of-listed-crimes trigger remains)

bills.title: Wabeno Economic Development Act
bills.official_title: To provide for the conveyance of certain Federal land in Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Tiffany (R-WI); passed the House and was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Single-parcel land conveyances at market value are usually low-controversy and clear the Senate when floor time allows.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

bills.summary: Directs the Forest Service to sell about 14 acres of national forest land in Wisconsin to a local company at market value, and orders a federal review of stone, sand, and gravel permitting.
bills.brief: Conveys about 14 acres of Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest to a Wisconsin company at market value, plus a permitting review.

top_lines.headline: National Forest Land Sale
subs: About 14 acres in Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest
Sold to Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix, LLC at appraised market value
Buyer pays survey, appraisal, and environmental costs

top_lines.headline: Permitting Review
subs: Interior review of stone, sand, and gravel permitting on federal land
Report to Congress within 180 days

items.main: Names the Act the “Wabeno Economic Development Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Conveyance of Certain National Forest System Land

items.main: Directs the Forest Service to convey about 14 acres of national forest land to Tony's Wabeno Redi-Mix, LLC at market value.
items.detail: If the company offers market value (set by a required appraisal) within 180 days of the appraisal's approval, the Secretary of Agriculture must convey the roughly 14-acre parcel in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest in Wisconsin, including mineral rights, by quitclaim deed within 180 days. The buyer pays the purchase price plus survey, appraisal, and environmental-analysis costs.

sections.label: Section 3 — Comprehensive Review of Federal Permitting Processes for Stone, Sand, and Gravel Development

items.main: Requires an Interior Department review of federal permitting for stone, sand, and gravel development on federal lands.
items.detail: Within 180 days, the Secretary of the Interior must report to the House Natural Resources and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committees (and publish online) on the current permitting process and timelines, inefficiencies and duplicative steps, recommendations to streamline, and the economic impact of current timelines.

gaps: The bill conveys the parcel including mineral rights but does not restrict how the land may be used after sale.
The bill is silent on liability for hazardous substances, pollutants, or contaminants on the parcel — it neither imposes nor waives CERCLA cleanup obligations.

added: Conveyance of about 14 acres of Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest land to a private company at market value
Interior review and report on federal stone, sand, and gravel permitting

removed: Struck the Hazardous Materials carve-out (subsection (e)) that had limited the Secretary to only CERCLA section 120(h) disclosure and exempted any duty to remediate or abate disclosed contaminants — full CERCLA cleanup obligations now apply

bills.summary: Makes permanent a NASA program that buys commercial satellite imagery and Earth data for scientific research, building on a pilot the agency started in 2019.
bills.brief: Establishes a permanent NASA program to acquire and share commercial Earth remote sensing data and imagery.

Prioritizes U.S. vendors

Annual report to Congress on vendors and license terms

items.main: Names the Act the “Accessing Satellite Capabilities to Enable New Discoveries Act” (the “ASCEND Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Directs NASA to establish a permanent program to acquire and share commercial Earth remote sensing data and imagery.
items.detail: Adds Section 60307 to title 51. The Administrator must establish, within the Earth Science Division, a program to acquire cost-effective commercial Earth remote sensing data and imagery for NASA's scientific, operational, and educational needs and, where appropriate, for other agencies and researchers. Acquisition terms may not prevent publication of the data for scientific purposes; the Administrator may set license terms for the widest possible use; and data is to be procured from U.S. vendors to the maximum extent practicable. An initial and then annual report to the Senate Commerce and House Science Committees must list agreements, vendors, license terms, and uses.

gaps: The bill establishes the program but does not authorize a specific funding level for data purchases.
It prioritizes U.S. vendors 'to the maximum extent practicable' but does not define when foreign data may be bought instead.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hurd
featured_quotes.text: This bill builds on a model that already works. In 2017, NASA launched the Commercial Small Satellite Data Acquisition Pilot Program to test whether commercially available Earth observation data could support NASA's scientific missions. The results were clear: Participating scientists found the data reliable, valuable, and highly effective across a broad range of research applications. The ASCEND Act takes that successful pilot and makes it permanent.

added: Permanent NASA Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program with annual reporting (new Section 60307 of title 51)

bills.title: Faster Labor Contracts Act
bills.official_title: To accelerate workplace time-to-contract under the National Labor Relations Act.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Norcross (D-NJ) with 110 cosponsors from both parties; passed the House. The unusually broad bipartisan cosponsorship is a strong signal, but binding interest arbitration for first contracts is contested by employer groups, so the 60 votes needed in the Senate are not assured.
bills.summary: Speeds up first union contracts: it sets deadlines to start bargaining, then routes unresolved disputes to mediation and, if needed, binding arbitration that sets the contract for two years.
bills.brief: Sets deadlines and a mediation-then-binding-arbitration process for reaching a first union contract under the National Labor Relations Act.

top_lines.headline: First Contract Deadlines
subs: Bargaining must begin within 10 days of a union's request
Mediation available if no deal after 90 days

top_lines.headline: Binding Arbitration
subs: Unresolved disputes go to a 3-person arbitration panel
Panel decision binds both sides for 2 years

items.main: Names the Act the “Faster Labor Contracts Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: States congressional findings that first-contract bargaining is often protracted, citing a 2021 Bloomberg Law study finding an average of 465 days between a representation vote and a contract, and that delays primarily benefit employers opposed to representation.
items.detail: Findings section — sets out the rationale; no substantive operative effect.

sections.label: Section 3 — Facilitating Initial Collective Bargaining Agreements

items.main: Creates a timeline and binding-arbitration backstop for reaching a first union contract.
items.detail: Amends Section 8 of the National Labor Relations Act (29 U.S.C. 158). After a union is newly certified or recognized, the parties must begin bargaining within 10 days of a written request. If no agreement is reached after 90 days, either party may request Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service mediation. If mediation does not produce a deal within 30 more days, the dispute goes to a 3-person arbitration panel (one member each side, one neutral) whose majority decision binds both parties for 2 years, based on the employer's finances, operations, employees' cost of living and ability to sustain themselves, and comparable wages. Current wages and terms continue pending an agreement. A GAO report on average time-to-contract is due within one year.

sections.label: Section 4 — GAO Report Examining Average Workplace Time-to-Contract

items.main: Requires the Comptroller General to report to Congress within 1 year on the average number of days between certification/recognition under section 9(a) of the NLRA (29 U.S.C. 159(a)) after enactment and entry into an initial collective bargaining agreement.
items.detail: GAO study provision measuring time-to-contract.

gaps: The bill imposes binding arbitration on first contracts but does not address renewals or later contracts.
It lists factors the arbitration panel must weigh but does not provide a way to appeal the panel's decision.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Mrvan
featured_quotes.text: The men and women who pour our steel and power our grid built the middle class with a union card in their pocket. This bill makes sure the next generation of workers can earn one without waiting to be heard for months, years, or decades. I rise today to express my strong support for H.R. 5408, the Faster Labor Contracts Act. My good friend, the chairman of the Education and Workforce Committee, mentioned this administration and how much they like the working public, working men and women.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Allen
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, under the leadership of this House majority and the Trump administration, we are working to deliver  a 21st century economy that benefits the working class. We are putting workers first and giving them the freedom to champion their own future and achieve the American Dream. This legislation before us today, to put it simply, is a significant step backward. There is a reason this bill is opposed by hundreds of organizations and stakeholder groups, including H.R. professionals, franchise businesses, retailers, and more.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Miller
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I join the majority of my Republican colleagues in voicing strong opposition to H.R. 5408, the Faster Labor Contracts Act. This bill puts the selfish needs of the union bosses above the welfare of American workers. It would force employers to begin bargaining with new unions within 10 days of certification. It would force Federal mediation to intervene if no contract is signed. It would force the arbitrated contracts to last 2 years, and they cannot be appealed. Let me be clear.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Krishnamoorthi
featured_quotes.text: Across America, workers exercise one of the most fundamental rights protected under our labor laws--namely, the right to organize and bargain collectively. Yet, far too often, after workers vote to form a union, they are forced to wait months and even years before seeing the benefits of that decision. In fact, the average time to secure a first contract exceeds 450 days. During that time, workers can face uncertainty, delays, and frustration while negotiations drag on with no clear path to resolution. There are countless examples.

added: Mediation-then-binding-arbitration process and bargaining deadlines for first union contracts (National Labor Relations Act Section 8)
GAO report on average time-to-contract within one year

bills.title: Emergency Reporting Act
bills.official_title: To direct the Federal Communications Commission to issue reports after activation of the Disaster Information Reporting System and to make improvements to network outage reporting, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Matsui (D-CA) with Rep. Bilirakis (R-FL) and 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. A bipartisan reporting-and-transparency measure on disaster communications has a reasonable path through the Senate.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.summary: Requires the FCC to hold hearings and publish reports on communications outages after disasters, and to study how to improve network-outage and 9-1-1 reporting.
bills.brief: Requires FCC hearings and reports on disaster communications outages and a study of network-outage reporting.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Outage Reports
subs: Annual FCC hearings after 7-day-plus disaster activations
Reports on broadband, phone, and mobile outages
Includes 9-1-1 outage effects and resiliency recommendations

top_lines.headline: Outage Reporting Study
subs: FCC study on improving network outage notifications to 9-1-1 centers

items.main: Names the Act the “Emergency Reporting Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reports After Activation of Disaster Information Reporting System

items.main: Requires the FCC to hold hearings and publish reports on communications outages after disasters.
items.detail: After each event lasting at least 7 days for which the FCC's Disaster Information Reporting System was activated, the Commission must hold at least one annual public hearing and, within 120 days, publish a report on the number and duration of broadband, internet-phone, and mobile outages, the users and infrastructure affected, 9-1-1 outages that block caller location or emergency calls, and resiliency recommendations. Separately, within one year the FCC must investigate and report on improving network outage reporting — including the value and burden of visual information in 9-1-1 outage notifications and outages that go unreported under current thresholds. The section grants no new FCC authority over broadband providers beyond what it specifies.

gaps: The bill requires reporting on disaster outages but does not impose any new outage-prevention or resiliency requirements on providers.
It studies unreported 9-1-1 outages but does not itself change the reporting thresholds.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Matsui
featured_quotes.text: Emergencies can happen anywhere at any time, and in those moments every second counts. When a family calls 911, they should never be met with silence. During major disasters, we have seen communications fail, and too often we are left without clear answers about what went wrong or how to prevent it from happening again. That is why I am proud to lead the Emergency Reporting Act, a bipartisan bill, with Congressman Bilirakis that helps fix this.

added: FCC annual hearings and reports on disaster communications outages
FCC study on improving network outage and 9-1-1 reporting

bills.title: Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act
bills.official_title: To amend title 31, United States Code, to authorize pausing and segmenting payments, and for other purposes.
