bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Comer (R-KY) with Rep. Arrington (R-TX) and 2 cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity measures aimed at fraud tend to attract bipartisan support, though the bill has not yet received a Senate vote.
bills.summary: Lets federal agencies and the Treasury pause or split up payments that show signs of fraud, while requiring payees to be notified and given a chance to contest, with the payment due within 45 days.
bills.brief: Authorizes agencies and the Treasury to pause or segment federal payments flagged for fraud risk, with payee notice and time limits.

top_lines.headline: Pausing Risky Payments
subs: Agencies must pause or segment payments flagged for fraud risk
Treasury can return a payment voucher and order corrective action
Triggered by fraud-risk indicators or the Do Not Pay system

top_lines.headline: Payee Protections
subs: Payee notified and given a chance to contest
Payment due within 45 days of the determination
Routine, low-risk portions allowed to proceed

items.main: Names the Act the “Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Authority To Pause and Segment Payments

items.main: Authorizes agencies and the Treasury to pause, condition, or segment federal payments that present an elevated fraud risk.
items.detail: Adds Section 3337 to title 31. Before certifying a payment voucher, an agency must temporarily delay, condition, or segment a disbursement that an official determines presents an elevated risk of fraud or improper payment, or when ordered by the Treasury. The Treasury may return a certified voucher and issue a corrective-action order based on a fraud-risk indicator or a Do Not Pay system flag. Actions must be objective, narrowly applied, and time-limited; the payee must be notified and given a process to contest; and the payment must be issued within 45 days of the determination (or 7 days after the payee contests). Routine, historically consistent payment amounts may proceed while an anomalous portion is held. Law-enforcement exemptions and good-faith liability protection apply, and the Treasury must issue implementing regulations within 180 days.

gaps: The bill sets a 45-day limit to issue a paused payment but does not specify a consequence if an agency misses it.
It relies on 'fraud-risk indicators' and the Do Not Pay system but does not address erroneous flags that wrongly delay legitimate payments beyond the contest process.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: let me translate that 5 minutes of gibberish from my colleague. They don't care about fraud. When you do find fraud, like we found in Minnesota and California, they don't want to cut off the money. They want the money to keep going so the fraudsters can stay in business. That is why we have to support this bill.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Boebert
featured_quotes.text: I strongly support H.R. 8464, the Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act. This legislation is a commonsense, taxpayer-first bill that finally puts an end to the reckless pay-and-chase scam that has drained billions from hardworking American families. For too long, the Washington bureaucracy has operated like an open checkbook for fraudsters. They cut the checks first, ask the questions later while American taxpayers foot the bill for waste, abuse, and outright theft.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bell
featured_quotes.text: no one in this Chamber disputes that improper and fraudulent payments are a serious problem. The question before us is not whether to fight fraud; it is how we fight fraud. If this bill actually does that--and I will give you a hint: It does not. The Stopping Fraudulent Payments Act allows agency officials to block payments whenever they have sufficient reason to believe there is an elevated risk of fraud. This bill sets the standard so low that any administration can use it to cut off legitimate recipients before a single fact is even proven.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walkinshaw
featured_quotes.text: I will just give one agency, Social Security, an agency that has been under assault by this administration. It is estimated that 10,000 times a year, Social Security falsely declares somebody dead. Imagine that. You wake up one morning, and your own government says you are dead. It happens oftentimes because States send bad information to the Social Security Administration. Time after time after time, the IG has recommended that Social Security and this body make improvements in that process.

added: Authority for agencies and the Treasury to pause, condition, or segment fraud-risk federal payments, with payee notice and a 45-day limit (new Section 3337 of title 31)
modified: Relief of accountable officers (Section 3527 of title 31) extended to good-faith actions under the new pause authority

added: New pause trigger: agency may act on a State or local government official's notification for State-administered, federally-funded programs
Regulations must now specify the minimum seniority of the official who can order a corrective action
New agency dispute/appeal path: agencies may contest a returned voucher to the Fiscal Assistant Secretary, who must respond within five days
New Treasury report to Congress 18 months after enactment, then annually — number of orders, percentage of payments issued, total savings, and recommendations
Conforming amendments added covering payment disbursing officials (section 3325(a)(3)) and certifying officials (section 3528)
Effective date set to 1 year after enactment
modified: Pause authority broadened from agencies administering a "federally funded financial assistance or public benefit program" to the head of any agency
Treasury must issue its corrective-action order not later than 2 days after determining elevated fraud risk, tied to a Do Not Pay system output under section 3354
Payee notification must now be given within 2 days of the determination or notification (previously "prompt notice" with no deadline)
Payment-issuance deadline shortened from 45 days to 30 days after a corrective-action determination
Fraud-risk determinations now must be made "in accordance with the statutorily-defined eligibility requirements" of the program
False Claims Act reference rewritten to cite sections 3729 through 3733 of title 31
removed: Drops the Do Not Pay "flagged payee" as a standalone Treasury trigger and the separate reference to other Treasury payee-validation programs in subsection (b)

bills.title: Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To establish a program to Beautify the District of Columbia and establish the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. McGuire (R-VA) with 4 cosponsors. A federal program directing immigration enforcement and law-enforcement coordination in the District would need 60 votes in the Senate and is likely to draw strong Democratic opposition over federal control of D.C., making passage unlikely.
bills.summary: Creates a federal program to clean up the District of Columbia and a commission to coordinate federal law enforcement there, including immigration enforcement and support for the D.C. police.
bills.brief: Establishes a federal D.C. beautification program and a commission to coordinate federal law enforcement and immigration enforcement in the District.

top_lines.headline: D.C. Beautification Program
subs: Interior Department program to clean up D.C. public spaces
Includes graffiti removal and monument restoration
Sunsets January 2, 2029

top_lines.headline: Safe and Beautiful Commission
subs: Federal commission chaired by a White House official
Coordinates federal law enforcement and immigration enforcement in D.C.
Reviews D.C. sanctuary-city status and supports the D.C. police

items.main: Names the Act the “Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Program To Beautify District of Columbia

items.main: Directs the Interior Department to create a program to clean up and restore D.C. public spaces.
items.detail: Within 30 days, the Secretary of the Interior must develop a program — in consultation with the Attorney General, Transportation, the D.C. Mayor, the U.S. Attorney for D.C., and others — to coordinate cleanliness of federal and D.C. facilities, monuments, public spaces, and transit (including graffiti removal), restore damaged or defaced monuments, and encourage private-sector participation. An annual report is required, and the program sunsets January 2, 2029.

sections.label: Section 3 — District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission

items.main: Establishes a federal commission to coordinate law enforcement in the District.
items.detail: Creates a Commission with members from Interior, Transportation, Homeland Security, the FBI, U.S. Marshals, ATF, and U.S. Attorneys, chaired by a senior White House official. Its functions are to recommend and review actions on maximum enforcement of federal immigration law in D.C., monitor the District's sanctuary-city status, accredit the D.C. forensic crime lab, support recruitment and capabilities of the D.C. police, speed concealed-carry license processing, review pretrial-detention policies, address transit fare evasion, and expand federal and local law-enforcement presence in D.C. The Commission reports to Congress and sunsets January 2, 2029.

criticisms.why: I strongly oppose this bill. I include in the Record letters opposing this bill from the District of Columbia Mayor and every member of the D.C. Council. September 10, 2025.

gaps: The bill directs maximum federal immigration enforcement in D.C. but does not provide funding for the additional law-enforcement activity.
It establishes a commission to recommend actions but the commission's recommendations are not binding on the District or federal agencies.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Norton
featured_quotes.text: I strongly oppose this bill. I include in the Record letters opposing this bill from the District of Columbia Mayor and every member of the D.C. Council. September 10, 2025.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Higgins
featured_quotes.text: I rise to support H.R. 5103. As a proud cosponsor of H.R. 5103, I stand with Representative McGuire and my Republican colleagues to deliver on President Trump's vision for our Nation's capital. This bill codifies Executive Order 14252 and turns words into law to make Washington, D.C., safe, clean, and beautiful once again.

added: Interior Department program to beautify D.C. (sunsets January 2, 2029)
District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Commission to coordinate federal law enforcement and immigration enforcement in D.C. (sunsets January 2, 2029)
Adds the Executive Office of the Mayor of the District of Columbia as a Commission member entity
Commission functions list reworded to be open-ended — "with respect to, but not limited to" the listed items
modified: Program purpose changed from establishing a plan to "establish and implement" a plan; monument restoration now covers "District of Columbia and Federal" monuments and is qualified "to the extent practicable"
Short title becomes "Make the District of Columbia Safe and Beautiful Act of 2025"
removed: Drops the United States Park Police from the list of authorities the Commission may request operational assistance from

bills.title: District of Columbia Cash Bail Reform Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To require mandatory pretrial and post conviction detention for crimes of violence and dangerous crimes and require mandatory cash bail for certain offenses that pose a threat to public safety or order in the District of Columbia, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Stefanik (R-NY) with 3 cosponsors; passed the Republican-majority House. Federal changes to the District of Columbia's bail and detention laws would need 60 votes in the Senate and are likely to draw strong Democratic opposition over federal intervention in D.C., making passage unlikely.
bills.summary: Requires judges in the District of Columbia to detain people charged with violent or dangerous crimes before trial, and to require cash bail for certain public-safety offenses.
bills.brief: Mandates pretrial detention for violent and dangerous crimes and cash bail for certain offenses in the District of Columbia.

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Detention
subs: Judges must detain those charged with violent or dangerous crimes before trial
Same mandatory detention applies after conviction
Expands the 'dangerous crime' and 'crime of violence' definitions

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Cash Bail
subs: Secured cash bail required for 'public safety or order' crimes
Covers offenses such as rioting, stalking, and fleeing police

items.main: Names the Act the “District of Columbia Cash Bail Reform Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Mandatory Pretrial and Post Conviction Detention for Crime of Violence or Dangerous Crime

items.main: Requires D.C. judges to detain people charged with a crime of violence or dangerous crime before trial, and after conviction.
items.detail: Amends the D.C. Official Code so a judicial officer must order pretrial detention for anyone charged with a crime of violence or dangerous crime, and applies mandatory detention after conviction for the same. The definitions of 'dangerous crime' and 'crime of violence' are expanded to include first-degree burglary and robbery, attempts, and those committed with a dangerous weapon.

sections.label: Section 3 — Requiring Cash Bail for Release of Individuals Charged With Public Safety or Order Offenses

items.main: Requires a secured cash bail bond for release of people charged with 'public safety or order' crimes.
items.detail: Adds a category of 'public safety or order crime' — including failure to appear, obstruction of justice, fleeing law enforcement, rioting, inciting a riot, destruction of property, stalking, and certain burglary or robbery — for which a person may be released only on a secured appearance bond (cash or surety). It defines 'secured appearance bond' and adds surety-arrest provisions. The changes apply to offenses charged 30 days after enactment.

items.main: Applies the Act and its amendments to individuals charged with an offense in D.C. on or after 30 days after enactment.
items.detail: Effective-date/applicability provision — sets when the changes take effect; no independent substantive effect.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, I strongly oppose this bill which amends the District of Columbia's pretrial release and detention law. Last year, violent crime in D.C. was down 35 percent, reaching an over-30-year low. This year, violent crime in D.C. is down 28 percent compared to the same period last year.

gaps: The bill mandates detention and cash bail but does not provide funding for additional D.C. jail capacity.
It requires secured bonds for certain offenses but does not address defendants who cannot afford to post bail.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Norton
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I strongly oppose this bill which amends the District of Columbia's pretrial release and detention law. Last year, violent crime in D.C. was down 35 percent, reaching an over-30-year low. This year, violent crime in D.C. is down 28 percent compared to the same period last year.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walkinshaw
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, 2 months ago, I was a local government official not far from here, in Fairfax County. In the 6 years I spent in that role, I learned that the people best positioned to make decisions about the local policies in their local communities are local leaders after listening to that local community. My colleagues across the aisle who are advocating for these bills, with due respect, know very little about the District of Columbia, know very little outside of perhaps their walk from their apartment in Navy Yard to this Capitol complex.

added: Mandatory cash bail (secured appearance bond) for D.C. 'public safety or order' crimes
modified: D.C. Official Code requires pretrial and post-conviction detention for crimes of violence and dangerous crimes; the definitions of those crimes are expanded
"Public safety or order crime" definition narrows robbery the same way as burglary — excluding first-degree or dangerous-weapon robbery, instead of treating all robbery as a qualifying offense

bills.title: MAPWaters Act of 2025
bills.official_title: An Act to provide for the standardization, consolidation, and publication of data relating to public outdoor recreational use of Federal waterways among Federal land and water management agencies, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Became Public Law 119-62 on December 26, 2025. Passed the House on January 21, 2025 and the Senate on December 16, 2025.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

bills.summary: Requires federal land and water agencies to create and publish standardized digital maps showing where the public can boat, fish, and access federal waterways, and what restrictions apply.
bills.brief: Requires federal agencies to standardize and publish digital maps of public access and restrictions on federal waterways.

top_lines.headline: Digital Waterway Maps
subs: Agencies must publish online maps of waterway access and restrictions
Covers boating, fishing, and navigation rules
Five-year deadline to digitize and publish

top_lines.headline: Data Standards and Reports
subs: Interagency data standards within 30 months
Annual progress reports through 2034

items.main: Names the Act the “Modernizing Access to our Public Waters Act of 2025” (the “MAPWaters Act of 2025”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines key terms used throughout the Act: Federal fishing restriction, Federal land or water management agency, Federal waterway, Federal waterway restriction, Secretaries, and State.
items.detail: Definitions apply throughout. "Secretaries" means the Secretary of Agriculture (acting through the Chief of the Forest Service) and the Secretary of the Interior; "Federal land or water management agency" covers the Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, and Forest Service.

items.main: Requires federal agencies to adopt common data standards for waterway recreation data within 30 months.
items.detail: The Secretaries of Agriculture (Forest Service) and the Interior, coordinating with the Federal Geographic Data Committee, must jointly develop interagency standards so federal databases on public recreational access to federal waterways and federal fishing restrictions are compatible and interoperable.

items.main: Requires agencies to digitize and publish online maps of waterway restrictions, access, and fishing rules within five years.
items.detail: Within five years, the Bureau of Reclamation, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service, and Forest Service must publish geographic data on waterway open/closed status, seasonal closures, motorized and anchoring restrictions, allowed watercraft, boat ramps and fishing access sites, and federal fishing restrictions (closures, no-take zones, and gear, bait, and catch-and-release rules). Data must be updated at least twice a year (in real time for fishing restrictions), with a public comment process. The Act does not change the definition of navigable waters or federal and state fishing jurisdiction.

items.main: Lets the Secretaries partner with non-Federal, private, nonprofit, and Tribal entities, and the U.S. Geological Survey, to carry out the Act.
items.detail: Authorizes coordination with State and Tribal natural resource agencies, technology and geospatial data companies, and data-science experts, plus third-party agreements. Data must be developed under applicable Federal, State, and Tribal laws with a notice to that effect, and existing efforts (the Modernizing Access to Our Public Land Act and section 103 of division DD of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023) should be reused where practicable.

items.main: Requires the Secretaries to report progress to named House and Senate committees within 1 year and annually through March 30, 2034.
items.detail: Reports go to the House Committees on Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Agriculture, and the Senate Committees on Energy and Natural Resources and on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry.

items.main: States the Act does not change the definition of "navigable waters," State or Federal authority over navigable waters or fisheries, or the current accessibility of waters for hunting, fishing, or recreation.
items.detail: Rule-of-construction/savings provision — preserves existing law; no independent substantive effect.

gaps: The bill requires publishing access and restriction data but does not change any actual access rules or restrictions.
It sets a five-year publication deadline but does not provide dedicated funding for the mapping work.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moore
featured_quotes.text: This legislation builds upon the success of my MAPLand Act, enacted in 2022, and MAP Army Corps language included in last year's Water Resources Development Act to ensure Americans can quickly see the public resources around them and spend more time recreating on the land and water they love.

added: Federal agencies must standardize and publish digital maps of public access and restrictions on federal waterways (new 16 U.S.C. 6871 et seq.)

bills.title: Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Act to promote the protection of the resources of the Northwest Straits, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Larsen (D-WA) with 6 cosponsors; passed the House and was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar. A modest, regionally focused conservation reauthorization tends to clear the Senate when floor time allows.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass, as Amended

bills.summary: Renews and updates a federal program that supports local efforts to protect and restore the marine waters of the Northwest Straits in Washington's Puget Sound, funded at $10M a year through 2031.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative through fiscal year 2031 at $10M per year.

top_lines.headline: Northwest Straits Program
subs: Reauthorizes the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative
$10M per year authorized for fiscal years 2026-2031
Supports local marine protection in Puget Sound

top_lines.headline: Commission Structure
subs: 14-member advisory commission with county, tribal, and state seats
Commission advises and reports; cannot issue regulations

items.main: Names the Act the “Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reauthorization of Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative Act

items.main: Reauthorizes and rewrites the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative (title IV of Public Law 105-384).
items.detail: Authorizes $10M per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031 (and such sums as necessary thereafter) to the Under Secretary of Commerce for Oceans and Atmosphere. It rewrites the program's findings, definitions, and the 14-member Advisory Commission (county marine resources committee appointees, two tribal representatives, and Washington gubernatorial appointees), whose goal is to protect and restore the marine waters, habitats, and species of the Northwest Straits region of Puget Sound. The Commission advises, collects data, and reports annually against benchmarks but has no authority to issue regulations.

gaps: The bill authorizes $10M a year but the actual funding depends on later appropriations.
It reauthorizes an advisory commission that cannot itself implement or enforce any protections.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: I support this bill to reauthorize the Northwest Straits Advisory Commission. I commend my colleague, the gentleman from the State of Washington (Mr. Larsen), not only for his work on this bill but for his leadership to pass the successful highway transportation reauthorization bill recently. Again, I support the legislation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Larsen
featured_quotes.text: The Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative started as a bipartisan, homegrown idea. Thanks to the foresight and hard work of Democratic Senator Patty Murray and my predecessor here in the U.S. House of Representatives, former Representative Jack Metcalf, and local stakeholders, Congress created the Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Commission in 1998. The commission works with seven county-based marine resources committees, or MRCs, in northwest Puget Sound.

modified: Northwest Straits Marine Conservation Initiative (title IV of Public Law 105-384) reauthorized at $10M per year for fiscal years 2026-2031, with a rewritten commission structure and duties

added: New sunset: authority to carry out the title terminates 7 years after enactment
removed: Drops the entire funding section — including the authorization of $10,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2031 and "such sums as may be necessary" for FY2032 and after
Removes the assistance provisions, including funding the Commission through a contract with the Director of the Padilla Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve subject to the Governor's objection
Removes the section 403 "Findings" (declines in marine health, climate-change threats, NOAA partnership history)
Removes the Commission's authority to solicit and accept gifts, devises, and bequests

bills.title: ZOMBIE Act
bills.official_title: To reform the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 to ensure executive agencies focus on fraud prevention, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Palmer (R-AL) with no cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity and fraud-prevention reforms are often bipartisan, but the lack of cosponsors and the need for 60 votes leave its Senate path uncertain.
bills.summary: Refocuses federal improper-payment law on payments that actually cause financial loss to the government — rather than all paperwork errors — and adds fraud-risk management requirements for agencies.
bills.brief: Reforms the Payment Integrity Information Act to focus agencies on improper payments that cause real financial loss and on fraud prevention.

top_lines.headline: Focus on Financial Loss
subs: Targets improper payments that cause actual financial loss
Excludes payments that were correct but missed paperwork steps
Defines 'financial loss to the Government'

top_lines.headline: Fraud Risk Management
subs: Treasury risk-assessment guidance within 1 year
Agencies adopt the GAO fraud-risk framework
Shifts some reviews from annual to every 3 years

items.main: Names the Act the “Zeroing Out Monetary Benefits Improperly Expended Act” (the “ZOMBIE Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reforms to Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019

items.main: Refocuses federal improper-payment requirements on payments that result in financial loss to the government and strengthens fraud-risk management.
items.detail: Amends the Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (31 U.S.C. 3351-3352). It adds a definition of 'financial loss to the Government' — payments above the legally correct amount that cause a loss, excluding correct-amount payments that missed certain administrative procedures — and reorients agency estimates, reports, and reduction plans around such payments. It requires the Treasury to develop risk-assessment guidance within one year; agencies to run risk assessments and adopt fraud-risk-management practices (including the GAO 'Framework for Managing Fraud Risks in Federal Programs'); designates agency liaisons who meet with OMB, the Treasury, Inspectors General, and the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee; and changes several reviews and reports from annual to at least once every three years.

gaps: The bill narrows the focus to payments causing financial loss but does not change the penalties for improper payments.
It shifts several reviews from annual to once every three years, which could reduce how often improper payments are reassessed.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Palmer
featured_quotes.text: every year, hardworking Americans dutifully pay their taxes to support Federal public programs and other priorities. Unfortunately, the Federal Government has too often squandered their money through mismanagement. For example, just last year, the Federal Government lost an estimated $186 billion in improper payments. Six years ago, the COVID-19 pandemic produced what is now often referred to as the greatest theft of taxpayer dollars in history. This is not new.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Gill
featured_quotes.text: I encourage my colleagues to support H.R. 8467, the Zeroing Out Monetary Benefits Improperly Expended Act, which reforms the Payment Integrity Information Act to refocus Federal agencies on proactively identifying and preventing improper payments before they happen, rather than wasting resources on backward-looking compliance activities. Mr. Speaker, we need reforms like this bill that force agencies to focus on preventing improper payments in the first place, and this smart legislation does just that.

added: Definition of 'financial loss to the Government' and a Treasury risk-assessment guidance requirement within one year
modified: Payment Integrity Information Act of 2019 (31 U.S.C. 3351-3352) refocused on improper payments that cause financial loss, with added fraud-risk-management requirements and some reviews shifted from annual to triennial

added: New Section 3 added: reforms to the annual Inspector General compliance report (section 3353) — OMB and CIGIE must revise existing guidance rather than develop new guidance, keyed to ZOMBIE Act enactment, with "financial loss to the Government" inserted throughout

New Federal-State coordination meeting: OMB Director and Treasury Secretary must convene State program- and payment-integrity officials at least once each fiscal year to review fraud-prevention performance and share best practices

Rewrites section 3352(d)(6) to require a description of how planned or completed agency actions matched the level of improper payments resulting in financial loss, with a category breakdown and specific completion timelines
modified: Section 3352(g)(2)(B) prepayment terminology now becomes "pre-award, pre-payment, and post-payment" (the introduced version had only "pre-award and pre-payment," dropping post-payment)
The statistically-valid-estimate review recommendation relocated into the high-priority report clause (subsection (b)(2)(E)(i)) instead of being added as a new subsection (b)(1)(A)
Table-of-sections conforming amendments added for the section 3352 heading changes

bills.title: Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act
bills.official_title: To modify the appointment and removal process for certain legislative branch officers, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Griffith (R-VA) with 4 cosponsors; passed the House. The bill reassigns appointment and removal power over the Librarian of Congress, the GPO Director, and the Register of Copyrights, a structural change that faces a 60-vote threshold and likely scrutiny over shifting appointment authority between the branches.
bills.summary: Shifts how Congress's own agency heads are chosen: the Librarian of Congress and the Government Publishing Office Director would be appointed and removed by congressional leaders rather than the President, and the Register of Copyrights would become a Presidential appointee independent of the Library of Congress.
bills.brief: Changes the appointment and removal of the Librarian of Congress, the GPO Director, and the Register of Copyrights.

top_lines.headline: Librarian of Congress Appointed by Congress
subs: Removes the President from appointing the Librarian of Congress
A congressional commission picks from 3 names recommended by oversight committee leaders
Removable at any time by a majority of House and Senate leadership

top_lines.headline: GPO Director Under the Same Model
subs: GPO Director appointed by the congressional commission, not the President
Drops Senate advice-and-consent for the Director
Adds Deputy Director appointment and acting-officer succession rules

top_lines.headline: Copyright Office Split From the Library
subs: Register of Copyrights becomes a Presidential appointee with Senate consent
10-year term, renewable for 5-year terms; must have a copyright-law background
Ratifies Copyright Office actions taken from May 8, 2025 through enactment

items.main: Names the Act the “Legislative Branch Agencies Clarification Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Replaces Presidential appointment of the Librarian of Congress with appointment by a congressional commission.
items.detail: Amends the Librarian of Congress Succession Modernization Act of 2015. A vacancy is filled by 'oversight committee leadership' (the chair and ranking member of the House Committee on House Administration and the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration) jointly recommending 3 individuals, from whom the 'House and Senate leadership' (the Speaker, the Senate majority leader, and the House and Senate minority leaders) selects the Librarian by majority vote, without regard to political affiliation. The Librarian may be removed at any time by a majority vote of the House and Senate leadership, and is no longer treated as a political appointee for purposes of section 747 of the Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act, 2024.

items.main: Creates a Deputy Librarian of Congress and an acting-Librarian succession line.
items.detail: The Librarian must appoint a Deputy Librarian within 120 days of being appointed or of a vacancy arising. If the Librarian fails to do so, the oversight committee leadership recommends an individual whom the House and Senate leadership appoint by majority vote. The Deputy Librarian acts as Librarian during an absence, disability, or vacancy; if both positions are empty, the leadership designates an acting Librarian.

sections.label: Section 4 — Director of the Government Publishing Office

items.main: Applies the same commission-appointment and leadership-removal model to the GPO Director.
items.detail: Amends chapter 3 of title 44, U.S. Code. The Director of the Government Publishing Office is appointed by the congressional commission from 3 individuals recommended by the oversight committee leadership, striking the prior 'by and with the advice and consent of the Senate' language, and may be removed at any time by a majority vote of the House and Senate leadership. The Director is likewise no longer treated as a political appointee for the same appropriations-law purpose.

sections.label: Section 5 — Deputy Director of the Government Publishing Office

items.main: Establishes a Deputy Director of the GPO with acting-Director succession rules.
items.detail: Rewrites sections 302 and 304 of title 44 so the Director appoints a Deputy Director (within 120 days of appointment or a vacancy), with a leadership-appointment fallback if the Director does not act, and the Deputy Director serves as acting Director during an absence, disability, or vacancy.

items.main: Removes the Library of Congress supervisory authority over the Copyright Office and makes the Register of Copyrights a Presidential appointee.
items.detail: Amends title 17, U.S. Code, replacing the Librarian of Congress with the Register of Copyrights across many provisions. The Register would be appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate after the chairs and ranking members of the House and Senate Judiciary Committees jointly recommend 3 individuals; the Register must be a U.S. citizen with a background in copyright law, serves a 10-year term, and may be reappointed for additional 5-year terms. It establishes an Inspector General for the Copyright Office and ratifies actions taken by the Copyright Office, the Register, the Copyright Royalty Judges, and the Copyright Claims Board between May 8, 2025 and the date of enactment.

sections.label: Section 7 — Government Publishing Office Personnel Reforms

items.main: Brings the GPO under the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995.
items.detail: Adds the Government Publishing Office to the entities covered by section 101(a) of the Congressional Accountability Act of 1995 and makes conforming amendments to title 5 that remove the GPO from several executive-branch personnel provisions.

sections.label: Section 8 — Human Capital Management System for the GPO

items.main: Directs the GPO Director to establish a merit-based human capital management system.
items.detail: Adds a new section 306A to title 44 requiring the Director to establish and maintain a human capital system that incorporates the merit-system principles of section 2301(b) of title 5, prohibits the prohibited personnel practices and political activity barred under title 5, appoints and promotes employees only on merit and fitness, and gives a hiring preference consistent with the executive-branch veterans' preference. Regulations require public notice and comment and the approval of the Joint Committee on Printing.

items.main: Updates which entities the GPO may provide printing and publishing services to.
items.detail: Rewrites section 501 of title 44 so the Government Publishing Office may perform printing, binding, blank-book work, and publishing services for Congress, the Executive Office of the President, the Judiciary, and every executive department, independent office, and establishment of the Government, and repeals a 1993 conforming provision.

items.main: Sets when the appointment and removal changes apply.
items.detail: The new appointment procedures apply to appointments made on or after enactment, while the new removal provisions apply to individuals serving before, on, or after enactment — meaning current officeholders become removable under the new leadership-vote standard.

underreported: Actions taken by the Copyright Office, the Register, the Copyright Royalty Judges, and the Copyright Claims Board between May 8, 2025 and enactment would be ratified and given full force and effect.
gaps: The bill does not specify what happens if the oversight committee leaders cannot agree on the 3 individuals to recommend for a vacancy.
Removal of the Librarian and the GPO Director 'at any time' by a leadership majority sets no for-cause standard or fixed term of office.

added: A congressional commission and House/Senate leadership vote to appoint and remove the Librarian of Congress and the GPO Director; an Inspector General for the Copyright Office; a merit-based human capital system for the GPO
modified: Register of Copyrights becomes a Presidential appointee (with Senate consent) independent of the Librarian of Congress, with a 10-year renewable term; Librarian and GPO Director appointments drop Presidential nomination and Senate advice-and-consent
removed: Library of Congress supervisory authority over the Copyright Office; Senate advice-and-consent for the Librarian of Congress and the GPO Director

added: New Sec. 11 Severability clause added — unconstitutional provisions severed without affecting the rest of the Act

Sec. 6(g) Transition Provisions added — through September 30, 2029, Register and Librarian may transfer appropriations to effectuate the Copyright Office/Library separation, plus personnel-law transition rules

Copyright Office Inspector General now established as a separate Office of Inspector General with detailed appointment, removal (30-day written notice), pay (above GS-15, no bonuses), law-enforcement (arrest/firearm) authority, peer review, and budget-independence provisions

Section 702 amendment now inserts language requiring the Register to consult the Librarian before regulations affecting deposits under sections 407 and 704 or the Library's access to deposited material
modified: Register of Copyrights nominee recommendation now requires joint recommendation from chair/ranking member of four committees (House Administration, House Judiciary, Senate Rules and Administration, Senate Judiciary) instead of just the two Judiciary Committees
Sec. 7 GPO personnel reforms restructured — Congressional Accountability Act application and conforming title 5 amendments reorganized into separate lettered subsections
removed: Original Sec. 6(c) two-paragraph Inspector General approach (amending title 5 sec. 415 and adding a 'no oversight authority' clause to sec. 1307) replaced by the new standalone IG office

bills.title: Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act
bills.official_title: To establish governmentwide requirements for pre-payment fraud prevention actions, to provide the U.S. Treasury appropriate data resources, to facilitate participation in governmentwide anti-fraud data sharing, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Comer (R-KY) with 3 cosponsors; passed the House. Payment-integrity measures often draw bipartisan support, but the expanded Treasury access to IRS and Social Security data may draw privacy scrutiny, and Senate passage requires 60 votes.
bills.summary: Builds new fraud checks into the federal payment process: before the Treasury pays out money, agencies would have to verify the payee, the amount, and the bank account, and the Treasury's 'Do Not Pay' screening system would gain statutory footing and broad access to tax, Social Security, and new-hire data.
bills.brief: Adds governmentwide pre-payment fraud checks and expands the Treasury's Do Not Pay system and its data access.

top_lines.headline: Checks Before the Government Pays
subs: Agencies must clear pre-certification checks before certifying a payment voucher
Verify payee identity, amount, fund availability, and that the payee is not deceased
Confirm the bank account on the voucher belongs to the payee

top_lines.headline: Do Not Pay System in Statute
subs: Gives the Treasury-run Do Not Pay system explicit statutory authority
Adds New Hires, IRS, and Social Security data to the screening pool
Up to a $5,000 fine and 5 years in prison for unlawful disclosure

top_lines.headline: First-Time Recipient Reporting & Data Access
subs: First-time recipients of awards of $50,000 or more file a one-time use-of-funds report
Treasury gains privacy-limited access to select tax return information
Most provisions take effect 180 days after enactment

items.main: Names the Act the “Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention Requirements for Agencies

items.main: Bars agencies from certifying a payment voucher until a set of pre-certification checks is met.
items.detail: Adds a new section 3325a to title 31, U.S. Code. An agency head may not certify a voucher under section 3325 until pre-certification requirements are met, and the Treasury must issue implementing regulations within 180 days. The checks include confirming funds are available, the amount and payee name are correct, a valid Social Security, taxpayer, employer, or individual taxpayer identification number is provided, the appropriation is available with the correct Treasury Account Symbol, the payee is not deceased, and the account belongs to the payee. Disbursing officials must verify bank-account accuracy to the extent practicable. It also renames the Do Not Pay 'Initiative' as a 'System' and defines a 'fraud-risk indicator.'

sections.label: Section 3 — Treasury Do Not Pay System

items.main: Puts the Do Not Pay system in statute and expands the data the Treasury can use to screen payments.
items.detail: Amends section 3354 of title 31 so each executive agency screens all recipients of federal awards or payments against Do Not Pay data assets before an award or payment. Notwithstanding the Internal Revenue Code, the Social Security Act, and the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act, the Treasury gains access to the National Directory of New Hires, certain IRS information under section 6103(i)(9)(A), and Social Security information under a new section 235. The Secretary may designate additional data assets after at least 30 days of public notice; such data comparisons are not treated as a Privacy Act 'matching program'; use is limited to improper-payment and law-enforcement purposes; and unlawful disclosure carries a fine of not more than $5,000, imprisonment of not more than 5 years, or both. State, local, judicial, and legislative entities get access, and the Treasury must file an annual report to Congress.

sections.label: Section 4 — Single Report on First-Time Use of Funds

items.main: Requires first-time recipients of larger federal awards to file a one-time report on how they used the money.
items.detail: Adds section 6107 to title 31. A 'covered recipient' — an entity receiving a 'covered award' (a federal award of not less than $50,000 in fiscal year 2027 constant dollars) from a program for the first time — must submit a one-time use-of-funds report within 180 days. OMB must issue governmentwide content and format rules within 1 year, updated at least every 5 years. Noncompliance triggers written notice and a halt to further disbursements until the report is filed, and reports are kept on file for at least 5 years.

sections.label: Section 5 — Treasury Data Access for Program Integrity

items.main: Grants the Treasury access to New Hires, IRS, and Social Security data for payment screening.
items.detail: Amends section 453(j) of the Social Security Act to give the Treasury access to the National Directory of New Hires for preventing improper payments, including for the Do Not Pay system. It amends section 6103(i) of the Internal Revenue Code to allow disclosure of limited return information — taxpayer identity, filing status, adjusted gross income, Schedule C net profit or loss, bank and routing information, the fact of no return filed, the taxable year, and reported identity theft — for the Do Not Pay system, covering an applicable period of at least 3 taxable years. A new section 235 of the Social Security Act sets up name and Social Security number confirmation, with the Treasury paying the Social Security Administration's full costs.

items.main: Sets the effective date 180 days after enactment.
items.detail: The Act and its amendments take effect on the date that is 180 days after the date of enactment.

underreported: The Treasury would gain access to IRS return information and Social Security records for payment screening, with redisclosure allowed to its agents, contractors, and entities connected to the Do Not Pay system.
gaps: Agencies may request exemptions from some or all payment-verification requirements, and the bill leaves the scope of those exemptions to Treasury guidance.
The bill treats Do Not Pay data comparisons as outside the Privacy Act's 'matching program' protections while still requiring some privacy notices.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Subramanyam
featured_quotes.text: I also rise in support of H.R. 8463, the Pre-Payment Fraud Prevention and Treasury Data Access Act. This bill will help prevent improper payments by requiring that agencies verify with the U.S. Treasury that payments are going to the right place before they are made. Agencies would be required to use the Treasury's Do Not Pay system to confirm that recipients, one, have a valid Social Security number; two, are not deceased; and, three, have a valid bank account. The bill would also impose heavy fines for any misuse of the Do Not Pay system.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: Every year, the Federal Government loses hundreds of billions of dollars to fraud and improper payments. The Government Accountability Office estimates that the Federal Government has lost over $2.8 trillion since 2003 to payments that should never have been made or were made incorrectly. Annual improper payments ballooned to nearly $236 billion in fiscal year 2023, more than six times the amount in 2003.

added: A new pre-payment certification step (31 U.S.C. 3325a) with identity, amount, and bank-account checks; a one-time first-use-of-funds report for first-time recipients of awards of $50,000 or more; statutory Treasury access to New Hires, IRS, and Social Security data
modified: The Do Not Pay 'Initiative' becomes a statutory Do Not Pay 'System' run by the Treasury's Fiscal Service, with expanded data assets, a use limitation, and a disclosure penalty

added: New voluntary expedited computer-matching process — agencies adopting a standard OMB/Treasury template are deemed to satisfy Privacy Act 552a(o) without Data Integrity Board review; agreements capped at under 5 years
New System of Records Notice requirement — Treasury must publish a SORN identifying each data asset and its routine uses before any data asset may be disclosed from the Do Not Pay system
New 'data matching is not a matching program' safe harbor conditions added — binary response, results not retained over 30 days, max 20 record requests at a time
New limitation-on-use safeguards — match queries return only confirm/deny plus confidence and sources; no adverse action on the data alone; independent verification required before adverse action
New Confidentiality Maintenance paragraph requiring Treasury to preserve each data asset's source-law confidentiality level
New annual Evaluation by the agency Evaluation Officer (under section 313 of title 5) estimating fraud/improper-payment reductions and dollar savings
modified: Penalty for unlawful disclosure raised from a fine of not more than $5,000 to not more than $250,000 (imprisonment stays not more than 5 years)
Do Not Pay reporting changed from an annual report to quarterly reports to the appropriate committees
Public comment period before designating sensitive data assets shortened from not less than 30 days to not less than 15 days
Report retention period in section 3354(d) extended — '3 years' struck and replaced with '5 years' in two places
Exemption process now requires the agency to provide a plan and reasonable timeframe to remediate the need for the exemption
Section 3354 data-asset access reframed from a 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' override to access 'consistent with the routine use authority under section 552a of title 5'
State/local government provision changed from a duty to 'establish and maintain' procedures to access granted 'if procedures are established'
removed: Entire Sec. 5 'U.S. Treasury Data Access for Purposes of Program Integrity' removed — dropping new access to the National Directory of New Hires, IRS section 6103(i)(9) return-information disclosure, and new SSA section 235 verification
Section 3354 data assets G (National Directory of New Hires), H (IRS 6103(i)(9) info), and I (SSA section 235 info) that the introduced version added were removed

bills.title: Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act
bills.official_title: To establish fraud prevention and program integrity functions and data sharing authorities within the Department of Treasury and a permanent governmentwide Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Sessions (R-TX) with 1 cosponsor; passed the House. Anti-fraud oversight tends to attract bipartisan interest, but creating a new Senate-confirmed Inspector General and Treasury data role is a larger lift, and the bill needs 60 votes in the Senate with key provisions delayed to 2028.
bills.summary: Stands up a new permanent, Senate-confirmed Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery inside the Treasury, gives the Treasury's Fiscal Service a governmentwide fraud-data analysis role, and folds in the pandemic-era oversight committee's assets.
bills.brief: Creates a permanent governmentwide fraud Inspector General and fraud-data functions inside the Treasury.

top_lines.headline: New Governmentwide Fraud Inspector General
subs: Creates a permanent IG for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery in the Treasury
Presidential appointment with Senate confirmation; oversight of "covered funds"
$10M authorized annually beginning in fiscal year 2035

top_lines.headline: Treasury Fiscal Service Fraud Role
subs: Bureau of the Fiscal Service runs the Do Not Pay system and a governmentwide data-analysis program
Makes the DATA Act analysis center mandatory ('may' becomes 'shall')
Functions explicitly exclude any investigative or law-enforcement role

top_lines.headline: Pandemic Oversight Wound Down Into the New Office
subs: Ends the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee on December 31, 2028 (moved up from 2034)
Transfers PRAC's assets, data, and staff to the new office
Treasury must flag fraud risks in any relief bill over $100B or new program over $100M

items.main: Names the Act the “Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Fraud Prevention and Financial Integrity Functions in Treasury

items.main: Rewrites the Fiscal Service's statutory functions around fraud prevention, data analysis, and improper-payment prevention.
items.detail: Rewrites section 306 of title 31, U.S. Code. The Bureau of the Fiscal Service maintains financial-integrity, spending-transparency, and improper-payment-prevention functions — explicitly excluding any investigative or law-enforcement function. It administers the Do Not Pay system and establishes a governmentwide data-analysis program (using the DATA Act's authority) that shares data and analysis with federal agencies, states, and nongovernmental entities, requires agencies to share known or suspected fraud data and to screen awardees and payees against a centralized fraud database, and provides the new Inspector General access to data. The Treasury must report to Congress within 2 years and annually thereafter, and the bill makes the DATA Act data-analysis center mandatory by changing 'may' to 'shall.'

sections.label: Section 3 — Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery

items.main: Establishes a permanent, Senate-confirmed Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery within the Treasury.
items.detail: Adds section 317 to title 31. The Inspector General is appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, without regard to political affiliation, and oversees 'covered funds' through audits and investigations, support to agency Inspectors General, an independent data-analytics platform (incorporating the platform built by the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee), coordination with the Department of Justice, an advisory committee of Inspectors General, and reporting suspected criminal violations to the Attorney General. The office may hire staff, employ annuitants, and enter contracts. The bill authorizes $10M annually beginning in fiscal year 2035, transfers the PRAC's assets and obligations to the office, and takes effect on December 31, 2028.

sections.label: Section 4 — Data Sharing for Fraud Prevention

items.main: Gives the Treasury authority to negotiate data-sharing agreements and to flag fraud risks in large spending measures.
items.detail: Amends section 321(a) of title 31 to let the Treasury enter memoranda of understanding with federal agencies, Inspectors General, law enforcement, and private entities to secure data access for fraud and improper-payment prevention. For any supplemental or emergency relief measure totaling more than $100B, or any new program with more than $100M in anticipated additional annual spending, the Treasury must give Congress's leadership and the relevant committees legislative recommendations so that existing fraud-prevention functions are used or expanded rather than duplicated and adequate resources are provided. OMB must issue implementing guidance within 270 days.

sections.label: Section 5 — Termination and Transfer of PRAC Assets

items.main: Winds the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee down into the new office.
items.detail: Amends the CARES Act to move the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee's termination date up from September 30, 2034 to December 31, 2028. On that date, the committee's assets and obligations — including contracts, data, records, unobligated balances, and identified personnel — transfer to the new Office of the Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery, and CARES Act section 15010 is repealed.

underreported: The new office would inherit the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee's data-analytics platform, assets, and personnel rather than starting from scratch.

criticisms.why: you will not hear anything more rich in this body today than listening to a Democrat who did absolutely nothing about fraud for the last 4 years talk about why we should oppose a very good measure to prevent and oppose fraud. Madam Speaker, I yield 7 minutes to the gentleman from Texas (Mr. Sessions), the sponsor of this good legislation.

Mr. Comer has begun telling the story about H.R. 8312, Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act, which we today will discuss, but I think it is important that we probably tell a story because this has two tales, but one truth to it. The bottom line is that our friends, if they oppose this today, it is because they are embarrassed.

gaps: The new Inspector General’s funding is not authorized until fiscal year 2035, though the office and its duties take effect December 31, 2028.
'Covered funds' is defined by a fixed list of pandemic-era and other laws plus federal awards of $50,000 or more, with expansion left to future legislation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: you will not hear anything more rich in this body today than listening to a Democrat who did absolutely nothing about fraud for the last 4 years talk about why we should oppose a very good measure to prevent and oppose fraud.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Sessions
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Comer has begun telling the story about H.R. 8312, Fraud Prevention and Accountability Act, which we today will discuss, but I think it is important that we probably tell a story because this has two tales, but one truth to it. The bottom line is that our friends, if they oppose this today, it is because they are embarrassed.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Boebert
featured_quotes.text: The American people expect their government to be a responsible steward of taxpayer dollars, yet every year, the Federal Government loses hundreds of billions of dollars to fraud, waste, and abuse of our hard-earned money. While the Federal Government provides families, workers, and businesses with the support they need, several COVID-era spending programs exposed serious weaknesses in our ability to prevent fraud. Once those dollars were lost, it has proven to be nearly impossible to recover them.

added: A permanent, Senate-confirmed Inspector General for Fraud, Accountability, and Recovery within the Treasury ($10M authorized annually from fiscal year 2035); a governmentwide fraud-data analysis program in the Fiscal Service; a Treasury duty to recommend fraud safeguards for relief bills over $100B or new programs over $100M
modified: Rewrites the Fiscal Service's statutory functions (31 U.S.C. 306) around fraud prevention and data analysis; makes the DATA Act data-analysis center mandatory; moves the Pandemic Response Accountability Committee's sunset up to December 31, 2028
removed: The Pandemic Response Accountability Committee (repealed December 31, 2028, with its assets transferred to the new office)

added: State definition for the data program expanded inline to include the District of Columbia, territories/possessions, and federally recognized Indian Tribes
modified: Treasury Fiscal Service governmentwide data analysis program changed from mandatory to a 'voluntary' program, facilitating services 'upon request and on a voluntary basis in accordance with all applicable privacy and security laws'

Agency data-sharing reframed from mandatory commands ('requiring each agency to share/screen') to voluntary services agencies may request — and added 'but for no other purpose including any policy analysis and enforcement action purpose'

Fraud-data sharing narrowed to entities 'resulting from final adverse action determinations, payment denials, referrals for criminal investigation, or equivalent findings' rather than from any internal agency investigation
Inspector General access to Treasury IT/data (sec. 306(c)(3)) now simply 'in accordance with applicable law' instead of subject to a Secretary discretion-to-deny carve-out with congressional notice
Sec. 4(a)(10) data-access authority reworded to 'agreements with private entities' (was 'and private entities') as may be appropriate

bills.title: SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To reauthorize certain programs that provide for opioid use disorder prevention, treatment, and recovery, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-44. Passed the House June 4, 2025 and the Senate September 18, 2025, and was signed into law December 1, 2025. A reauthorization of existing opioid programs originally created by the bipartisan 2018 SUPPORT Act.
bills.summary: Reauthorizes the opioid prevention, treatment, and recovery programs created by the 2018 SUPPORT Act through fiscal year 2030, mostly at higher funding levels, and adds new provisions covering fetal alcohol spectrum disorder services, cybersecurity for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, fentanyl-contamination coordination, at-home drug disposal, and expanded prescriber training.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the 2018 SUPPORT Act's opioid programs through 2030 at higher funding, plus new FASD, 988 cybersecurity, and fentanyl provisions.

top_lines.headline: Reauthorizes the Opioid Response Through 2030
subs: Extends dozens of prevention, treatment, and recovery programs from the 2018 SUPPORT Act through fiscal year 2030
Most reauthorized programs get funding increases (e.g., overdose prevention rises to $505.58M/year; first-responder training $36M to $57M/year)
Allows fentanyl and xylazine test strips under State and Tribal opioid response grants

top_lines.headline: New and Expanded Health Programs
subs: Creates a standalone Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder program with $12.5M/year through 2030
Adds cybersecurity reporting requirements for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline plus a GAO study
Raises authorizations for recovery, trauma, and treatment-workforce programs (e.g., Building Communities of Recovery $5M to $17M/year)

top_lines.headline: Fentanyl, Disposal, and Prescriber Provisions
subs: "Bruce's Law" sets up a federal interagency work group on fentanyl contamination of illegal drugs
Directs HHS guidance on at-home drug disposal systems within one year
Expands the list of organizations whose courses satisfy controlled-substance prescriber training

sections.label: Section 103 — Preventing Overdoses of Controlled Substances

items.main: Broadens the CDC overdose-prevention program beyond opioids and reauthorizes it at a higher level.
items.detail: Amends section 392A of the Public Health Service Act so the surveillance and rapid-response grant program covers "substances causing overdose" and associated risk factors rather than opioids alone, and explicitly allows innovative approaches such as wastewater surveillance. The authorization rises from $496M to $505.58M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

sections.label: Section 104 — Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder Program

items.main: Replaces the existing FASD provisions with a new prevention, intervention, and services program.
items.detail: Rewrites Part O of title III of the Public Health Service Act to establish an FASD education, prevention, identification, intervention, and services-delivery program, with grants and technical assistance to states, Tribes, local governments, and nonprofits, and a separate capacity-building and clearinghouse role. It authorizes $12.5M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 and requires HHS to report to Congress within four years and annually thereafter.

items.main: Expands the first-responder overdose training program beyond opioids and increases its funding.
items.detail: Amends section 546 of the Public Health Service Act to cover overdose-reversal drugs that are "approved, cleared, or otherwise legally marketed" and to address heroin and other drug overdoses, not just opioids. The authorization rises from $36M to $57M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

sections.label: Section 107 — Donald J. Cohen National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative

items.main: Reauthorizes the National Child Traumatic Stress Initiative and adds a dissemination role for grantees.
items.detail: Amends section 582 of the Public Health Service Act to require NCTSI grantees to develop trainings and resources that support implementation of the evidence-based practices they develop. It authorizes $98.89M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2028 and $100M for each of fiscal years 2029 and 2030.

sections.label: Section 108 — Protecting the 988 Lifeline From Cybersecurity Incidents

items.main: Adds cybersecurity protection and reporting requirements for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline.
items.detail: Amends section 520E-3 of the Public Health Service Act to require the Lifeline program to take steps to protect against cybersecurity incidents and eliminate known vulnerabilities, and to require the program's network administrator and participating crisis centers to report identified vulnerabilities and incidents to the Assistant Secretary in a privacy-protective manner. It also directs the Comptroller General to complete a study of cybersecurity risks to the 988 Lifeline within 180 days of enactment.

items.main: Strengthens youth fentanyl-awareness work and creates a federal work group on fentanyl-contaminated illegal drugs.
items.detail: Amends the youth prevention provisions of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to add education on the potency and dangers of synthetic opioids, including drugs contaminated with fentanyl. It directs the Interdepartmental Substance Use Disorders Coordinating Committee to establish a Federal Interagency Work Group on Fentanyl Contamination of Illegal Drugs, which consults with families of overdose victims and reports annually with recommendations. The Coordinating Committee is set to terminate September 30, 2030.

sections.label: Section 113 — State and Tribal Opioid Response Grants

items.main: Allows opioid response grant funds to be used for drug-detection tools such as fentanyl and xylazine test strips.
items.detail: Clarifies that activities under the 21st Century Cures Act State and Tribal opioid response grant program may include facilitating access to products that detect substances such as fentanyl and xylazine test strips, to the extent their purchase and possession is consistent with federal and state law.

sections.label: Section 204 — Loan Repayment for the Treatment Workforce

items.main: Reauthorizes the substance use disorder treatment workforce loan-repayment program at a higher level.
items.detail: Amends section 781 of the Public Health Service Act, raising the authorization from $25M to $40M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

items.main: Directs HHS to review the controlled-substance scheduling of approved buprenorphine-naloxone combination products.
items.detail: Requires the Secretary of HHS to review data on the scheduling of FDA-approved products containing a combination of buprenorphine and naloxone and, if appropriate, ask the Attorney General to begin rulemaking to revise the schedules. The Attorney General must review any such request under the Controlled Substances Act criteria.

items.main: Sharply increases funding for the Building Communities of Recovery program.
items.detail: Amends section 547 of the Public Health Service Act, raising the authorization from $5M to $17M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

items.main: Reauthorizes and expands the youth prevention and recovery program with a rising funding schedule.
items.detail: Amends section 7102(c) of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to broaden eligible applicants (including consortia of local educational agencies and secondary schools) and require sustainability plans. It authorizes $10M for fiscal year 2026, $12M for 2027, $13M for 2028, $14M for 2029, and $15M for 2030.

items.main: Reauthorizes the CAREER Act workforce grants and the recovery housing pilot, with new performance reporting.
items.detail: Amends section 7183 of the 2018 SUPPORT Act to rename the program, update the targeting formula to use 2018-2022 overdose, unemployment, and labor-force data, allow up to 5 percent of grant funds for transportation, and add employment-and-earnings outcome reporting. It raises the authorization from $5M to $12M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2030 and reauthorizes the recovery housing pilot program through 2030.

sections.label: Section 401 — Pharmacy Delivery to a Prescribing Practitioner

items.main: Adjusts when a pharmacy may deliver a controlled substance to a prescribing practitioner for administration.
items.detail: Amends section 309A of the Controlled Substances Act so the exception covers schedule III, IV, or V drugs administered by injection or implantation for maintenance or detoxification treatment, or drugs subject to an FDA risk evaluation and mitigation strategy that includes post-administration monitoring by a health care provider.

items.main: Expands the list of organizations and schools whose courses satisfy controlled-substance prescriber training.
items.detail: Amends section 303 of the Controlled Substances Act to add organizations such as the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American Podiatric Medical Association, the Academy of General Dentistry, the American Optometric Association, the American Pharmacists Association, and others, and to include podiatric medicine and accredited schools of pharmacy. The amendment takes effect as if enacted on December 29, 2022.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Latta
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate it. The SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act of 2025 is one of the most impactful bills the Committee on Energy and Commerce has worked on during my time in Congress. Simply put, we came together to implement bipartisan policies that would save lives. Gone are the days that substance abuse and addiction are a far off problem that doesn't impact each one of our districts.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Dunn
featured_quotes.text: This bill is a critical piece of legislation that will help bolster prevention, treatment, and recovery for millions of Americans suffering from substance abuse disorders. Thanks to the investments from the original SUPPORT for Patients and Communities Act in 2018 and the efforts of the Trump administration, we are finally starting to see a decrease in the overdose death rate. Florida is a shining example of this progress.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Dexter
featured_quotes.text: I rise today not just as a Member of this body but as a physician who has spent nearly two decades caring for patients in the intensive care unit, many of them fighting for their lives because of a system that has failed to support them before a crisis hit. In Oregon's Third District, we see every day how critical prevention, treatment, and recovery programs are. We need those programs that my colleague from New Jersey just referred to as being cut. This bill does nothing to repair those cuts. These aren't abstract policy ideas.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hassan
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to pass into law a lifesaving bipartisan legislation that will enable us to keep fighting the opioid and fentanyl epidemic, an epidemic that has destroyed families and devastated communities all across our country. Our country faces many challenges, and I am sure we will continue to debate in the coming weeks how to address those, but today we will advance, on a bipartisan basis, lifesaving legislation that we know is working to combat fentanyl.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cassidy
featured_quotes.text: It is part of, as a doctor, I would say, a pro-patient--we would say pro-family--agenda that we wish to deliver for the American people. About a month and a half ago, President Trump had a signing ceremony for the HALT Fentanyl Act at the White House. That was my bill, so I was privileged to be there. Behind him were families holding the pictures of their children who had died from fentanyl overdose. Incredibly moving. I had a similar ceremony in Baton Rouge where, across Louisiana, people came and held a picture of their child who had died.

added: New Sec. 210 — HHS must make any reference to an opioid overdose reversal drug (such as naloxone) in grant-program regulations/guidance inclusive of any FDA-approved reversal drug; existing references updated within one year

New Sec. 211 — National Coordinator for Health IT must convene a public roundtable within 180 days on using electronic health records to improve mental health and substance use care outcomes, then report
New Sec. 307 — HHS must convene a public meeting within one year to improve awareness of and access to SAMHSA funding opportunities, improve Grants.gov, and report

bills.title: Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
bills.official_title: Making further continuing appropriations and other extensions for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2025, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-4 on March 15, 2025. This was the full-year measure that funded the federal government for the rest of fiscal year 2025 and averted a shutdown after the prior stopgap expired.

votes.question: On Passage of the Bill H.R. 1968

bills.summary: Funds the federal government for the rest of fiscal year 2025 (through September 30, 2025) by continuing fiscal year 2024 appropriations, but with the Department of Defense funded at new line-item levels and given added flexibility while most nondefense agencies stay at prior-year amounts. It also extends a set of expiring health programs — community health centers, telehealth, and several Medicare and Medicaid provisions — and a handful of other authorities.
bills.brief: Full-year stopgap funding the government through September 30, 2025: continues FY2024 levels, sets new defense amounts, and extends expiring health programs.

top_lines.headline: Full-Year Funding Through September 30, 2025
subs: Continues fiscal year 2024 appropriations for most of the government for the rest of FY2025
Funds run through September 30, 2025, replacing the expiring short-term stopgap
Strips out the earmarks (community project funding) that were carried in the FY2024 bills

top_lines.headline: Defense Funded in Full; Nondefense Held Flat
subs: Sets specific, account-by-account funding levels for the Department of Defense rather than simply continuing prior-year amounts
Most nondefense agencies remain at FY2024 levels, an effective cut after inflation
Requires agencies to submit detailed FY2025 spending plans and OMB to report monthly on obligations

top_lines.headline: Health Program Extensions
subs: Extends funding for community health centers, the National Health Service Corps, and teaching health centers through September 30, 2025
Extends Medicare telehealth flexibilities and hospital-at-home authority and delays Medicaid DSH payment cuts
Extends the temporary scheduling order for fentanyl-related substances through September 30, 2025

items.main: Continues fiscal year 2024 funding levels, authorities, and conditions for most of the government.
items.detail: Appropriates, for the listed FY2024 appropriations Acts, the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions, for projects and activities not otherwise specifically provided for. It applies to all twelve appropriations subcommittees' bills, subject to specific exceptions and dollar substitutions ('anomalies') spelled out account by account.

items.main: Sets the funding to run through the end of fiscal year 2025.
items.detail: Unless otherwise provided, appropriations and authority under the division are available through September 30, 2025.

items.main: Nullifies the earmarks that were attached to the FY2024 appropriations.
items.detail: Provides that any language specifying an earmark in an FY2024 appropriations Act, or in an accompanying committee report or joint explanatory statement, has no legal effect for funds appropriated by the division. 'Earmark' is defined by reference to House Rule XXI and Senate Rule XLIV (congressional earmarks, community project funding, congressionally directed spending).

items.main: Requires departments and agencies to submit detailed FY2025 operating plans.
items.detail: Within 45 days of enactment, each of the listed departments and agencies must submit to the Appropriations Committees a spending, expenditure, or operating plan at the program, project, or activity level (or, for foreign assistance, by country and program). Section 1114 separately requires OMB to report monthly, from May 15 through November 1, 2025, on obligations by account compared to the same period in FY2024.

items.main: Sets specific dollar levels for Defense accounts instead of simply continuing prior-year funding.
items.detail: Notwithstanding the general continuing-appropriations rule, the division specifies funding account by account for the Department of Defense — for example, $51.18B for Military Personnel, Army and $73.66B for Operation and Maintenance, Navy — and provides new line-item procurement and research figures. This gives the Pentagon updated amounts and reprogramming room that the rest of the government, held at FY2024 levels, does not get.

sections.label: Section 2101 — Community Health Center and Workforce Extensions

items.main: Extends mandatory funding for community health centers and related workforce programs through September 30, 2025.
items.detail: Amends the Affordable Care Act and Public Health Service Act to add $2.14B for community health centers, $172.97M for the National Health Service Corps, and $87.74M for teaching health centers that operate graduate medical education programs, each for the period April 1 through September 30, 2025.

items.main: Extends the Special Diabetes Program and the Special Diabetes Program for Indians.
items.detail: Adds $79.83M for each program for the period April 1 through September 30, 2025, to remain available until expended.

items.main: Extends the pandemic-era Medicare telehealth flexibilities by six months.
