items.detail: Pushes the expiration of multiple telehealth provisions in the Social Security Act from March 31, 2025 to September 30, 2025 — including the removal of geographic and originating-site restrictions, the expanded list of eligible practitioners, audio-only services, telehealth for federally qualified health centers and rural health clinics, and the delay of in-person requirements for tele-mental-health.

items.main: Increases the Medicare Improvement Fund balance.
items.detail: Amends section 1898(b)(1) of the Social Security Act to change the fund amount from $1.25B to $1.80B.

items.main: Delays scheduled cuts to Medicaid Disproportionate Share Hospital payments.
items.detail: Amends section 1923(f)(7)(A) of the Social Security Act to remove the reduction for the April 1 through September 30, 2025 period and to extend the schedule of reductions through fiscal year 2028 instead of 2027.

items.main: Extends the temporary class-wide scheduling of fentanyl-related substances.
items.detail: Amends the Temporary Reauthorization and Study of the Emergency Scheduling of Fentanyl Analogues Act to push the order's expiration from March 31, 2025 to September 30, 2025.

items.main: Exempts the health and other-matters divisions from PAYGO scorecards.
items.detail: Provides that the budgetary effects of divisions B and C are not entered on the statutory or Senate PAYGO scorecards.

criticisms.why: I rise to oppose this cruel betrayal of America's veterans, seniors, and working families. This 1-year CR doesn't make rent or healthcare bills more affordable, which is what keeps my constituents up at night. Instead, it actually cuts housing aid that could force 32,000 veterans, domestic violence survivors, seniors, and people with disabilities into homelessness. What does this spending patch do as we all now stare down the barrel of another Trump recession?

and still I rise, to oppose a Continuing Resolution that will allow a chainsaw to, among other things: minimize Medicaid with underfunded block grants to states, marginalize Medicare's ``Dual Eligibles'' long-term Medicaid care, and privatize Social Security by allowing private investment of Social Security funds in the stock market with no protections from market downturns. Mr. Speaker, the costs of the cuts in spending will be measurable. However, the human cost in pain and suffering will be immeasurable.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Wasserman Schultz
featured_quotes.text: I rise to oppose this cruel betrayal of America's veterans, seniors, and working families. This 1-year CR doesn't make rent or healthcare bills more affordable, which is what keeps my constituents up at night. Instead, it actually cuts housing aid that could force 32,000 veterans, domestic violence survivors, seniors, and people with disabilities into homelessness. What does this spending patch do as we all now stare down the barrel of another Trump recession?

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Green
featured_quotes.text: and still I rise, to oppose a Continuing Resolution that will allow a chainsaw to, among other things: minimize Medicaid with underfunded block grants to states, marginalize Medicare's ``Dual Eligibles'' long-term Medicaid care, and privatize Social Security by allowing private investment of Social Security funds in the stock market with no protections from market downturns. Mr. Speaker, the costs of the cuts in spending will be measurable. However, the human cost in pain and suffering will be immeasurable.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rutherford
featured_quotes.text: I really appreciate all the hard work that got us here today. Mr. Speaker, I have to tell you, as I sat here on this floor listening to the conversation, it reminded me of an old saying that my father had. For many, many years, I heard this: A lie can travel around the world three times before the truth can get up and put its pants on. That was before the internet. Now, after what I have heard today, I would say it is probably more like 100 times that a lie can travel around the world before the truth can get up and put its pants on.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Bice
featured_quotes.text: I think my colleagues on the other side of the aisle are confused about what is in this bill and what is not. They keep talking about impacts to mandatory spending, Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid. That is not in this bill. Just because you keep repeating the same dishonest talking points doesn't make it true. This legislation continues funding and prevents a government shutdown, which would have a devastating impact on my home State of Oklahoma and communities across the country.

modified: Reference date corrected — a striking instruction changed from "March 14, 2025" to "March 31, 2025" (in a provision inserting "September 30, 2025")
removed: Afghan Special Immigrant Visa cap increase dropped — the introduced bill's amendment raising the section 602(b)(3) cap from "50,500" to "70,500" was removed

Afghan SIV deadline extension dropped — the introduced bill's change of "December 31, 2025" to "December 31, 2027" in the Afghan Allies Protection Act was removed; only the subparagraph heading "2024"→"2025" change remains

bills.title: Pay Our Homeland Defenders Act
bills.official_title: Making appropriations for the Department of Homeland Security for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2026, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House and was received in the Senate. Sponsored by Rep. Ciscomani (R-AZ). It pairs full-year Homeland Security funding with provisions to cover a funding lapse and pay employees, which creates pressure to act, but full-year DHS appropriations are contentious over immigration enforcement and it still needs 60 votes in the Senate.
bills.summary: Provides full-year fiscal year 2026 funding for the Department of Homeland Security — including Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the TSA — and, in a second division, retroactively covers a lapse in appropriations that began around February 13, 2026 and makes the pay and benefits of affected employees available, effectively reopening the government and authorizing back pay.
bills.brief: Full-year DHS funding for FY2026 plus a division that covers a February 2026 funding lapse and pays affected employees.

top_lines.headline: Full-Year Homeland Security Funding
subs: Funds Customs and Border Protection operations at $17.73B and ICE operations at $10.04B
Funds the Transportation Security Administration at $10.64B (about $7.6B from the general fund after security fees)
Covers the Department through the end of fiscal year 2026

top_lines.headline: Covers a Funding Lapse and Back Pay
subs: Treats the period of the appropriations lapse that began around February 13, 2026 as covered by the FY2026 continuing resolution
Makes employee pay, allowances, and benefits available for payment under the Antideficiency Act's exception
Ratifies obligations incurred during the lapse to protect life and property

top_lines.headline: Enforcement Funding and Controls
subs: Authorizes CBP to buy up to 7,500 police-type vehicles and ICE up to 3,790
Earmarks ICE funds for forced-child-labor enforcement, intellectual-property investigations, and child-rescue apprenticeships
Requires congressional notification before larger reprogrammings (over $5M or 10%) and most fund transfers

sections.label: Title II — Customs and Border Protection

items.main: Funds CBP operations and procurement for fiscal year 2026.
items.detail: Appropriates $17.73B for CBP operations and support — covering air and marine support, transportation of unaccompanied minors, and up to 7,500 police-type vehicles (6,500 for replacement) — with $550M available through September 30, 2027, plus $222.89M for procurement, construction, and improvements.

sections.label: Title II — Immigration and Customs Enforcement

items.main: Funds ICE operations and sets aside amounts for specific enforcement priorities.
items.detail: Appropriates $10.04B for ICE operations and support (including up to 3,790 police-type vehicles), of which Homeland Security Investigations amounts include not less than $6M for enforcing laws against forced child labor, not less than $15M for intellectual-property-rights investigations, and $3M for child-rescue apprenticeships, plus $5M for procurement, construction, and improvements.

items.main: Funds the TSA, offset by aviation security fees.
items.detail: Appropriates $10.64B for TSA operations and support, with security service fees credited as offsetting collections so that the net general-fund appropriation is estimated at not more than $7.61B for fiscal year 2026.

items.main: Sets limits and notification requirements on moving DHS funds between purposes.
items.detail: Bars reprogrammings that create or eliminate programs, augment a program by more than $5M or 10 percent, or cut a program or personnel by 10 percent or more, unless the Appropriations Committees are notified 30 days in advance, and limits transfers between appropriations to 5 percent (and no more than a 10 percent increase to any account).

sections.label: Section 1001 — Coverage of the Appropriations Lapse

items.main: Retroactively treats a funding lapse as covered by the FY2026 continuing resolution.
items.detail: Provides that, for purposes of the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2026 (division A of Public Law 119-37), the time covered includes the period beginning on or about February 13, 2026 during which a lapse in appropriations occurred.

items.main: Makes pay, allowances, and benefits available to affected employees.
items.detail: Provides that amounts under the FY2026 continuing resolution and the DHS appropriations in division A for personnel pay, allowances, and benefits are available for payments under the Antideficiency Act exception (31 U.S.C. 1341(c)), and that such payments shall be made.

items.main: Ratifies obligations incurred during the lapse.
items.detail: Ratifies and approves obligations incurred in anticipation of the FY2026 continuing resolution and division A for maintaining the essential level of activity to protect life and property and to bring about an orderly termination of government functions, if otherwise in accord with the applicable Act.

bills.title: Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
bills.official_title: Making appropriations for Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House and was received in the Senate. This is one of the twelve annual appropriations bills; standalone House-passed appropriations bills typically are not taken up as-is by the Senate but instead get renegotiated and folded into a year-end package, and it would need 60 votes there.
bills.summary: Sets fiscal year 2027 funding for the Department of Agriculture, rural development programs, the Food and Drug Administration, and related agencies. The largest pieces are the domestic nutrition programs — SNAP, WIC, and child nutrition — which together account for most of the bill, alongside farm, research, conservation, and FDA accounts.
bills.brief: FY2027 funding for Agriculture, rural development, and the FDA, dominated by the SNAP, WIC, and child-nutrition programs.

top_lines.headline: Domestic Nutrition Programs
subs: $101.24B for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), including a $3B reserve
$8B for WIC and $37.9B for child nutrition programs
Sets the WIC fruit-and-vegetable cash voucher at 267% (children) and 428% (women) of the fiscal year 2020 amount

top_lines.headline: Food and Drug Administration
subs: $7.11B total for the FDA, including industry user fees
$1.28B for the Human Foods Program and $2.54B for the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research
Sets aside funds for unannounced foreign drug inspections and foreign seafood inspections

top_lines.headline: Farm, Research, and Rural Programs
subs: Funds USDA departmental offices, the Agricultural Research Service ($1.8B), and farm and conservation programs
Funds rural development, foreign food assistance, and related agencies
Caps USDA's vehicle fleet at its 2018 size absent advance congressional approval

sections.label: Title I — Agricultural Programs and Research

items.main: Funds USDA departmental offices and research agencies.
items.detail: Provides salaries and expenses for the Office of the Secretary and USDA management offices and funds the research mission area, including $1.8B for the Agricultural Research Service (with per-building construction and alteration limits) and $99.97M for the Office of Inspector General.

sections.label: Title IV — Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program

items.main: Funds SNAP, the largest single program in the bill.
items.detail: Appropriates $101.24B to carry out the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, of which $3B is placed in reserve (available through September 30, 2029) for use only as needed for program operations, and continues work-registration and program-integrity conditions.

items.main: Funds the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children.
items.detail: Appropriates $8B for WIC through September 30, 2028, requires at least $90M for breastfeeding peer counselors, and directs that the fruit-and-vegetable cash-value voucher be set at 267 percent of the fiscal year 2020 amount for children and 428 percent for women.

items.main: Funds school meals and other child nutrition programs.
items.detail: Appropriates $37.9B (available through September 30, 2028) to carry out the National School Lunch Act and Child Nutrition Act, including $18M to carry out section 19 of the Child Nutrition Act, $22.38M for studies and evaluations, and farm-to-school grants capped at $500,000 per recipient for fiscal year 2027.

items.main: Funds commodity and disaster food assistance.
items.detail: Appropriates $546.07M, of which $460M is for the Commodity Supplemental Food Program, $75M for the Emergency Food Assistance Act, and $10M for the Farmers' Market Nutrition Program.

sections.label: Title VI — Food and Drug Administration

items.main: Funds the FDA, including amounts derived from industry user fees.
items.detail: Appropriates $7.11B for FDA salaries and expenses, including $1.64B from prescription-drug user fees, $712M from tobacco product user fees, and other fee streams. Of the total, $1.28B is for the Human Foods Program, $2.54B for the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (with at least $10M for pilots to increase unannounced foreign inspections), $985.57M for the Center for Devices and Radiological Health, and $687.12M for the Center for Tobacco Products.

items.main: Caps the USDA vehicle fleet at its 2018 level.
items.detail: Allows the Secretary to purchase passenger vehicles only so long as the total purchased in fiscal year 2027 does not exceed the number owned or leased in fiscal year 2018, and bars increasing the fleet above the 2018 level without advance written approval from the Appropriations Committees.

criticisms.why: I can't say that I am surprised that my Republican colleagues want to cut yet another resource to help women and children get food. This bill reduces the fruit and vegetable benefit for mothers and young children under WIC, and this goes against actual science-based evidence that tells us what families need to stay healthy. Cutting these benefits leaves 5.3 million moms and kids without reliable access to fresh fruits and vegetables.
Pursuant to the provisions of clause 3(a)(1) of House rule XIII and sec.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Bynum
featured_quotes.text: I can't say that I am surprised that my Republican colleagues want to cut yet another resource to help women and children get food. This bill reduces the fruit and vegetable benefit for mothers and young children under WIC, and this goes against actual science-based evidence that tells us what families need to stay healthy. Cutting these benefits leaves 5.3 million moms and kids without reliable access to fresh fruits and vegetables.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Taylor
featured_quotes.text: Through this bill, Republicans are making critical investments in American agriculture, considering to fund broadband expansion programs in rural regions like mine in Appalachian Ohio, and providing funding for critical community projects. Counties like those in my district have been left behind for too long when it comes to internet connectivity and repairing water infrastructure that our communities rely on every day. This bill delivers long-overdue support for rural Ohio families so they can have the tools they need to thrive.

added: New Sec. 781 — bars FDA's CDER, CBER, or CDRH from issuing or finalizing guidance recommending or requiring testing in dogs

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on November 12, 2025 as Public Law 119-37 — the deal that ended the record-long October–November 2025 government shutdown. The House passed it 217-212 on September 19, but the Senate rejected cloture more than a dozen times before agreeing 60-40 on November 10; the House concurred in the Senate amendment 222-209 on November 12. It funds most agencies at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026, with full-year budgets for Agriculture/FDA, the Legislative Branch, and Military Construction-VA, plus health, farm, and veterans extensions.

bills.summary: This is the law that ended the October–November 2025 government shutdown. It keeps most agencies running at last year's levels through January 30, 2026, gives full-year budgets to Agriculture and the FDA, Congress, and military construction and veterans programs, and renews a long list of expiring health, farm, and veterans authorities.
bills.brief: A hybrid funding law that ended the 2025 shutdown — a stopgap for most of government plus full-year appropriations for three areas and broad program extensions.

top_lines.headline: Division A — Stopgap & Shutdown Reversal
subs: Funds most agencies at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026
Reverses October 2025 layoffs and provides federal worker back pay

subs: $2.08B for the House of Representatives

items.main: A stopgap that funds all agencies not covered by Divisions B–D at FY2025 rates through January 30, 2026, and undoes the October 2025 shutdown.
items.detail: Keeps the rest of the federal government running at last year's spending levels through January 30, 2026, after the October 2025 funding lapse. It ends the shutdown, pays workers their missed wages, and reverses layoffs that agencies started during the gap.

sections.label: Division B — Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agency Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for USDA, the FDA, and domestic nutrition programs, led by $107.48B for food stamps and $37.84B for child nutrition.
items.detail: Funds the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the Food and Drug Administration, and the country's main food-aid programs for 2026. The biggest pieces are food assistance for low-income families, school meals, and aid for mothers and infants.

sections.label: Division C — Legislative Branch Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for the legislative branch, led by $2.08B for the House of Representatives and roughly $852M for the Capitol Police.
items.detail: Funds Congress itself and its support agencies for 2026 — the House, the Senate, the Capitol Police, the Library of Congress, and government watchdogs. The largest share goes to running the House of Representatives.

sections.label: Division D — Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: A full-year appropriation for military construction and the VA, anchored by a $246.63B advance appropriation for veterans' compensation and pensions and $59.86B for VA medical services.
items.detail: Pays for building and maintaining military bases and family housing, and funds the Department of Veterans Affairs — veterans' disability checks, pensions, and medical care. Most of the VA money is set a year ahead so veterans' benefits keep flowing without interruption.

sections.label: Division E — Extension of Agricultural Programs

items.main: Extends the 2018 Farm Bill (Agriculture Improvement Act) and its programs through the later of September 30, 2026.
items.detail: Keeps the 2018 Farm Bill alive by extending its programs and authorities, which had lapsed on September 30, 2025. Without this, dozens of farm, conservation, and rural programs would expire.

items.main: Short-term extensions of public health, Medicare, and Medicaid programs through January 30, 2026, plus a renewal of FDA over-the-counter drug user fees.
items.detail: Keeps a long list of health programs from expiring — community health centers, special diabetes programs, and Medicare rules for rural and home care. Most are extended only to January 30, 2026, the same cliff as the stopgap. It also renews the FDA's fee program for over-the-counter drugs and delays scheduled Medicaid cuts to safety-net hospitals.

sections.label: Division G — Department of Veterans Affairs Extenders

items.main: One-year extensions of VA health, benefits, and housing authorities, including $660M for supportive services for very low-income veteran families.
items.detail: Renews a set of expiring VA authorities covering veterans' health care, benefits, and housing for homeless and disabled veterans. Most simply push expiration dates from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2026.

items.main: Exempts the extension divisions from PAYGO budget scorecards and zeroes out the scorecard balances.
items.detail: A bookkeeping division that controls how this law's costs are counted against federal budget rules. It keeps the extender divisions from triggering automatic spending cuts.

underreported.summary: Voids reduction-in-force layoffs taken October 1, 2025 through enactment and reinstates affected federal workers with back pay.
underreported.why_unreported: The shutdown-ending law also rolls back layoffs already issued, not just funds forward operations.

underreported.summary: Rescinds $15.89B of prior-year VA medical services funds and $610M of medical support funds even as it adds new advance appropriations.
underreported.why_unreported: A multi-billion-dollar VA health clawback is paired with the new funding.

underreported.summary: Keeps the extender divisions off PAYGO scorecards and zeroes accumulated balances, avoiding an automatic sequestration trigger.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision resets PAYGO balances rather than only changing forward accounting.

criticisms.why: They cut SNAP by 20 percent in the big, ugly bill this summer, dismantled and defunded Federal programs, fired Federal workers, and illegally ignored court orders. This bill fails to address the healthcare crisis, and bipartisan outrage has erupted over language in this bill to pay millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of Senators whose phone records were subpoenaed in relation to the January 6 investigation. It is a bad bill, and I oppose it.

gaps: Sets a January 30, 2026 funding cliff for most of government while only three areas get full-year budgets.
Many health and farm programs are extended only to late January 2026, recreating the same deadline within weeks.
Delays rather than resolves scheduled Medicaid safety-net hospital cuts and prior-year VA rescissions.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bishop
featured_quotes.text: They cut SNAP by 20 percent in the big, ugly bill this summer, dismantled and defunded Federal programs, fired Federal workers, and illegally ignored court orders. This bill fails to address the healthcare crisis, and bipartisan outrage has erupted over language in this bill to pay millions of taxpayer dollars to a handful of Senators whose phone records were subpoenaed in relation to the January 6 investigation. It is a bad bill, and I oppose it.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: I look forward to reopening the government. The shutdown has gone on long enough, and it is time to end it. Yesterday was Veterans Day. It is a timely reminder of the commitment our Armed Forces personnel have made and the responsibility we have to take care of those who serve our Nation. The military construction and veterans affairs component of the legislation meets that goal. The legislation includes $133.3 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs, including $113.8 billion in discretionary funding for VA medical care.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Harris
featured_quotes.text: Millions of Americans have suffered because Democrats have refused to reopen the government, harming those who depend on SNAP benefits, Federal workers, Border Patrol agents, and our troops, who were uncertain about their next paycheck. This legislation extends government funding to the end of January 2026, thereby blocking attempts to force a budget-busting omnibus at the last minute before Christmas. It also includes the FY 2026 Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Espaillat
featured_quotes.text: Today's backroom deal does nothing to stop 20 million Americans who will see their healthcare premiums double or triple. It does absolutely nothing to stop provisions in the reconciliation package that will strip 15 million people of their Medicaid coverage. These cuts will have a resounding impact on individuals and the healthcare industry and economy as a whole. Safety net hospitals like Montefiore in my district and federally funded clinics like Boriken in East Harlem face having to eliminate services or completely close.

bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law on January 23, 2026 as Public Law 119-74. This consolidated package bundles 3 of the 12 regular FY2026 appropriations bills — Commerce-Justice-Science, Energy and Water Development, and Interior-Environment — funding those departments and agencies through September 30, 2026. It passed the House 397-28 on January 8 and the Senate 82-15 on January 15, both with broad bipartisan majorities.

bills.summary: A consolidated full-year appropriations law (Public Law 119-74) funding three of the twelve regular 2026 spending bills: Commerce-Justice-Science (Division A), Energy and Water Development (Division B), and Interior-Environment (Division C). It sets the 2026 budgets for the FBI, federal prisons, NASA, the National Science Foundation, the Army Corps of Engineers, the nuclear-weapons complex, the National Park Service, the EPA, the Forest Service and the Indian Health Service, among many others.

sections.label: Division A — Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: Full-year FY2026 budgets for the Departments of Commerce and Justice, NASA and the National Science Foundation, and related agencies.
items.detail: Funds the Commerce Department (including the Census Bureau, NIST, NOAA and the Patent and Trademark Office), the Justice Department (the FBI, federal prisons, the DEA, ATF and federal prosecutors), NASA, the National Science Foundation, and smaller related agencies for the full 2026 budget year. It also permanently cancels some unspent prior-year balances.

sections.label: Division B — Energy and Water Development and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: Full-year FY2026 budgets for the Army Corps of Engineers, the Bureau of Reclamation, the Department of Energy and the nuclear-weapons complex.
items.detail: Funds the Army Corps of Engineers civil works (locks, dams, harbors and flood control), the Bureau of Reclamation’s Western water projects, the Department of Energy’s science and energy programs, and the National Nuclear Security Administration, which maintains the U.S. nuclear arsenal. Nuclear weapons activities are the single largest account in this division.

sections.label: Division C — Department of the Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2026

items.main: Full-year FY2026 budgets for the Interior Department, the EPA, the Forest Service, the Indian Health Service and related agencies.
items.detail: Funds the National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management, Fish and Wildlife Service, U.S. Geological Survey and Indian Affairs within the Interior Department; the Environmental Protection Agency, including state water-infrastructure grants; and related agencies such as the Forest Service and the Indian Health Service. Wildfire suppression and tribal health and education programs are major components.

underreported: NNSA nuclear Weapons Activities at $20.38B is the single largest account anywhere in the bill, exceeding any individual Commerce, Justice, NASA, Interior or EPA account.

The Patent and Trademark Office’s $4.96B and the Indian Health Service’s $4.79B are structured unusually — the first is fully fee-offset (net $0 to the general fund) and the second is forward-funded into FY2027.

criticisms.why: I will start with a constituent from Canon City. I am writing to express my strong opposition to the administration's recent plans to dismantle the National Center for Atmospheric Research, NCAR. NCAR is a cornerstone of American scientific leadership and public safety. Since 1960, it has provided the essential infrastructure, including super computers, research, aircraft, and sophisticated modeling that protects American lives and our economy every single day. I urge you to push back against the move for the following reasons: public safety.

gaps: The enacted bill delegates account-by-account allocations to an explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record rather than itemizing them in the law itself, so the public statute shows lump-sum totals rather than program-level detail.

items.main: Full-year funding for Commerce agencies, led by NOAA, the Patent and Trademark Office, NIST and the Census Bureau.
items.detail: NOAA receives $4.54B for operations and $1.58B for procurement, ships, satellites and construction. NIST gets $1.25B for research plus $212M for industrial technology services (including $175M for the Hollings Manufacturing Extension Partnership). The Census Bureau receives $1.17B for periodic programs and $318.5M for current surveys.

items.main: Funds federal law enforcement, prosecution, prisons and justice grants.
items.detail: The FBI receives $10.61B and the Bureau of Prisons (Federal Prison System) $8.1B for salaries and expenses. U.S. Attorneys get $2.62B, the DEA $2.58B, the ATF $1.59B, and federal prisoner detention (handled by the U.S. Marshals) $2.24B. State and local justice assistance grants total $2.4B.

items.main: Funds NASA and the National Science Foundation.
items.detail: NASA accounts include Exploration $7.78B, Science $7.25B, Space Operations $4.18B, and a combined Science/Aeronautics/Space Technology/Education account of $3.0B. The National Science Foundation receives $7.18B for research and related activities.

sections.label: Titles IV–V — Related Agencies, General Provisions and Rescissions

items.main: Funds smaller related agencies and permanently cancels some unspent prior-year balances.
items.detail: Related agencies (Title IV) include the Legal Services Corporation, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the International Trade Commission and others. Section 521 permanently rescinds prior-year balances: $250M from the Office of Justice Programs, $36M from Violence Against Women Act prevention programs, $25M from Community Oriented Policing Services, $210M from the DOJ Working Capital Fund, $113.2M from the Assets Forfeiture Fund, $60M from the Economic Development Administration, and $15M from the Census Working Capital Fund.

underreported: The Patent and Trademark Office’s $4.96B is fully offset by patent and trademark fees, so the headline number overstates its draw on the general fund — the estimated net appropriation is $0.
NOAA’s operations account also draws $399.64M transferred from the Promote and Develop Fishery Products fund and $28M from prior-year recoveries, on top of the $4.54B direct appropriation.
criticisms: Section 521 permanently cancels $250M from the Office of Justice Programs, $36M from Violence Against Women Act prevention programs and $25M from Community Oriented Policing Services — reductions to state and local grant pipelines drawn from unspent prior-year balances.
gaps: Detailed account-by-account allocations are delegated to the explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record, not the bill text, so the public bill does not itemize how the lump-sum totals are distributed across programs.

HIV/AIDS programs (PEPFAR) are $5.88B (including $1.25B to the Global Fund); humanitarian assistance $5.4B; Global Health Programs $3.53B. underreported: The SEC’s $2.15B is fully offset by section 31 transaction fees, so its net draw on the general fund is reduced to essentially zero; the Small Business Administration’s $16.5B and $35.5B figures are loan-guarantee ceilings, not appropriations.

Two of the largest dollar figures in Division B — $3.2B for the World Bank’s 21st IDA replenishment and $7.8B for a callable-capital subscription — are authorizations that require separate future appropriations, not money provided by this bill.
gaps: The bill text states lump-sum account totals but leaves most program- and country-level allocations to the accompanying explanatory statement, so the public bill does not itemize how the totals are distributed.

divisions.label: Division A — Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act, 2026
divisions.brief: Full-year FY2026 funding for the Treasury Department and IRS, the federal Judiciary, the District of Columbia, the Executive Office of the President, and independent financial-regulatory and small-business agencies.
divisions.summary: Division A is one of the twelve regular annual appropriations bills, covering the Treasury Department (including the IRS), the Executive Office of the President, the federal courts, the District of Columbia, and a set of independent agencies such as the SEC, the GSA, the Small Business Administration and the FCC. The largest single line is the General Services Administration’s Federal Buildings Fund; the IRS is funded across three separate accounts; and the SEC and Patent-style fee agencies are written to draw on collections rather than the general fund.

sections.label: The Judiciary, the District of Columbia and independent agencies

items.main: Pays for the federal courts, federal-payment support to the District of Columbia, and independent regulators and agencies.

The General Services Administration’s Federal Buildings Fund is set at an aggregate $9.69B (including $5.57B for rental of space and $3.01B for building operations). The Securities and Exchange Commission is funded at $2.15B but offset entirely by section 31 transaction fees, leaving essentially no net draw on the general fund. The Small Business Administration’s business-loan guarantee authority is set by ceiling rather than appropriation; its disaster-loan account is $282M.

underreported: The Securities and Exchange Commission’s $2.15B is fully offset by section 31 transaction fees, so the headline figure overstates its cost — the bill provides that the net general-fund appropriation is reduced to essentially zero as fees come in.

The Small Business Administration’s large dollar figures ($16.5B and $35.5B) are loan and guarantee commitment ceilings, not money appropriated; the actual SBA appropriations (disaster loans $282M, loan administration $158M) are far smaller.
criticisms: IRS Enforcement is funded at $5.0B in annual appropriations, separate from the multi-year IRS funding provided in prior laws; the bill does not itself restore or rescind those separate balances.
gaps: Account-by-account allocations below the headline totals are delegated to the explanatory statement printed in the Congressional Record, so the public bill text does not itemize how lump sums are distributed across programs.

divisions.label: Division B — National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2026
divisions.brief: Full-year FY2026 funding for the State Department, U.S. diplomacy and embassy security, global health and humanitarian aid, security assistance including Foreign Military Financing, and U.S. contributions to international organizations.
divisions.summary: Division B is the State-Foreign Operations appropriations bill. It funds the day-to-day operations of the State Department and U.S. embassies, U.S. dues to the United Nations and other international organizations, global health programs including HIV/AIDS, humanitarian and refugee assistance, and security assistance such as Foreign Military Financing. It carries extensive country-specific earmarks (notably for Israel and Jordan) and policy conditions, and renames the former Economic Support Fund as “National Security Investment Programs.”

International Narcotics Control and Law Enforcement receives $1.4B, and the U.S. contribution to the World Bank’s International Development Association is $1.07B.

underreported: Two of the bill’s largest dollar figures are authorizations, not appropriations: it authorizes $3.2B for the World Bank’s 21st IDA replenishment and $7.8B for a U.S. callable-capital subscription to a development bank, both of which require separate future appropriations to take effect.

The Economic Support Fund — historically the main U.S. economic-aid account — is renamed “National Security Investment Programs” ($6.77B), and a new “America First Opportunity Fund” is created by consolidating portions of several existing accounts.
criticisms: Division C bars any U.S. contribution, grant or payment to the United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA) for prior years and FY2026, and through March 25, 2027 for FY2027 funds.

Israel’s $3.3B in Foreign Military Financing must be disbursed within 30 days of enactment, a faster cash-flow than for most other recipients, and the bill conditions or restricts a range of other contributions through country- and organization-specific provisos.
gaps: As with Division A, detailed allocations within each foreign-assistance account are set by the explanatory statement rather than the bill text, so the public bill does not itemize most country and program funding levels below the account headlines.

bills.official_title: An Act to provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of S. Con. Res. 33.

bills.summary: Provides about $69.55B in new funding through fiscal year 2029 to U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the Department of Homeland Security for border security, immigration enforcement, and removal operations. It was enacted as a budget reconciliation bill.

$13.02B for CBP agents carrying out immigration enforcement
$3.45B for border technology, including AI inspection and surveillance systems

$7.45B for Homeland Security Investigations, including $108.5M for child-exploitation investigators
At least $350M to arrest released aliens in non-cooperating jurisdictions

top_lines.headline: DHS and State Coordination
subs: $2.5B in additional DHS funding under Title I and $2.5B under Title II
Funds expanded use of 287(g) agreements with state and local police
All funds remain available through September 30, 2029

sections.label: Section 1 — Short Title; Table of Contents

items.main: Names the Act the “Secure America Act” and lists its titles and sections.
items.detail: Short-title and table-of-contents section — citation name and a navigational list of the two titles; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Title I — Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs

items.main: $9.55B for CBP to hire, pay, train, and equip Border Patrol agents and support personnel for functions other than immigration and customs enforcement (Sec 101).
items.detail: Section 102 provides $7.45B for ICE Homeland Security Investigations agents and support, of which $108.5M is for child-exploitation investigators and forensic analysts at the HSI Victim Identification Laboratory. No funds under Section 101 may be used to recruit or train processing coordinators after October 31, 2028.

items.main: $3.45B for border security, technology, and screening (Sec 103).
items.detail: Funds nonintrusive inspection equipment using artificial intelligence and machine learning, air and marine response platforms, border surveillance technology, the biometric entry-and-exit system, and counter-fentanyl efforts. None of the funds may buy surveillance towers that CBP has not tested and accepted as delivering autonomous capabilities.

items.main: $2.5B in additional DHS appropriations for the purposes of Title I (Sec 104).
items.detail: Appropriated to the Secretary of Homeland Security for fiscal year 2026, to remain available until September 30, 2029.

sections.label: Title II — Committee on the Judiciary

items.main: $13.02B for CBP to hire, pay, train, and equip agents and support staff to carry out immigration enforcement (Sec 201).
items.detail: Appropriated for fiscal year 2026 and available until September 30, 2029, for immigration-enforcement activities and related mission support and operations.

items.main: $31.08B for ICE immigration enforcement and removal operations (Sec 202).
items.detail: Covers ICE personnel and directorates, removal transportation, information technology including body-worn cameras, facility and fleet maintenance, 287(g) agreements with state and local authorities, and attorneys in the Office of the Principal Legal Advisor. At least $350M is set aside to arrest "covered unlawful aliens" released in jurisdictions that are not qualified cooperating jurisdictions; those funds may not be used to release such individuals.

items.main: $2.5B in additional DHS appropriations for the purposes of Title II (Sec 203).
items.detail: Available for purposes in this title or in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21, to remain available until September 30, 2029.

underreported.summary: Within the $7.45B ICE/HSI appropriation, $108.5M is directed to child-exploitation investigators and forensic analysts at the HSI Victim Identification Laboratory and Special Agent in Charge offices, to support identifying and rescuing victims of child sexual exploitation.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned "U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement," but this line item funds a victim-identification mission distinct from the bill's headline immigration-enforcement purpose.

underreported.summary: None of the $3.45B may be used to buy or deploy southwest- or northern-border surveillance towers that CBP has not tested and accepted as delivering autonomous capabilities.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision narrows what border-surveillance procurement is allowed, conditioning it on an "autonomous" performance standard defined in the same section.

underreported.summary: The at-least-$350M for arresting "covered unlawful aliens" may not be used to release, parole, place on alternatives to detention, or otherwise facilitate the community release of such individuals, except as required by existing law.
underreported.why_unreported: The provision appropriates funds to arrest covered unlawful aliens, but its operative effect is also a spending restriction tied to whether a jurisdiction has a 287(g) agreement or an 8 U.S.C. 1373 certification.

gaps: The bill funds hiring of CBP and ICE personnel through FY2029 but does not set numeric hiring targets for agents.
Section 101 funds Border Patrol for "functions other than immigration enforcement and customs functions" but does not define which functions those are.
The bill appropriates funds available through September 30, 2029 but specifies no reporting or oversight mechanism on how the funds are spent.
Section 203 makes funds available for purposes in paragraph (3) or (7) of section 100051 of Public Law 119-21 but does not restate what those purposes are.

bills.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bills.official_title: An Act to require covered platforms to remove nonconsensual intimate visual depictions, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-12 on May 19, 2025. Sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX) with 21 cosponsors; its child-protection and anti-deepfake provisions drew bipartisan support and it passed both chambers before being signed.
bills.summary: Makes it a federal crime to knowingly publish nonconsensual intimate images of a person online — including AI-generated "deepfake" forgeries — and requires online platforms to remove such images within 48 hours of a valid request.
bills.brief: Creates federal criminal penalties for nonconsensual intimate-image publication (real or AI-generated) and requires covered platforms to remove flagged images within 48 hours.

top_lines.headline: New Federal Crime for Nonconsensual Intimate Images
subs: Bans knowingly publishing nonconsensual intimate images of adults that cause harm
Covers AI-generated "digital forgeries" indistinguishable from real images
Up to 2 years in prison for images of adults, 3 years for minors

top_lines.headline: Threats and Forfeiture
subs: Threatening to publish such images is also a crime
Courts must order forfeiture of proceeds and equipment used
Mandatory restitution to victims

top_lines.headline: 48-Hour Platform Takedown
subs: Covered platforms must build a removal-request process within 1 year
Must remove flagged images within 48 hours of a valid request
FTC enforces noncompliance as an unfair or deceptive practice

items.main: Names the Act the “Tools to Address Known Exploitation by Immobilizing Technological Deepfakes on Websites and Networks Act” (the “TAKE IT DOWN Act”).
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Criminal Prohibition on Intentional Disclosure

items.main: Makes it unlawful to knowingly publish, over an interactive computer service, an intimate visual depiction of an identifiable adult where the subject had a reasonable expectation of privacy and publication is intended to or does cause harm.
items.detail: Adds subsection (h) to Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934. A parallel prohibition covers "digital forgeries" — AI- or computer-generated images indistinguishable from authentic ones. Penalties are up to 2 years for offenses involving adults and up to 3 years for minors. Exceptions cover law-enforcement and intelligence activity, good-faith reporting, legal proceedings, and medical or educational use.

items.main: Threatening to publish such images for intimidation, coercion, or extortion is a separate crime, with mandatory forfeiture and restitution on conviction.
items.detail: Threats involving digital forgeries carry up to 18 months for adults and 30 months for minors. Courts must order forfeiture of any material distributed, proceeds, and equipment used, and must order restitution under section 2264 of title 18.

sections.label: Section 3 — Notice and Removal of Nonconsensual Intimate Visual Depictions

items.main: Within one year of enactment, covered platforms must establish a process for individuals to request removal of nonconsensual intimate images and must remove valid-request images within 48 hours.
items.detail: Platforms must post a clear, plain-language notice of the process and make reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies. A failure to comply is treated as an unfair or deceptive practice enforced by the Federal Trade Commission. Platforms acting in good faith to remove material claimed to be nonconsensual are shielded from liability even if the image is later found lawful.

items.main: Defines "covered platform" as a public website, online service, or application that primarily hosts user-generated content or regularly publishes nonconsensual intimate depictions.
items.detail: Excludes broadband internet access providers, electronic mail, and services that consist primarily of provider-selected (non-user-generated) content where any interactive feature is incidental.

items.main: If any provision of the Act or its amendments is held unenforceable or invalid, the remaining provisions are unaffected.
items.detail: Standard severability clause — preserves the rest of the Act if part is struck down; no substantive effect.

underreported.summary: A covered platform is not liable for good-faith removal of material claimed to be a nonconsensual intimate depiction, "regardless of whether the intimate visual depiction is ultimately determined to be unlawful or not."
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned notice-and-removal, but this clause grants platforms immunity for removing content even when the claim turns out to be unfounded.

underreported.summary: The crime applies to "digital forgeries" — images created with software, machine learning, or AI that a reasonable person cannot distinguish from authentic.
underreported.why_unreported: The prohibition extends beyond real photographs to computer-generated depictions, defining the Act's reach over deepfake media.

underreported.summary: Broadband providers, email, and content-curated services with only incidental interactivity are excluded from the "covered platform" definition.
underreported.why_unreported: The exclusions narrow which services carry the 48-hour takedown duty, separate from the headline platform obligation.

gaps: The bill requires covered platforms to remove images within 48 hours but provides no penalty for individual late removals beyond FTC unfair-practice enforcement.
The bill criminalizes publication but does not create a private civil cause of action for victims against the publisher.
The takedown duty applies to platforms hosting user-generated content but does not address search engines that index rather than host such images.
The bill defines consent but does not specify how platforms verify a removal requester's identity or resolve a disputed consent claim.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Dingell
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I rise today as a strong and unwavering advocate for women, children, and survivors of abuse and in support of a bill that I helped lead, S. 146, the TAKE IT DOWN Act. The rise of deepfake pornography and nonconsensual intimate images is a growing crisis that demands urgent action now. We need to work together to protect women and children from these evolving threats. New generative artificial intelligence tools are being weaponized to humiliate, silence, and terrorize women and children.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Salazar
featured_quotes.text: every generation of Congress faces moments that test our commitment to justice, and today is one of those moments. The Senate has already done its job. They passed this legislation unanimously. Now, it is our turn in the House of Representatives. This is our moment to stand up to protect our children and make this the law of the land. The name of the legislation is the TAKE IT DOWN Act. The mission of this bill is simple, profound, and long lasting. It stops cyber abuse.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Guthrie
featured_quotes.text: I echo the sentiments of Representative Dean and my friend Representative Salazar. I appreciate the comments that they just made. Last month, I joined a bipartisan group convened by the First Lady. We heard from young survivors and their parents who were targeted by those abhorrent practices. I am sad to say that this issue struck close to home with the heartbreaking death of my constituent, 16-year-old Elijah Heacock.

added: New federal crime (47 U.S.C. 223(h)) for nonconsensual publication of intimate images, including AI deepfakes
48-hour platform takedown requirement enforced by the FTC (Sec 3)
Mandatory criminal forfeiture and restitution for violations (Sec 2)
modified: Amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 to add the new prohibition and extend its existing defenses to the new subsection
