bills.title: ACES Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To provide for a study by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine on the prevalence and mortality of cancer among individuals who served as active duty aircrew in the Armed Forces, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-32 on August 14, 2025. Introduced by Sen. Mark Kelly (D-AZ) with 3 cosponsors; ordering a National Academies study of cancer among military aircrew is a low-cost veterans-health measure that drew no recorded opposition, clearing both chambers before being signed.
bills.summary: Orders an independent scientific study of how often cancer occurs, and how often it is fatal, among military members who served as aircrew on fixed-wing aircraft. The Department of Veterans Affairs must arrange for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to conduct it.
bills.brief: Directs a National Academies study on the prevalence and mortality of cancer among military fixed-wing aircrew.

top_lines.headline: National Academies Cancer Study
subs: VA must seek an agreement with the National Academies within 30 days of enactment
Study covers cancer prevalence and mortality among fixed-wing aircrew
Must report to Congress if the agreement is not finalized within 60 days of negotiations

top_lines.headline: Scope of the Study
subs: Identifies exposures tied to aircrew occupations (chemicals, compounds, agents)
Reviews 11 named cancer types, including brain, lung, prostate, and thyroid
Uses VA, DoD, and CDC death-index data where available

items.main: Names the Act the “ACES Act of 2025”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — National Academies Study on Cancer Among Active Duty Aircrew

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, within 30 days of enactment, to seek an agreement with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine to study the prevalence and mortality of cancers among covered individuals.
items.detail: The Secretary must finalize the agreement within 60 days of entering negotiations; if not, the Secretary must report to the Senate and House Veterans’ Affairs Committees explaining the delay and give a briefing at least every 60 days until it is finalized. "Covered individual" means a person who served on active duty in the Army, Navy, Air Force, or Marine Corps as an aircrew member of a fixed-wing aircraft (pilot, navigator, weapons systems operator, or other regular crew).

items.main: Requires the study to identify occupational exposures and review associations with overall cancer morbidity and mortality and 11 specified cancers.
items.detail: The named cancers are brain; colon and rectal; kidney; lung; melanoma skin; non-Hodgkin lymphoma; pancreatic; prostate; testicular; thyroid; and urinary bladder, plus others the Secretary deems appropriate. The study draws on VA, DoD, and Service health databases, the National Death Index, and the aircrew study conducted under section 750 of the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act (Public Law 116-283). The National Academies reports the results to the Secretary and the Veterans’ Affairs Committees.

underreported.section: Section 2(a)(2)(B) — reporting consequences for a missed deadline
underreported.summary: If the VA does not finalize the study agreement within 60 days of negotiations, the Secretary must report the reasons to Congress and brief the Veterans’ Affairs Committees at least every 60 days until it is done.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond ordering a study, the bill attaches a recurring congressional-reporting consequence to the VA missing the agreement deadline.

gaps: The bill orders a study of cancer among aircrew but does not itself establish or change any benefit, presumption, or treatment for affected veterans.
The study covers fixed-wing aircrew but does not address members who served as aircrew on rotary-wing aircraft.

added: New requirement for a National Academies study on cancer prevalence and mortality among military fixed-wing aircrew

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pfluger
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I rise today not just as a Member of Congress but as a wingman, a servicemember, and a friend to those in uniform and in strong support of S. 201, the Aviator Cancers Examination Study Act, or the ACES Act. Far too many of our military aviators and aircrew are being diagnosed with cancer at troubling rates.

added: VA must seek the study agreement with the National Academies within 30 days of enactment
Agreement must be finalized within 60 days after the Secretary enters negotiations

If the 60-day finalization deadline is missed, VA must report to the Veterans' Affairs Committees explaining the delay and estimating a completion date, plus brief them at least every 60 days until finalized
modified: Short title changed from "ACES Act" to "ACES Act of 2025"
Subsection (a) retitled from "In General" to "Agreement" and split into a deadline-bearing structure

bills.title: Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act
bills.official_title: To reauthorize funding to monitor, assess, and research the Great Lakes Basin, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-67 on December 26, 2025. Introduced by Sen. Gary Peters (D-MI) with 1 cosponsor; extending an existing Great Lakes research funding authorization is a narrow regional measure that drew no recorded opposition, clearing both chambers before being signed.
bills.summary: Extends the existing federal authorization to fund monitoring, assessment, and research of the Great Lakes Basin. The prior authorization was set to run through 2025; this law continues it through 2030.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes funding to monitor, assess, and research the Great Lakes Basin through 2030.

top_lines.headline: What the Great Lakes Authorization Does
subs: Authorizes federal funding to monitor, assess, and research the Great Lakes Basin

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extends the funding authorization from 2025 through 2030

items.main: Names the Act the “Great Lakes Fishery Research Reauthorization Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Reauthorization of Great Lakes Basin Funding

items.main: Extends the authorization of funding to monitor, assess, and research the Great Lakes Basin from 2025 through 2030.
items.detail: The change amends Section 201(d) of title II of division P of the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020 (16 U.S.C. 941h(d)) by striking "2025" and inserting "2030." The bill makes no other change to the underlying program.

gaps: The bill extends the funding authorization through 2030 but does not itself appropriate funds or change the amount authorized for the Great Lakes Basin program.

modified: Extends the Great Lakes Basin monitoring and research funding authorization from 2025 to 2030 (16 U.S.C. 941h(d))

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Dingell
featured_quotes.text: The Great Lakes aren't just a part of Michigan and the heartland's landscape. They are part of our economy, our identity, and our heritage. They are more than 20 percent of the world's freshwater and must be protected. They provide drinking water to millions. They are home to a thriving ecosystem for a wide breadth of species. They support countless jobs. Our Great Lakes' fishing economy alone is worth more than $5 billion.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Stauber
featured_quotes.text: this bill supports effective fishery management, which starts with accurate data.

bills.title: SECURE Grid Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to require States to include supporting the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local distribution systems in State energy security plans.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Robert E. Latta (R-OH) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill folds local-distribution-system security into existing State energy security plans and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Updates the federal law on State energy security plans so States also plan for the physical security, cybersecurity, and resilience of local electric distribution systems — the lower-voltage lines and equipment that deliver power to communities. It adds these systems and their equipment suppliers to what State plans must address.
bills.brief: Requires State energy security plans to address the security and resilience of local electric distribution systems.

top_lines.headline: Local Distribution Systems in State Plans
subs: Defines a local distribution system as utility energy infrastructure at 100 kilovolts or less
State plans must address physical attacks on local distribution and the bulk-power system
State plans must address cybersecurity threats that may impact the bulk-power system

top_lines.headline: Equipment Suppliers and Supply Chain
subs: Adds suppliers of electricity generation, transmission, and distribution equipment to consultation
State plans must address supply chain risks for that equipment
Plans must address weather-related threats and vulnerabilities

top_lines.headline: State Determination and Timeline
subs: A State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary
Statutory year reference in subsection (i) changed from 2025 to 2030
Adds a risk mitigation approach for reliability and end-use resilience

items.main: Names the Act the "Securing Community Upgrades for a Resilient Grid Act" or the "SECURE Grid Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Consideration of the Security of Local Distribution Systems in State Energy Security Plans

items.main: Amends Section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (42 U.S.C. 6326) to add "local distribution system," defined as any energy infrastructure owned and operated by an electric utility at a voltage of 100 kilovolts or less.
items.detail: The new definition is added to subsection (a). Subsection (h) is also amended to insert "local distribution system" after "electric utility," extending existing plan provisions to cover these systems.

items.main: Rewrites the hazards a State plan must address to include physical threats, physical attacks on local distribution systems and the bulk-power system, supply chain risks for electricity equipment, and cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems that may impact the bulk-power system.
items.detail: Subsection (c)(3) is replaced to list weather-related threats, physical attacks, and supply chain risks as physical threats, plus a separate cybersecurity category. Subsection (c)(5) is replaced to require a risk mitigation approach to enhance reliability and end-use resilience, including responding to, mitigating, and recovering from those hazards.

items.main: Adds suppliers of electricity generation, transmission, and distribution equipment to the parties States consult (subsection (b)(2)); adds suppliers of generation and transmission equipment to the coordination provision (subsection (d)(3)); and lets States submit plans without the Secretary’s approval.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(2) and subsection (d)(3) are amended to add equipment suppliers. Subsection (e) is restructured to state that a plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary. Subsection (i) is amended by striking "2025" and inserting "2030."

underreported.summary: A State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary; States self-determine the content submitted.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill expands what plans must address, but this provision establishes that the Secretary does not approve the submission, leaving plan sufficiency to the State rather than federal review.

underreported.summary: The provision striking "2025" and inserting "2030" changes the year referenced in subsection (i) of the amended statute.
underreported.why_unreported: The date change is a single-word amendment separate from the bill headline on security and resilience, adjusting the timeframe in the underlying statute.

gaps: The bill requires plans to address cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems but does not specify security standards, funding, or penalties for those systems.
The bill adds equipment suppliers to consultation but does not define which suppliers qualify or address foreign-sourced equipment beyond a general supply chain risk category.
The bill states a plan submission need not be approved by the Secretary but does not describe any federal review or consequence if a plan omits the newly required hazards.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Latta
featured_quotes.text: State energy security plans, or SESPs, provide States with an opportunity to identify threats and vulnerabilities in their respective energy networks. This collaborative process ensures that States can stay on the cutting edge of an evolving threat landscape. While the initial exercise of SESPs has meaningfully assisted States in managing their energy systems, there is room for improvement to enhance visibility and threat detection and to holistically consider disparate vulnerabilities across the sector.

added: New statutory definition of "local distribution system" as utility energy infrastructure at 100 kilovolts or less
New requirement that State plans address physical attacks and supply chain risks for electricity equipment, and cybersecurity threats to local distribution systems
New provision that a State plan submission is not required to be approved by the Secretary
modified: Amends Section 366 of the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (42 U.S.C. 6326) to add equipment suppliers to consultation and to rewrite the hazards and risk mitigation paragraphs
Changes the year reference in subsection (i) from 2025 to 2030

bills.title: Energy Emergency Leadership Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Department of Energy Organization Act with respect to functions assigned to Assistant Secretaries, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Laurel M. Lee (R-FL) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill assigns energy emergency and security functions to an Assistant Secretary at the Department of Energy and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Adds energy emergency and energy security duties to the list of functions the Secretary of Energy may assign to an Assistant Secretary. These duties cover energy infrastructure security, cybersecurity, and helping state, local, and Tribal governments respond to energy threats when they ask.
bills.brief: Assigns energy emergency and energy security functions to an Assistant Secretary at the Department of Energy.

top_lines.headline: Energy Emergency and Security Functions
subs: Adds a new function class to Assistant Secretary duties under the DOE Organization Act
Covers infrastructure security, resilience, emerging threats, cybersecurity, and supply
Includes emergency planning, preparedness, coordination, response, and restoration

top_lines.headline: Technical Assistance to Governments
subs: Provides technical assistance on request of a State, local, or Tribal government
Also available on request of an energy sector entity
Aims to protect against, detect, and respond to energy security threats and incidents

top_lines.headline: Interagency Coordination
subs: Secretary must ensure the new functions are performed with relevant Federal agencies

items.main: Names the Act the "Energy Emergency Leadership Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Functions Assigned to Assistant Secretaries

items.main: Amends subsection (a) of section 203 of the Department of Energy Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7133(a)) to add a new paragraph (12) listing energy emergency and energy security functions among those assigned to Assistant Secretaries.
items.detail: The new functions include responsibilities for energy infrastructure, security and resilience, emerging threats, cybersecurity, supply, and emergency planning and preparedness, coordination, response, and restoration, as appropriate.

items.main: The new paragraph authorizes, upon request of a State, local, or Tribal government or energy sector entity, the provision of technical assistance and support to protect against, detect, and respond to energy security threats, risks, and incidents.
items.detail: Such assistance is to be provided in coordination with other Federal agencies as appropriate. It is triggered by a request from the covered government or energy sector entity rather than initiated unilaterally.

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Energy to ensure the functions described in the new section 203(a)(12) are performed in coordination with relevant Federal agencies.
items.detail: This coordination requirement applies to the functions added by this Act. The bill states no funding, deadline, or reporting requirement for the new functions.

underreported.section: Section 203(a)(12)(B) — technical assistance to energy sector entities
underreported.summary: Beyond governments, the new paragraph lets the Department provide technical assistance and support to an "energy sector entity" upon its request to protect against, detect, and respond to energy security threats.
underreported.why_unreported: The short title frames the change as internal leadership on energy emergencies, but the operative text extends Department technical support directly to private energy sector entities on request.

gaps: The bill assigns energy emergency and energy security functions but does not appropriate any funds or specify staffing for carrying them out.
The bill authorizes technical assistance upon request but sets no deadline, standard, or eligibility criteria for responding to such requests.
The bill directs coordination with relevant Federal agencies but does not name the agencies or specify how coordination is to occur.

added: New paragraph (12) in section 203(a) of the Department of Energy Organization Act listing energy emergency and energy security functions
New authority to provide technical assistance and support to State, local, or Tribal governments and energy sector entities upon request
modified: Amends subsection (a) of section 203 of the Department of Energy Organization Act (42 U.S.C. 7133(a)) by adding the new function class at the end

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: This legislation passed out of the Subcommittee on Energy unanimously because both Republicans and Democrats on the Committee recognized how critical it is to have accountable leadership protecting our electric grid. Today, the United States is experiencing record energy demand, driven by artificial intelligence, data centers, renewed domestic manufacturing, and widespread electrification across our economy. Meeting that demand safely requires not only robust and reliable generation but also a secure and resilient grid to deliver it.

bills.title: Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to reauthorize the Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-IA) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill reauthorizes an existing utility-cybersecurity grant program and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Renews a federal program that helps rural, municipal, and small electric utilities defend their systems against cyberattacks. It gives the Secretary $250M over five years to hand out grants, technical assistance, and prizes to utilities that often lack their own cybersecurity resources.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program and authorizes $250M for it through 2030.

top_lines.headline: What the Utility Cybersecurity Program Does
subs: The Secretary awards grants, cooperative agreements, and prizes to eligible utilities
Deploys cybersecurity technology and expands threat information sharing
Provides technical assistance to protect, detect, respond to, and recover from cyber threats

top_lines.headline: Who Is Eligible and Prioritized
subs: Covers rural co-ops, municipal utilities, and investor-owned utilities selling under 4,000,000 MWh/year
Includes not-for-profits partnered with at least 6 qualifying utilities
Priority for entities with limited cyber resources or bulk-power/defense-critical assets

top_lines.headline: Funding and Information Protection
subs: Authorizes $250M for the program for fiscal years 2026 through 2030
Information shared under the program is exempt from FOIA and state open-records laws
Awards may be made on a competitive or noncompetitive basis

items.main: Names the Act the "Rural and Municipal Utility Cybersecurity Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program

items.main: Amends Section 40124 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (42 U.S.C. 18723) to have the Secretary maintain the Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program, providing technical assistance and funding to eligible electric utilities to protect against, detect, respond to, and recover from cybersecurity threats.
items.detail: The Secretary awards funding through grants, cooperative agreements, and prizes on a competitive or noncompetitive basis, develops award criteria, and establishes a process to inform all eligible entities of opportunities. The program's objectives are to deploy advanced cybersecurity technologies for electric utility systems and to increase eligible entities' participation in cybersecurity threat information sharing programs.

items.main: Defines eligible entities as rural electric cooperatives, municipally owned or other political-subdivision utilities, not-for-profits partnered with at least 6 such utilities, and investor-owned utilities that sell less than 4,000,000 megawatt hours per year.
items.detail: In awarding funding and technical assistance, the Secretary must give priority to an eligible entity that has limited cybersecurity resources, owns assets critical to the reliability of the bulk-power system, or owns or operates defense critical electric infrastructure. The terms bulk-power system and defense critical electric infrastructure take their meanings from sections 215(a) and 215A(a) of the Federal Power Act.

items.main: Deems information shared by or with government under the program to be voluntarily shared and exempts it from the Freedom of Information Act and any state, Tribal, or local open-records, open-meetings, or sunshine law.
items.detail: Authorizes $250M to be appropriated to the Secretary to carry out the section for the period of fiscal years 2026 through 2030. Awards and technical assistance are subject to the availability of appropriations.

underreported.summary: Information shared by or with the Federal Government or a State, Tribal, or local government under the program is deemed voluntarily shared and exempted from FOIA and from any state, Tribal, or local freedom-of-information, open-government, open-meetings, open-records, or sunshine law.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is titled and structured as a grant and technical-assistance program (subsections (b) through (d)), but subsection (e) also creates a broad disclosure exemption reaching state, Tribal, and local transparency laws, an effect not apparent from the program's funding-and-assistance label.

underreported.summary: Investor-owned electric utilities qualify as eligible entities if they sell less than 4,000,000 megawatt hours of electricity per year.
underreported.why_unreported: The program is titled for rural and municipal utilities, but the eligibility definition also extends to smaller investor-owned utilities meeting the sales threshold.

gaps: The bill authorizes $250M for the program but does not specify how the funds are allocated across fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
The program prioritizes entities that own defense critical electric infrastructure but does not set a minimum share of funding for that category.
The bill exempts shared information from disclosure laws but does not address how long that information is retained or when the exemption ends.
The program is directed at eligible entities with limited cybersecurity resources but sets no numeric threshold defining what counts as limited.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Miller-Meeks
featured_quotes.text: Just this spring, national security experts warned that hostile nation-states are shifting from isolated cyber incidents to sustained campaigns against U.S. critical infrastructure, including the energy sector. Yet, many small and rural utilities lack the capacity and expertise to act on this information. RMUC is designed to close that gap. In Iowa's First District, rural electric cooperatives serve ratepayers across 20 counties and face the same threats as major urban systems but with fewer resources.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. McClellan
featured_quotes.text: This bill represents the sort of bipartisan work that is important for the security and stability of the American grid and the safety of the American people. This bill reauthorizes the vital RMUC program, which helps rural and small municipalities to protect themselves against ever-multiplying and more sophisticated cybersecurity threats that could prove severely disruptive to small and rural communities alike, just like the ones I represent in Virginia's Fourth Congressional District.

added: Authorizes $250M for the Rural and Municipal Utility Advanced Cybersecurity Grant and Technical Assistance Program for fiscal years 2026 through 2030
modified: Amends Section 40124 of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (42 U.S.C. 18723) by replacing it with the reauthorized program text

bills.title: Energy Threat Analysis Center Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To amend the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act to reauthorize the Department of Energy's Energy Sector Operational Support for Cyberresilience Program to provide operational support for energy sector cybersecurity and resilience.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Kathy Castor (D-FL) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill reauthorizes an existing Department of Energy energy-sector cybersecurity program and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Continues a Department of Energy program that helps protect the country's energy systems — the energy sector — from cyberattacks by sharing threat information between the government and energy companies. It renews the program's funding authorization for five more years and lets the Department run it through a dedicated Energy Threat Analysis Center.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Department of Energy's energy-sector cybersecurity support program through fiscal year 2031 and authorizes an Energy Threat Analysis Center to carry it out.

top_lines.headline: What the Cyberresilience Program Does
subs: Shares classified and unclassified cyber threat information with the energy sector
Jointly analyzes threats to energy systems and recommends fixes
Builds technical infrastructure for advanced analytics on energy-sector threats

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Extends the program's authorization from fiscal years 2022-2026 to 2027-2031
Authorizes an Energy Threat Analysis Center at one or more physical locations
Makes program participation a discretionary, unreviewable choice of the Secretary

top_lines.headline: Information Handling Rules
subs: Information shared under the program is exempt from Freedom of Information Act disclosure
Shared information deemed voluntarily shared and withheld from the public without discretion
Program is not an advisory committee under federal advisory-committee law

items.main: Names the Act the "Energy Threat Analysis Center Act of 2026".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Energy Sector Operational Support for Cyberresilience Program

items.main: Amends Section 40125(c) of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (42 U.S.C. 18724(c)) to add a new stated purpose of strengthening the collective defense, response, and resilience of the U.S. energy sector.
items.detail: The new purpose directs the program to enhance government-energy sector collaboration to analyze threats and deny, disrupt, and mitigate operational impacts to energy systems — by exchanging information at classified and unclassified levels and by building technical infrastructure to house, access, and perform advanced analytics. It also directs the program to advance understanding of national security risks and vulnerabilities and of threat-actor tactics, techniques, and procedures. The existing purposes are redesignated as subparagraphs (B) through (F), and one redesignated subparagraph (F) is struck.

items.main: Authorizes the Secretary to carry out program activities through an Energy Threat Analysis Center, which may be established at one or more physical locations.
items.detail: The Center is added as a new paragraph (2). The Secretary may use it to carry out any activity of the program developed under paragraph (1); the bill does not require that the Center be established or specify a location.

items.main: Sets the terms on which program assistance is provided and shields program-related information from disclosure.
items.detail: Provision of assistance or information is at the sole and unreviewable discretion of the Secretary and creates no right or benefit to similar assistance for any other entity. The program is not an advisory committee under chapter 10 of title 5. Information shared by or with federal, State, Tribal, or local governments is deemed voluntarily shared, exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act (5 U.S.C. 552), and withheld without discretion under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3)(B) and any State, Tribal, or local disclosure law.

items.main: Extends the program's authorization of appropriations from fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to fiscal years 2027 through 2031.
items.detail: The change is made by striking "2022 through 2026" and inserting "2027 through 2031" in the redesignated authorization paragraph (renumbered from paragraph (2) to paragraph (6)). The bill states no dollar figure for the authorization.

underreported.summary: Information shared under the program with or by federal, State, Tribal, or local governments is deemed voluntarily shared, exempt from the Freedom of Information Act, and withheld from the public without discretion, overriding State, Tribal, and local disclosure laws.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is titled and structured as a program reauthorization, but subsection (c)(5) also creates a standing public-disclosure exemption that reaches State, Tribal, and local records laws, not only federal FOIA.

underreported.summary: Program assistance and information are provided at the sole and unreviewable discretion of the Secretary and create no enforceable right or benefit for any entity to similar assistance.
underreported.why_unreported: The reauthorization label suggests continuity, but this clause forecloses judicial review of who receives program assistance and bars entities from claiming equal access.

gaps: The bill authorizes an Energy Threat Analysis Center but does not specify where it will be located, how it will be staffed, or a deadline to establish it.
The bill reauthorizes the program's appropriations for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 but states no dollar amount for that authorization.
The bill extends and expands a threat-information-sharing program but does not set any reporting requirement to Congress on the program's activities or results.

added: New program purpose to strengthen the collective defense, response, and resilience of the U.S. energy sector through government-industry threat analysis and collaboration
Authority to carry out the program through an Energy Threat Analysis Center at one or more physical locations

New provisions making program assistance discretionary and unreviewable, exempting the program from advisory-committee law, and exempting shared information from Freedom of Information Act and State/Tribal/local disclosure
modified: Reauthorizes appropriations for the Energy Sector Operational Support for Cyberresilience Program: fiscal years 2022 through 2026 → fiscal years 2027 through 2031
removed: Strikes one existing program-purpose subparagraph (redesignated subparagraph (F)) of Section 40125(c)(1)

bills.title: KIDS Act
bills.official_title: To protect children and teens online, empower parents and strengthen families, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-KY) and passed the House 267-117 on June 29, 2026; the bill creates FTC-enforced online-safety duties across obscenity sites, social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots, and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Sets new federal rules to protect people under 17 online. It requires adult-content sites to check whether users are minors, makes social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots add safety tools and parental controls, limits messaging features for young users, and orders several studies — all enforced by the Federal Trade Commission.
bills.brief: Creates federal online-safety duties for adult sites, social platforms, video games, and AI chatbots aimed at users under 17, enforced by the FTC.

top_lines.headline: Age Checks for Adult Content Sites
subs: Sites where over one-third of material is harmful sexual content must verify users' age
Verification takes effect 1 year after enactment
Confirming you are not a minor is not enough to pass
Cannot be required to submit government-issued ID

top_lines.headline: Platform Safeguards and Parental Tools
subs: Covered platforms must give known minors safety controls, set most-protective by default
Must provide parental tools to manage settings, purchases, and screen time
Independent third-party audit required within 18 months, then annually

top_lines.headline: Messaging Limits for Young Users
subs: Bans disappearing (ephemeral) messaging features for known minors
Bans direct messaging for known users under 13
Parental direct-messaging controls required for teen users

top_lines.headline: AI Chatbot Rules
subs: Chatbots must disclose they are AI, not a person, to known minors
Must show suicide/crisis hotline resources when a minor raises suicide
Must advise a break after 3 continuous hours of use

top_lines.headline: Studies and FTC Enforcement
subs: Orders studies on social media, fentanyl access, chatbots, and safety tools
Violations treated as unfair or deceptive acts under the FTC Act
State attorneys general may sue on behalf of residents

sections.label: Section 1 — Short Title; Table of Contents

items.main: Names the Act the "Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act" or the "KIDS Act".
items.detail: Short-title and table-of-contents section — citation name and structure only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines terms used across the Act, including "minor" as an individual under age 17 and "chatbot," "design feature," and "personalized recommendation system."
items.detail: Ties several terms to existing law (artificial intelligence to 15 U.S.C. 9401; personal information and verifiable parental consent to the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act at 15 U.S.C. 6501). "Design feature" includes infinite scrolling, autoplay, push notifications, and personalized recommendation systems.

sections.label: Title I — Shielding Minors From Obscenity

items.main: Requires providers of "covered platforms" — sites where more than one-third of the material is sexual material harmful to minors — to adopt commercially available technology verification measures to identify minors and prevent them from accessing that material, beginning 1 year after enactment.
items.detail: Titled the "SCREEN Act." Providers must use an age-verification measure (a user's self-confirmation is not sufficient), give clear notice, limit retention of verification data, and maintain data-security practices. Providers may not be required to have users submit government-issued ID. The FTC must consult specified experts, and the Comptroller General must report to Congress within 3 years on effectiveness, compliance, privacy, and speech effects. States are preempted from requiring covered platforms to use technology verification measures.

sections.label: Title II — Addressing Harms to Minors on Online Platforms

items.main: Requires social-media-style "covered platforms" to maintain policies addressing enumerated harms to minors and to give known minors safety safeguards and parents parental tools, set to the most-protective level by default.
items.detail: Subtitle A ("Kids Online Safety Act") lists harms to address (threats of violence, sexual exploitation and abuse, drug/tobacco/gambling/alcohol activity, deceptive financial practices), requires reporting mechanisms with a response no later than 10 days, bars advertising illegal products to known minors, and requires an independent third-party audit within 18 months and annually thereafter (results to the FTC within 30 days, public report within 45 days). It states it does not impose a duty of care or require age gating.

items.main: Subtitle B ("Safe Messaging for Kids Act") bans ephemeral messaging features for known minors, bans direct messaging for known users under 13, and requires parental direct-messaging controls for teen users age 13 and up.
items.detail: Parental controls must, by default, alert parents to requests from unapproved contacts, let them approve or deny contacts, and let them disable messaging or hide a teen's profile. A rule of construction bars overriding strong encryption. Subtitle C ("SPY Kids Act") bars market or product research on known minors except to improve privacy, security, or safety, or as needed for legal compliance.

items.main: Requires online video game providers to give parents of known-minor users safeguards to limit communication with other players, enabled and set to the most protective level by default.
items.detail: Titled the "Safer GAMING Act." Providers must also give minors and parents easy-to-use tools to prevent a minor's profile from being recommended to non-minors, restrict purchases and financial transactions, and limit playing time, plus give clear notice when safeguards are in effect. States are preempted from regulating these communication tools and safeguards, except for general tort, contract, and consumer-protection law.

items.main: Sets rules for chatbot providers with respect to known-minor users, including a bar on falsely claiming the chatbot is a licensed professional and required disclosures.
items.detail: Titled the "SAFE BOTs Act." Providers must disclose the chatbot is an AI system and not a person at the first interaction and when a minor asks, and must provide suicide and crisis hotline resources when a minor raises suicide. Providers must maintain policies advising a break after 3 continuous hours of use and addressing minors' access to harmful sexual material, gambling, and restricted drugs, tobacco, or alcohol.

sections.label: Title V — Research, Education, and Best Practices

items.main: Orders multiple federal studies, education efforts, and a new partnership on protecting minors online.
items.detail: The FTC (with HHS) must study social media use by minors and report within 3 years; report on minors' access to fentanyl through social media within 1 year; and review industry safety tools, reporting within 3 years. HHS through NIH must run a 4-year longitudinal study on chatbots and minors' mental health. Section 522 amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking sections 211 through 214 and 216 and inserting a new FTC public-awareness campaign, annual report for 10 years, and definitions. The AWARE Act directs FTC chatbot educational resources, and the Kids Internet Safety Partnership Act establishes a Commerce-led partnership that sunsets 5 years after it is established.

items.main: Sets enforcement, judicial review, rules of construction, severability, and the effective date for the Act.
items.detail: Violations are treated as unfair or deceptive acts under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act and enforced by the FTC; state attorneys general may bring civil actions on behalf of residents after notice to the FTC. Constitutional challenges may be filed only in the D.C. Circuit, within 90 days of enactment. Rules of construction protect First Amendment-protected viewpoints, bar requiring decryption or weakening encryption, and bar altering section 230. Except as otherwise provided, the Act takes effect 1 year after enactment.

underreported.section: Section 522 — amendment to the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act
underreported.summary: Strikes sections 211 through 214 and 216 of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) and replaces them with a new FTC public-awareness and education campaign, an annual report for 10 years, and definitions.
underreported.why_unreported: This part sits in Title V under an education heading, but the operative text repeals and rewrites parts of a separate existing statute rather than only adding new study or education activity.

underreported.summary: Each of Titles I through IV, and Subtitles B and C of Title II, bars states from maintaining or enforcing laws that conflict with or regulate the same subject as the relevant title, while preserving general tort, contract, product-liability, criminal, and consumer-protection law.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is protecting minors online, but multiple sections also limit state authority to regulate these areas — a preemption effect distinct from the safety mandates in the same titles.

underreported.section: Section 602 — judicial review in the D.C. Circuit
underreported.summary: Constitutional challenges to the Act may be filed only in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, which has exclusive jurisdiction, and only within 90 days of enactment for facial challenges.
underreported.why_unreported: This channels and time-limits constitutional litigation to a single court, an effect not apparent from the bill's child-safety framing.

gaps: The bill requires covered platforms to give safeguards to users the provider "knows" is a minor but does not require platforms to determine users' ages outside the Title I obscenity-site context.
Title I requires adult-content sites to verify age but does not specify penalties or amounts for a provider that fails to comply, relying on general FTC Act enforcement.
The Act repeatedly turns on whether a provider "knows" a user is a minor but does not define what steps establish such knowledge for platforms outside the technology-verification requirement.
The bill orders studies on chatbots, social media, and fentanyl access but does not set requirements that follow automatically from those findings.
Title IV addresses chatbot conduct toward minors but does not require chatbot providers to determine which users are minors.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bilirakis
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to speak in strong in support of H.R. 7757, the Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act, or the KIDS Act. This package will finally give parents real tools to protect their kids online. A key provision in the KIDS Act is my Kids Online Safety Act, or KOSA. I have been working on KOSA, Mr. Speaker, for 3 years, and I am proud to see it finally reach the House floor. The need for action has never been clearer.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Lee
featured_quotes.text: Children today are growing up in a digital world that looks dramatically different than it did just a generation ago. While technology has created tremendous opportunities to learn and to connect, it has also exposed young people to online predators, sexual exploitation, privacy violations, and increasingly sophisticated threats driven by artificial intelligence. Parents are doing everything they can to protect their children online but should not have to navigate these challenges alone.

added: New requirement that adult-content "covered platforms" (over one-third harmful sexual material) use technology verification measures to identify minors, effective 1 year after enactment (Title I)
New safeguards, parental tools, reporting mechanisms, and annual third-party audits for social-media-style covered platforms serving known minors (Title II Subtitle A)
New prohibitions on ephemeral messaging for known minors and direct messaging for known users under 13, plus required parental direct-messaging controls for teens (Title II Subtitle B)
New default-on communication safeguards and parental controls for online video game providers (Title III)
New disclosure, break-reminder, and content-policy requirements for AI chatbot providers serving known minors (Title IV)
New Kids Internet Safety Partnership at the Department of Commerce, sunsetting 5 years after establishment (Section 526)
New federal studies on social media use, fentanyl access, industry safety tools, and a 4-year NIH study on chatbots and minors' mental health (Title V Subtitle A)
modified: Amends the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act (15 U.S.C. 6551 et seq.) by striking sections 211 through 214 and 216 and inserting a new FTC public-awareness campaign, a 10-year annual report, and definitions (Section 522)
removed: Repeals sections 211 through 214 and 216 of the Protecting Children in the 21st Century Act as they previously read (Section 522)

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

bills.title: TRIA Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To extend the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Mike Flood (R-NE) and passed the House 373-15 on June 29, 2026; the bill extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program sunset from 2027 to 2034 and revises its certification process, and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Extends the federal Terrorism Risk Insurance Program, which is set to end after 2027, so that it now runs through 2034. It also changes how the government decides whether an event counts as an "act of terrorism" for the program, including raising a dollar figure in that definition and adding public-notice steps.
bills.brief: Extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program through 2034 and revises how acts of terrorism are certified under it.

top_lines.headline: Program Extension
subs: Extends the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program's sunset from 2027 to 2034
Amends Section 108(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002

top_lines.headline: Certification Process Changes
subs: Raises a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M
Adds a lapse trigger if no certification within 90 days of a Federal Register notice
Requires a Federal Register notice within 30 days of starting a certification review

top_lines.headline: Technical Amendments
subs: Updates statutory year references in Section 103(e)(7)(E)(i)
Renames "Terrorism Insurance Program" to "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout

items.main: Names the Act the "TRIA Program Reauthorization Act of 2026".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends Section 108(a) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002 (15 U.S.C. 6701 note) by striking "2027" and inserting "2034", extending the program's end date.
items.detail: The change moves the sunset year in Section 108(a) from 2027 to 2034. The bill text states only the year substitution; the program's operating terms are set in the underlying Act, which is not reproduced in this bill.

items.main: Amends Section 102(1) of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act of 2002 to raise a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M and to add a new condition tied to a 90-day certification window.
items.detail: In subparagraph (B), the bill strikes "$5M" and inserts "$25M", and adds a new clause (iii) providing that the definition is affected if the Secretary did not certify an act as an act of terrorism before the end of the 90-day period following a Federal Register notice under subparagraph (D)(i).

items.main: Replaces subparagraph (D) with new notice requirements directing the Secretary to publish Federal Register notices about the certification process.
items.detail: The Secretary must publish a Federal Register notice, not later than 30 days after beginning the process of determining whether to certify an act as an act of terrorism, informing the public that this determination is underway. The Secretary may also notify the public, through the Federal Register or otherwise, that an act is not being evaluated for certification.

items.main: Updates year references in Section 103(e)(7)(E)(i) of the Act and standardizes the program's name throughout the statute.
items.detail: In subclause (I), "2022" becomes "2029" and "2024" becomes "2031"; in subclause (II), "2023" becomes "2030", "2029" becomes "2036", and "2024" becomes "2031"; in subclause (III), "2029" becomes "2036" and "2024" becomes "2031". Separately, the Act is amended by striking "Terrorism Insurance Program" each place it appears and inserting "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program".

underreported.summary: Adds a condition to the certification definition tied to the Secretary not certifying an act within the 90-day period following a Federal Register notice under subparagraph (D)(i).
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned "Improvements to Certification Process," but beyond the threshold change it inserts a time-based condition into the definition itself, keyed to the new 90-day notice window rather than to the certification decision alone.

criticisms.why: Too often, Congress reflexively renews sprawling federal backstops that the market no longer needs--quietly gambling with taxpayers' exposure to potentially massive losses while ignoring the absence of any real market breakdown. This TRIA reauthorization fits the pattern perfectly: another automatic green light for an open-ended federal guarantee, despite no evidence of a genuine market failure.

gaps: The bill raises a dollar figure in the certification definition from $5M to $25M but the bill text does not state the program's other operating parameters it is extending, so a reader cannot see from this text what the program does when triggered.
The bill adds a 90-day certification window and Federal Register notice steps but does not state a consequence within the bill text for the Secretary missing the 30-day or 90-day deadlines.
Section 5 renames "Terrorism Insurance Program" to "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout but the bill text does not address whether references in other statutes or regulations are conformed.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Flood
featured_quotes.text: I will start today by thanking Chairman Hill, Ranking Member Waters, and my co-lead on this bill, Congressman Andrew Garbarino. All of us have worked together on legislative text that would reauthorize the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program while also making changes that will protect taxpayers. This legislation would reauthorize TRIA, the program established by Congress in the aftermath of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, through 2034. We are so fortunate that we have never seen a TRIA claim in the program's entire history.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cleaver
featured_quotes.text: I would like to enter into a colloquy with the chairman. I was appalled by reports that a FEMA employee used their authority entrusted by the United States to determine access to Federal aid based on a political yard sign. Whether we are talking about FEMA or the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, this type of action violates the mission of Federal programs that Congress designs to work for all Americans. Likewise, H.R. 7128 is also designed to avoid anything like that from happening in the future with regard to the Terrorism Risk Insurance Program.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hill
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate the gentleman yielding, and I agree with his assessment. It is true that TRIA was designed to create certainty, not doubt, for our businesses, indeed our economy at large after something unthinkable takes place. It requires insurance companies to make stand-alone terrorism coverage available to their clients, who can choose to purchase it or not in addition to their traditional business insurance coverage.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rose
featured_quotes.text: Too often Congress reflexively renews sprawling federal backstops that the market no longer needs--quietly gambling with taxpayers' exposure to potentially massive losses while ignoring the absence of any real market breakdown. This TRIA reauthorization fits the pattern perfectly: another automatic green light for an open-ended federal guarantee, despite no evidence of a genuine market failure.

added: New clause (iii) in Section 102(1)(B) tying the certification definition to a 90-day period following a Federal Register notice
New Federal Register notice requirement: the Secretary must publish notice within 30 days of beginning a certification determination
modified: Section 108(a) sunset year: 2027 → 2034
Section 102(1)(B) certification dollar figure: $5M → $25M
Program name standardized: "Terrorism Insurance Program" → "Terrorism Risk Insurance Program" throughout the Act
removed: Prior subparagraph (D) of Section 102(1), struck and replaced with the new notice requirements

bills.title: Health Care Efficiency Through Flexibility Act
bills.official_title: To amend title XVIII of the Social Security Act to ensure the availability of appropriate collection types for quality reporting under the Medicare Shared Savings Program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-FL) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill amends Medicare Shared Savings Program quality reporting and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Requires Medicare to keep several ways of reporting quality data available to the doctor-and-hospital groups (called ACOs) that take part in the Medicare Shared Savings Program. It also tells Medicare to run a test program letting some of those groups report quality measures digitally.
bills.brief: Requires Medicare to keep specified quality-reporting methods available to ACOs and to run a digital reporting pilot for the Medicare Shared Savings Program.

top_lines.headline: What the Medicare Shared Savings Program Does
subs: Lets provider groups form ACOs to coordinate care for Medicare fee-for-service patients
ACOs that hit quality standards can share in the savings they generate
ACOs must report quality-of-care data in the form Medicare specifies

top_lines.headline: Required Reporting Methods
subs: For performance years 2025-2029, three collection types must stay available
Covers electronic clinical, MIPS clinical, and Medicare CQMs for ACOs
Data not deemed unrepresentative solely because one ACO participant couldn't collect it

top_lines.headline: Digital Reporting Pilot
subs: New pilot for performance years 2028-2032 using a digital collection type
Selected ACOs report only 2 Medicare-specified measures, waiving the rest
Public analysis and recommendations due by December 31, 2032

items.main: Names the Act the "Health Care Efficiency Through Flexibility Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Ensuring Availability of Appropriate Collection Types for Quality Reporting

items.main: Amends Section 1899(b)(3)(B) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395jjj(b)(3)(B)) to require, for performance years 2025 through 2029, that the Secretary keep three collection types available for each quality measure an ACO must report.
items.detail: The Medicare Shared Savings Program lets provider groups act as ACOs coordinating care for Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries and submit quality data the Secretary determines necessary. This section requires that Electronic Clinical Quality Measures, MIPS Clinical Quality Measures, and Medicare Clinical Quality Measures for ACOs (as described in 42 CFR 414.1305) all remain available for reporting.

items.main: Adds a data-completeness clarification: for performance years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, the Secretary may not treat an ACO's data as unrepresentative solely because it excludes data from one or more ACO participants.
items.detail: The exclusion is protected only if the submitted data otherwise meets the completeness requirements of 42 CFR 414.1340 (as applied under 42 CFR 425.512) and the ACO shows to the Secretary's satisfaction that the participant could not collect the data through the selected collection type. "ACO participant" takes the meaning in 42 CFR 425.20, and the Secretary may implement the clause by program instruction or otherwise.

sections.label: Section 3 — Pilot Program for Digital Quality Measure Reporting

items.main: Further amends Section 1899(b)(3)(B) to require the Secretary to establish a digital quality measure reporting pilot program for each of performance years 2028 through 2032.
items.detail: The Secretary selects ACOs from among applicants; for each performance year the Secretary specifies 2 measures the selected ACOs report through a digital quality measure collection type, and may not require them to report other measures. Data for those measures is not counted toward quality performance standards or an ACO participant's quality performance category score, and the Secretary provides technical assistance as practicable.

items.main: Requires the Secretary, not later than December 31, 2032, to publicly post (or include in annual rulemaking) an analysis of the pilot and related recommendations.
items.detail: The posting must include recommendations for increasing submissions through the digital collection type and a proposed timeline for eventually requiring measures to be submitted through it.

underreported.summary: Data an ACO submits for the pilot's specified measures, and any measures it is relieved from reporting, are not taken into account in judging whether the ACO met quality performance standards or in a participant's quality performance category score.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is labeled a reporting pilot, but this provision means a participating ACO's pilot-year quality results carry no consequence for its quality-standard determinations.

gaps: The bill requires three collection types be available for performance years 2025-2029 but does not specify what collection types must be available after 2029.
The bill establishes a digital reporting pilot through 2032 but does not set criteria for how the Secretary selects participating ACOs beyond requiring an application.
The bill directs a proposed timeline for eventually requiring digital submission but does not itself set any deadline for making digital reporting mandatory.

added: New requirement that three collection types (eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, and Medicare CQMs for ACOs) remain available for ACO quality reporting for performance years 2025-2029
New data-completeness protection barring the Secretary from deeming ACO data unrepresentative solely for excluding a participant that could not collect through the selected collection type
New digital quality measure reporting pilot program for performance years 2028-2032, with a public analysis due by December 31, 2032
modified: Amends Section 1899(b)(3)(B) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395jjj(b)(3)(B)) to restructure the ACO reporting-requirements clause and add the collection-type, data-completeness, and pilot provisions

bills.title: Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act
bills.official_title: To recover unclaimed pandemic-era unemployment compensation funds held by financial institutions or escheated to State unclaimed property administrators, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Beth Van Duyne (R-TX) and passed the House by voice vote (no recorded roll call); the bill directs recovery of improper pandemic unemployment payments and extends the related fraud statute of limitations to 10 years, and now awaits Senate consideration.
bills.summary: Sets up a federal task force to find and get back pandemic unemployment money that was paid out improperly and is still sitting in banks or with state unclaimed-property offices. It also gives prosecutors more time to bring fraud cases tied to those pandemic unemployment programs.
bills.brief: Creates a federal task force to recover improper pandemic unemployment payments held by banks and states, and extends the fraud statute of limitations to 10 years.

top_lines.headline: Pandemic Fund Recovery Task Force
subs: Task force convened within 30 days of enactment
Targets improper payments on prepaid debit cards held by banks or states
Labor Secretary reimburses states for related administrative costs

top_lines.headline: Fraud Statute of Limitations
subs: Extends the fraud prosecution deadline to 10 years
Covers PUA, FPUC/MEUC, and PEUC unemployment claims
Does not revive cases whose limitations period already expired

top_lines.headline: Coordination and Guidance
subs: National Recovery Coordinator designated by the Labor Secretary
Guidance issued to banks and state unclaimed-property offices
Model notice developed for identity-theft victims

items.main: Names the Act the "Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — National Recovery Coordinator and Task Force

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Labor, in consultation with the Treasury Secretary, the Labor Department Inspector General, and the Attorney General, to designate a National Recovery Coordinator who convenes a "Recover Pandemic Unemployment Funds in Banks Task Force" not later than 30 days after enactment.
items.detail: The Task Force includes the Attorney General, the Secretary of Labor, the Labor Department Inspector General, the Secretary of the Treasury, the Chairman of the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, and the Director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, or their designees. It coordinates with state agencies to identify federal pandemic unemployment payments issued on prepaid debit cards that are held by financial institutions or that were transferred to and are held by a state unclaimed-property agency.

items.main: Requires the Task Force to develop model recovery processes and issue guidance to state agencies, financial institutions, and state unclaimed-property administrators for returning improper payments to the appropriate state agency.
items.detail: Guidance to states covers reviewing whether a payment was improper, whether cost-effective recovery is possible (including a dollar threshold or a methodology for calculating one), and actions to take if fraud is determined. Guidance to banks is issued with the Comptroller of the Currency and the FDIC Chairman; guidance to unclaimed-property administrators is issued with the Treasury Secretary. The Task Force must consult states and incorporate best practices from prior state recovery attempts.

items.main: Requires the Secretary of Labor to reimburse states for all administrative costs incurred from coordinating with the Task Force by reason of an agreement under section 2102, 2104, or 2107 of the CARES Act.
items.detail: Defines "Federal pandemic unemployment compensation" as payments under CARES Act sections 2102(b), 2104(b)(1), and 2107(a)(2), and defines "improper payment" as any amount of a pandemic unemployment payment to which the individual is not entitled. State-law terms take the meanings in section 205 of the Federal-State Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 1970.

sections.label: Section 3 — Extension of the Statute of Limitations

items.main: Amends CARES Act sections 2102, 2104, and 2107 to require that any criminal prosecution or civil enforcement action for fraud tied to a claim funded in whole or in part by those pandemic unemployment programs be brought not later than 10 years after the violation or conspiracy.
items.detail: The 10-year period applies to violations of, or conspiracies to violate, sections 371, 641, 1028A, 1029, 1341, 1343, 1344, 1349, 1956, and 1957 of title 18 and sections 3729 and 3802 of title 31. It does not apply where the applicable statute of limitations already expired before the Act's enactment. The amendments take effect on the date of enactment.

underreported.summary: The 10-year limitations period does not apply to any prosecution or enforcement action whose applicable statute of limitations already expired before the Act's enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned as an extension of the statute of limitations, but this carve-out means it does not revive cases that were already time-barred, limiting which claims the longer window can reach.

underreported.summary: The Secretary of Labor must reimburse states for all administrative costs incurred from coordinating with the Task Force under CARES Act sections 2102, 2104, or 2107.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is framed around recovering funds held by banks, but it also creates a federal reimbursement obligation to states for the administrative work of that coordination.

gaps: The bill directs recovery of improper payments held by banks and states but does not appropriate funds for the Task Force's own operating costs.
The bill defines "improper payment" as any amount to which the individual is not entitled but does not set the dollar threshold for cost-effective recovery, leaving it to Task Force guidance.
The bill requires guidance to identity-theft victims but does not specify a remedy or restitution process for individuals whose identities were fraudulently used.
The bill extends the fraud statute of limitations for individuals but does not address limitations periods for the financial institutions holding the funds.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Van Duyne
featured_quotes.text: This commonsense legislation creates a Federal task force to work with States to recover unspent Federal pandemic unemployment funds that remain frozen in financial institutions and return those taxpayer dollars to the U.S. Treasury, but Congress must act quickly. Last December, the Department of Labor's Office of Inspector General issued two fraud alerts identifying nearly $1 billion in unspent Federal unemployment funds frozen by banks because of suspected fraud.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Suozzi
featured_quotes.text: H.R. 8873, the Recover COVID Unemployment Fraud in Banks Act, is a commonsense bill that helps eliminate waste, fraud, and abuse; recovers stolen taxpayer dollars; and protects some of our most vulnerable citizens, including older Americans. At a time when too many families face the uncertainty of unemployment, high gas and grocery prices, and seniors are forced to choose between food, rent, and healthcare, we can't allow fraudsters to get away with stealing funds meant to help hardworking families.

added: New National Recovery Coordinator position and Recover Pandemic Unemployment Funds in Banks Task Force, convened within 30 days of enactment
New requirement that the Secretary of Labor reimburse states for administrative costs of coordinating with the Task Force
modified: Amends CARES Act section 2102 (15 U.S.C. 9021) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Pandemic Unemployment Assistance claims
Amends CARES Act section 2104 (15 U.S.C. 9023) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Federal Pandemic Unemployment Compensation and Mixed Earner Unemployment Compensation claims
Amends CARES Act section 2107 (15 U.S.C. 9025) to add a 10-year statute of limitations for fraud tied to Pandemic Emergency Unemployment Compensation claims

bills.title: Semiquincentennial Congressional Time Capsule Act
bills.official_title: To provide for the creation of a congressional time capsule in commemoration of the semiquincentennial of the United States, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-79 (PL 119-79) on February 18, 2026. Introduced by Sen. Thomas Tillis (R-NC); directing the Architect of the Capitol to create and bury a commemorative time capsule is a narrow ceremonial measure that drew no recorded opposition, passing the Senate and House before being signed.
bills.summary: Directs the Architect of the Capitol to build a congressional time capsule marking the 250th anniversary of the United States. The capsule is to be sealed and buried in the Capitol Visitor Center, then opened on July 4, 2276.
bills.brief: Creates a congressional time capsule to be sealed and buried at the Capitol and unsealed in 2276.

top_lines.headline: Congressional Time Capsule
subs: Architect of the Capitol builds the capsule
Capsule limited to 50 in. wide, 32 in. deep, 48 in. high
Sealed and buried in the Capitol Visitor Center

top_lines.headline: Contents and Materials
subs: Congressional leadership offices jointly choose contents
Must include one joint letter from those offices
Items must use low-degradation materials such as metal or archival paper

top_lines.headline: Sealing and Unsealing
subs: Prepared and buried on or before July 4, 2026
Sealed until July 4, 2276
Presented to the 244th Congress on unsealing

items.main: Names the Act the “Semiquincentennial Congressional Time Capsule Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Directs the Architect of the Capitol to create, seal, and bury a congressional time capsule, with contents chosen by congressional leadership.
items.detail: The Speaker, House Minority Leader, Senate Majority Leader, and Senate Minority Leader jointly determine the contents, which must include a single joint letter from those offices and may include other items they agree on. Items must be made of low-degradation materials such as metal or archival paper, and the capsule may be no more than 50 inches wide, 32 inches deep, and 48 inches high. The Architect prepares it to be sealed and buried in the Capitol Visitor Center on or before July 4, 2026, with the approval of the Senate Committee on Rules and Administration and the House Committee on House Administration, installs a plaque, and the capsule stays sealed until July 4, 2276, when it is presented to the 244th Congress.

gaps: The Act sets the burial to coincide with a time capsule buried at Independence Mall in Philadelphia but does not address what happens if the July 4, 2026 deadline is not met.
The Act specifies the maximum capsule dimensions and material requirements but does not name a funding source for building, sealing, or installing the capsule and its plaque.
The Act directs that the capsule be presented to the 244th Congress in 2276 but does not specify how or where it is to be stored or safeguarded during the intervening 250 years.

added: Creates the Semiquincentennial Congressional Time Capsule, built by the Architect of the Capitol and buried in the Capitol Visitor Center
Requires a single joint letter from the four congressional leadership offices to be included in the capsule
Requires a plaque describing the capsule to be installed

bills.title: Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Congressional Award Act.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-66 on December 26, 2025. Introduced by Sen. Cynthia M. Lummis (R-WY); reauthorizing an existing youth-recognition program by extending its board's termination date is a narrow measure that drew no recorded opposition, clearing both chambers before being signed.
bills.summary: Keeps the Congressional Award Program running by pushing back the date its governing board is set to shut down. The program gives medals to young people aged 14 through 23 for achievement in public service, personal development, and physical fitness.
bills.brief: Extends the Congressional Award Board's termination date to October 1, 2028, keeping the youth award program alive.

top_lines.headline: What the Congressional Award Program Does
subs: Awards medals to youths aged 14 through 23 nationwide
Recognizes public service, personal development, and physical/expedition fitness
Run by the Congressional Award Board, not a federal agency

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Board termination date moved from Oct. 1, 2023 to Oct. 1, 2028
Extension applies retroactively as if enacted Oct. 1, 2023
Drops the fixed gold-plate/rhodium/bronze medal material requirement

items.main: Names the Act the "Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Extends the Congressional Award Board's termination date from October 1, 2023 to October 1, 2028.
items.detail: Amends Section 108 of the Congressional Award Act (2 U.S.C. 808), which sets the date the Board shall terminate. The extension takes effect retroactively as if enacted on October 1, 2023, so the Board is treated as never having lapsed. The Board administers the Congressional Award Program that awards medals to young people aged 14 through 23.

items.main: Removes the fixed material specification for Congressional Award medals.
items.detail: Amends Section 102 of the Congressional Award Act (2 U.S.C. 802). It strikes the sentence in subsection (a) requiring each medal to consist of gold-plate over bronze, rhodium over bronze, or bronze and be struck per subsection (f), and in subsection (f)(1) strikes "Subject to subsection (a), the" and inserts "The". The Secretary of the Treasury strikes the medals in such quantity, design, and specifications as the Secretary determines after consulting the Board.

underreported.summary: Strikes the statutory requirement that each medal be gold-plate over bronze, rhodium over bronze, or bronze, and removes the cross-reference tying the Treasury's striking authority to that material list.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is captioned a reauthorization and its termination-date extension is in Section 2, but Section 3 makes a separate substantive change to what the medals must be made of rather than to the program's authorization.

gaps: The bill extends the Board's termination date to October 1, 2028 but does not itself appropriate funds or change how the program is funded.
Section 3 removes the required medal materials but does not specify any replacement material standard, leaving composition to the Secretary of the Treasury's determination.
The bill reauthorizes the Board through October 1, 2028 but sets no new standards, conditions, or oversight requirements on the program it revives.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Dingell
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to share my strong support for S. 284, the Congressional Award Program Reauthorization Act. Mr. Speaker, I am proud to co-lead it with my colleague, Representative Hudson, whom you just heard from, and also Congressmen Mike Levin and John Rutherford. This bill will reauthorize the Congressional Award program, which has been responsible for printing and distributing awards to young Americans across this country since 1979. This important program expired nearly 18 months ago, and it is in desperate need of reauthorization.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hudson
featured_quotes.text: This bill simply reauthorizes the Congressional Award program, Congress' official youth recognition program and the highest honor that Congress can award our Nation's youth. This program has helped generations of young people set goals, serve others, and push themselves to achieve more. Specifically, young Americans have to set and complete rigorous personal goals focused on volunteer service, personal development, exploration, and physical fitness.

modified: Congressional Award Board termination date extended from October 1, 2023 to October 1, 2028, retroactive to October 1, 2023 (2 U.S.C. 808)

Medal material requirement changed: strikes the gold-plate-over-bronze / rhodium-over-bronze / bronze specification and the "Subject to subsection (a)" limit on the Treasury's striking authority (2 U.S.C. 802)
removed: The statutory requirement that each Congressional Award medal consist of gold-plate over bronze, rhodium over bronze, or bronze (2 U.S.C. 802(a))
