bills.title: VA Budget Shortfall Accountability Act
bills.official_title: To direct the Secretary of Veterans Affairs and the Comptroller General of the United States to report on certain funding shortfalls in the Department of Veterans Affairs.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-71 on January 20, 2026. Sponsored by Rep. Jack Bergman (R-MI) with 1 cosponsor; per the printed legislative history, the measure passed the House on May 19, 2025 and the Senate on December 18, 2025 before being signed.
bills.summary: Orders GAO to investigate why the VA ran short of money — the fiscal year 2024 shortfall in the Veterans Benefits Administration and the expected fiscal year 2025 shortfall in the Veterans Health Administration — and to repeat the review every year for five years. The VA Secretary must send each report to Congress within 30 days of receiving it.
bills.brief: Requires GAO reviews of the VA's fiscal year 2024 and 2025 funding shortfalls, repeated annually for five years, with every report forwarded to Congress.

top_lines.headline: VA Shortfall Investigation
subs: GAO review must begin within 30 days of enactment
Covers the fiscal year 2024 Veterans Benefits Administration shortfall
Covers the expected fiscal year 2025 VHA shortfall

top_lines.headline: Five Years of Follow-Up Reviews
subs: New GAO review in each of the next five calendar years
Each review covers the most recent completed fiscal year

top_lines.headline: Reports to Congress
subs: VA Secretary forwards each GAO report within 30 days
Goes to the Veterans' Affairs and Appropriations committees

items.main: Names the Act the "VA Budget Shortfall Accountability Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Funding Shortfalls in Certain Administrations of the Department of Veterans Affairs: Reviews; Reports

items.main: Directs the Comptroller General to begin, within 30 days of enactment, a review of the circumstances and causes of the Veterans Benefits Administration's fiscal year 2024 funding shortfall and the expected Veterans Health Administration shortfall in fiscal year 2025.
items.detail: The review must compare monthly obligations and expenditures in the relevant accounts against the VA's spending plan, examine transfers between those accounts, explain any significant diversions from the plan, and analyze the accuracy of the projections behind them. GAO submits a written report of its findings to the VA Secretary within 30 days of completing the review.

items.main: Requires a follow-up GAO review and report in each of the five calendar years after enactment, covering VA funding for the most recent completed fiscal year.
items.detail: Each subsequent review must include the same elements as the first, including remedial actions the Secretary may take to improve the accuracy of the Department's budget-submission supporting information and to prevent future shortfalls. The VA Secretary must forward every GAO report to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs and Appropriations Committees within 30 days of receiving it.

underreported.summary: Each review must identify remedial actions the Secretary may take to improve the accuracy of supporting information the VA submits for the President's annual budget under section 1105(a) of title 31 and to prevent future funding shortfalls.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and review triggers concern past shortfalls, but this element points GAO at the accuracy of the VA's future budget projections — a forward-looking budget-process element rather than a backward-looking accounting.

gaps: The bill orders reviews of the funding shortfalls but does not itself provide any additional funding to address them.
GAO reports go to the Secretary and four congressional committees, but the bill does not require public release of the findings.
The reviews must list remedial actions the Secretary may take, but nothing in the bill requires the Secretary to adopt any of them.
The bill covers shortfalls in the benefits and health administrations but does not address funding in the Department's other administrations or offices.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bergman
featured_quotes.text: Last July, the VA came to Congress with a dire warning: the agency was facing major funding shortfalls, nearly $3 billion for veterans' benefits and additional $12 billion for healthcare. The message was urgent: Without immediate action, benefits could be delayed for millions of veterans. Congress acted quickly and responsibly to approve supplemental funding because when it comes to our veterans and their families, there can be no margin for error. Their peace of mind, their financial security, and their access to care are not negotiable.

added: GAO review, beginning within 30 days of enactment, of the fiscal year 2024 Veterans Benefits Administration shortfall and the expected fiscal year 2025 Veterans Health Administration shortfall
Annual follow-up GAO reviews and reports in each of the five calendar years after enactment
Requirement that the VA Secretary forward each GAO report to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs and Appropriations Committees within 30 days

bills.title: Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act with respect to molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Republican sponsor with 313 cosponsors — well over half the House signed on across both parties — and the House passed the bill by voice vote. No organized opposition to the pediatric-study or voucher provisions appears in the metadata; the main risk is Senate floor time rather than substantive resistance.
bills.summary: Requires drug companies to study whether their targeted adult cancer drugs work in children — including when used in combination with other cancer drugs — and lets FDA seek penalties from companies that skip required pediatric studies without a good-faith effort. It also extends the rare pediatric disease priority review voucher program through September 30, 2029, modernizes the organ transplant network, and raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.
bills.brief: Extends required pediatric cancer studies to combination therapies, extends the rare pediatric disease priority review voucher program through September 30, 2029, and raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.

top_lines.headline: Pediatric Cancer Drug Studies
subs: Required studies now reach combination cancer therapies
Applies to drug applications filed 3 years after enactment
Penalties possible for sponsors lacking due diligence on studies

top_lines.headline: Rare Disease Incentives
subs: Priority review voucher awards extended through September 30, 2029
Vouchers grant 6-month FDA review and can be sold
Orphan-drug exclusivity narrowed to the approved use or indication

top_lines.headline: Transplant Network and Medicare Fund
subs: Transplant-network registration fees authorized for 3 years
Electronic health-record integration for organ donor referrals
Medicare Improvement Fund raised from $1.40B to $2.62B

sections.label: Sections 2-4 — Pediatric Study Requirements and Enforcement

items.main: Expands required molecularly targeted pediatric cancer investigations so they can cover the application drug used in combination with other active ingredients — either standard-of-care pediatric cancer ingredients or the sponsor's own approved adult cancer ingredients directed at a molecular target relevant to a pediatric cancer.
items.detail: Investigations must be designed to yield clinically meaningful pediatric data on dosing, safety, and preliminary efficacy, using age-appropriate formulations. Combination investigations may be required only for drugs with a single new active ingredient, or for unapproved combinations of ingredients each previously approved for adult cancer. The changes apply to applications submitted 3 years or more after enactment; FDA must issue draft implementation guidance within 12 months.

items.main: Allows FDA to pursue penalty action under section 303 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act against sponsors who fail pediatric-study requirements — but only after finding the sponsor demonstrated a lack of due diligence.
items.detail: Prior law expressly excluded pediatric-study noncompliance from section 303 action. FDA must first issue a noncompliance letter, give the sponsor 45 days to respond in writing, and review the response before making a due-diligence determination. No enforcement is allowed for drugs no longer marketed, and only failures occurring 180 days or more after enactment can be pursued.

items.main: Adds to FDA's PREA-tracking report an evaluation of compliance with deferral deadlines and a public listing of every penalty, settlement, or payment for pediatric-study noncompliance, naming the drug, its sponsor, and the amount.
items.detail: The listing is added to the report required under section 508(b) of the Food and Drug Administration Safety and Innovation Act.

sections.label: Sections 5-7 — Rare and Pediatric Disease Incentives

items.main: Extends FDA's authority to award rare pediatric disease priority review vouchers through September 30, 2029, replacing the December 20, 2024 cutoff.
items.detail: Under the program, a sponsor that wins approval of a rare pediatric disease product receives a voucher entitling the holder to a 6-month priority FDA review of a later drug application; vouchers may be transferred or sold without limit. The bill also makes the priority-review user fee due when the voucher is actually used, and orders a GAO study of the program's effectiveness with findings due within 5 years.

items.main: Narrows orphan-drug exclusivity: the 7-year exclusive-approval window now blocks competitors only for the same approved use or indication within the rare disease, instead of the same disease or condition.
items.detail: The change applies to every drug designated as an orphan drug, regardless of when it was designated or approved.

items.main: Authorizes $25M for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2028 for the Public Health Service Act program for pediatric studies of drugs.
items.detail: Amends section 409I(d)(1) of the Public Health Service Act, which funds pediatric studies of drugs that still need testing in children.

sections.label: Sections 8-9 — Transplant Network and an FDA Office Abroad

items.main: Modernizes the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network: encourages electronic health-record integration for automated donor referrals, allows a 24-hour telephone or information technology service, and calls for considering a public transplant-statistics dashboard.
items.detail: The Secretary may also collect registration fees from network members for each transplant candidate listed — usable only to support network operations, with per-member amounts and uses posted publicly each quarter. The fee authority expires 3 years after enactment, and GAO must review the fee program within 2 years.

items.main: Creates an Abraham Accords Office within FDA, to be located in an Abraham Accords country within two years of enactment.
items.detail: The office will provide technical assistance to regulatory partners in Abraham Accords countries — including on good manufacturing practices — and facilitate interactions between FDA and interested parties there. HHS must report to Congress on the office's results within 3 years.

sections.label: Sections 10-11 — Generic Drug Transparency and Medicare Fund

items.main: Requires FDA, on request, to tell a generic-drug applicant whether its product is qualitatively and quantitatively the same as the brand-name listed drug — and if not, to identify the differing ingredients and the amount of any quantitative deviation.
items.detail: Once FDA determines a generic matches, it cannot change that determination after the application is filed except for a safety-based formulation change in the listed drug or a written error finding with notice to the applicant. Draft guidance is due within one year of enactment.

items.main: Raises the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B.
items.detail: Amends section 1898(b)(1) of the Social Security Act to increase the amount available to the Secretary for improvements to the original Medicare program.

underreported.summary: Increases the Medicare Improvement Fund from $1.40B to $2.62B by amending the Social Security Act.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and stated subject are pediatric cancer drug investigations; this provision changes a Medicare fund balance and is unrelated to drug studies.

underreported.summary: Establishes a new FDA office physically located in an Abraham Accords country to provide regulatory technical assistance and facilitate industry interactions there.
underreported.why_unreported: A foreign-based FDA office serving international regulatory cooperation is a different subject from the pediatric-drug provisions named in the bill's title.

underreported.section: Section 3 — Ensuring Completion of Pediatric Study Requirements
underreported.summary: Strikes the clause that shielded pediatric-study noncompliance from section 303 penalty action and replaces it with penalty exposure whenever the sponsor lacked due diligence.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label reads as administrative housekeeping, but the operative text reverses a prior statutory exemption from penalties.

gaps: The bill authorizes $25M a year for pediatric drug studies only through fiscal 2028, while the voucher authority it extends runs through September 30, 2029.
Sponsors get a 45-day window to respond to a noncompliance letter, but the bill sets no deadline for FDA to act after reviewing the response.
The transplant-statistics dashboard is only something the network must consider establishing; the bill does not require it or set a deadline.
The Abraham Accords Office must be established within two years, but the bill provides no dedicated appropriation for the office or its staffing.
FDA must answer generic applicants' sameness requests, but the bill sets no deadline for providing that answer.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bilirakis
featured_quotes.text: I am rising in strong support of H.R. 1262, the Mikaela Naylon Give Kids a Chance Act, led by my friend, the gentleman from Texas, Congressman McCaul. This piece of legislation is comprised of bipartisan solutions to increase access to innovative treatments for those living with rare diseases, particularly children and adolescents. Ten years ago, Mr. Speaker, the idea that we would be able to not just treat but cure sickle cell disease sounded like a dream that was too far out of reach. Today, we are curing sickle cell disease.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Obernolte
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I rise in strong support as both a member of the Health Subcommittee and a proud cosponsor of this bill, H.R. 1262, the Give Kids a Chance Act. Mr. Speaker, we live in the most technologically advanced society in the history of human civilization, and modern medicine has recently come up  with amazing solutions and cures for many of the physical ailments that have afflicted humanity. Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, we have many rare pediatric diseases for which there is no cure.

added: Combination-therapy pediatric cancer investigations — required studies may cover the application drug used with standard-of-care or same-sponsor adult cancer ingredients
Due-diligence enforcement path: FDA may seek section 303 penalties for pediatric-study noncompliance after a noncompliance letter and 45-day response period
Abraham Accords Office within FDA, located in an Abraham Accords country within 2 years
Binding FDA sameness determinations for generic-drug formulations, with disclosure of differing ingredients
Transplant-network registration fees (3-year authority) with quarterly public posting of amounts and uses
$25M per year authorized for pediatric drug studies for fiscal years 2026 through 2028
modified: Rare pediatric disease priority review voucher authority — award cutoff moved from December 20, 2024 to September 30, 2029
Orphan-drug 7-year exclusivity — narrowed from the same disease or condition to the same approved use or indication
Medicare Improvement Fund — $1.40B to $2.62B
Priority-review user fee — now due when the voucher is used, upon submission of the application
removed: Statutory exclusion that kept pediatric-study noncompliance outside section 303 penalty action

bills.title: ACRES Act
bills.official_title: To require that the Secretary of Agriculture and the Secretary of the Interior submit accurate reports regarding hazardous fuels reduction activities, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors, but the bill cleared the House by voice vote and the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee ordered it reported favorably without amendment — the metadata shows no organized opposition. A transparency mandate with no new spending attached rarely draws floor resistance; the main variable is Senate scheduling.
bills.summary: Makes the Forest Service and Interior Department report honestly on how many acres of federal land they actually treated to reduce wildfire fuel each year — counting each acre only once, even if it was treated multiple times. The reports go to Congress with the President's budget and must be posted publicly.
bills.brief: Requires annual, publicly posted counts of acres treated for wildfire fuel reduction, with each completed acre counted only once and no credit for awarding contracts.

top_lines.headline: Wildfire Treatment Reporting
subs: Annual acre counts filed with the President's budget materials
Each treated acre counted once — no double counting
Only completed treatments count toward the total

top_lines.headline: Data Quality Rules
subs: Standardized tracking procedures due within 90 days
Reports must show cost per acre and wildfire risk levels
Every report posted on the agencies' websites

top_lines.headline: Oversight and Cost
subs: GAO studies implementation within 2 years
No additional funds authorized

items.main: Names the Act the "Accurately Counting Risk Elimination Solutions Act" or the "ACRES Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Accurate Hazardous Fuels Reduction Reports

items.main: Requires the Agriculture and Interior Secretaries to report each year, in the materials supporting the President's budget, the number of federal acres where hazardous fuels reduction work was completed the prior fiscal year.
items.detail: Only completed activities are recorded, and each acre is counted once regardless of how many treatments it received. Reports must break out which acres sit in the wildland-urban interface, wildfire risk levels (high, moderate, or low) at the start and end of the period, whether work came from a managed wildfire or a planned project, cost per acre, the region or system unit, and the treatments' effectiveness at reducing wildfire risk. Each report must be posted on the departments' websites.

items.main: Orders standardized data-tracking procedures within 90 days of enactment, with a report to Congress due 2 weeks after the procedures are in place.
items.detail: The procedures must include regular accuracy reviews, verification methods tying data to actual work performed, analysis of short- and long-term effectiveness, and methods to distinguish acres inside versus outside the wildland-urban interface. The report to Congress must describe the procedures and recommend fixes for any tracking limitations.

items.main: Directs a GAO study of the Act's implementation within 2 years, and authorizes no additional funds for any of it.
items.detail: "Hazardous fuels reduction activity" is defined as vegetation management that reduces wildfire risk — including mechanical treatments and prescribed burning — and expressly excludes the mere awarding of contracts. The Agriculture Secretary covers National Forest System lands; the Interior Secretary covers public lands and National Park System units.

underreported.summary: Each acre is recorded once per reporting period regardless of how many hazardous fuels reduction activities occurred on it, and only completed activities are recorded.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label promises accurate reports; the operative rule changes the counting method itself, which mechanically produces lower acre totals than counting every treatment on the same land.

underreported.summary: The definition of hazardous fuels reduction activity excludes the awarding of contracts to conduct such activities.
underreported.why_unreported: This bars agencies from counting acres as treated when a contract has been signed but no work completed — a definitional limit not apparent from the bill's title.

gaps: Reports must state the effectiveness of treatments at reducing wildfire risk, but the bill does not define how effectiveness is to be measured.
The bill mandates new tracking procedures, reviews, and reports but authorizes no additional funds to carry them out.
Reports must give wildfire risk levels (high, moderate, or low) at the start and end of each period, but the bill does not say who assigns those levels or by what standard.
The report on tracking limitations must include policy recommendations, but the bill sets no process or deadline for acting on them.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: This is, I think, a small step in the right direction, and it shouldn't cost any more to report accurate data than to report inaccurate data. I look forward to passing this bill as well as some larger bills like the Fix Our Forests Act that we hope to have before the body this week.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Tiffany
featured_quotes.text: In spite of what was just said on the other side of the aisle, I want to invite the gentleman from California to Wisconsin. He can get some good fishing in in northern Minnesota, good musky fishing, but if the gentleman wants the best, then come to northern Wisconsin. I have an invitation for my friend. This bill will bring transparency, Mr. Speaker, to the misleading and inaccurate way hazardous fuels treatments are reported.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Huffman
featured_quotes.text: I look forward to working with our friends across the aisle on the accounting issue that has been discussed here today. Obviously, we want to make sure that the Forest Service is not taking advance credit for phases of projects that haven't happened yet. I think that is for the most part what has happened that the gentleman from Arkansas identified. I don't believe there has been any actual double or triple counting, but either way, we want it to be accurate. We all need good, accurate data on that reporting. We will work together on that.

added: Annual hazardous-fuels-reduction report submitted with the President's budget materials and posted publicly
Once-per-acre, completed-work-only counting rules for reported acreage
Standardized data-tracking procedures due within 90 days of enactment, with a report to Congress 2 weeks after implementation
GAO study of implementation due within 2 years

bills.title: Emergency Conservation Program Improvement Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Agricultural Credit Act of 1978 to remove barriers to agricultural producers in accessing funds to carry out emergency measures under the emergency conservation program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Republican sponsor (R-LA) with 4 cosponsors; the House cleared it 395-10 on a suspension vote, a strong bipartisan margin. Disaster-recovery cost-share help for farmers has no natural opposition bloc; the open question is whether the Senate gives floor time to a standalone farm-disaster bill.
bills.summary: Lets farmers hit by natural disasters collect more of their federal repair money up front — up to 75% before rebuilding fences or rehabilitating farmland, up from 25% for fencing only — and extends the same advance option to private forest owners restoring disaster-damaged woodland. Damage from wildfires the government caused now qualifies too, when the fire spread naturally.
bills.brief: Raises Emergency Conservation Program advance payments from 25% (fencing only) to up to 75%, covers federally caused wildfires, and creates 75% advances for private forest restoration.

top_lines.headline: Disaster Advance Payments for Farmers
subs: Advance option grows from 25% to up to 75%
Now covers farmland rehab and conservation structures, not just fencing
Repairs qualify for 50% up front

top_lines.headline: Government-Caused Wildfires Covered
subs: Non-natural wildfires qualify, including fires caused by the Federal Government
Applies when damage comes from the fire's natural spread

top_lines.headline: Forest Owner Advances
subs: Private forest owners can get 75% of restoration costs up front
Unspent funds must be returned after 180 days

items.main: Names the Act the "Emergency Conservation Program Improvement Act of 2025".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Expands the Emergency Conservation Program's advance-payment option: producers may take up to 75% of a payment before replacing fencing or rehabilitating farmland or a conservation structure — up from 25% for fencing work only — and up to 50% before making repairs.
items.detail: The program pays agricultural producers who carry out emergency measures to rehabilitate farmland damaged by floods, hurricanes, wildfires, wind erosion, or other natural disasters. Advances are based on the fair market value of the work as determined by the Secretary of Agriculture; the existing rule requiring unspent advance funds to be returned after 60 days is not changed.

items.main: Makes damage from wildfires that were not caused naturally — including fires caused by the Federal Government — eligible for program payments when the damage results from the fire's spread due to natural causes.
items.detail: The new subsection defines which wildfires count for payment purposes under the program's existing damage-payment authority.

sections.label: Section 3 — Improving the Emergency Forest Restoration Program

items.main: Gives owners of nonindustrial private forest land the option of receiving up to 75% of the cost of emergency restoration measures before carrying them out.
items.detail: Advances are valued using the estimated practice costs published in each state's Field Office Technical Guide by the Natural Resources Conservation Service. Funds unspent after 180 days must be returned on a timeline the Secretary sets. The underlying program pays forest owners to restore land damaged by natural disasters, with total payments capped at 75% of cost.

underreported.summary: Extends Emergency Conservation Program payment eligibility to damage from non-naturally-caused wildfires, including fires caused by the Federal Government, when the damage arises from the fire's natural spread.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's stated purpose is removing barriers to accessing funds; this provision instead changes which disasters qualify at all, reaching fires the government itself started.

underreported.summary: New forest-restoration advances must be returned if unspent after 180 days, while farmland advances remain subject to the existing 60-day return window, which the bill does not amend.
underreported.why_unreported: Two advance-payment options under the same Act now run on different clocks — a difference not visible from either section's title.

gaps: The bill raises how much can be advanced but leaves the program's underlying eligibility conditions unchanged, including the requirement that damage be so costly that federal assistance is needed.
Advance amounts are based on fair market value as determined by the Secretary, but the bill sets no deadline for making that determination.
The wildfire rule covers fires that are not caused naturally, but the bill does not say how causation is determined or documented.
Forest-restoration advances rely on estimated practice costs in each state's Field Office Technical Guide, but the bill does not address practices missing from a state's guide.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Letlow
featured_quotes.text: Across this country, farmers, ranchers, and forest landowners are on the front lines of natural disasters. Whether it is hurricanes in my home State of Louisiana, wildfires in Nebraska, or severe storms across rural America,  these events do not just damage land. They threaten livelihoods, local economies, and our Nation's food and fiber supply.

added: Wildfire causation rule — non-naturally-caused wildfires, including federally caused fires, qualify for payments when damage results from natural spread
Advance payments of up to 75% for emergency forest-restoration measures on nonindustrial private forest land, with a 180-day return rule
modified: Emergency Conservation Program advance-payment option — expanded beyond fencing to farmland rehabilitation and conservation structures, at up to 75% for replacement or rehabilitation and up to 50% for repair

bills.title: Wetlands Conservation and Access Improvement Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Act to provide that interest on obligations held in the Federal aid to wildlife restoration fund shall become available for apportionment at the beginning of fiscal year 2033.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-40 on November 25, 2025. Sponsored by Rep. Jeff Hurd (R-CO) with 3 cosponsors; per the printed legislative history, it passed the House on July 14, 2025 and the Senate on October 23, 2025 before being signed.
bills.summary: Money from federal excise taxes on firearms and ammunition sits in a wildlife restoration fund, and the interest it earns is allocated to wetlands conservation projects. This law delays until fiscal year 2033 — instead of fiscal year 2026 — the date that interest becomes available to be divided among state wildlife programs.
bills.brief: Delays from fiscal year 2026 to fiscal year 2033 the date Pittman-Robertson fund interest becomes available for apportionment, leaving it allocated to wetlands conservation projects in the meantime.

top_lines.headline: Wildlife Fund Interest Timing
subs: Interest apportionment date moves from fiscal 2026 to 2033
Interest is credited to the wildlife restoration fund

top_lines.headline: Wetlands Project Funding
subs: Fund interest is allocated to wetlands conservation projects
30-60% goes to projects in Canada and Mexico
Non-federal sponsors generally must match the federal amount

items.main: Names the Act the "Wetlands Conservation and Access Improvement Act of 2025".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Availability of Interest on Obligations Held in Federal Aid to Wildlife Restoration Fund

items.main: Delays from the beginning of fiscal year 2026 to the beginning of fiscal year 2033 the date when interest earned by the federal aid to wildlife restoration fund becomes available for apportionment under the Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Act.
items.detail: The fund holds revenue from federal excise taxes — 10% on pistols and revolvers, 11% on other firearms and on shells and cartridges — and the Treasury invests balances not needed for current withdrawals in interest-bearing U.S. obligations. The interest is credited to the fund and constitutes the sums the Secretary allocates under section 4407 of title 16.

items.main: Keeps fund interest running through the North American Wetlands Conservation allocation formula rather than state apportionment for seven more years.
items.detail: Under that formula, between 30% and 60% of available sums goes to approved wetlands conservation projects in Canada and Mexico and the remainder to projects in the United States. Non-federal sponsors generally must at least match the federal amount, though projects on federal lands and waters may be fully federally funded.

underreported.section: Section 2 — the Act's only operative provision
underreported.summary: The entire Act consists of striking "2026" and inserting "2033" in the Pittman-Robertson interest-availability clause.
underreported.why_unreported: The title promises wetlands conservation and access improvements; mechanically the Act only postpones the date when fund interest shifts from wetlands-project allocation to apportionment among state wildlife programs.

gaps: The title references access improvement, but the Act contains no provision addressing public access.
The Act moves the apportionment date to fiscal 2033 but does not change how much interest the fund earns or how wetlands allocations are divided.
The Act sets a new 2033 date without stating any criteria for whether the shift to state apportionment should occur then.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Hurd
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan legislation ensures that the interest earned on unallocated Pittman-Robertson funds will continue to support wetlands restoration through the North American Wetlands Conservation Act for years to come. For nearly a century, the Pittman-Robertson Act has stood as one of the most successful conservation funding models in the world. It works because sportsmen and sportswomen pay a dedicated excise tax on firearms, ammunition, and archery equipment.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: By passing this commonsense legislation, the House will ensure that we can continue conserving vital waterfowl habitats for years to come. This is important for sportsmen and -women who depend on healthy wetland habitats for hunting, fishing, and other forms of wildlife- centered recreation. H.R. 2316 is a win for conservation and the sportsmen and -women communities alike. NAWCA has proven to be a very successful program.

modified: Pittman-Robertson fund interest — becomes available for apportionment at the beginning of fiscal year 2033 instead of fiscal year 2026

bills.title: Medal of Honor Act
bills.official_title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to increase the rate of the special pension payable to Medal of Honor recipients, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-43 on December 1, 2025. Sponsored by Rep. Troy Nehls (R-TX) with 4 cosponsors; per the printed legislative history, it passed the House on February 26, 2025 and the Senate on November 7, 2025 before being signed.
bills.summary: Raises the VA's special monthly pension for Medal of Honor recipients by replacing the fixed $1,406.73 rate with a rate tied to the veterans' disability-compensation schedule. It also extends through January 31, 2033 the rule capping VA pension at $90 a month for certain veterans in Medicaid-funded nursing homes.
bills.brief: Replaces the fixed Medal of Honor special pension of $1,406.73 a month with a higher schedule-based rate, and extends the Medicaid nursing-home pension cap of $90 a month through January 31, 2033.

top_lines.headline: Medal of Honor Pension Increase
subs: Fixed rate of $1,406.73 replaced with a schedule-based rate
New rate tied to compensation for a veteran without dependents
No double increases in the same year

top_lines.headline: Pension Cap Extension
subs: Cap of $90 a month for Medicaid nursing-home veterans extended
Cap now expires January 31, 2033 instead of November 30, 2031

items.main: Names the Act the "Medal of Honor Act" and sets out findings on the Medal of Honor and the special pension paid to those on the Medal of Honor Roll.
items.detail: The findings state that Medal of Honor recipients have earned a substantial and historic increase to the special pension paid monthly under section 1562 of title 38.

sections.label: Section 3 — Increase in Department of Veterans Affairs Special Pension Payable to Medal of Honor Recipients

items.main: Replaces the fixed special pension of $1,406.73 a month for Medal of Honor recipients with a rate equal to the monthly compensation paid to a veteran without dependents under section 1114(m) of title 38, increased to the next intermediate rate under section 1114(p).
items.detail: The special pension is paid by the VA to each living person whose name is on the Army, Navy, Air Force, and Coast Guard Medal of Honor Roll, with surviving spouses also eligible under existing law. Tying the rate to the compensation schedule replaces the prior fixed dollar amount.

items.main: Bars the pension's annual cost-of-living adjustment in any year when the amount was already otherwise increased that year.
items.detail: Existing law raises the special pension every December 1 by the same percentage as the Social Security benefit increase. The new rule prevents that adjustment from stacking on top of another increase in the same year.

sections.label: Section 4 — Extension of Certain Limits on Payments of Pension

items.main: Extends from November 30, 2031 to January 31, 2033 the expiration of the rule capping VA pension at $90 per month for certain veterans receiving Medicaid-covered nursing-facility care.
items.detail: Under that rule, a veteran with no spouse or child who is covered by a Medicaid plan for nursing-facility services cannot be paid more than $90 a month in VA pension after the month of admission; the same limit applies to surviving spouses with no child. The extension lengthens the cap's life by 14 months.

underreported.section: Section 4 — Extension of Certain Limits on Payments of Pension
underreported.summary: Extends by 14 months, through January 31, 2033, the $90-per-month VA pension cap for veterans with no spouse or child receiving Medicaid-covered nursing-facility care, and for surviving spouses with no child.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and findings concern honoring Medal of Honor recipients; this provision extends a limit on pension payments to a different group of veterans entirely.

underreported.summary: The Secretary may not apply the annual December cost-of-living increase to the special pension in a year when the amount was otherwise increased.
underreported.why_unreported: The section is labeled as a pension increase; this clause withholds the routine annual adjustment in any year another increase occurs.

gaps: The bill pegs the new pension to the section 1114 rate schedule but states no dollar figure, leaving the actual amount to the compensation tables in effect at any given time.
The findings call for a substantial and historic increase, but the bill does not state the size of the increase in dollars.
The bill extends the Medicaid nursing-home pension cap to January 31, 2033 without stating any criteria for whether the cap should continue past that date.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Nehls
featured_quotes.text: First and foremost, it has been a sincere pleasure to work with the chairman and his staff to advance this important legislation to the House floor. It is an honor to stand with him today. I also extend my gratitude and thanks to my colleague, Mr. Pappas, for co-leading this bipartisan legislation with me for the last two Congresses. Mr. Speaker, today, I rise in strong support of H.R. 695, the Medal of Honor Act. The Medal of Honor is our Nation's highest and most prestigious military decoration that can be awarded.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cruz
featured_quotes.text: Since 1863, Presidents of the United States have awarded the Medal of Honor to more than 3,500 of the bravest men and women ever to wear the uniform of this Nation. Each one has demonstrated valor, gallantry, and heroism above and beyond the call of duty, with acts so selfless, so extraordinary that they stand as beacons of courage for future generations. In 1960, Congress passed Public Law 6556, establishing the Army and Navy Medal of Honor Roll and entitling each Medal of Honor recipient to a modest special pension of $10 per month for life.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Pappas
featured_quotes.text: The Medal of Honor is our Nation's highest military decoration. It recognizes the extraordinary valor that distinguished men and women of our military demonstrated in critical moments during their service to our great Nation. There are 63 living Medal of Honor recipients, including heroes like Army Staff Sergeant Ryan Pitts of New Hampshire, who served two tours in Afghanistan. During his second deployment, hundreds of insurgents attacked the Army base where he was stationed.

added: Rule barring the annual cost-of-living adjustment to the Medal of Honor special pension in any year the amount was otherwise increased
modified: Medal of Honor special pension — fixed monthly rate of $1,406.73 replaced by the section 1114(m) compensation rate for a veteran without dependents, increased to the next intermediate rate under section 1114(p)
Medicaid nursing-facility pension cap — expiration extended from November 30, 2031 to January 31, 2033

bills.title: Disapproving the behavior of Representative Jesús G. Chuy García of Illinois.
bills.official_title: Disapproving the behavior of Representative Jesús G. Chuy García of Illinois.
bills.likelihoodReason: Adopted by the House 236-183 with 4 voting present (Roll no. 292) on November 18, 2025. A simple resolution takes effect on House adoption — no Senate or presidential action is involved. Sponsored by Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-WA), a member of García's own party, with no cosponsors.
bills.summary: The House went on record disapproving the behavior of Rep. Jesús "Chuy" García of Illinois. The resolution recounts that García filed for reelection, that his chief of staff filed as the only other Democrat on the last day of filing at his direction, and that García then withdrew after the deadline — leaving her the lone Democrat on the March 2026 primary ballot.
bills.brief: Formally disapproves of Rep. Chuy García's conduct around Illinois primary ballot filing, finding he directed his chief of staff to file before he withdrew after the deadline.

top_lines.headline: Formal Rebuke
subs: House disapproves of Rep. García's behavior
Finds his actions beneath the dignity of his office

top_lines.headline: Ballot Timeline
subs: García filed for reelection October 27, 2025
Chief of staff filed November 5, the last day
García withdrew November 6, after the deadline

sections.label: Resolved Clause — Disapproval of Representative García

items.main: Places the House on record disapproving the behavior of the Representative from Illinois, Mr. García.
items.detail: The resolution's findings state that García filed nominating petitions on October 27, 2025 for the March 2026 Democratic primary; that his chief of staff, Patty Garcia, submitted her own paperwork on November 5, the last day of filing; that on November 6 — after the filing deadline — García confirmed he would not seek another term and would withdraw his petitions; and that his chief of staff was the only Democrat who filed, at his direction, which the findings describe as undermining the process of a free and fair election.

gaps: The resolution disapproves of the behavior but imposes no sanction, referral, or further action.
The findings describe the conduct as undermining a free and fair election, but the resolution directs no election-related remedy.
The resolution states the chief of staff filed at Representative García's direction but cites no investigation or source for that finding.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Espaillat
featured_quotes.text: Since 2019, I have been proud to call the gentleman from Illinois both a colleague and a trusted friend. During the build back better negotiations, we stood shoulder to shoulder to defend immigrant communities when it mattered the most. That is who Chuy Garcia is. He leads with conviction, courage, and integrity, even when he stands alone. Chuy Garcia came up during the era of the late and great Harold Washington in Chicago who took down the political machine.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Morelle
featured_quotes.text: I once again remind the Members that any one of the citizens of this district could have filed petitions. In fact, Mr. Garcia has faced primaries before and general elections before.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I stand here, believe it or not, with a grateful heart. Over the last several days, many of my colleagues have reached out with kindness and understanding. I appreciate their concern for me and their desire to keep our Caucus united. I wasn't expecting to stand here to debate my retirement, but before any of us are Members of Congress, we are husbands, we are grandfathers, we are sons, we are mothers, and we are sisters. We are regular people, but life reminds us that our jobs come second to the people waiting for us at home.

added: Formal House record of disapproval of Representative García's behavior

bills.title: Directing the Committee on Ethics to preserve and publicly release records relating to monetary settlements involving acts of sexual harassment.
bills.official_title: Directing the Committee on Ethics to preserve and publicly release records relating to monetary settlements involving acts of sexual harassment.
bills.likelihoodReason: Adopted by the House 420-0 with 1 voting present (Roll no. 233) on June 30, 2026 — unanimous across both parties. A simple resolution takes effect on House adoption, and the 60-day disclosure clock runs from that date. Sponsored by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) with no cosponsors.
bills.summary: Orders the House Ethics Committee and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights to publish, within 60 days, a list naming every House member whose sexual-harassment or sexual-abuse case ended in a taxpayer-funded payment — with the total amount shown next to each name. Aggregate totals must also be published for other taxpayer-funded settlements involving members and for House-employee cases.
bills.brief: Requires public, name-by-name disclosure within 60 days of taxpayer-funded sexual-harassment settlements involving House members, plus aggregate totals for other member and employee settlements.

top_lines.headline: Naming Names
subs: Members with taxpayer-funded harassment settlements listed publicly
Total taxpayer amount shown next to each name
Disclosure due within 60 days of adoption

top_lines.headline: Aggregate Totals
subs: Totals disclosed for member settlements not involving harassment
House-employee settlement totals split the same way

top_lines.headline: What Counts
subs: Any settlement with a sexual-misconduct component counts in full

sections.label: Resolved Clauses — Public Release of Settlement Records

items.main: Requires a single consolidated public list naming each Member, Delegate, or Resident Commissioner who was the subject of a review or investigation involving sexual harassment under clause 9 or clause 18 of House Rule XXIII — or any sexual-harassment or sexual-abuse case — that resulted in a payment of taxpayer funds, with the total taxpayer amount adjacent to each name.
items.detail: The duty falls on the Committee on Ethics and the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights for matters they reviewed, conducted, or facilitated, and the list is due not later than 60 days after adoption.

items.main: Requires aggregate totals of taxpayer funds paid in three other categories: member settlements with no sexual-misconduct component, House-employee settlements involving sexual harassment or abuse, and House-employee settlements not involving it.
items.detail: These categories are disclosed as lump totals rather than by name.

items.main: Counts a settlement as involving sexual harassment, abuse, or misconduct if that was any component of the matter, regardless of how the case was classified or resolved.
items.detail: This classification rule prevents matters from being excluded because they were settled under a different claim or category.

underreported.summary: Requires disclosure of aggregate taxpayer-funded settlement totals for matters that did not involve sexual harassment, covering both members and House employees.
underreported.why_unreported: The resolution's title concerns sexual-harassment settlement records, but these clauses also compel totals for every other kind of taxpayer-funded settlement, in aggregate.

gaps: Members are named individually, but House employees' settlements are disclosed only as aggregate totals.
The resolution sets a 60-day deadline but provides no enforcement mechanism if the committee or office misses it.
The disclosure covers names and amounts but not case details, dates, or the outcomes of the underlying investigations.
The resolution reaches matters the Ethics Committee or the Office of Congressional Workplace Rights handled, but does not address settlements resolved outside those two bodies.

added: Public, name-by-name disclosure of taxpayer-funded sexual-harassment settlements involving House members, with amounts, due within 60 days of adoption
Aggregate disclosure of other taxpayer-funded settlement totals for members and House employees
Classification rule counting any settlement with a sexual-misconduct component in full

bills.title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon.
bills.official_title: Directing the President pursuant to section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon.
bills.likelihoodReason: Failed in the House 189-235 (Roll no. 232) on June 30, 2026. Sponsored by Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) with 43 cosponsors — a Democratic war-powers directive brought to the floor in a Republican-majority chamber, where the majority voted it down.
bills.summary: Directs the President, under section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution, to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days of adoption. Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities could continue.
bills.brief: Directs removal of U.S. Armed Forces from hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days, with carve-outs for security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities.

top_lines.headline: War Powers Directive
subs: Forces out of Lebanon hostilities within 7 days
Invokes section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution

top_lines.headline: Carve-Outs
subs: Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces may continue
Diplomatic-facility protection unaffected
Nothing in it authorizes military force

sections.label: Section 1 — Removal of United States Armed Forces From Any Hostilities in Lebanon

items.main: Directs the President to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon no later than 7 days after adoption of the resolution, invoking section 5(c) of the War Powers Resolution.
items.detail: The directive covers any hostilities in Lebanon, and the 7-day clock runs from the date the concurrent resolution is adopted.

items.main: Preserves security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and the protection of diplomatic facilities, and states that nothing in the resolution authorizes the use of military force.
items.detail: The non-authorization clause is stated to be consistent with section 8(a)(1) of the War Powers Resolution.

underreported.section: Section 2 — Rule of Construction Relating to Certain Activities
underreported.summary: Security cooperation with the Lebanese Armed Forces and protection of diplomatic facilities may continue even after forces are removed from hostilities.
underreported.why_unreported: The title reads as a full removal of U.S. forces from hostilities in Lebanon; the carve-out keeps two categories of U.S. military activity there running.

gaps: The resolution does not define which U.S. activities in Lebanon count as hostilities — the term that triggers removal.
The 7-day removal clock runs from adoption, but the resolution sets no reporting or verification requirement to confirm removal.
Security cooperation is preserved but not defined, leaving open how it differs from participation in hostilities.

added: Directive to remove U.S. Armed Forces from any hostilities in Lebanon within 7 days of adoption

bills.title: To repeal certain provisions relating to notification to Senate offices regarding legal process on disclosure of Senate data, and for other purposes.
bills.official_title: To repeal certain provisions relating to notification to Senate offices regarding legal process on disclosure of Senate data, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Austin Scott (R-GA) with 39 cosponsors; the House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Repeals Section 213 of title II of division C of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026 — the provision that established notification requirements for Senate offices regarding legal process on the disclosure of Senate data — and all amendments made by that section.
bills.brief: Wipes out Section 213 of the FY2026 continuing appropriations extensions act and the amendments it made, ending the Senate-notification regime it created around legal process on Senate data.

top_lines.headline: Section 213 Repealed
subs: Repeals Section 213 of title II of division C of the FY2026 continuing appropriations extensions act
The amendments made by that section are also repealed
The section is declared to have no force or effect

sections.label: Section 1 — Repeal of Senate Notification Requirements Relating to Legal Process on Disclosures of Senate Data

items.main: Repeals Section 213 of title II of division C of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026, together with the amendments made by that section.
items.detail: The bill states that the repealed section and its amendments "shall have no force or effect." The bill contains no other operative provisions.

gaps: The bill repeals the underlying section without stating an alternative notification standard for legal process on Senate data.
The bill does not describe transitional treatment for any notifications already issued under the repealed section.
The bill does not fetch or restate the language of the repealed section, so its full scope is not visible in this Act's own text.
The bill provides no effective date and no severability clause.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walkinshaw
featured_quotes.text: These eight Senators provided support to President Trump's attempt to overturn the results of a free and fair election. It is a brazen attempt by Republicans to further whitewash a conspiracy and a violent insurrection while lining their own pockets with taxpayer dollars. It is a trifecta of the type of corruption that shakes Americans' faith in Congress: contempt for the rule of law, a secret backroom deal, and self-enrichment. This Republican Senator slush fund is yet another example of the corruption that has taken hold here.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: Included in the Senate amendment to H.R. 5371 was a section providing for a private right of action for those Senators who were targeted by the Biden administration to access their cell phone data. I support repealing this particular provision, not because I think that these Senators and others should not be able to sue the Federal Government for these acts, but because they already have the ability to do so.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Austin Scott
featured_quotes.text: Wow. There has been a lot said in the last few minutes. Let's be clear: Senate Democratic leadership knew about the language, as well as Senate Republican leadership. Both sides knew about this language. Nobody in the House supported this language. This language did not go through any committee in the Senate, did not go through any committee in the House, and could never be passed and signed into law if it was discussed openly where the American citizens could actually see and understand what was happening.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Morelle
featured_quotes.text: I need to say, as someone who served on the House Rules Committee for 4 years, that we clearly could have put on the floor and made in order an amendment to strike this provision from the bill that had been passed by the Senate. Most people who took social studies in elementary school understand the bill has to pass the Senate and the House before it is sent to the President. Had we had the opportunity, we would have voted on an amendment.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Roy
featured_quotes.text: We both immediately raised this issue in front of the Rules Committee and for the entire body. There is nobody, to the best of my knowledge, in this body who supports this language that was inserted in the end of the funding bill that we passed last week. I don't know anybody. I have yet to meet one person who supports it.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rose
featured_quotes.text: It would repeal the indefensible Senate payday provision that was snuck into the critical funding legislation to reopen the government last week. With the goal of ending the suffering caused by the Schumer shutdown top of mind, I voted yes on the CR. It was the right thing to do.

removed: Section 213 of title II of division C of the Continuing Appropriations, Agriculture, Legislative Branch, Military Construction and Veterans Affairs, and Extensions Act, 2026, and all amendments made by that section

bills.brief: Extends TSA's reimbursable screening services program from fiscal year 2026 through fiscal year 2031 and raises the participation cap from eight to 14.

bills.title: FEC Administrative Improvements Act

bills.brief: Requires electronic FEC filing for persons making electioneering communications and lets political committees pay by methods other than check.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steil
featured_quotes.text: There is a lot of work to be done to update our campaign finance laws for the digital age, and this is an important piece of legislation. I encourage all my colleagues to vote in favor of H.R. 8738.
