bills.title: Protect America's Workforce Act
bills.official_title: To nullify the Executive Order relating to Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME) with 226 cosponsors — one of the largest cosponsor blocs in the batch. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Section 2 declares the March 27, 2025 Executive Order titled "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs" of no force or effect and bars any federal funds from being obligated or expended to carry it out. Section 3 preserves any collective bargaining agreement in effect as of March 26, 2025 between an executive branch federal agency and an exclusive representative of federal employees through the stated term of that agreement.
bills.brief: Nullifies the March 27, 2025 executive order excluding federal agencies from federal labor-management relations programs and preserves collective bargaining agreements that were in effect the day before the order.

top_lines.headline: Executive Order Nullified
subs: Applies to the Executive Order titled "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs" issued March 27, 2025
The order "shall have no force or effect"
No federal funds may be obligated or expended to carry it out

top_lines.headline: Existing CBAs Preserved
subs: Covers collective bargaining agreements in effect as of March 26, 2025
Agreements between executive branch federal agencies and exclusive representatives of federal employees
They have full force and effect through the stated term of the applicable agreement

items.main: Names the Act the "Protect America's Workforce Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Nullification of Executive Order Relating to Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs

items.main: The March 27, 2025 Executive Order titled "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs" is declared to have no force or effect, and no federal funds may be obligated or expended to carry it out.
items.detail: The section identifies the order by title and issuance date but does not list which specific agencies or bargaining units it addressed.

items.main: Any collective bargaining agreement in effect as of March 26, 2025 between any executive branch federal agency and any labor organization that is an exclusive representative of federal employees has full force and effect through the stated term of the applicable agreement.
items.detail: The section fixes eligibility to the day before the executive order but does not distinguish among agencies or bargaining units.

gaps: The bill does not restate which agencies or units the March 27, 2025 executive order covered; the scope of what is being nullified is not described in the Act itself.
The bill does not address collective bargaining agreements negotiated after March 26, 2025 or renewals during the covered agreements' stated terms.
The bill does not provide a remedy or enforcement mechanism for actions taken between March 27, 2025 and enactment.
The bill does not set an effective date beyond the general rule for enactment.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: That was a long minute for the leader of the Democratic Party to advocate for more work-from-home policies for our Federal employees. I think the American people have spoken loud and clear. They support our Federal employees, like the Republican Party, but we expect them to show up for work, not get paid to be home and not be accessible by phone or by computer or by email. That is what we heard from the leader of the Democratic Party.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cloud
featured_quotes.text: The proposed legislation is designed to nullify President Trump's lawful executive order to exclude agencies with national security missions from collective bargaining agreements. Article II of the Constitution is crystal clear: The executive power is invested in the President of the United States. Let me repeat: All authority in the executive branch flows from the people to the duly elected executive.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: This legislation reaffirms a core principle: A government that serves the people must also respect the rights of those who serve within it. Federal employees work tirelessly every day, often behind the scenes. They process Social Security benefits, safeguard our food and water, care for our veterans, and respond whenever a disaster strikes. Their work is essential, and its impact reaches every community across this Nation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Biggs
featured_quotes.text: This bill would nullify President Trump's Executive Order No. 14251, which rightly excluded 40 national security agencies from collective bargaining. Agencies like FEMA, the Coast Guard, the CDC, and the VA cannot afford to be paralyzed by union red tape when lives are on the line. I want to emphasize that this is going to nullify an executive order. It is going to attack his agenda, the America First agenda, that he was overwhelmingly elected to enact. These unions are not neutral actors.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Norcross
featured_quotes.text: Earlier this year, President Trump launched one of the largest attacks on labor in the history of the United States, on the working people who voted to join a union and have a voice. President Trump suggests that this is a problem of national security. Quite frankly, it has not been. They cited that there would be strikes. There hasn't been, and it is illegal to strike. In fact, we are looking for workers to help build our military at the very time that the President is trying to beat down those workers. This is where the real problem is.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Krishnamoorthi
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan bill reverses an illegal executive order that stripped collective bargaining rights from roughly 67 percent of the Federal workforce, so more than two-thirds of the Federal workforce. Removing their limited bargaining rights does not improve efficiency. It threatens the integrity of our civil service. These rights exist for one essential reason: to shield Federal employees from political pressure so that they serve the American people, not the agenda of any one President or political party.

added: Preservation of collective bargaining agreements in effect between executive branch federal agencies and exclusive representatives as of March 26, 2025, through their stated terms
removed: Force and effect of the Executive Order titled "Exclusions from Federal Labor-Management Relations Programs" issued March 27, 2025, together with any federal funding to carry it out

bills.title: Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 to apply the prohibition against contributions and donations by foreign nationals in connection with elections to contributions or donations in connection with ballot initiatives and referenda.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-PA) with 2 cosponsors. Cleared the House per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Amends section 319(a)(1)(A) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 (52 U.S.C. 30121(a)(1)(A)) by inserting ", including a State or local ballot initiative or referendum or recall election" after "State, or local election." The amendment applies to contributions and donations made on or after the date of enactment.
bills.brief: Extends the Federal Election Campaign Act's ban on foreign national contributions and donations to state and local ballot initiatives, referenda, and recall elections, applying to contributions made on or after enactment.

top_lines.headline: Foreign National Ban Extended to Ballot Measures
subs: Adds ", including a State or local ballot initiative or referendum or recall election" after "State, or local election"

top_lines.headline: Forward-Looking Effective Date
subs: Applies to contributions and donations made on or after the date of enactment

items.main: Names the Act the "Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act".
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Prohibition on Contributions and Donations by Foreign Nationals in Connection with Ballot Initiatives and Referenda and Recall Elections

items.main: Amends section 319(a)(1)(A) of the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 (52 U.S.C. 30121(a)(1)(A)) by inserting ", including a State or local ballot initiative or referendum or recall election" after "State, or local election."
items.detail: The bill does not modify any of the other elements of section 319, including the definition of "foreign national" or the range of covered persons; it only widens the list of election-related activities that the prohibition reaches.

items.main: Sets an effective date under which the amendment applies with respect to contributions and donations made on or after the date of enactment.
items.detail: The Act does not create a retroactive remedy; contributions made before enactment are not covered by the amended clause.

criticisms.why: Madam Speaker, this legislation is built on a simple principle: American elections should be decided by the American people, not by the influence of foreign actors. The Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act closes a dangerous and longstanding loophole in our current election system. While current Federal law already prohibits foreign nationals from contributing to candidates running for office, there remains gaps when it comes to State and local ballot measures.

gaps: The bill does not restate the definition of "foreign national" used in section 319; the term's scope is set by the underlying statute, which is not reproduced here.
The bill does not create a new enforcement mechanism or private right of action for the expanded prohibition.
The bill does not preempt or accommodate state-level laws that already restrict foreign contributions to ballot measures.
The bill does not authorize any funding for Federal Election Commission implementation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: Madam Speaker, this legislation is built on a simple principle: American elections should be decided by the American people, not by the influence of foreign actors. The Stop Foreign Funds in Elections Act closes a dangerous and longstanding loophole in our current election system. While current Federal law already prohibits foreign nationals from contributing to candidates running for office, there remains gaps when it comes to State and local ballot measures.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Morelle
featured_quotes.text: Again, I reiterate my support for the bill, and I want to thank the bill's sponsors, Mr. Fitzpatrick as well as Mr. Golden, for their work on this bill and continue to believe that there is much we can do and much that we need to do. This is an important step along the way.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steil
featured_quotes.text: I will close by saying I thank my colleague Brian Fitzpatrick from Pennsylvania and Ranking Member Morelle for their work on closing this gap in Federal law.

added: ", including a State or local ballot initiative or referendum or recall election" added to 52 U.S.C. 30121(a)(1)(A) — expands the foreign-national contribution/donation ban to those categories

bills.title: To lower the age at which a minor may be tried as an adult for certain criminal offenses in the District of Columbia to 14 years of age.
bills.official_title: To lower the age at which a minor may be tried as an adult for certain criminal offenses in the District of Columbia to 14 years of age.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) with 6 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Amends two sections of the District of Columbia Official Code to lower the age at which a minor may be treated as an adult in criminal proceedings for certain offenses. In section 16-2301(3) the exclusion threshold moves from "sixteen years of age" to "fourteen years of age." In section 16-2307(a) the ages at which a minor may be transferred to a criminal proceeding drop from "fifteen," "sixteen," and "eighteen" to "fourteen" in paragraphs (1), (2), and (3) respectively. The changes apply to criminal offenses committed on and after the date of enactment.
bills.brief: Amends the D.C. Official Code to lower the age at which a minor may be excluded from Family Court jurisdiction, or transferred to a criminal proceeding, from sixteen/fifteen/eighteen to fourteen — applying to offenses committed on or after enactment.

top_lines.headline: Family Court Exclusion Age Lowered to 14
subs: Section 16-2301(3), D.C. Official Code: "sixteen years of age" struck and "fourteen years of age" inserted
In the matter following subparagraph (C): "the age of sixteen" replaced with "the age of fourteen"

top_lines.headline: Criminal Transfer Ages All Reset to 14
subs: Section 16-2307(a)(1): "fifteen" → "fourteen"
Section 16-2307(a)(2): "sixteen" → "fourteen"
Section 16-2307(a)(3): "eighteen" → "fourteen"

top_lines.headline: Applies Prospectively
subs: Applies with respect to criminal offenses committed on and after the date of enactment

sections.label: Section 1 — Lowering Age at Which a Minor May Be Tried as Adult for Certain Criminal Offenses in District of Columbia

items.main: Subsection (a) amends section 16-2301, D.C. Official Code, paragraph (3), by striking "sixteen years of age" and inserting "fourteen years of age," and by striking "the age of sixteen" and inserting "the age of fourteen" in the matter following subparagraph (C).
items.detail: The bill leaves the surrounding structure of paragraph (3) intact; only the two age references are changed.

items.main: Subsection (b) amends section 16-2307(a), D.C. Official Code, striking "fifteen" in paragraph (1) and inserting "fourteen," striking "sixteen" in paragraph (2) and inserting "fourteen," and striking "eighteen" in paragraph (3) and inserting "fourteen."
items.detail: All three paragraph-level age thresholds for transfer to a criminal proceeding are moved to the same fourteen-year figure.

items.main: Subsection (c) applies the Act and its amendments only to criminal offenses committed on and after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Offenses committed before enactment remain governed by the pre-amendment ages.

gaps: The bill does not restate which categories of offenses trigger the exclusion or transfer, since those criteria are set in the surrounding text of sections 16-2301 and 16-2307 rather than in this Act.
The bill does not modify the procedural safeguards that accompany a transfer determination in section 16-2307.
The bill does not address parallel age references elsewhere in the D.C. Official Code that govern juvenile custody, records, or sentencing.
The bill does not include an appropriation or resource plan for the D.C. courts or corrections agencies that would handle the change.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Comer
featured_quotes.text: We have debated these bills in a sincere effort to work with the President of the United States to lower crime in D.C. We have heard nothing from the Democrats other than there is no crime problem in D.C., and that a solution is to make Washington, D.C., a State. We are serious about lowering crime. We applaud the efforts of the President of the United States. We will continue to work with him to make our Capital City as safe as possible. I appreciate Brandon Gill, the sponsor of the bill, and Byron Donalds for sponsoring the last bill.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Pressley
featured_quotes.text: This bill seeks to create 14-year-old prisoners in the adult criminal legal system. We know this approach doesn't improve public safety. It only traumatizes our babies. History tells us as much. Antron McCray, 15 years old; Yusef Salaam, 15 years old; Raymond Santana, 14 years old; Korey Wise, 16 years old; and Kevin Richardson, 14 years old. These five boys with big smiles and bright futures ahead of them went on to experience fear and manipulation that no child should.

modified: Section 16-2301(3), D.C. Official Code: exclusion age reduced from sixteen to fourteen years
Section 16-2307(a)(1), D.C. Official Code: transfer age reduced from fifteen to fourteen
Section 16-2307(a)(2), D.C. Official Code: transfer age reduced from sixteen to fourteen
Section 16-2307(a)(3), D.C. Official Code: transfer age reduced from eighteen to fourteen

bills.title: FAST VETS Act
bills.official_title: To amend title 38, United States Code, to modify the conditions under which the Secretary of Veterans Affairs is required to redevelop the individualized vocational rehabilitation plan for a veteran, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-72 on January 20, 2026. Per the printed legislative history for H.R. 4446, the House considered and passed the measure on September 15, 2025 and the Senate considered and passed it on December 18, 2025.
bills.summary: Modifies the redevelopment step of the Department of Veterans Affairs' individualized vocational rehabilitation plan process. Section 3107(b) of title 38, United States Code, is restructured so that after the required review, the Secretary either (A) redevelops the plan when the veteran's long-range rehabilitation goals are no longer feasible due to changes in the veteran's employment handicap and are likelier under a different plan formulated under subsection (a), or (B) disapproves redevelopment when the Secretary determines it is not appropriate.
bills.brief: Amends 38 U.S.C. 3107(b) so that, after reviewing a veteran's vocational rehabilitation plan, the VA Secretary either redevelops it under specified conditions or disapproves redevelopment when not appropriate.

top_lines.headline: Restructured Redevelopment Decision
subs: Amends 38 U.S.C. 3107(b) (Section 3107 of title 38)
Existing review sentence becomes paragraph (1)
The prior second sentence is struck

top_lines.headline: Two-Path Determination
subs: Redevelop when long-range rehabilitation goals are no longer feasible due to changes in the employment handicap AND likelier under a different plan under subsection (a)
Disapprove redevelopment when the Secretary determines redevelopment is not appropriate

items.main: Names the Act the "Focused Assistance and Skills Training for Veterans' Employment and Transition Success Act" or the "FAST VETS Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Conditions Under Which Secretary of Veterans Affairs Shall Redevelop Individualized Vocational Rehabilitation Plan

items.main: Amends subsection (b) of section 3107 of title 38, United States Code, by striking "The Secretary shall review" and inserting "(1) The Secretary shall review"; by striking the second sentence; and by adding a new paragraph (2).
items.detail: The rewrite converts the existing single-sentence review requirement into a numbered paragraph (1) and clears out the prior second sentence, making room for the new determination framework.

items.main: New paragraph (2) directs the Secretary, on the basis of the review, to (A) redevelop the plan when long-range rehabilitation goals are no longer feasible due to changes in the veteran's employment handicap and are likelier under a different plan formulated under subsection (a), or (B) disapprove redevelopment when it is determined not to be appropriate.
items.detail: Both criteria in prong (A) — infeasibility due to changes in the employment handicap and higher likelihood under a different plan — must be met before the Secretary redevelops the plan.

gaps: The bill does not describe how the Secretary must document a determination that redevelopment is not appropriate.
The bill does not set a deadline within which the Secretary must act on the review before the veteran's plan status is resolved.
The bill does not create appeal rights specific to the new redevelopment or disapproval determinations.
The bill does not authorize additional funding for the vocational rehabilitation program to support the restructured review.

added: New 38 U.S.C. 3107(b)(2): two-path Secretary determination — redevelop under specified conditions or disapprove redevelopment when not appropriate
modified: 38 U.S.C. 3107(b): existing review sentence renumbered as paragraph (1)
removed: The prior second sentence of 38 U.S.C. 3107(b)

bills.title: Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserves Tuition Fairness Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To Amend title 38, United States Code, to direct the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to disapprove courses of education offered by a public institution of higher learning that does not charge the in-State tuition rate to a veteran using certain educational assistance under title 10 of such Code, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-55 on December 12, 2025. Per the printed legislative history for H.R. 983, the House considered and passed the measure on April 7, 2025 and the Senate considered and passed it on November 20, 2025.
bills.summary: Extends the Department of Veterans Affairs' in-State tuition disapproval regime in section 3679(c) of title 38, United States Code, to cover educational assistance under chapter 1606 of title 10 (Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserves). It inserts ", or chapter 1606 of title 10," after existing chapter citations in paragraph (1) and paragraph (6), adds a new subparagraph (E) covering individuals entitled to assistance under section 16131 of title 10, and makes conforming changes to subsection (e). The amendments apply to an academic period that begins on or after August 1, 2026.
bills.brief: Extends the VA in-State tuition disapproval rule in 38 U.S.C. 3679 to Selected Reserves educational assistance under chapter 1606 of title 10, effective for academic periods beginning on or after August 1, 2026.

top_lines.headline: Chapter 1606 Added to the Disapproval Rule
subs: 38 U.S.C. 3679(c)(1): inserts ", or chapter 1606 of title 10," after the existing chapter list
38 U.S.C. 3679(c)(6): inserts ", or chapter 1606 of title 10" before the period at the end

top_lines.headline: New Eligible Individual
subs: 38 U.S.C. 3679(c)(2)(E): individual entitled to assistance under section 16131 of title 10

top_lines.headline: Effective for Academic Periods Beginning On or After Aug. 1, 2026
subs: Amendments take effect on the date of enactment
But apply with respect to an academic period that begins on or after August 1, 2026

items.main: Names the Act the "Montgomery GI Bill Selected Reserves Tuition Fairness Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Department of Veterans Affairs Disapproval of Courses Offered by Public Institutions of Higher Learning That Do Not Charge Veterans In-State Tuition Rate for Purposes of Selected Reserve Educational Assistance Program

items.main: Subsection (a) amends 38 U.S.C. 3679(c) by (1) inserting ", or chapter 1606 of title 10," after "chapter 30, 31, 33, or 35 of this title" in paragraph (1); (2) adding new subparagraph (E) to paragraph (2), covering an individual entitled to assistance under section 16131 of title 10; and (3) inserting ", or chapter 1606 of title 10" before the period at the end of paragraph (6).
items.detail: The three changes extend the disapproval rule to the chapter 1606 (Selected Reserves) program in title 10, while leaving the paragraph (2)(A)-(D) categories in place.

items.main: Subsection (b) makes conforming amendments to 38 U.S.C. 3679(e): paragraph (1)(A) adds ", or chapter 1606 of title 10," after "chapter 31, 33, or 35 of this title"; paragraph (1)(B) replaces "chapter 31 33, or 35 of this title" with "chapter 31, 33, or 35 of this title, or chapter 1606 of title 10"; paragraph (2) makes the same replacement.
items.detail: Subsection (e) references are updated so the covered-chapter lists stay parallel to the amended subsection (c).

items.main: Subsection (c) sets the effective date: amendments take effect on the date of enactment and apply with respect to an academic period that begins on or after August 1, 2026.
items.detail: The two-tier effective date lets institutions and the VA adjust before the change binds any given academic period.

gaps: The bill does not restate the in-State tuition disapproval rule itself; that mechanism is set by the surrounding text of 38 U.S.C. 3679, which is not reproduced in this Act.
The bill does not create a private right of enforcement for a Selected Reserves student denied the in-State rate.
The bill does not authorize additional funding for the VA's disapproval or oversight activities.
The bill does not describe how existing state residency policies at public institutions must be modified to comply.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Van Orden
featured_quotes.text: This bill holds particular significance for me because the issue was first brought to my attention by one of my constituents, Mr. Greg Tremelling, a fellow veteran, during our Veterans Day listening session hosted last Congress. His voice, joined by countless other reservists and veterans, highlighted the urgent need for policy change, and this is precisely what this government  should be doing: listening to our constituents and acting on their needs.

modified: 38 U.S.C. 3679(c)(1): chapter 1606 of title 10 added to the covered-chapter list

bills.title: Improving Care in Rural America Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To reauthorize certain programs regarding rural health care.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) with 5 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate and been placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar (General Orders, Calendar No. 377).
bills.summary: Reauthorizes and adjusts three rural health grant programs administered under section 330A of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c). Subsections (a) and (b) add a new paragraph (4) to sections 330A(e) and 330A(f), directing the Director, when awarding Rural Health Care Services Outreach Grants and Rural Health Network Development Grants, to ensure that funds are used to meet the health care needs of, and involve, rural underserved populations in the local community or region to be served. Subsection (c) amends section 330A(j) by striking "2021 through 2025" and inserting "2026 through 2030," reauthorizing the programs for the next five-year window.
bills.brief: Adds a rural-underserved-population use-of-funds paragraph to two rural health grant programs in 42 U.S.C. 254c and reauthorizes the programs from fiscal years 2021 through 2025 to fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

top_lines.headline: Outreach Grants: Rural Underserved Populations Focus
subs: Amends section 330A(e) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c(e))
New paragraph (4): funds used to meet the health care needs of rural underserved populations and to ensure their involvement in the project

top_lines.headline: Network Development Grants: Same Focus
subs: Amends section 330A(f) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c(f))
New paragraph (4): funds used to increase access via integrated health care networks and involve rural underserved populations in planning, development, and ongoing implementation

top_lines.headline: Reauthorization Window Extended
subs: Amends section 330A(j)
Strikes "2021 through 2025"
Inserts "2026 through 2030"

items.main: Names the Act the "Improving Care in Rural America Reauthorization Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Rural Health Care Services Outreach, Rural Health Network Development, and Small Health Care Provider Quality Improvement Grant Programs

items.main: Subsection (a) amends section 330A(e) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c(e)) by adding a new paragraph (4) directing the Director, in awarding a grant under that subsection, to ensure the funds are used to (A) meet the health care needs of rural underserved populations in the local community or region to be served, and (B) support other activities that ensure the involvement of those populations in the development and ongoing operations of the project.
items.detail: The paragraph is a use-of-funds directive; it does not change the eligibility criteria or matching requirements that govern the grants elsewhere in section 330A.

items.main: Subsection (b) amends section 330A(f) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c(f)) by adding a new paragraph (4) with the same structure — funds used to (A) increase access to quality health care services through integrated health care networks for rural underserved populations, and (B) support other activities to involve those populations in the planning, development, and ongoing implementation of the network.
items.detail: The Network Development Grants program picks up the same rural-underserved-populations focus, expressed in network terms.

items.main: Subsection (c) amends section 330A(j) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 254c(j)) by striking "2021 through 2025" and inserting "2026 through 2030."
items.detail: The single-line reauthorization moves the covered fiscal years without changing the dollar authorization language in subsection (j).

underreported.section: Section 2 heading — Small Health Care Provider Quality Improvement
underreported.summary: The section heading names the "Small Health Care Provider Quality Improvement Grant Programs" alongside the Outreach and Network Development programs, but the operative text of subsections (a), (b), and (c) only amends section 330A subsections (e), (f), and (j) — no discrete change is directed at a Quality Improvement grant subsection.
underreported.why_unreported: The heading is broader than the operative changes; readers scanning the section title may expect provider-quality-specific edits that this Act does not include.

gaps: The bill does not restate the dollar authorization figures in section 330A(j); the reauthorization changes only the fiscal-year window.
The bill does not define "rural underserved populations" for purposes of the new paragraph (4) directives.
The bill does not require the Director to report to Congress on how funds are being used to reach the newly emphasized populations.
The bill does not modify the underlying eligibility criteria for either grant program in sections 330A(e) or 330A(f).

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: Let me be clear, healthcare outcomes should not depend on your ZIP Code. Today, for millions of Americans living in rural communities, that is exactly the reality. Rural residents face serious barriers to care: provider shortages, long travel distances, hospital closures, and limited access to specialists. The consequences are real. Rural Americans experience a 43-percent higher mortality rate compared to those in urban and suburban areas. That is simply unacceptable. This legislation is about addressing those disparities head-on.

New paragraph (4) at 42 U.S.C. 254c(f) — Rural Health Network Development Grants use-of-funds directive for rural underserved populations

bills.title: District of Columbia Judicial Nominations Reform Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to terminate the District of Columbia Judicial Nomination Commission, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Pete Sessions (R-TX) with 2 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Terminates the District of Columbia Judicial Nomination Commission by striking section 434 of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (sec. 1-204.34, D.C. Official Code). Conforming amendments to section 431(b) hand designation of chief judges to the President, section 433(a) removes the President's obligation to nominate from a Commission list, section 433(b) drops Commission-service credit from the judicial qualifications, and section 11-1528(a)(2) of the D.C. Official Code strikes subparagraph (C). The amendments apply to appointments made on or after the date of enactment.
bills.brief: Strikes section 434 of the D.C. Home Rule Act to shut down the D.C. Judicial Nomination Commission, hands chief-judge designation and nominee selection to the President, and applies to appointments made on or after enactment.

bills.title: Improving Travel for American Families Act
bills.official_title: To improve travel for American families, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Ryan Mackenzie (R-PA) with 2 cosponsors. Cleared the House per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Directs the TSA Administrator to establish a two-year pilot program at a minimum of five airports to implement alternative security screening lanes and approaches for passengers and accompanying child passengers twelve years of age and under. The bill is issued "notwithstanding any other provision of law," including the Administrative Procedure Act, the Congressional Review Act, and the Paperwork Reduction Act. Airport selection must prioritize high-family-volume airports and consider space and staffing. A briefing to House Homeland Security and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and Commerce, Science, and Transportation committees is required within one year of enactment.
bills.brief: Sets up a TSA pilot program at five or more airports to test alternative screening lanes for passengers traveling with children twelve or under, running two years, with a one-year briefing to committee.

Consider adequate space and sufficient personnel to keep other lanes staffed

items.main: Names the Act the "Improving Travel for American Families Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Improving Travel for American Families Pilot Program

items.main: Subsection (a) directs the TSA Administrator to establish a pilot program, to be carried out at a minimum of five airports, to implement alternative security screening lanes and approaches for passengers and accompanying child passengers twelve years of age and under. The Administrator acts "notwithstanding any other provision of law," including provisions applicable to issuance of regulations such as chapters 5 and 8 of title 5 (the APA and Congressional Review Act) and chapter 35 of title 44 (the Paperwork Reduction Act).
items.detail: The bill uses shall — not may — for establishing the pilot, and names the APA/CRA/PRA carve-outs by title.

items.main: Subsection (b) sets airport-selection factors: priority to airports the Administrator determines have a high volume of passengers traveling with accompanying child passengers, consideration of airports with adequate space to accommodate additional or larger screening lanes and sufficient personnel to maintain adequate staffing of other lanes, and any other consideration the Administrator determines necessary. Subsection (c) requires a briefing to the House Homeland Security Committee and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committees not later than one year after enactment.
items.detail: Selection criteria are permissive and enumerated; the briefing recipients are three named committees.

items.main: Subsection (d) sets a two-year sunset: the Administrator shall carry out the pilot program for a period of two years.
items.detail: The sunset applies to the pilot program itself, not to the briefing requirement.

underreported.summary: The Administrator's authority to establish the pilot is stated "notwithstanding any other provision of law," including the APA (chapters 5 and 8 of title 5), the Congressional Review Act, and the Paperwork Reduction Act (chapter 35 of title 44).
underreported.why_unreported: The public-facing framing of the bill is a family-lane pilot; the bypass of standard rulemaking and paperwork-approval statutes is a legally distinct feature not evident from the title.

gaps: The bill does not require a public evaluation or metrics report at the end of the pilot; only a one-year briefing to committees is required.
The bill does not authorize funding for the pilot or require reallocation from existing TSA appropriations.
The bill does not set eligibility criteria that airports must meet to volunteer, beyond the Administrator's discretionary considerations.
The bill does not specify how children ages 13-17 traveling as "accompanying family" are treated, since the pilot text names only twelve years of age and under.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Mackenzie
featured_quotes.text: Americans everywhere understand that there are better, easier, and more efficient ways to manage safety screenings at our airports. That was made clear when this legislation was reported unanimously by the Committee on Homeland Security by a vote of 30-0. We are bringing both sides together to give families the more convenient air travel experience that they deserve. As the father of two young children, I know firsthand that family travel can be challenging.

bills.title: One-Stop Pilot Program Extension Act
bills.official_title: To amend title 49, United States Code, to authorize an extension of a program to permit screened passengers and their property arriving on direct flights or flight segments originating at certain foreign last point of departure airports to continue on additional flights or flight segments originating in the United States without additional screening, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-FL) with 1 cosponsor. Cleared the House per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Rewrites subsection (d) of section 7132 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263; 49 U.S.C. 44901 note) so the TSA Administrator, in coordination with the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, may permit checked baggage arriving from participating foreign last point of departure airports to continue on additional flights originating in the United States without additional TSA re-screening if four conditions are met. Subsection (b) also amends subsection (k) of section 7132 by striking "six" and inserting "ten," extending the associated authority.
bills.brief: Rewrites section 7132(d) of the FY2023 NDAA to let TSA and CBP allow checked-baggage transfers from participating foreign airports to continue without re-screening on U.S. connecting flights when four conditions are met, and changes "six" to "ten" in subsection (k).

subs: Amends 49 U.S.C. 44901 note (section 7132(d) of the FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263)

subs: Initial checked baggage screening at the foreign airport used an explosives detection system under an aviation security screening agreement described in subsection (e)
Passengers cannot access their checked baggage until arrival at their final destination
CBP has received timely images meeting CBP requirements before U.S. arrival
CBP has not identified any such passenger or baggage for further inspection

top_lines.headline: Extension — "six" to "ten"

items.main: Names the Act the "One-Stop Pilot Program Extension Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Subsection (a) amends subsection (d) of section 7132 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263; 49 U.S.C. 44901 note) by rewriting it so that, subject to subsection (f), the TSA Administrator, in coordination with the Commissioner of U.S. Customs and Border Protection, may permit checked baggage arriving on direct flights or flight segments arriving from participating foreign last point of departure airports (referred to in subsection (b)) to continue on additional flights or flight segments originating in the United States without additional TSA security re-screening if four conditions are satisfied.
items.detail: The rewrite retains the subsection heading ("Re-Screening of Checked Baggage") and the subject-to-(f) limitation while restructuring the substantive conditions.

items.main: The four conditions in the new subsection (d) are: (1) initial checked baggage screening at the foreign airport was conducted using an explosives detection system in accordance with an aviation security screening agreement described in subsection (e); (2) passengers arriving from such airports cannot access their checked baggage until arrival at their final destination; (3) CBP has received timely images of the baggage prior to arrival in the United States that satisfy CBP requirements, corresponding to the checked baggage, to ensure appropriate border security enforcement can be completed in an efficient manner; and (4) CBP has not identified any such passenger or baggage for further inspection.
items.detail: All four conditions must be met; the coordination with CBP is baked into the granting authority and further reinforced by the CBP-specific conditions in paragraphs (3) and (4).

items.main: Subsection (b) amends subsection (k) of section 7132 of the FY2023 NDAA by striking "six" and inserting "ten."
items.detail: Subsection (k) is not otherwise reproduced in this Act; the change is a single numeric substitution.

gaps: The bill does not restate what subsection (k) of section 7132 measures (the "six" being changed to "ten"), so the practical effect of that change is not visible in the Act's own text.
The bill does not authorize funding for TSA or CBP implementation.
The bill does not describe how the aviation security screening agreements in subsection (e) are negotiated or approved.
The bill does not require public reporting on which foreign airports participate or how often the no-re-screening authority is used.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Gimenez
featured_quotes.text: In south Florida, Miami International Airport is one of the busiest international gateways in the United States. Every day, millions of passengers pass through airports like Miami International Airport throughout the country. We have a responsibility to keep those passengers and our airports moving efficiently while maintaining the highest security standards. This bill does exactly that.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: This bipartisan measure will modernize our aviation system, reduce unnecessary delays, and strengthen our international security partnership that keeps our skies safe. Today, the international passengers connecting to domestic flights must often retrieve their checked bags, clear customs, and undergo yet another screening process through TSA before re-entering the terminal, creating congestion, long connection times, and avoidable operational strain on airports and the airlines.

bills.title: District of Columbia Policing Protection Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To establish standards for law enforcement officers in the District of Columbia to engage in vehicular pursuits of suspects, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Clay Higgins (R-LA) with 2 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Amends the D.C. Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 (D.C. Law 24-345) to rewrite the vehicular pursuit standard. Section 128 is replaced with a rule that an officer who encounters a suspect fleeing in a motor vehicle shall engage in a vehicular pursuit unless the officer, or a higher-ranking official with supervisory authority over the officer, reasonably believes pursuit would entail an unacceptable risk of harm to a person other than the suspect or be futile, or that the suspect can be apprehended more effectively or expeditiously by another means. Section 127(a) is trimmed to eliminate paragraphs (1)-(5) and (8)-(11) and renumber the survivors, and the subtitle S heading is updated. Subsection (b) requires the Attorney General, within three years, to evaluate PursuitAlert or a similar technology and report to four named congressional committees.
bills.brief: Rewrites the D.C. vehicular-pursuit standard to a shall-pursue default with three narrow exceptions, cuts most of section 127(a)'s limitations, and requires a DOJ PursuitAlert cost-benefit evaluation within three years.

top_lines.headline: Shall-Pursue Default with Three Exceptions
subs: Section 128 of the Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 is rewritten (subsections (a), (b), and (c) struck and replaced)

Officer shall engage in vehicular pursuit unless the officer or a supervisor reasonably believes it (A) would entail an unacceptable risk of harm to a person other than the suspect, (B) would be futile, or (C) the suspect can be apprehended more effectively or expeditiously by another means

items.main: Names the Act the "District of Columbia Policing Protection Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Vehicular Pursuits by Law Enforcement Officers in District of Columbia

items.main: Subsection (a) amends the Comprehensive Policing and Justice Reform Amendment Act of 2022 (D.C. Law 24-345) by striking "LIMITATIONS ON THE" from the subtitle S heading of title I and by striking paragraphs (1) through (5) of section 127(a) (sec. 5-365.01(a), D.C. Official Code), redesignating paragraphs (6) and (7) as (1) and (2), striking paragraphs (8) through (11), and redesignating paragraph (12) as (3).
items.detail: The section leaves the surviving paragraphs intact but strips out the surrounding limitations.

items.main: Subsection (a) also amends section 128 (sec. 5-365.02, D.C. Official Code) by striking subsections (a), (b), and (c) and inserting a new rule: if a law enforcement officer encounters a suspect fleeing in a motor vehicle, the officer shall engage in a vehicular pursuit unless the officer or a higher-ranking official with supervisory authority reasonably believes that (1)(A) pursuit would entail an unacceptable risk of harm to a person other than the suspect, (1)(B) pursuit would be futile, or (2) the suspect can be apprehended more effectively or expeditiously by a means other than vehicular pursuit. The table of contents item for subtitle S of title I is updated to "SUBTITLE S. USE OF VEHICULAR PURSUITS BY LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS."
items.detail: The shall-pursue default reverses the prior orientation of section 128 by making pursuit the presumptive response.

items.main: Subsection (b) requires the Attorney General, not later than three years after enactment, to evaluate the costs and benefits of the Metropolitan Police Department of the District of Columbia adopting PursuitAlert or another similar technology capable of alerting members of the public to the presence of a police pursuit in their immediate vicinity, publish a report on the evaluation, and submit it to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, the Senate Committee on the Judiciary, the House Committee on Oversight, and the House Committee on the Judiciary.
items.detail: The three-year timer runs from enactment; the report must be both published and submitted to the four named committees.

underreported.summary: The amendments to section 127(a) strike paragraphs (1)-(5) and (8)-(11), leaving only three surviving paragraphs. The bill does not restate the content of the struck paragraphs.
underreported.why_unreported: The vehicular-pursuit rewrite in section 128 gets the headline treatment, but the substantive effect on D.C. policing turns equally on which limitations in section 127(a) are being removed.

gaps: The bill does not restate the content of the struck paragraphs of section 127(a); the substance of what is being removed is not visible in the Act's own text.
The bill does not describe how compliance with the new section 128 standard will be reviewed or enforced.
The bill does not authorize funding for MPD training, PursuitAlert deployment, or the DOJ evaluation.
The bill does not address parallel D.C. Code provisions or MPD general-order regimes that reference the deleted section 127 language.

We met with D.C. officials, including in hearings, and we advised against what they intended to do.

bills.title: Weatherizing Infrastructure in the North and Terrorism Emergency Readiness Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To require the Secretary of Homeland Security to conduct a collective response to a terrorism exercise that includes the management of cascading effects on critical infrastructure during times of extreme cold weather, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Timothy Kennedy (D-NY) with 1 cosponsor. Cleared the House per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to develop and conduct a collective response to terrorism exercise that includes management of cascading effects on critical infrastructure (as defined in section 1016(e) of Public Law 107-56, 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e)) in accordance with six scenario requirements. The scenario must include an extreme cold weather event (such as one caused by a polar vortex) affecting access to critical services, cascading effects on critical infrastructure, mitigation options, community resilience, coordination with federal, state, local, Tribal, and territorial agencies, and coordination with private sector and community stakeholders. Not later than 60 days after completion of the exercise, the Secretary must submit an after-action report to the House Homeland Security and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committees.
bills.brief: Requires DHS to run a collective terrorism-response exercise focused on cascading effects to critical infrastructure during an extreme cold weather event, followed by an after-action report to House Homeland Security and Senate HSGAC within 60 days of completion.

top_lines.headline: Collective Response Exercise
subs: Secretary of Homeland Security shall develop and conduct the exercise
In addition to or as part of exercise programs currently carried out by the Department

top_lines.headline: Six Scenario Requirements
subs: Extreme cold weather event, such as one caused by a polar vortex, affecting access to critical services
Cascading effects on critical infrastructure (as defined in section 1016(e) of Public Law 107-56, 42 U.S.C. 5195c(e))

Community resilience bolstering

Coordination with private-sector and community stakeholders

subs: To the House Homeland Security Committee and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
Must be consistent with protection of classified information

items.main: Names the Act the "Weatherizing Infrastructure in the North and Terrorism Emergency Readiness Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Exercise on Terrorist Attack During Extreme Cold

items.main: Subsection (a) directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, acting through appropriate offices and components of the Department, to develop and conduct a collective response to terrorism exercise that includes management of cascading effects on critical infrastructure — using the definition of "critical infrastructure" in section 1016(e) of Public Law 107-56 (42 U.S.C. 5195c(e)) — in accordance with the scenario requirements in subsection (b).
items.detail: The exercise is authorized as an addition to or part of existing DHS exercise programs; the definition anchor is section 1016(e) of Public Law 107-56.

items.main: Subsection (b) specifies six scenario requirements: (1) an extreme cold weather event, such as an event caused by a polar vortex, with respect to access to critical services; (2) any cascading effects on critical infrastructure; (3) how the effects of a successful terrorist attack against critical infrastructure could be mitigated by emergency managers, State officials, and appropriate private sector and community stakeholders; (4) how community resilience could be bolstered; (5) coordination with appropriate federal departments and agencies and State, local, Tribal, and territorial agencies; and (6) coordination with appropriate private sector and community stakeholders.
items.detail: All six elements are required to appear in the exercise scenario as written; the Secretary retains discretion over specific design choices within each element.

items.main: Subsection (c) requires the Secretary, not later than 60 days after the completion of the exercise, to submit an after-action report — consistent with the protection of classified information — to the House Committee on Homeland Security and the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs. The report must present initial findings, any immediate and longer-term plans for incorporating lessons learned into future DHS operations, and any proposed legislative changes informed by the exercise.
items.detail: The 60-day report clock runs from exercise completion, not from enactment.

gaps: The bill does not fix a date by which the exercise itself must be completed, only a 60-day report clock after completion.
The bill does not authorize funding for the exercise or the after-action report.
The bill does not require a public version of the after-action report; the classified-information protection may keep findings inside the two named committees.
The bill does not describe how state, local, Tribal, and territorial agencies will be resourced to participate in the coordination elements.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Kennedy
featured_quotes.text: As a nation, we must be prepared to prevent and respond to terrorist threats in every circumstance, including during the harshest winter weather. That is why I introduced the WINTER Act, to strengthen our Homeland Security posture during extreme cold weather conditions and ensure that the Department of Homeland Security is prepared to respond. My hometown of Buffalo, New York, is no stranger to cold weather events. In December of 2022, Winter Storm Elliott hit western New York with historic force.

bills.title: Improving Travel for Military Members Act
bills.official_title: To improve travel for active-duty military personnel and accompanying family, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Sheri Biggs (R-SC) with 2 cosponsors. Cleared the House per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Authorizes the TSA Administrator, not later than 60 days after enactment, to establish a pilot program at airports to expedite access to security screening for traveling active-duty military personnel and accompanying family members, so long as such access does not compromise security protocols. The pilot must screen each covered passenger under Secure Flight per paragraph (2) of section 44903(j) of title 49, prevent access to TSA PreCheck or other expedited lanes without an eligibility-indicating boarding pass under section 44901 of title 49, and permit local management to open or close checkpoint lanes and reallocate resources based on passenger volume. Selection criteria prioritize airports within an Administrator-set distance of a military installation (as defined in section 2801 of title 10) meeting an active-duty threshold. A briefing to House Homeland Security and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committees is due nine months after establishment, and the pilot has a three-year sunset.
bills.brief: Lets TSA set up a pilot within 60 days to expedite airport screening for active-duty military personnel and accompanying family, under three security-preserving requirements, a nine-month briefing, and a three-year sunset.

top_lines.headline: TSA Pilot Program Within 60 Days
subs: Administrator may establish the pilot not later than 60 days after enactment

top_lines.headline: Three Security Requirements
subs: Screen each passenger per Secure Flight, in accordance with paragraph (2) of section 44903(j) of title 49
No TSA PreCheck or other expedited lane access without a boarding pass indicating eligibility under section 44901 of title 49
Permit local management to open or close lanes and reallocate resources as needed

top_lines.headline: Selection, Briefing, and Three-Year Sunset
subs: Priority to airports within an Administrator-set distance of a military installation (as defined in section 2801 of title 10) with an Administrator-set active-duty threshold

Pilot runs for a period of three years

items.main: Names the Act the "Improving Travel for Military Members Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Improving Travel for Active-Duty Military Personnel and Accompanying Family

items.main: Subsection (a) authorizes the TSA Administrator, not later than 60 days after enactment, to establish a pilot program at airports to expedite access to security screening for traveling active-duty military personnel and accompanying family members. The Administrator may carry out this subsection only to the extent such access does not compromise security protocols.
items.detail: Authority is may, not shall — the pilot is discretionary. Subsections (c), (d), and (e) only apply if the Administrator establishes the pilot.

items.main: Subsection (b) sets three security requirements the Administrator must carry out: (1) ensure each passenger described in subsection (a) is screened in accordance with the vetting status under the TSA's Secure Flight program, in accordance with paragraph (2) of section 44903(j) of title 49; (2) prevent individuals carrying out screening functions under section 44901 from allowing any passenger into a TSA PreCheck or other expedited security screening lane unless the passenger has received a boarding pass indicating eligibility for TSA PreCheck or such other expedited security screening; and (3) permit local Administration management to open or close checkpoint lanes and reallocate available resources as needed to maximize security effectiveness and efficiency based on passenger volume.
items.detail: The three requirements preserve Secure Flight-based screening, enforce the boarding-pass-eligibility precondition for expedited lanes, and preserve local flexibility over lane configuration.

items.main: Subsection (c) directs the Administrator, in selecting airports for the pilot program, to (1) give priority to an airport that is not more than a certain distance, as determined by the Administrator, from a military installation (as defined in section 2801 of title 10) to which not fewer than a certain number, as determined by the Administrator, of active-duty military personnel are stationed; (2) consider airports with adequate space to accommodate dedicated screening lanes for the covered population; and (3) use any other consideration the Administrator determines necessary. Subsection (d) requires a briefing to the House Homeland Security Committee and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committees not later than nine months after establishment. Subsection (e) sunsets the pilot at three years.
items.detail: The distance threshold and the active-duty personnel threshold are both delegated to the Administrator; the briefing recipients are three named committees.

underreported.summary: Every operative subsection except (a) and (b) is conditioned on "if the Administrator establishes the pilot program." The Administrator retains discretion over whether to establish the pilot at all.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title suggests a program will exist; the operative text authorizes but does not require it.

gaps: The bill does not fix the distance from a military installation or the active-duty threshold; both are set by the Administrator.
The bill does not authorize funding for the pilot.
The bill does not require a public evaluation or metrics beyond the nine-month committee briefing.
The bill does not specify how accompanying family members are identified for purposes of the expedited lane.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Biggs
featured_quotes.text: I don't speak on this legislation as an outside observer. As a Member currently serving in the Air National Guard, I have worn the uniform. I have seen firsthand what it asks of servicemembers and their families. This legislation is written from experience, not just policy.

added: Three-year TSA pilot program at airports to expedite screening for active-duty military personnel and accompanying family members

bills.title: Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program Amendment Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To establish an interest-bearing account for the non-Federal contributions to the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Ken Calvert (R-CA) with 5 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Amends section 9402 of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (Public Law 111-11; 123 Stat. 1328) by adding a new subsection (c) that establishes a Non-Federal Funding Account for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program in the Treasury. The account holds any unexpended non-Federal contributions provided before enactment and any provided on or after enactment, together with any investment interest. The Treasury Secretary transfers previously contributed funds within 90 days of enactment and moves future contributions as soon as practicable. Amounts and any interest are made available to the Secretary, without further appropriation, for expenditure as provided in the Program Documents and this section. Investment is limited to interest-bearing U.S. obligations; State Parties are not responsible for investment losses.
bills.brief: Creates a Treasury account for non-Federal contributions to the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program, mandates a 90-day transfer of previously contributed funds, and lets those amounts plus interest be spent without further appropriation.

top_lines.headline: New Treasury Account for Non-Federal Contributions
subs: Amends section 9402 of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (Public Law 111-11; 123 Stat. 1328) by adding subsection (c)
Establishes the Non-Federal Funding Account for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program in the Treasury
Account holds pre- and post-enactment non-Federal contributions plus investment interest

top_lines.headline: Transfers Within 90 Days
subs: Previously contributed funds transferred from the general fund of the Treasury within 90 days of enactment
Future non-Federal contributions transferred as soon as practicable after receipt

top_lines.headline: Available Without Further Appropriation
subs: Fund amounts and interest available to the Secretary for expenditure without further appropriation
Investments limited to interest-bearing obligations of the United States
State Parties not responsible for losses due to investment

items.main: Names the Act the "Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program Amendment Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends section 9402 of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009 (Public Law 111-11; 123 Stat. 1328) by adding a new subsection (c) titled "Interest-Bearing Account for Non-Federal Contributions." The subsection defines "Agreement" as the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program Funding and Management Agreement dated April 4, 2005; "Fund" as the Non-Federal Funding Account established by paragraph (2); "non-Federal contribution" as an amount contributed by a State Party for the non-Federal cost share described in section 8 of the Agreement; and "State Party" per section 3 of the Agreement.
items.detail: The four definitions anchor the rest of the subsection to the referenced Agreement.

items.main: Paragraph (2) establishes in the Treasury of the United States a fund known as the Non-Federal Funding Account for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program, consisting of amounts deposited under paragraph (3) plus any interest earned on investment under paragraph (4). Paragraph (3) directs the Treasury Secretary, pursuant to section 8.4 of the Agreement, to deposit any unexpended non-Federal contributions provided before the date of enactment of the subsection and any provided on or after that date; amounts and any interest are made available to the Secretary, without further appropriation, for expenditure as provided in the Program Documents and in accordance with this section.
items.detail: The reference is specifically to section 8.4 of the Agreement; deposit authority is not open-ended.

items.main: Paragraph (4) permits the Treasury Secretary to invest any portion of the Fund not required to meet current needs, only in interest-bearing obligations of the United States. Paragraph (5)(A) requires transfer of previously contributed amounts from the general fund of the Treasury to the Fund not later than 90 days after the date of enactment of the subsection. Paragraph (5)(B) requires transfer of future amounts as soon as practicable after they are contributed. Paragraph (5)(C) provides that in accordance with the Agreement, on deposit of amounts under paragraph (3), the State Parties are not responsible for any losses due to investment of those amounts in the Fund.
items.detail: The 90-day transfer clock applies only to the previously contributed portion; ongoing contributions are handled on an as-soon-as-practicable basis.

gaps: The bill does not restate what the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program does; the substantive program is set by the referenced Agreement and by section 9402 of the 2009 Act.
The bill does not describe the total amount of non-Federal contributions expected to move into the Fund.
The bill does not require public reporting on Fund balances, investment returns, or expenditures.
The bill does not set a sunset for the Fund's availability without further appropriation.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Stanton
featured_quotes.text: The Colorado River is the lifeblood of our region. More than 40 million people across the seven basin States depend on it for drinking water, agriculture, and economic vitality. In Arizona alone, it supports our cities, our farmers, our Tribal communities, and our economy, including our critical semiconductor industry. But this river is under enormous pressure from a drought now entering its 25th year, from overuse, and from a changing climate that is reshaping the West as we know it.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Calvert
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to urge my colleagues to approve my bipartisan legislation, H.R. 831, the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program Amendment Act of 2025. My bill is simple and straightforward: it would establish an interest-bearing account for the nonfederal contributions for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program, a cooperative effort between federal and nonfederal entities in Arizona, California, and Nevada to recover endangered species.

added: New subsection (c) to section 9402 of the Omnibus Public Land Management Act of 2009: Non-Federal Funding Account in the Treasury for the Lower Colorado River Multi-Species Conservation Program, with definitions, deposit/investment rules, and 90-day transfer of previously contributed amounts
Availability of Fund amounts and interest to the Secretary without further appropriation, per the Program Documents and the new subsection

bills.title: Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act
bills.official_title: To establish consumer standards for lithium-ion batteries.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) with 23 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), not later than 180 days after enactment, to promulgate three named voluntary standards as final consumer product safety standards under section 553 of title 5, U.S. Code: ANSI/CAN/UL 2271 (Batteries for Use in Light Electric Vehicle Applications), ANSI/CAN/UL 2849 (Electrical Systems for eBikes), and ANSI/CA/UL 2272 (Electrical Systems for Personal E-Mobility Devices), as in effect on the date of enactment. The Commission must limit the standards' application to consumer products as defined in section 3(a)(5) of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5)). Future revisions of the standards become consumer product safety standards effective 180 days after notice unless the CPSC rejects them within 90 days. Promulgated standards are treated as consumer product safety rules under section 9 of the CPSA (15 U.S.C. 2058). Not later than five years after enactment, the CPSC must report to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on fires, explosions, and other hazards involving lithium-ion batteries in micromobility products.
bills.brief: Requires the CPSC to adopt three UL micromobility-battery standards as final consumer product safety standards within 180 days, treats future revisions as effective 180 days after notice absent CPSC rejection, and requires a five-year hazards report to House Energy and Commerce and Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

top_lines.headline: Three UL Standards Adopted Within 180 Days
subs: CPSC shall promulgate under section 553 of title 5 not later than 180 days after enactment
ANSI/CAN/UL 2271 — Batteries for Use in Light Electric Vehicle Applications
ANSI/CAN/UL 2849 — Electrical Systems for eBikes
ANSI/CA/UL 2272 — Electrical Systems for Personal E-Mobility Devices
As in effect on the date of enactment

top_lines.headline: Automatic Revision Adoption Absent CPSC Rejection
subs: Revisions become consumer product safety standards effective 180 days after notice
Unless CPSC notifies the standards organization within 90 days that the revision does not improve safety
Treated as consumer product safety rules under section 9 of the CPSA (15 U.S.C. 2058)

top_lines.headline: Five-Year Hazards Report
subs: Not later than 5 years after enactment
To Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Covers fires, explosions, and other hazards involving lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility products

items.main: Names the Act the "Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Consumer Product Safety Standard for Certain Batteries

items.main: Subsection (a) requires the CPSC, not later than 180 days after enactment, to promulgate under section 553 of title 5, U.S. Code, the provisions of ANSI/CAN/UL 2271, ANSI/CAN/UL 2849, and ANSI/CA/UL 2272 — as in effect on the date of enactment — as final consumer product safety standards. Subsection (b) requires the CPSC, in adopting the standards, to limit their application to consumer products as defined in section 3(a)(5) of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. 2052(a)(5)).
items.detail: The three UL standards named in the bill are the operative reference set; the scope limitation is fixed by the existing CPSA definition of "consumer product."

items.main: Subsection (c) requires the standards organization to notify the CPSC after final approval of any revision. The revised voluntary standard is considered a consumer product safety standard issued by the CPSC under section 9 of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. 2058), effective 180 days after notification (or such later date specified by the Commission in the Federal Register), unless within 90 days after receiving that notice the CPSC notifies the organization that it has determined the proposed revision (in whole or in part) does not improve safety and that the Commission is retaining the existing standard.
items.detail: The default rule flips the usual rulemaking presumption for revisions: adoption is automatic unless the CPSC affirmatively rejects within 90 days.

items.main: Subsection (d) treats standards promulgated under section 2 (including revisions adopted by the Commission) as consumer product safety rules promulgated under section 9 of the CPSA (15 U.S.C. 2058). Subsection (e) requires the CPSC, not later than 5 years after enactment, to report to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee on fires, explosions, and other hazards relating to lithium-ion batteries used in micromobility products during the period beginning on enactment and ending on the report date, including source of information, make and model, standard-compliance status if known, and manufacturer/country of manufacture if known.
items.detail: The five-year report window runs from enactment; the four required content elements are enumerated.

underreported.summary: Revisions to any of the three UL standards become binding CPSC standards 180 days after the organization notifies the CPSC, unless the CPSC rejects within 90 days.
underreported.why_unreported: The public-facing framing is that Congress is adopting current UL standards; the automatic-adoption default for future revisions delegates ongoing rulemaking authority to a private standards body.

gaps: The bill does not authorize additional funding for CPSC rulemaking or enforcement of the new standards.
The bill does not preempt or coordinate with state-level battery-safety requirements.
The bill does not require a public docket for the CPSC's 90-day review of proposed revisions.
The bill does not describe how imports will be certified or tested for compliance.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Torres

At the heart of our legislative progress has been the tireless advocacy of the FDNY, the finest and bravest fire department in the Nation. The sheer speed and scale of destruction caused by a lithium-ion battery fire is nothing short of staggering.
