bills.title: Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Education Amendments of 1972 to provide that for purposes of determining compliance with title IX of such Act in athletics, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. W. Gregory Steube (R-FL) with 83 cosponsors. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate per the latest recorded action.
bills.summary: Amends section 901 of the Education Amendments of 1972 (20 U.S.C. 1681) by adding a new subsection (d). Paragraph (1) makes it a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates an athletic program or activity to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls. Paragraph (2) provides that for the purposes of the new subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth. Paragraph (3) defines "athletic programs and activities" to include, but not be limited to, all programs or activities provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team. Paragraph (4) allows a recipient to permit males to train or practice with a female-designated program so long as no female is deprived of a listed benefit. Paragraph (5) directs the Comptroller General to study the meaning of "any other benefit" and to submit a report to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
bills.brief: Adds subsection (d) to 20 U.S.C. 1681 defining a title IX violation for federally funded recipients that permit males to participate in athletic programs designated for women or girls (sex defined by reproductive biology and genetics at birth), and orders a Comptroller General report to House Education and Workforce and Senate HELP.

top_lines.headline: New Title IX Violation for Athletics
subs: Amends section 901 of the Education Amendments of 1972 (20 U.S.C. 1681) by adding subsection (d)
Violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity designated for women or girls

top_lines.headline: Sex Defined by Reproductive Biology and Genetics at Birth
subs: Paragraph (2): sex recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth
Paragraph (3): athletic programs and activities include (but are not limited to) all programs or activities provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team
Paragraph (4) practice/training carve-out: allowed only if no female is deprived of a roster spot, practice/competition opportunity, scholarship, admission, or other benefit

top_lines.headline: Comptroller General Study and Report
subs: Study to determine the meaning of "any other benefit" as used in paragraph (4)
Document adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results
Report to House Education and Workforce Committee and Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee

items.main: Names the Act the "Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Amends section 901 of the Education Amendments of 1972 (20 U.S.C. 1681) by adding a new subsection (d). Paragraph (1) makes it a violation of subsection (a) for a recipient of Federal financial assistance who operates, sponsors, or facilitates an athletic program or activity to permit a person whose sex is male to participate in an athletic program or activity that is designated for women or girls.
items.detail: The prohibition binds only recipients of Federal financial assistance and only in the athletic-program/activity context.

items.main: Paragraph (2) provides that for the purposes of the new subsection, sex shall be recognized based solely on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth. Paragraph (3) defines "athletic programs and activities" to include, but not be limited to, all programs or activities that are provided conditional upon participation with any athletic team. Paragraph (4) provides a carve-out permitting males to train or practice with a female-designated program so long as no female is deprived of a roster spot, opportunity to participate in a practice or competition, scholarship, admission to an educational institution, or any other benefit that accompanies participating in the program.
items.detail: The four terms in paragraph (4) frame the training/practice exception, and the phrase "any other benefit" triggers the paragraph (5) study.

items.main: Paragraph (5) directs the Comptroller General to carry out a study to determine the meaning of the phrase "any other benefit" as used in paragraph (4), documenting adverse psychological, developmental, participatory, and sociological results to girls of allowing males to compete, be members of a sports team, or participate in athletic programs designed for girls, including displacement or discouragement from sports participation, deprivation of a roster spot, loss of practice or competition opportunity, loss of a scholarship or scholarship opportunities, loss or displacement of admission to an educational institution, deprivation of an environment free of hostility based on sexual assault or harassment, or loss of any other benefit. The Comptroller General must submit the results to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
items.detail: The paragraph enumerates the categories of adverse results the study must cover; the two named committees receive the report.

gaps: The bill does not describe how a recipient's compliance with the new subsection (d) will be enforced beyond incorporation into subsection (a) of section 901.
The bill does not authorize funding for the Comptroller General study or CPSC-style enforcement of the standard.
The bill does not set a deadline for the Comptroller General to submit the paragraph (5) study.
The bill does not describe how a recipient must verify a participant's reproductive biology and genetics at birth for eligibility purposes.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Bonamici
featured_quotes.text: As trans student and successful athlete Rebekah said: ``I know what it is like to have my gender questioned. . . . It is invasive and embarrassing. I wouldn't want anyone else to have to go through that,'' and, ``It is awful. Legislators are bullying kids.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Takano
featured_quotes.text: I rise in strong, unequivocal opposition to H.R. 28, the Republican child predator empowerment act. This bill lets politicians in Washington dictate to parents, school districts, and athletic associations across the country who can and cannot participate in their local sports leagues. It creates a one-size-fits-all policy that holds a kindergartner wanting to play soccer to the same standards as an elite athlete.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Walberg
featured_quotes.text: I would call attention to the fact that, in this bill, we offer no requirement for any type of invasive checks on women or men. They simply have to go to the birth certificate. That will give the answer.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rulli
featured_quotes.text: There is no reason we should even be having this conversation right now. H.R. 28 is a women's rights bill to protect Title IX, which was constructed to protect women's rights. This first came on my radar while I was a member of the Ohio Senate. I had a lesbian couple shopping in my store, and they asked me to step aside to talk to me for a minute. They said that I needed to protect women's sports. We had Title IX. Since we had Stonewall 50 years ago, this couple told me, they have worked their entire life for women's rights.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Adams
featured_quotes.text: I rise because this bill threatens the principles that make our schools and sports fields places of opportunity. This bill does not protect anyone. It unjustly targets transgender women and girls under the guise of fairness, but exclusion is not fairness, Mr. Speaker. Fairness is ensuring that every athlete can participate, grow, and thrive. For this reason, at the appropriate time, I will offer a motion to recommit this bill back to the committee.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Ansari
featured_quotes.text: I rise today to oppose the GOP child predator empowerment act. This bill is an egregious attack on young women and girls. Everyone in this room knows that this legislation has the power to threaten the physical and mental safety of minors. Schools and athletic institutions already have rules around fairness and safety in children's sports. This is literally why we have the NCAA. This bill is textbook government overreach meant to fuel division.

added: New subsection (d) of 20 U.S.C. 1681: paragraph (1) makes it a violation of subsection (a) for federally funded recipients to permit males to participate in athletic programs designated for women or girls
Paragraph (2) definition of sex based solely on reproductive biology and genetics at birth for purposes of the new subsection
Paragraph (3) definition of "athletic programs and activities" (including programs conditional on athletic-team participation)
Paragraph (4) train/practice carve-out conditioned on no deprivation of enumerated female benefits
Paragraph (5) Comptroller General study on the meaning of "any other benefit" and report to House Education and Workforce Committee and Senate HELP Committee

bills.title: Informing Consumers about Smart Devices Act
bills.official_title: To require the disclosure of a camera or recording capability in certain internet-connected devices.
bills.likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-ID) with 1 cosponsor. The House-passed measure has moved to the Senate and been placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar (General Orders, Calendar No. 64).
bills.summary: Requires each manufacturer of a "covered device" to disclose, clearly and conspicuously and prior to purchase, whether the device contains a camera or microphone as a component. Enforcement is handled by the Federal Trade Commission under the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.), with a violation treated as a violation of a rule defining an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of that Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)). Within 180 days of enactment, the FTC must issue guidance on best practices for making the disclosure clear, conspicuous, and age-appropriate, including on use of pictorial representations as defined in section 2(a) of the Consumer Review Fairness Act of 2016 (15 U.S.C. 45b(a)). A "covered device" is a consumer product (per 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)) capable of connecting to the internet with a camera or microphone component, but not phones, laptops, tablets, devices marketed as cameras/microphones/telecom devices, or devices covered by named subsections of the Communications Act of 1934. The Act applies to devices manufactured after 180 days from FTC guidance and is not retroactive.
bills.brief: Requires manufacturers of certain internet-connected devices to disclose (before purchase) whether the device has a camera or microphone; enforced by the FTC under the FTC Act, with 180-day FTC guidance and a no-retroactive-application effective date tied to that guidance.

top_lines.headline: Pre-Purchase Camera/Microphone Disclosure
subs: Each manufacturer of a covered device shall disclose "clearly and conspicuously and prior to purchase" whether the device contains a camera or microphone as a component

top_lines.headline: FTC Enforcement Under the FTC Act
subs: Violation treated as a violation of a rule defining an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B))
FTC enforces with the same jurisdiction, powers, and duties as under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.)
180-day FTC guidance on clear, conspicuous, age-appropriate disclosure — including pictorial representations under section 2(a) of the Consumer Review Fairness Act of 2016 (15 U.S.C. 45b(a))

top_lines.headline: Covered Device Definition and Effective Date
subs: Covered device: consumer product (as defined in 15 U.S.C. 2052(a)) capable of connecting to the internet with a camera or microphone component

Excludes phones/laptops/tablets, devices marketed as cameras/microphones/telecom devices, and devices covered by sections 255, 716, and 718 and subsections (aa) and (bb) of section 303 of the Communications Act of 1934
Applies only to covered devices manufactured after 180 days from issuance of FTC guidance under section 3(c); not retroactive

items.main: Names the Act the "Informing Consumers about Smart Devices Act."
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Required Disclosure of a Camera or Recording Capability in Certain Internet-Connected Devices

items.main: Each manufacturer of a covered device shall disclose, clearly and conspicuously and prior to purchase, whether the covered device manufactured by the manufacturer contains a camera or microphone as a component of the covered device.
items.detail: The requirement is unqualified for covered devices and applies at the manufacturer level. The disclosure trigger is presence of a camera or microphone as a component.

sections.label: Section 3 — Enforcement by the Federal Trade Commission

items.main: Subsection (a) treats a violation of section 2 as a violation of a rule defining an unfair or deceptive act or practice under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)). Subsection (b) authorizes the FTC to enforce the Act with the same jurisdiction, powers, and duties (and to impose the same penalties and privileges) as under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.), and contains a savings clause preserving the Commission's other authority.
items.detail: The enforcement construction routes the disclosure obligation directly into the FTC's existing UDAP toolkit; no new enforcement office is created.

items.main: Subsection (c) requires the FTC, not later than 180 days after enactment, through outreach to relevant private entities, to issue guidance to assist manufacturers in complying with the Act, including guidance on best practices for making the disclosure clear, conspicuous, and age-appropriate and on the use of a pictorial (as defined in section 2(a) of the Consumer Review Fairness Act of 2016 (15 U.S.C. 45b(a))) visual representation of the information disclosed. Subsection (d) allows a manufacturer to petition the FTC for tailored guidance; subsection (e) limits the effect of guidance so that it confers no rights and does not bind the Commission or any person and cannot be the sole basis for an enforcement action.
items.detail: The 180-day clock runs from enactment; the tailored-guidance petition and no-binding-effect limits preserve FTC discretion.

items.main: "Covered device" means a consumer product, as defined by section 3(a) of the Consumer Product Safety Act (15 U.S.C. 2052(a)), that is capable of connecting to the internet, a component of which is a camera or microphone. The definition excludes (A) a telephone (including a mobile phone), a laptop, tablet, or any device that a consumer would reasonably expect to have a microphone or camera; (B) any device that is specifically marketed as a camera, telecommunications device, or microphone; and (C) any device or apparatus described in sections 255, 716, and 718, and subsections (aa) and (bb) of section 303 of the Communications Act of 1934 (47 U.S.C. 255; 617; 619; and 303(aa) and (bb)), and any regulations promulgated thereunder.
items.detail: The exclusions are drafted at the device-category level and rely on cross-references to the Communications Act; the reasonable-expectation exclusion in clause (A) is drafted broadly.

items.main: The Act applies to all covered devices manufactured after the date that is 180 days after the date on which the FTC guidance under section 3(c) is issued, and does not apply to covered devices manufactured or sold before that date, or otherwise introduced into interstate commerce before that date.
items.detail: The effective-date clock is tied to the FTC guidance date, not to the date of enactment; the Act does not sweep in existing inventory.

underreported.summary: The FTC's guidance under section 3(c) "shall confer any rights" on no person, does not bind the Commission or any person, and cannot be used as the sole basis for an enforcement action.
underreported.why_unreported: The section's headline is that the FTC must issue guidance; the same subsection substantially limits what the guidance can do in an enforcement setting.

gaps: The bill does not describe how the manufacturer must physically present the disclosure (labeling, packaging, online listing) beyond "clearly and conspicuously and prior to purchase."
The bill does not authorize funding for FTC guidance or enforcement.
The bill does not extend the disclosure duty to importers or retailers when the manufacturer is offshore.
The bill does not address parallel state disclosure requirements or preemption.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Dingell
featured_quotes.text: I strongly recommend my colleagues on both sides of the aisle support H.R. 859, the Informing Consumers About Smart Devices Act, and protect Americans' privacy.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fulcher
featured_quotes.text: This bill would require manufacturers of internet-connected so-called smart appliances to disclose to consumers prior to purchase when their product is equipped with a camera or microphone. Manufacturers today produce appliances that connect to software applications that can be set, managed, and monitored through one's computing device. They are designed to capture voice commands from around the vicinity, recording information to adapt to the way individuals give commands.

added: Manufacturer disclosure duty: clearly and conspicuously and prior to purchase, disclose whether a covered device contains a camera or microphone as a component
FTC enforcement construction routing the duty into the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.) as a UDAP rule violation under 15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)
180-day FTC guidance mandate on clear, conspicuous, age-appropriate disclosure and pictorial representation under 15 U.S.C. 45b(a)
Covered-device definition tied to 15 U.S.C. 2052(a) with named exclusions and a Communications Act cross-reference
Effective date tied to 180 days after FTC guidance, with no retroactive application

bills.title: ELO Realignment and Strategic Engagement Reform Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To provide for the reorganization and realignment of the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office of the Department of Homeland Security, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with two cosponsors; referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Directs the Secretary of Homeland Security to submit a comprehensive plan within 120 days for reorganizing the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office (ELO) inside the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) and realigning its essential functions and personnel into the Partner Engagement directorate of I&A. The plan must identify redundant or non-essential positions, programs, or functions; establish clear communication protocols with priority law enforcement agencies; centralize points of contact; enhance information-sharing; reduce outreach duplication across DHS components; and improve accountability and performance metrics. The Secretary must certify commencement of implementation within 60 days of starting the plan, and until both the plan is submitted and implementation is certified, the Secretary may not expand ELO's staffing, budget, or programmatic scope, nor establish new offices duplicating ELO's or the Partner Engagement directorate's mission without specific congressional authorization.
bills.brief: Requires DHS to submit within 120 days a plan to reorganize the Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office and fold its essential functions into I&A's Partner Engagement directorate, and freezes ELO expansion until the plan is submitted and implementation is certified.

top_lines.headline: 120-Day DHS Reorganization Plan
subs: Secretary must submit a comprehensive plan to the House Homeland Security Committee and the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee
Plan must identify redundant or non-essential ELO positions, programs, or functions
Plan must realign ELO's essential functions and personnel within I&A's Partner Engagement directorate

top_lines.headline: Coordination Requirements
subs: Establish clear communication protocols with priority law enforcement agencies
Centralize points of contact for law enforcement engagement
Enhance information-sharing mechanisms
Reduce outreach duplication across DHS components
Improve accountability and performance metrics related to stakeholder engagement

top_lines.headline: Plan Content Requirements
subs: Organizational analysis with cost-benefit estimates
Detailed staffing proposals, including reassignment plans
Transition timeline for realignment within I&A's Partner Engagement directorate
Internal oversight mechanisms to monitor implementation
Recommendations for future engagement models
Assurance of continuity of intelligence support and convenings to State, local, Tribal, and territorial (SLTT) entity partners, including relevant HSIN-INTEL access

top_lines.headline: Certification and Freeze
subs: Certification of implementation commencement due within 60 days of starting the plan
Until plan is submitted and implementation is certified, Secretary may not expand ELO's staffing, budget, or programmatic scope
Secretary may not establish new offices duplicating ELO or Partner Engagement mission without specific congressional authorization

items.main: Names the Act the "ELO Realignment and Strategic Engagement Reform Act of 2026."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Plan for Reorganization and Realignment of DHS Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach Office

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Secretary must submit to the House Homeland Security Committee and Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee a comprehensive plan to identify redundant or non-essential ELO positions, programs, or functions; realign ELO's essential functions and personnel within the Partner Engagement directorate of I&A; and improve coordination with priority law enforcement agencies.
items.detail: The coordination improvements listed in subsection (a)(3) are establishing clear communication protocols, centralizing points of contact, enhancing information-sharing, reducing outreach duplication across DHS components, and improving accountability and performance metrics.

items.main: Plan must include an organizational analysis justifying the reorganization (with cost-benefit estimates), detailed staffing proposals including reassignment plans, a transition timeline for the realignment, internal oversight mechanisms, recommendations for future engagement models, and assurance of continuity of intelligence support and convenings to SLTT entity partners, including relevant HSIN-INTEL access.
items.detail: Subsection (b) enumerates six specific plan requirements. Continuity of intelligence support to State, local, Tribal, and territorial partners is called out separately in paragraph (6).

items.main: Not later than 60 days after commencing implementation of the plan, the Secretary must submit a certification to the same congressional committees.
items.detail: Subsection (c) sets the certification-of-commencement requirement.

items.main: Until the Secretary submits the plan and certifies implementation, the Secretary may not expand ELO's staffing, budget, or programmatic scope, and may not establish new offices in DHS duplicating ELO's or the Partner Engagement directorate's mission without specific congressional authorization.
items.detail: Subsection (d) is the pre-plan expansion freeze — it applies until both the plan is submitted (subsection (a)) and implementation commencement is certified (subsection (c)).

items.main: Defines "Department" (DHS), "ELO Office" (Engagement, Liaison, and Outreach office within I&A), "I&A" (Office of Intelligence and Analysis), "Secretary" (of Homeland Security), "SLTT entity" (via section 2200 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, 6 U.S.C. 650), and "priority law enforcement agencies" (Federal, State, and local law enforcement agencies identified by the Secretary as key partners for national security, counterterrorism, emergency response, or other mission-critical operations).
items.detail: Definitions section in subsection (e).

gaps: The bill does not specify the total number of ELO positions or the current ELO budget baseline that the reorganization applies to.
The bill does not describe consequences if the Secretary fails to submit the plan within the 120-day deadline.
The bill does not define what a "non-essential" position or function is beyond leaving the determination to the plan itself.
The bill does not authorize any additional funds for the reorganization or transition.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Evans
featured_quotes.text: This bill consolidates the functions of two existing Department of Homeland Security offices tasked with public safety coordination into one centralized point of contact. DHS' Office of Intelligence and Analysis, also known as I&A, is the only entity in the U.S. intelligence community responsible for delivering intelligence directly to State and local law enforcement agencies.

added: 120-day DHS plan requirement to reorganize ELO and fold its essential functions into I&A's Partner Engagement directorate
60-day certification-of-implementation-commencement requirement
Pre-plan freeze on ELO staffing, budget, or programmatic scope expansion
Prohibition on establishing new DHS offices duplicating ELO or Partner Engagement mission without specific congressional authorization

bills.title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026
bills.official_title: To amend title 49, United States Code, to establish funds for investments in aviation security, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with six cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Amends title 49, United States Code, to dedicate portions of the 9/11 Security Fee (collected under section 44940) to two aviation security funds beginning in fiscal year 2027. Under subsection (h) of section 44923 as amended, the first $500M in fees each fiscal year is deposited in the existing Aviation Security Capital Fund and the TSA Administrator is directed to impose the fee so as to collect at least $500M for that fund. A new subsection (i) creates the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund (ASCT Fund) into which the next $250M in fees is deposited each fiscal year — available until expended for testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment of aviation security checkpoint technology, again with a fee-setting instruction to collect not less than $250M. A sense of Congress declares that the 9/11 Security Fee is airline-passenger-paid and should be used exclusively for aviation security, and that diversion should end no later than 2027. A conforming amendment updates the cross-reference in section 44940(j)(1) from "section 44923(h)" to "subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923."
bills.brief: Dedicates the first $500M of the 9/11 Security Fee each fiscal year to the Aviation Security Capital Fund and creates a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund that receives the next $250M, both starting in fiscal year 2027.

top_lines.headline: $500M to the Aviation Security Capital Fund
subs: Beginning FY2027 and each fiscal year thereafter, the first $500M from 9/11 Security Fee receipts is deposited in the Aviation Security Capital Fund
TSA Administrator directed to set the fee so as to collect at least $500M annually
Amounts available to the Administrator to make grants or enter related agreements under section 44923

top_lines.headline: New Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund
subs: Establishes ASCT Fund within DHS
Beginning FY2027 and each fiscal year thereafter, the next $250M in fees (after the $500M Capital Fund deposit) is deposited in the ASCT Fund
TSA Administrator directed to set the fee so as to collect not less than $250M annually
Amounts available until expended for testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment of aviation security checkpoint technology

top_lines.headline: Sense of Congress
subs: 9/11 Security Fee is an airline-passenger-paid fee established to sustain aviation security
Revenue should be used exclusively for aviation security (screening, technology upgrades, personnel support)
Use of the fee for unrelated purposes undermines public trust
Diversion of fee revenue should end no later than 2027, per section 44940(i)(4) of title 49, U.S.C., as in effect on the date of enactment

top_lines.headline: Conforming Cross-Reference
subs: Section 44940(j)(1) reference updated from "section 44923(h)" to "subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923"

items.main: Names the Act the "Spending Aviation Fees for Equipment, Guaranteeing Upgraded and Advanced Risk Detection and Safety Act of 2026" or the "SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

items.main: States that the 9/11 Security Fee (49 U.S.C. 44940) is an airline-passenger-paid fee established with the express purpose of sustaining aviation security; that revenue should be used exclusively to fund activities, programs, equipment, and initiatives directly improving commercial aviation security (including passenger and baggage screening, security technology upgrades, and personnel support); that use for unrelated purposes undermines public trust; and that diversion should be ended no later than 2027 in accordance with section 44940(i)(4) as it read on the date of enactment.
items.detail: Sense-of-Congress declarations are non-binding but frame the operative amendments in section 3.

items.main: Amends subsection (h) of section 44923 of title 49, U.S.C., so that beginning FY2027 and for each fiscal year thereafter, the first $500M derived from fees received under section 44940(a)(1) is available to be deposited in the Aviation Security Capital Fund, and the TSA Administrator is directed to impose the fee so as to collect at least $500M annually for that Fund.
items.detail: Strikes the second, third, and fourth sentences of paragraph (1) of subsection (h) and inserts the new $500M-floor sentences. Paragraphs (2) and (3) are struck and replaced with a single paragraph (2) making Fund amounts available to the TSA Administrator for grants and related agreements under section 44923.

items.main: Establishes the Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology (ASCT) Fund within DHS. Beginning FY2027 and each fiscal year thereafter, after the first $500M is deposited into the Aviation Security Capital Fund, the next $250M from fees received under section 44940(a)(1) is available to be deposited in the ASCT Fund; the Administrator must set the fee so as to collect not less than $250M annually for the ASCT Fund. Amounts are available until expended for testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment of aviation security checkpoint technology.
items.detail: Adds new subsection (i) to section 44923 (redesignating the existing subsection (i) as (j)). ASCT Fund disbursement authority mirrors the Capital Fund's — available to the TSA Administrator to make grants or enter related agreements.

items.main: Conforming amendment: paragraph (1) of section 44940(j) (as redesignated) is amended by striking "section 44923(h)" and inserting "subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923."
items.detail: Updates the 9/11 Security Fee statute's cross-reference to reflect that the fee now flows into both the Capital Fund and the new ASCT Fund.

gaps: The bill does not identify what happens to 9/11 Security Fee receipts above the combined $750M ($500M + $250M) floors — the current allocation to general revenues or other uses is not described within this Act's text.
The bill does not define "aviation security checkpoint technology" for the ASCT Fund beyond authorizing testing, procurement, deployment, installation, and sustainment.
The bill does not specify grant-application procedures, matching requirements, or eligibility criteria for either fund.
The bill does not include an oversight or reporting requirement on how deposited amounts are spent.

added: $500M annual floor from 9/11 Security Fee to Aviation Security Capital Fund starting FY2027
New Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund receiving the next $250M annually starting FY2027
New fee-setting directives requiring TSA to collect at least $500M for Capital Fund and not less than $250M for ASCT Fund
Sense of Congress that the 9/11 Security Fee should be used exclusively for aviation security and that diversion should end no later than 2027
modified: 49 U.S.C. 44923(h) restructured: prior second, third, and fourth sentences of paragraph (1) replaced; paragraphs (2) and (3) replaced with a single disbursement-authority paragraph
49 U.S.C. 44940(j)(1) cross-reference updated to point to both subsections (h) and (i) of section 44923
removed: Second, third, and fourth sentences of prior 49 U.S.C. 44923(h)(1)
Prior paragraphs (2) and (3) of 49 U.S.C. 44923(h)

bills.title: Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Small Business Act to clarify the responsibilities of the Office of Rural Affairs of the Small Business Administration, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on December 2, 2025 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 282). Sponsored by a Democratic member with three cosponsors; referred in the House to the Committee on Small Business.
bills.summary: Amends section 26 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 653) to clarify the Office of Rural Affairs (ORA) of the Small Business Administration. The Office is to be administered by an Assistant Administrator who is an employee in the competitive service and who must have education, professional experience, or knowledge of rural affairs and small business issues, as well as experience providing development assistance to rural small business concerns. The bill rewrites the duties in subsection (c) — replacing references to "small business concerns located in rural areas" with "rural small business concerns," changing "provide information" to "promote" the policies and programs of SBA and other federal agencies, updating the cross-reference from the United States Tourism and Travel Administration to the National Travel and Tourism Office of the Department of Commerce, and adding a new duty to host webinars and outreach events. New subsection (d) requires the Assistant Administrator to host webinars and outreach events across regions and to invite district-office representatives, resource partners, and Federal/State agencies. New subsection (e) requires the Administrator to submit annual reports (first due 180 days after enactment of the subsection) to the House Small Business Committee and the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, and make them publicly available, covering operational details, activities under subsection (c), number of webinars/events, an analysis of SBA lending programs' service to rural small businesses, and information gathered from outreach. New subsection (f) defines "Assistant Administrator," "resource partners" (small business development centers, women's business centers under section 29, SCORE chapters under section 8(b)(1)(B), and Veteran Business Outreach Centers under section 32), and "rural small business concern" (a small business concern in a rural area as defined in section 7(b)(16)).
bills.brief: Restructures the Office of Rural Affairs at SBA — sets qualifications for a competitive-service Assistant Administrator, rewrites the Office's duties, requires nationwide webinars and outreach events, and adds an annual public report to the House and Senate small business committees.

top_lines.headline: Competitive-Service Assistant Administrator
subs: Office of Rural Affairs to be administered by an Assistant Administrator who is an employee in the competitive service
Must have education, professional experience, or knowledge of rural affairs and issues relating to small business concerns
Must have experience providing development assistance to rural small business concerns

top_lines.headline: Rewritten Office Duties
subs: "Small business concerns located in rural areas" replaced with "rural small business concerns" throughout paragraph (1)
In paragraph (3), "provide information" changed to "promote" the policies and programs of SBA and other federal agencies for assisting rural small business concerns
In paragraph (5), reference updated from the United States Tourism and Travel Administration to the National Travel and Tourism Office of the Department of Commerce
New paragraph (6) added: host webinars and outreach events for rural small business concerns as described in subsection (d)

top_lines.headline: New Outreach Duties
subs: Assistant Administrator must host webinars and outreach events in various regions of the United States for rural small business concerns
Must invite representatives from SBA district offices, resource partners, Federal and State agencies, and other interested persons

top_lines.headline: Annual Public Report
subs: First report due 180 days after enactment of subsection (e); annually thereafter
Submitted to the House Small Business Committee and the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee, and made publicly available on an SBA website

Must include operational details (Assistant Administrator's name, Office budget, staffing), summary of subsection (c) activities, webinar/event counts, an analysis of SBA lending programs' service to rural small business concerns, and information gathered from outreach

items.main: Names the Act the "Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Office of Rural Affairs of the Small Business Administration

items.main: Amends section 26 of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 653), subsection (b), to require the Office to be administered by an Assistant Administrator who is an employee in the competitive service, and who has education/professional experience or knowledge of rural affairs and small business issues, plus experience providing development assistance to rural small business concerns.
items.detail: Paragraph (1) sets the appointment as a competitive-service position; paragraph (2) sets the qualifications.

items.main: Amends subsection (c) — changes references from "small business concerns located in rural areas" to "rural small business concerns," changes "provide information" to "promote" the policies and programs of SBA and other federal agencies, updates the reference from the United States Tourism and Travel Administration to the National Travel and Tourism Office of the Department of Commerce, and adds new paragraph (6) requiring the Office to host webinars and outreach events as described in subsection (d).
items.detail: Multiple striking-and-inserting amendments across paragraphs (1), (3), (4), and (5); paragraph (6) is the added item.

items.main: Adds new subsection (d) requiring the Assistant Administrator to host webinars and outreach events in various regions of the United States for rural small business concerns, and to invite representatives from SBA district offices, resource partners, Federal and State agencies, and other interested persons.
items.detail: Subsection (d) implements the new paragraph (6) duty added to subsection (c).

items.main: Adds new subsection (e) requiring the Administrator to submit annual reports to the House Committee on Small Business and the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship, and make each report publicly available on an SBA website. Reports must include operational details of the Office (Assistant Administrator's name, Office budget, number of full-time employees), a summary of subsection (c) activities, the number of webinars and outreach events, an analysis of SBA lending programs' service to rural small business concerns, and information gathered from outreach events.
items.detail: First report due not later than 180 days after enactment of subsection (e); annually thereafter.

items.main: Adds new subsection (f) definitions: "Assistant Administrator" (of the Office of Rural Affairs, appointed under subsection (b)); "resource partners" (small business development centers, women's business centers under section 29, SCORE chapters established under section 8(b)(1)(B), and Veteran Business Outreach Centers under section 32); "rural small business concern" (a small business concern located in a rural area as defined in section 7(b)(16)).
items.detail: Definitions in subsection (f).

gaps: The bill does not authorize additional funding to carry out the outreach or reporting requirements.
The bill does not specify the frequency of webinars or a minimum number of regions to be covered.
The bill does not describe consequences if the Administrator fails to meet the report deadlines.
The bill does not modify SBA lending program terms — only the reporting analysis of those programs' rural service.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Goodlander
featured_quotes.text: H.R. 4549 is a bill that will deliver a fair deal for America's rural small businesses and entrepreneurs by cutting red tape, delivering access to key Federal resources, and ensuring experienced and accountable representation and leadership within our government. It is a bill that will ensure the voices of rural America aren't just heard but are truly prioritized within our government. Running a small business is really an act of faith.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Cisneros
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I will, once again, thank my colleagues, Ms. Goodlander, Mr. Wied, and Mr. Golden, for their bipartisan efforts to pass this legislation. By strengthening the Office of Rural Affairs, we can ensure all small businesses have adequate access to the resources at their disposal.

New paragraph (6) in 15 U.S.C. 653(c): host webinars and outreach events for rural small business concerns
New subsection (d) requiring nationwide webinars and outreach events with invited district-office, resource-partner, and Federal/State agency representation
New subsection (e) requiring an annual public report to House and Senate small business committees, first due 180 days after enactment
New subsection (f) with definitions of "Assistant Administrator," "resource partners," and "rural small business concern"

15 U.S.C. 653(c)(1): "small business concerns located in rural areas" replaced with "rural small business concerns"
15 U.S.C. 653(c)(3): "provide information" changed to "promote" the policies and programs of SBA and other federal agencies

15 U.S.C. 653(c)(5): reference updated from the United States Tourism and Travel Administration to the National Travel and Tourism Office of the Department of Commerce, and "small businesses in rural areas" replaced with "rural small business concerns"

bills.title: Major Non-NATO Ally Terror Threat Assessment Act
bills.official_title: To require an assessment of terrorism threats to the United States posed by foreign terrorist organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists present in countries that are major non-NATO allies, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: House passage recorded July 13, 2026 per the latest action. Sponsored by a Republican member with one cosponsor; referred to the House Committee on Homeland Security. The measure now moves to the Senate.
bills.summary: Requires the Secretary of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of National Intelligence, to submit to the appropriate congressional committees an assessment of terrorism threats to the United States posed by foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs) and Specially Designated Global Terrorists (SDGTs) present in countries that are operating or designated as major non-NATO allies (MNNAs). The first assessment is due within 180 days after enactment; biennial assessments follow. Each assessment must identify each FTO or SDGT present in each MNNA; describe their activities within each ally (including use of artificial intelligence or critical and emerging technologies); describe the MNNA government's efforts to disrupt and degrade those activities and any cooperation with elements of the U.S. intelligence community; assess DHS's capability to identify, monitor, and mitigate the threats and to prevent members from entering the United States; and identify any additional resources required. Assessments are submitted in classified form and made available to every Member of Congress upon request; each assessment is followed by a congressional briefing. Definitions incorporate: "artificial intelligence" (section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020, 15 U.S.C. 9401), "critical and emerging technologies" (the February 2024 Critical and Emerging Technologies List Update issued by NSTC, or any successor), "intelligence community" (section 3(4) of the National Security Act of 1947, 50 U.S.C. 3003(4)), "foreign terrorist organization" (section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, 8 U.S.C. 1189), "major non-NATO ally" (section 644 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, 22 U.S.C. 2403), "specially designated global terrorist" (per Executive Order 13224, September 23, 2001; 66 Fed. Reg. 49079), and "terrorism" (section 2 of the Homeland Security Act of 2002, 6 U.S.C. 101).
bills.brief: Directs DHS, in consultation with State and ODNI, to submit a classified biennial assessment (first due 180 days after enactment) of FTO and SDGT presence and activity in major non-NATO ally countries — including use of AI and critical and emerging technologies — plus a congressional briefing on each.

top_lines.headline: 180-Day/Biennial DHS Assessment
subs: Secretary of Homeland Security submits the assessment, in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of National Intelligence
First assessment due not later than 180 days after enactment
Biennial thereafter

top_lines.headline: Elements for Each MNNA
subs: Identify each FTO or SDGT present in each MNNA
Describe each identified group's or individual's activities, including use of artificial intelligence or critical and emerging technologies
Describe MNNA government efforts to disrupt/degrade those activities and any cooperation with U.S. intelligence community elements
Assess DHS capability to identify, monitor, and mitigate the threats
Assess DHS capability to prevent identified members from entering the United States
Identify any additional resources required

top_lines.headline: Classified Form + Member Access
subs: Assessment submitted in classified form
Made available to every Member of Congress upon request
Secretary must provide a congressional briefing upon submission of each assessment

top_lines.headline: Cross-Referenced Definitions
subs: "Appropriate congressional committees": House Homeland Security + Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
"Artificial intelligence": section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401)
"Critical and emerging technologies": February 2024 Critical and Emerging Technologies List Update issued by NSTC, or any successor
"Foreign terrorist organization": section 219 of the Immigration and Nationality Act (8 U.S.C. 1189)
"Major non-NATO ally": section 644 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 (22 U.S.C. 2403)
"Specially designated global terrorist": per Executive Order 13224 (September 23, 2001; 66 Fed. Reg. 49079)

items.main: Names the Act the "Major Non-NATO Ally Terror Threat Assessment Act."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Assessment of Terrorism Threats to the United States by FTOs and SDGTs Present in Countries That Are Major Non-NATO Allies

items.main: Not later than 180 days after enactment and biennially thereafter, the Secretary of Homeland Security — in consultation with the Secretary of State and the Director of National Intelligence — must submit an assessment of terrorism threats to the United States posed by FTOs and SDGTs present in countries operating or designated as major non-NATO allies.
items.detail: Subsection (a) sets the recurring assessment requirement.

items.main: Each assessment must, for each MNNA: identify each FTO or SDGT present; describe all activities each identified group or individual is engaged in within that ally, including the extent to which they are using artificial intelligence or critical and emerging technologies; describe the government of each MNNA's disruption and degradation efforts, including cooperation with U.S. intelligence community elements; assess DHS's capability to identify, monitor, and mitigate the threats; assess DHS's capability to prevent identified members from entering the United States; and identify any additional resources required to counter the threats.
items.detail: Subsection (b) enumerates six required elements for each MNNA.

items.main: Each assessment is submitted in classified form and made available to every Member of Congress upon request. The Secretary must provide a congressional briefing on each assessment upon submission.
items.detail: Subsections (c) and (d) set form/availability and briefing requirements.

items.main: Definitions in subsection (e) tie all key terms to existing statutes and issuances: "artificial intelligence" to 15 U.S.C. 9401; "critical and emerging technologies" to the February 2024 NSTC list; "intelligence community" to 50 U.S.C. 3003(4); "foreign terrorist organization" to 8 U.S.C. 1189; "major non-NATO ally" to 22 U.S.C. 2403; "specially designated global terrorist" to Executive Order 13224; and "terrorism" to 6 U.S.C. 101.
items.detail: Definitions rely on incorporated cross-references rather than newly created terms.

gaps: The bill does not identify which countries currently qualify as major non-NATO allies — that list is maintained under other law and would need to be consulted separately.
The bill does not authorize additional funding to carry out the assessment or briefing requirements.
The bill does not specify consequences if the Secretary misses the 180-day or biennial deadline.
The bill does not require a public or unclassified summary of the assessment.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Van Epps
featured_quotes.text: When the United States designates a nation as a major non-NATO ally, MNNA, it comes with security cooperation and possible trade deals for defense equipment. This is an important designation that our Nation does not grant lightly. However, we cannot ignore the fact that foreign terrorist organizations continue to operate in or around some MNNA countries, creating threats that could have serious consequences for U.S. national security.

added: 180-day and biennial classified DHS assessment of FTO and SDGT activity in major non-NATO allies
Requirement to describe use of artificial intelligence and critical and emerging technologies by identified FTOs/SDGTs
Requirement to assess DHS capability to identify, monitor, and mitigate the threats, and to prevent identified members from entering the United States
Congressional briefing on each assessment upon submission
Any-Member-upon-request availability of the classified assessment

bills.title: D.C. CRIMES Act
bills.official_title: To limit youth offender status in the District of Columbia to individuals 18 years of age or younger, to direct the Attorney General of the District of Columbia to establish and operate a publicly accessible website containing updated statistics on juvenile crime in the District of Columbia, to amend the District of Columbia Home Rule Act to prohibit the Council of the District of Columbia from enacting changes to existing criminal liability sentences, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on September 17, 2025 after House action; no further Senate action recorded. Sponsored by a Republican member with eight cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.
bills.summary: Amends the District of Columbia Youth Rehabilitation Act of 1985 to lower the age ceiling for "youth offender" status from "24 years of age or younger" to "18 years of age or younger" (Section 2(6) of the Youth Rehabilitation Act, D.C. Official Code section 24-901(6)). Two conforming amendments follow: Section 3(a-1) of the Act (D.C. Official Code section 24-902(a-1)) is amended by striking paragraph (3) (which addressed strategic planning for individuals 18 through 24 in facilities, treatment, and services), and Section 4(a)(2) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(a)(2)) is amended to change "15 to 24 years of age" to "15 to 18 years of age." Section 4(b) (D.C. Official Code section 24-903(b)) is restructured — paragraph (2) (which addressed sentencing below the mandatory-minimum term) is struck and paragraph (3) is redesignated as paragraph (2). Section 3 adds a new section 16-2340a to Subchapter I of chapter 23 of title 16, D.C. Official Code, requiring the D.C. Attorney General to establish and operate a publicly accessible website with 11 juvenile-crime data measures (arrests by year, arrests broken down by age/race/sex, petty crime arrests, crime-of-violence arrests, first-offense arrests, prior-arrest history, declination rates, adult-court transfers, sentencing outcomes, and time-served information), updated monthly and archived, in a machine-readable bulk-download format, and without personally identifiable information. Conforming amendments (D.C. Code sections 16-2331, 16-2332, and 16-2333) allow the release of juvenile case, social, and law-enforcement records to the D.C. Attorney General for the website. The website must be established within 180 days of enactment. Section 4 amends section 602(a) of the District of Columbia Home Rule Act (D.C. Code section 1-206.02(a)) to prohibit the D.C. Council from enacting any act, resolution, or rule to change any criminal liability sentence in effect on the date of enactment of the D.C. CRIMES Act.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Donalds
featured_quotes.text: Now, in reference to what the gentleman was just talking about, Article I, Section 8, Clause 17 of the United States Constitution is quite clear. It grants Congress the power to exercise exclusive, exclusive jurisdiction over the Federal District, which all Americans know now is Washington, D.C., and it is the Nation's Capital. That is in the Constitution that was ratified by several States. Congress does have the constitutional authority to regulate activities within the Federal District.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Boebert
featured_quotes.text: This critical legislation is a direct response to the failed pro-crime policies that have turned our Nation's Capital into a war zone. Under failing leftist policies, Washington, D.C., has seen an epidemic of violence: carjackings surging 300 percent, homicides ravaging communities, and young thugs, some as old as 24, treated as juveniles, slapped with lenient sentences below mandatory minimums. It endangers young families and small businesses struggling in this crime-ridden city.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: There is no question that there has been a crime epidemic across the District of Columbia, and the citizens of this great city deserve better. President Trump recognized this fact and has exercised his authority to restore safety. It is now time for Congress to build on his good work. H.R. 4922 is designed to begin to address many of the problems that stem from the D.C. courts and their refusal to hold criminals accountable. We need to start with recognizing that 19- to 24-year-olds shouldn't be treated as youthful offenders.

bills.title: WIPPES Act
bills.official_title: To require certain products to be labeled with "Do Not Flush" labeling, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Received in the Senate on June 24, 2025 following House action. Sponsored by a Republican member with seven cosponsors and referred in the House to the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
bills.summary: Establishes a federal "Do Not Flush" labeling regime for premoistened, nonwoven disposable wipes marketed as baby or diapering wipes, and for household or personal-care wipes that are composed entirely or in part of petrochemical-derived fibers and have significant potential to be flushed (including antibacterial and disinfecting wipes, general and bathroom cleaning wipes, and body/personal-care wipes such as hand sanitizing, makeup removal, feminine and adult hygiene, and body cleansing). Covered entities (manufacturers, wholesalers, suppliers, individuals, or retailers responsible for the labeling or retail packaging of a covered product sold or offered for retail sale in the United States) must display both the phrase "Do Not Flush" (the "label notice") and the INDA/EDANA "Do Not Flush" symbol clearly and conspicuously in accordance with packaging-type rules. For cylindrical/near-cylindrical dispensing packages, the symbol and label notice must appear on the principal display panel or, alternatively, the symbol appears on the panel while the label notice (or combination) covers at least 8 percent of the flip lid. Flexible film packaging, rigid/refillable packaging, packaging not intended to dispense individual wipes, and bulk retail packaging each have their own placement rules. Outer packaging of combined products is exempt (with an accommodation for combined-product packages smaller than 3 inches by 3 inches). The symbol and label notice must each be equal in size to at least 2 percent of the principal display panel's surface area, and must have a contrast percentage of at least 70 percent against the background — light-on-dark or dark-on-light — except an embossed symbol or label notice on the flip lid of cylindrical or near-cylindrical packaging is exempt from the contrast rule. Covered entities may not make any express or implied representation that a covered product can or should be flushed. The Federal Trade Commission enforces the section: a violation is treated as a violation of a regulation under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices, and the FTC may promulgate implementing regulations under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C., consulting with EPA, FDA, and the Consumer Product Safety Commission as appropriate. State laws that are not identical to the federal requirements are preempted. The section applies to covered entities beginning 1 year after the date of enactment.
bills.brief: Requires baby/diapering wipes and specified household or personal-care wipes made even partly of petrochemical fibers to carry a "Do Not Flush" label notice and the INDA/EDANA symbol on packaging (with specific placement, size, and contrast rules), bars flushability claims, gives the FTC enforcement authority, preempts non-identical State laws, and takes effect 1 year after enactment.

top_lines.headline: Federal "Do Not Flush" Label + Symbol Requirement
subs: Covered entities must label covered products clearly and conspicuously with both the "Do Not Flush" label notice and the INDA/EDANA symbol
Covered entities may not make any express or implied representation that a covered product can or should be flushed
Effective 1 year after enactment

top_lines.headline: Placement Rules by Packaging Type
subs: Cylindrical dispensing packaging: symbol + label notice on principal display panel — or symbol on panel with label notice (or combination) covering at least 8 percent of the flip lid
Flexible film dispensing packaging: symbol on principal display panel and on dispensing side panel if different; label notice on principal display panel or dispensing side panel
Rigid/refillable dispensing packaging: symbol + label notice on principal display panel visible each time a wipe is dispensed
Packaging not intended to dispense individual wipes: symbol + label notice on principal display panel visible to the user
Bulk retail: symbol + label notice on both outer packaging and individual packaging, with two enumerated exemptions
Combined-product packaging: outer packaging exempt; individual covered-product packages smaller than 3 by 3 inches may satisfy the requirement with prominent placement

top_lines.headline: Size + Contrast Standards
subs: Symbol and label notice each must equal at least 2 percent of the principal display panel's surface area
Contrast percentage of at least 70 percent between symbol/notice and immediate background, using the formula (B1 − B2) / B1 × 100 where B1 and B2 are light reflectance values
Light on dark or dark on light
Embossed symbol or label notice on the flip lid of a cylindrical or near-cylindrical package is exempt from the contrast rule

top_lines.headline: FTC Enforcement + State Preemption
subs: Violations treated as violations of a regulation under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) — unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC enforcement with same jurisdiction, powers, and duties as under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.)
FTC may promulgate regulations under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C., and may consult with EPA, FDA, or the Consumer Product Safety Commission
State or local requirements not identical to the federal requirements are preempted

items.main: Names the Act the "Wastewater Infrastructure Pollution Prevention and Environmental Safety Act" or the "WIPPES Act."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Requires covered entities to label covered products clearly and conspicuously with both the label notice ("Do Not Flush") and the symbol (the INDA/EDANA "Do Not Flush" symbol from the most recent edition of the Guidelines for Assessing the Flushability of Disposable Nonwoven Products, or an FTC-adopted equivalent).
items.detail: Subsection (a) sets the core labeling duty. Definitions in subsection (g) tie "label notice" to the phrase "Do Not Flush" and "symbol" to the INDA/EDANA depiction.

items.main: Placement rules vary by packaging type: cylindrical dispensing packaging must display both on the principal display panel or, alternatively, the symbol on the panel with the label notice (or combination) covering at least 8 percent of the flip lid; flexible film dispensing packaging requires the symbol on the principal display panel and on the dispensing side panel if different, with the label notice on either; rigid/refillable dispensing packaging requires both on the principal display panel visible each time a wipe is dispensed; non-dispensing packaging requires both on the principal display panel; bulk retail requires both on outer and individual packaging (with two enumerated exemptions); combined-product outer packaging is exempt, and combined-product packages under 3 by 3 inches may satisfy the requirement with prominent placement.
items.detail: Subsection (b) contains the placement rules across six enumerated packaging categories.

items.main: Reasonable visibility: symbol and label notice must not be obscured by packaging seams, folds, or design elements; each must equal at least 2 percent of the principal display panel's surface area; each must have high contrast (at least 70 percent contrast percentage under the (B1 − B2) / B1 × 100 formula) with the immediate background — light on dark or dark on light. An embossed symbol or label notice on the flip lid of a cylindrical or near-cylindrical package is exempt from the contrast rule. The symbol and label notice may be adjacent or on separate areas of the principal display panel.
items.detail: Subsection (c) sets the size and contrast standards.

items.main: Prohibits covered entities from making any express or implied representation that a covered product can or should be flushed.
items.detail: Subsection (d) is the flushability-claim prohibition.

items.main: FTC enforcement: a violation of the section or an implementing regulation is treated as a violation of a regulation under section 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices. The Commission enforces with the same jurisdiction, powers, and duties as under the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. 41 et seq.), and violators are subject to the same penalties. The Commission may promulgate implementing regulations under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C., and may consult with the EPA Administrator, the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, the Consumer Product Safety Commission, or any other agency as appropriate. Nothing limits the Commission's other statutory authority.
items.detail: Subsection (e) is the enforcement and rulemaking framework.

items.main: State-law preemption: no State or political subdivision may establish or continue in effect requirements with respect to the "Do Not Flush" labeling of covered products that are not identical to the federal requirements and implementing regulations.
items.detail: Subsection (f) is the preemption clause.

items.main: Definitions in subsection (g) — including "covered product" (premoistened, nonwoven disposable wipes marketed as baby or diapering wipes, or household/personal care wipes composed entirely or in part of petrochemical-derived fibers and having significant potential to be flushed, with named inclusions covering antibacterial, disinfecting, general/bathroom cleaning, and personal-care wipes such as hand sanitizing, makeup removal, feminine hygiene, adult hygiene, and body cleansing); "combined product" (two or more products in shared retail packaging where at least one is a covered product and at least one is a consumer product intended to be used with it); "covered entity" (a manufacturer, wholesaler, supplier, individual or group of individuals, or retailer responsible for the labeling or retail packaging of a covered product sold or offered for retail sale in the U.S.); "high contrast," "label notice," "principal display panel," "State," and "symbol."
items.detail: Definitions in subsection (g).

items.main: Effective date: section applies to covered entities beginning on the date that is 1 year after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Subsection (h) sets the 1-year effective date.

gaps: The bill does not authorize any civil penalty amounts specific to this section — it relies on the general penalty structure under the FTC Act.
The bill does not define "significant potential to be flushed," leaving that judgment to covered entities and, ultimately, FTC enforcement.
The bill does not describe how existing State "Do Not Flush" labeling laws (already in place in some States) transition to the federal identical-requirement standard.
The bill does not set a deadline within which the FTC must issue implementing regulations.

added: Federal "Do Not Flush" label notice and symbol requirement for covered wipes, effective 1 year after enactment
Placement, 2 percent minimum size, and 70 percent contrast rules across six packaging categories
Prohibition on express or implied flushability representations by covered entities
FTC enforcement via section 18(a)(1)(B) of the FTC Act, with rulemaking authority under section 553 of title 5, U.S.C.
State-law preemption: only requirements identical to the federal rule are allowed
Definitions of "covered product," "covered entity," "combined product," "high contrast," "label notice," "principal display panel," "State," and "symbol"

bills.title: PRO Veterans Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To protect regular order for budgeting for the Department of Veterans Affairs, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Enacted as Public Law 119-33 on August 14, 2025. Per the printed legislative history for S. 423, the Senate considered and passed the measure on April 8, 2025 and the House considered and passed it on July 21, 2025.
bills.summary: Enacts two Department of Veterans Affairs administrative reforms in a single Act. Section 1 (the "Protecting Regular Order for Veterans Act of 2025") requires the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to provide quarterly, in-person briefings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs and Appropriations Committees on the VA's budget and any shortfall the Department may be experiencing, beginning the first quarter after enactment and continuing until the date that is 3 years after enactment; when a shortfall is reported, the Secretary must also present plans to address or mitigate it (a "shortfall" is defined as appropriations required to meet all statutory obligations exceeding the amount requested in the President's budget under 31 U.S.C. 1105(a)). Section 1(c) amends 38 U.S.C. 706(d) by adding a new paragraph (7): a critical skill incentive under paragraph (1) may not be provided to a Senior Executive Service (SES) employee (or comparable senior-level position, as defined by the Secretary) whose position is at the VA Central Office — including the Veterans Health Administration, Veterans Benefits Administration, and National Cemetery Administration — regardless of where the employee actually performs the functions of the position; for SES employees not at Central Office, incentives may only be provided on an individual basis (not to a group) and only with approval from a specified list of officers (Under Secretary for Benefits, Health, or Memorial Affairs; Assistant Secretary for Human Resources and Administration; Director of the Office of Management or CFO; Assistant Secretary for Accountability and Whistleblower Protection; General Counsel; and such other officers as the Secretary determines appropriate). For an SES employee whose position is primarily at Central Office but who performs some job function at other VA facilities, the employee is not considered a Central Office employee for the non-Central-Office portion of their job, and any critical skill incentive for that portion must be proportionate to the time spent at those facilities. The Secretary must submit an annual report to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees on SES employees who received critical skill incentives; reports may be incorporated into other required reports. Section 2 (the "Improving Veterans' Experience Act of 2025") adds new section 325 to chapter 3 of title 38, U.S.C., establishing the Veterans Experience Office within the Department under the Office of the Secretary, headed by a Chief Veterans Experience Officer appointed by and reporting directly to the Secretary. The Office's functions include carrying out customer experience initiatives; requiring other VA offices to report regularly on customer experience metrics and improvement efforts; collecting veteran-derived data on satisfaction and usage; providing strategic guidance for engagement; and assessing and advising on VA websites and customer service. The Chief Veterans Experience Officer must submit an annual summary to the Secretary, who must submit an annual analysis to Congress within 180 days of receiving that summary, including customer service data and satisfaction data disaggregated by benefit or service and by relevant demographic categories (with potential non-use reasons such as eligibility, lack of awareness, and barriers of technology, information, or time). The Office's information must exclude personally identifiable information unless the individual consents; funds from other VA organizations may be available to reimburse the Office at cost-recovery rates when the Secretary determines contributing will not undermine those organizations' ability to provide required services; nothing in the subsection authorizes an increase in the Department's overall full-time-employee count. The Office is subject to the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a). Section 325's requirements and authorities terminate on September 30, 2028. Section 2(c) requires the Comptroller General to complete, not later than 540 days after enactment, an analysis of the methodology, effectiveness, and implementation of veteran and beneficiary customer-experience findings and feedback used by VA (including through "trust-scores," VSignals, and related survey and data-collection activities), and submit a report on the findings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees.

sections.label: Section 1 — Protecting Regular Order for Veterans

items.main: Names the section the "Protecting Regular Order for Veterans Act of 2025" or the "PRO Veterans Act of 2025" (subsection (a); 38 U.S.C. 101 note).
items.detail: Short-title subsection.

items.main: Requires the VA Secretary to provide quarterly, in-person briefings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees and House and Senate Appropriations Committees on the VA budget and any shortfall the Department may be experiencing, beginning the first quarter after enactment and continuing until 3 years after enactment. When a shortfall is reported, the Secretary must present plans to address or mitigate it. "Shortfall" is defined as an amount of appropriations required by the Department for a fiscal year to meet all statutory obligations that exceeds the appropriations requested in the President's budget under 31 U.S.C. 1105(a).
items.detail: Subsection (b): quarterly briefings and definitions.

items.main: Amends 38 U.S.C. 706(d) by adding new paragraph (7): a critical skill incentive under paragraph (1) may not be provided to an SES employee (or comparable senior-level position, as defined by the Secretary) whose position is at the VA Central Office (including VHA, VBA, and NCA), regardless of where the employee actually performs the functions.
items.detail: Subsection (c); the Central-Office bar is in new subparagraph (A) of paragraph (7).

items.main: For SES employees not at Central Office, critical skill incentives may only be provided (i) on an individual basis (not to a group) and (ii) upon approval from a specified list of officers (or those in acting capacity): the Under Secretary for Benefits, Under Secretary for Health, or Under Secretary for Memorial Affairs; the Assistant Secretary for Human Resources and Administration; the Director of the Office of Management or the Chief Financial Officer; the Assistant Secretary for Accountability and Whistleblower Protection; the General Counsel; and such other officers as the Secretary determines appropriate.
items.detail: New 38 U.S.C. 706(d)(7)(B)(i) — enumerates the six approving-officer categories.

items.main: For an SES employee primarily at Central Office but performing some job function at other VA facilities, the employee is not treated as a Central Office employee with respect to the non-Central-Office portion, and any critical skill incentive for that portion must be proportionate to the time spent at those facilities.
