sections.label: Section 2 — Establishment of Veterans Experience Office

items.main: Names the section the "Improving Veterans' Experience Act of 2025" (subsection (a); 38 U.S.C. 101 note).
items.detail: Short-title subsection.

items.main: Adds new section 325 to chapter 3 of title 38, U.S.C., establishing the Veterans Experience Office within the Department under the Office of the Secretary. The head is the Chief Veterans Experience Officer, appointed by the Secretary from among individuals the Secretary considers qualified, reporting directly to the Secretary, and responsible for carrying out the functions of the Office.

Functions include: carrying out key customer experience initiatives (setting strategy, framework, policy, and other guidance for the Department, and ensuring coordination and non-duplication with other VA activities); requiring other VA organizations to report regularly on customer experience metrics, action plans, and other improvement efforts; collecting veteran-derived data to determine satisfaction and usage of benefits and services, to be considered during policymaking; providing strategic guidance and strategies for engaging with veterans and beneficiaries, including those not using benefits and services; assessing and advising the Secretary on the accuracy and helpfulness of VA websites and other customer-facing information; and assessing and advising on VA customer service efforts.
items.detail: New 38 U.S.C. 325(c) — six enumerated functions.

items.main: Reporting: Each year, the Chief Veterans Experience Officer must submit to the Secretary a summary of the data received under subsection (c)(2). Each year, not later than 180 days after the Secretary receives that summary, the Secretary must submit to Congress an annual summary and analysis. Annual summaries must include customer service and experience feedback data disaggregated by benefit or service (and by relevant demographic data), and satisfaction/usage data (disaggregated similarly) including potential reasons for not using benefits (eligibility; lack of knowledge or awareness; barriers of technology, information, or time; other related reasons) and an analysis of how such reasons may be addressed.

Staff and resources: the Secretary must ensure the Office has the necessary staff, resources, and access to customer service and experience information; information must exclude personally identifiable information of individual veterans, survivors, dependents, or other beneficiaries unless the individual provides appropriate consent. Funds available for basic pay and administrative expenses of other VA organizations may be used to reimburse the Office at cost-recovery rates for services provided to those organizations if the Secretary determines that contributing will not undermine those organizations' ability to provide required services. Nothing in the subsection authorizes an increase in the number of full-time employees otherwise authorized for the Department. The Office is subject to the Privacy Act of 1974 (5 U.S.C. 552a).
Sunset: the requirements and authorities of new section 325 terminate on September 30, 2028.
items.detail: New 38 U.S.C. 325(g). A clerical amendment adds "325. Veterans Experience Office." to the table of sections at the beginning of chapter 3 of title 38.

items.main: GAO review: not later than 540 days after enactment, the Comptroller General must complete an analysis of the methodology, effectiveness, and implementation of veteran and beneficiary customer-experience findings and feedback used by VA — including the Veterans Experience Office — through "trust-scores," VSignals, and related survey and data-collection activities. The Comptroller General must submit a report of the findings to the House and Senate Veterans' Affairs Committees.
items.detail: Subsection (c) of Section 2.

gaps: The Act does not describe consequences if the Secretary fails to provide a quarterly briefing or misses a report deadline.

The Act does not authorize additional appropriations for the Veterans Experience Office or the shortfall-mitigation plans — the Office is subject to a no-FTE-increase constraint and reimbursement-at-cost mechanism only.
The Act does not specify the criteria the Secretary uses to designate positions comparable to Senior Executive Service for purposes of the critical skill incentive restrictions.
The Act does not describe how the Veterans Experience Office's activities are to continue (or be transferred) after the September 30, 2028 sunset.

New 38 U.S.C. 706(d)(7): SES critical-skill-incentive bar at VA Central Office and approval-officer/individual-basis limits elsewhere
Annual report to Veterans' Affairs Committees on SES critical-skill-incentive recipients

Cost-recovery reimbursement mechanism for the Veterans Experience Office; no authorized increase in the Department's overall FTE count
September 30, 2028 sunset for the Veterans Experience Office requirements and authorities
GAO review of VA customer-experience methodology (including trust-scores and VSignals) due 540 days after enactment

bills.title: Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To establish a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce, and to secure American leadership in deploying emerging technologies, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Passed the House by voice vote on 2025-04-28 (no recorded opposition), a bipartisan-consent signal. Sponsored by a Republican member with 4 cosponsors. Senate advancement still faces the 60-vote cloture threshold.
bills.summary: Establishes a critical supply chain resiliency and crisis response program in the Department of Commerce administered by the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis. Section 2 adds eight responsibilities for the Assistant Secretary: promoting the stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the new Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks; encouraging reduced reliance of domestic manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of critical-good manufacturing to the United States and allies/partners. Section 3 requires the Assistant Secretary to establish, not later than 120 days after enactment, a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis (including the Departments of State, Defense, Homeland Security, Transportation, Energy, Agriculture, the Interior, and Health and Human Services; the Office of the Director of National Intelligence; and the Small Business Administration). Within 1 year of enactment, the Assistant Secretary must carry out enumerated assessment, mapping, modeling, gap-identification, workforce, and coordination activities in consultation with the Working Group. The Assistant Secretary must designate — within 120 days of enactment, with public comment — critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods, updating those designations at least every 4 years. An implementation report is due to the relevant committees within 1 year after enactment. A national strategy and review of critical supply chain resiliency and manufacturing is due to the relevant committees within 18 months after enactment and annually thereafter — covering critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-critical supplies and services, substitutes, authentication/traceability methods (including blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies), and allies/key international partner nations; assessing the manufacturing base, supply chains, and workforce; identifying threats and supply chain shocks (with threats originating from section 7(2)(B) countries listed); and developing a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains. Reports may not include non-aggregated critical supply chain information, confidential business information, or classified information; a public comment period is required; reports are unclassified with an optional classified annex. Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (accompanied by a specified express statement) is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), is not subject to ex parte communication rules, may not be used against the submitter in civil actions or by other authorities without written consent, may not be disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act (with narrow exceptions), and does not constitute a waiver of trade-secret or other protections. The subsection does not apply to voluntary submissions in an application for federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry NDAA for FY2021 (Public Law 116-283). Section 4 requires the Secretary to submit, within 2 years of enactment, a Department of Commerce capability assessment identifying the duties, responsibilities, resources, programs, and expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, plus recommendations to enhance those activities and a strategy to implement them as appropriate. Section 5 provides that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title. Section 6 provides that the title and all its requirements terminate 10 years after the date of enactment. Section 7 defines all key terms — including "ally or key international partner nation" (which excludes countries posing a significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564), "critical good," "critical industry," "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c), "critical supply chain," "critical supply chain information," "domestic enterprise," "domestic manufacturer," "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act (title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276) and a named list including artificial intelligence, automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems, blockchain and other distributed ledger technologies, quantum computing and sensing, additive manufacturing, advanced manufacturing and IoT, nanotechnology, robotics, microelectronics and advanced computer hardware/software, semiconductors, and advanced materials science), "institution of higher education" (via 20 U.S.C. 1001), "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing), "manufacturing technology," "production equipment," "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce), "resilient critical supply chain," "Secretary" (of Commerce), "State," and "supply chain shock."
bills.brief: Adds eight critical-supply-chain responsibilities to the Commerce Assistant Secretary for Industry and Analysis, establishes a 10-agency Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and a 120-day designation of critical industries/supply chains/goods, requires an implementation report (1 year), a national strategy and review (18 months + annual), a Department capability assessment (2 years), protects voluntarily-submitted supply chain information from FOIA/discovery, authorizes no additional funds, and sunsets the title 10 years after enactment.

items.main: Names the title the "Promoting Resilient Supply Chains Act of 2025."
items.detail: Short-title section only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Additional Responsibilities of Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Analysis

items.main: Adds eight new responsibilities on top of the Assistant Secretary's existing duties: promoting stability and resilience of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; leading the Supply Chain Resilience Working Group and consulting covered nongovernmental representatives, industry, higher education, and State and local governments; encouraging U.S. production and manufacturing of emerging technologies; assessing resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains and critical and emerging technologies; supporting availability of critical goods from domestic manufacturers and allies/key international partner nations (in consultation with the Secretary of State and USTR); assisting the Federal Government in preparing for and responding to supply chain shocks (including by improving flexible manufacturing capacities and capabilities); encouraging reduced reliance of domestic enterprises and manufacturers on critical goods from countries described in section 7(2)(B); and encouraging relocation of manufacturing facilities that manufacture critical goods from section 7(2)(B) countries to the United States and allies/partners.
items.detail: Section 2 enumerates the eight paragraphs of added responsibilities.

sections.label: Section 3 — Critical Supply Chain Resilience Working Group

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must establish a Supply Chain Resilience Working Group composed of the Federal agencies that rely on the Industry and Analysis business unit's analysis, including the Department of State, the Department of Defense, the Department of Homeland Security, the Department of Transportation, the Department of Energy, the Department of Agriculture, the Department of the Interior, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, and the Small Business Administration.
items.detail: Subsections (a) and (c) — 10 enumerated agencies.

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, must assess, map, and model critical supply chains (including for critical and emerging technologies); identify high-priority gaps and vulnerabilities; identify potential supply chain shocks; evaluate the capability and capacity of domestic and allied manufacturers to serve as sources for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology; evaluate market-stability effects of disruption, strain, or elimination of a critical supply chain; evaluate the state of the manufacturing workforce (including identifying opportunities to create high-quality manufacturing jobs); and identify tools — including commercially available risk assessment tools — that leverage data and industry expertise to provide insights into critical supply chain vulnerabilities.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(1) — assessment activities in consultation with the Working Group.

items.main: In consultation with State and local governments, the Working Group, and (as appropriate) allies/key international partner nations: identify opportunities to reduce gaps and vulnerabilities; encourage consultation between the Federal Government, industry, nongovernmental representatives, higher education, and State/local governments; encourage consultation between the Federal Government and governments of allies/partners; identify opportunities to build U.S. capacity in critical supply chains, critical industries, and emerging technologies; identify opportunities to build allies/partners' capacity in critical industries and critical supply chains; and develop and assess contingency plans and coordination mechanisms.
items.detail: Subsection (b)(2) — coordination activities.

items.main: Not later than 120 days after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must designate critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods; provide for a period of public comment and review; and update the designations not less than once every 4 years, including designations for technologies not described in section 7(12)(B) that the Assistant Secretary considers necessary.
items.detail: Subsection (d) — designations, public comment, and 4-year update cycle.

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must submit to the relevant committees of Congress an implementation report detailing supply chain activities conducted, describing supply chain data collected/retained/analyzed, identifying necessary tools including commercially available risk assessment tools, identifying all Federal agencies with authorities/responsibilities described in subsection (b), and identifying Federal agencies/programs/bureaus with duplicative purposes.
items.detail: Subsection (e) — 1-year implementation report.

items.main: Not later than 18 months after enactment, and annually thereafter, the Assistant Secretary, in consultation with the Working Group, covered nongovernmental representatives, industries, higher education, and State/local governments, must submit to the relevant committees a national strategy and review that identifies critical infrastructure, critical and emerging technologies, designated critical industries/supply chains/goods, other crisis-preparedness supplies and services, substitutes for critical goods/production equipment/manufacturing technology, methods and technologies for authentication and traceability of critical goods (including blockchain technology, distributed ledger technology, and other critical and emerging technologies as appropriate), and allies/partners; describes the U.S. manufacturing base, critical supply chains, and emerging technologies (including for critical goods, production equipment, and manufacturing technology) and the U.S. ability to maintain readiness and surge production; assesses and describes demand/supply, production by domestic manufacturers, and rural/Tribal/underserved-community effects; identifies threats and supply chain shocks — listing any threat or shock that may originate from a country (or entity/individual from a country) described in section 7(2)(B); assesses U.S. and allied manufacturing base resilience and workforce capacity; assesses flexible manufacturing capacity; and develops a Commerce Department strategy for resilience, diversity, and strength of critical supply chains.
items.detail: Subsection (f)(1) — 18-month national strategy and review with annual updates.

items.main: The national strategy report may not include critical supply chain information that is not aggregated, confidential business information of a private-sector entity, or classified information; the report is submitted in unclassified form and may include a classified annex; a public comment period is required.
items.detail: Subsection (f)(2)–(4).

items.main: Not later than 1 year after enactment, the Assistant Secretary must enter into an agreement with the head of any relevant agency to obtain any information, data, or assistance necessary to conduct subsection (b) activities.
items.detail: Subsection (g) — consultation agreements.

items.main: Rule of construction: nothing in the section requires any private entity to share information with the Secretary or Assistant Secretary, to request assistance, or to implement any recommendation.
items.detail: Subsection (h) — no private-entity mandate.

items.main: Voluntarily submitted critical supply chain information (identity of submitter included) — when accompanied by the specified express written or oral statement — is exempt from FOIA under 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3); is not subject to ex parte communication rules; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used directly by Commerce or any Federal, State, or local authority or third party in any civil action arising under Federal or State law when submitted in good faith; may not, without the submitter's written consent, be used or disclosed by federal officers for purposes other than the Act's purposes (with narrow exceptions for criminal investigation/prosecution and specified congressional/GAO oversight); may not, if provided to State or local governments, be made available under State/local disclosure law, distributed without consent, or used for purposes other than this section (or criminal investigation/prosecution); and does not constitute a waiver of any applicable privilege or protection under law, such as trade-secret protection.
items.detail: Subsection (i)(1)(A) — six enumerated protections tied to the express-statement mechanism in (i)(1)(B).

items.main: The voluntary submission mechanism does not apply to voluntary submissions of critical supply chain information in an application for Federal financial assistance under section 9902 of the William M. (Mac) Thornberry National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021 (Public Law 116-283).
items.detail: Subsection (i)(5) — semiconductor incentive program (FY2021 NDAA sec. 9902) application carveout.

sections.label: Section 4 — Department of Commerce Capability Assessment

items.main: Not later than 2 years after enactment, the Secretary must submit to the relevant committees a report — identifying duties/responsibilities/resources/programs/expertise within Commerce offices and bureaus relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing innovation, assessing the purpose/legal authority/effectiveness/efficiency/limitations of each identified office or bureau, and providing recommendations to enhance activities (including improving effectiveness and coordination, and consulting with agencies implementing similar activities) — along with a strategy to implement the recommendations as appropriate.
items.detail: Section 4 — Commerce capability assessment.

items.main: No additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out this title.
items.detail: Section 5 — no-additional-funds clause.

items.main: This title and all requirements, responsibilities, and obligations under this title terminate 10 years after the date of enactment.
items.detail: Section 6 — 10-year sunset.

items.main: Defines key terms used in the title, including: "agency" (5 U.S.C. 551); "ally or key international partner nation" (excludes countries posing significant risk to U.S. national or economic security and countries described in section 503(b) of the RANSOMWARE Act, title V of division BB of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023, Public Law 117-328, 136 Stat. 5564); "Assistant Secretary" (Assistant Secretary of Commerce directing Industry and Analysis); "critical good"; "critical industry"; "critical infrastructure" (via 42 U.S.C. 5195c); "critical supply chain"; "critical supply chain information"; "domestic enterprise"; "domestic manufacturer"; "emerging technology" (including technologies in the American COMPETE Act, title XV of division FF of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021, Public Law 116-260, 134 Stat. 3276, and a named list — artificial intelligence; automated vehicles and unmanned delivery systems; blockchain and other distributed ledger, data storage, data management, and cybersecurity technologies; quantum computing and quantum sensing; additive manufacturing; advanced manufacturing and the Internet of Things; nanotechnology; robotics; microelectronics, optical fiber ray, and high performance and advanced computer hardware and software; semiconductors; advanced materials science); "institution of higher education" (20 U.S.C. 1001); "manufacture" (excluding software unrelated to manufacturing); "manufacturing technology"; "production equipment"; "relevant committees of Congress" (Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; House Energy and Commerce); "resilient critical supply chain"; "Secretary" (of Commerce); "State" (each State, D.C., commonwealth, territory, possession, and each federally recognized Indian Tribe); and "supply chain shock" (an event causing severe or serious disruption, including a natural disaster, pandemic, biological threat, cyber attack, geopolitical conflict, terrorist or geopolitical attack, trade disruption caused by section 7(2)(B) countries or their entities/individuals, and Presidentially declared major disasters or emergencies under section 401 or 501 of the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act (42 U.S.C. 5170; 42 U.S.C. 5191)).
items.detail: Section 7 — full definition list.

gaps: Section 7(2)(B) refers to "a country that poses a significant risk to the national security or economic security of the United States" — no list of such countries is provided within this title, leaving that determination to other law or executive designation.

The bill authorizes no additional funds (Section 5) but imposes new assessment, mapping, modeling, working-group, designation, reporting, and consultation obligations on Commerce and 10 other agencies.

The bill does not create any enforcement mechanism for the private-sector no-mandate rule of construction (Section 3(h)) or provide any incentive to submit voluntary information beyond the Section 3(i) protections.
The bill does not describe how the Assistant Secretary's four-yearly redesignations under Section 3(d) interact with the annual national strategy updates under Section 3(f).

featured_quotes.name: Mr. James
featured_quotes.text: I especially thank my chairman, friend, and mentor, the gentleman from Florida (Mr. Bilirakis), for his leadership and support. The gentlewoman has been a family friend for such a long time. I also have the pleasure of sharing the opportunity on this bill with Erin Houchin, my classmate; Robin Kelly; and Pat Ryan, my West Point classmate. This is an example of Congress coming together, reaching across the aisle, and working in the best interests of the American people.

New Supply Chain Resilience Working Group of 10 named agencies, established within 120 days (Section 3)
120-day designation of critical industries, critical supply chains, and critical goods, with public comment and 4-year updates (Section 3(d))

18-month national strategy and review with annual updates and optional classified annex (Section 3(f))
2-year Department of Commerce capability assessment report (Section 4)
Voluntary-submission protections for critical supply chain information — FOIA exemption via 5 U.S.C. 552(b)(3), civil-action non-use, and disclosure restrictions (Section 3(i))
No-additional-funds clause (Section 5)

bills.title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Omnibus Crime Control and Safe Streets Act of 1968 to include certain retired law enforcement officers in the public safety officers' death benefits program.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV) with Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY) — a cross-aisle sponsor pairing on public-safety benefits. The measure passed the Senate by Unanimous Consent on July 29, 2025 and was received in the House on August 1, 2025 per the latest recorded action. The 2012 retroactivity window and the fiscal cost of new claims are the most likely points of pushback.
bills.summary: The Public Safety Officers' Benefits program, run by the Justice Department's Bureau of Justice Assistance, pays a $250,000 line-of-duty death benefit (adjusted each year for inflation) and matching disability benefit to the families of police, firefighters, and other public safety officers killed or permanently disabled on the job. This bill extends the same benefit to retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled as a direct and proximate result of a targeted attack because of their prior service as an officer.
bills.brief: Adds retired law enforcement officers targeted for their prior service to the federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits program, with claims applying retroactively to attacks on or after January 1, 2012.

top_lines.headline: What the Program Pays
subs: $250,000 death benefit, adjusted each October for inflation
Same amount payable for permanent and total disability
Interim benefit up to $6,000 while a claim is pending

top_lines.headline: New Eligibility for Retired Officers
subs: Covers officers who separated in good standing as a law enforcement officer
Trigger: death or permanent total disability from a targeted attack
Attack must be because of the officer's prior law enforcement service

top_lines.headline: Retroactive Window
subs: Applies to any qualifying attack on or after January 1, 2012
Also covers claims pending before the Bureau of Justice Assistance
Takes effect on the date of enactment

sections.label: Section 2 — Inclusion of Certain Retired Public Safety Officers in the Public Safety Officers' Death Benefits Program

items.main: Adds a new subsection (p) to 34 U.S.C. 10281 making retired law enforcement officers eligible for the Public Safety Officers' Benefits program when they die or become permanently and totally disabled from a targeted attack tied to their prior service.
items.detail: A "retired law enforcement officer" is defined as an individual who separated in good standing as a law enforcement officer in an official capacity at a public agency, with or without compensation. Eligibility requires that the death or permanent-and-total disability be the direct and proximate result of a personal injury from a targeted attack because of the officer's service as a law enforcement officer. Claims are processed by the Bureau of Justice Assistance under the existing benefits framework.

items.main: Sets a retroactive effective date so the new eligibility reaches back to targeted attacks occurring on or after January 1, 2012.
items.detail: The amendments take effect on the date of enactment and apply to any matter pending before the Bureau of Justice Assistance on that date, or filed or accruing after it. As an exception to that general rule, the amendment applies to any action taken against a retired law enforcement officer on or after January 1, 2012.

underreported.summary: The bill reaches back nearly 14 years before enactment, applying the new eligibility to any qualifying targeted attack on or after January 1, 2012.
underreported.why_unreported: The section heading names an "exception" to the general effective-date rule, but the operative effect is a broad retroactivity window that opens years of prior incidents to new claim filings — a scope not stated in the bill's short title or Section 2 heading.

gaps: The bill extends eligibility to retired officers but does not define "targeted attack" or list the evidence required to establish that an attack was "because of" the retiree's prior service.

The bill applies retroactively to January 1, 2012 but does not set a filing deadline for pre-enactment claims or address how the Bureau of Justice Assistance should prioritize backlogged retroactive claims against current-year filings.
The bill relies on the existing inflation-adjusted death benefit and disability-benefit mechanism in 34 U.S.C. 10281 but does not authorize additional appropriations to cover the new class of claims.

The bill uses "retired law enforcement officer" only and does not address whether retired firefighters, emergency medical responders, or other public safety officers targeted for prior service qualify.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Booker
featured_quotes.text: So, Mr. President, this casts a shadow over everything that was just said because I support these bills. Why do I support these bills? Because the officers of the State of New Jersey are going to benefit from them because Donald Trump hasn't targeted these and cut these, and these are things that are going to help all officers. That is what this body should do--not pick and choose one State over another, not pit one State against another, not pit so-called blue States over so-called red States. It is the United States of America.

added: New subsection 34 U.S.C. 10281(p) — eligibility for retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled from a targeted attack tied to their prior service
modified: 34 U.S.C. 10281 (Public Safety Officers' Death Benefits — Payment of death benefits) — expanded to cover certain retired officers, with retroactive reach to targeted attacks on or after January 1, 2012

bills.title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To extend the Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000.
bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law December 18, 2025 as Public Law 119-58. Sponsored by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID) with 28 cosponsors; passed the Senate June 18, 2025 and the House December 9, 2025.
bills.summary: The Secure Rural Schools (SRS) program, first enacted in 2000, pays counties that contain Forest Service or Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land a formula-based "State payment" or "county payment" for schools, roads, and other municipal services — an alternative to the traditional 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) share of receipts from timber sales and other federal-land revenues. This Act reauthorizes those SRS payments through fiscal year 2026, restores the lapsed payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 (which the Secretary of the Treasury must pay within 45 days of enactment), and extends the authority to initiate Resource Advisory Committee (RAC) Title II special projects on federal land and to spend Title III county funds through fiscal year 2028.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes the Secure Rural Schools program through fiscal year 2026, pays out the lapsed fiscal year 2024 and 2025 amounts within 45 days of enactment, and extends the Title II special-projects and Title III county-funds authorities through fiscal year 2028.

top_lines.headline: What SRS Pays For
subs: Formula payments to counties containing Forest Service or BLM land
Funds schools, roads, and other municipal services
Alternative to the 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) revenue share

top_lines.headline: SRS Payments Extended
subs: State/county payment authority extended through fiscal year 2026
Restores payments that lapsed for fiscal years 2024 and 2025
Treasury must issue those lapsed payments within 45 days of enactment

top_lines.headline: Election Waived for 2024-2025
subs: Counties skip the biennial election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025
Their fiscal year 2023 election choice carries over automatically

top_lines.headline: Title II & Title III Extensions
subs: RAC special-projects initiation authority extended from 2025 to 2028
Unobligated Title II funds return to Treasury deadline pushed from 2026 to 2029
County Title III fund-expenditure authority extended from 2025 to 2028
RAC composition waiver and pilot program authorities extended to 2026

sections.label: Section 2 — Extension of Secure Rural Schools and Community Self-Determination Act of 2000

items.main: Extends the SRS State and county payment authority in Section 101 (16 U.S.C. 7111) and the California-only county-share distribution rule in Section 103(d)(2) (16 U.S.C. 7113(d)(2)) by striking "2023" and inserting "2026" wherever those year references appear.
items.detail: Section 101 sets the formula the Secretary of Agriculture and Secretary of the Interior use to calculate the State payment (Forest Service counties) and county payment (BLM counties) for eligible jurisdictions. Section 103(d) is a California-only rule that distributes the State-payment share to California's eligible counties in the same proportion those counties received under the pre-2008 formula. The prior authorization covered fiscal years 2008-2015 and 2017-2023; the extension adds fiscal years 2024, 2025, and 2026.

items.main: Adds a new Section 101(e) with a special rule for fiscal year 2024 and 2025 payments and a 45-day prompt-payment deadline for the Secretary of the Treasury.
items.detail: For any eligible county that already received a share of the 25-percent (Forest Service) or 50-percent (BLM) payment for fiscal year 2024 or 2025, the corresponding State or county payment is reduced by the amount already received — preventing double payment. The Secretary of the Treasury must make all title I payments for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 not later than 45 days after enactment.

items.main: Amends Section 102 (16 U.S.C. 7112) so counties do not have to file a fresh biennial election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 — their fiscal year 2023 election choice carries over.
items.detail: Under existing law each affected county elects between the 25-percent/50-percent traditional payment and the State/county SRS payment on a two-fiscal-year cycle. The bill waives that election for fiscal years 2024 and 2025 for both the payment-type choice in subsection (b) and the intended use-of-funds choice in subsection (d), with the fiscal year 2023 elections treated as effective for those years.

items.main: Extends the Title II authority to initiate special projects on federal land under Section 208 (16 U.S.C. 7128) from September 30, 2025 to September 30, 2028, and pushes the deadline for depositing unobligated project funds in the Treasury from September 30, 2026 to September 30, 2029.
items.detail: Title II projects — proposed by Resource Advisory Committees for forest restoration, road maintenance, watershed work, and similar activities on Forest Service and BLM land — could no longer be initiated after September 30, 2025 under prior law. The bill gives RACs three more fiscal years to obligate project funds and three more years before unspent balances revert.

items.main: Extends the Title III authority for eligible counties to expend county funds under Section 305 (16 U.S.C. 7144) from 2025 to 2028, and the corresponding return-of-funds deadline from 2026 to 2029.
items.detail: Title III funds are the portion of the SRS payment a county may spend directly on carrying out the Firewise Communities program, reimbursing emergency services on federal land, or developing community wildfire protection plans. The bill extends both the authority to spend and the deadline to obligate by three fiscal years.

sections.label: Section 3 — Resource Advisory Committee Pilot Program Extension

items.main: Extends the Resource Advisory Committee pilot program in Section 205(g) (16 U.S.C. 7125(g)) from 2023 to 2026 by striking "2023" in the paragraph (5) termination-of-effectiveness clause, and strikes paragraph (6) (the post-termination "Report to Congress" requirement).
items.detail: Paragraph (5) is the pilot program's actual sunset — before this bill it terminated on October 1, 2023. Paragraph (6) required the Secretary to report back to Congress within 180 days of that termination date on how regional vs. national appointments compared. Extending paragraph (5)'s date to 2026 keeps the pilot running through fiscal year 2026, and striking paragraph (6) removes the accompanying report-to-Congress requirement.

items.main: Makes technical corrections to Section 205 (16 U.S.C. 7125) and Section 206(b)(2) (16 U.S.C. 7126(b)(2)) — punctuation, a missing article, and replacing "the date of the enactment of this Act" with the fixed date "October 3, 2008".
items.detail: The corrections replace "concerned," with "concerned" in two places (Section 205(c)(1) and Section 206(b)(2)), insert "the" into the phrase "to extent", and fix the ambiguous cross-reference to an enactment date by naming the specific date the underlying provisions took effect.

underreported.summary: The Secretary of the Treasury has 45 days after enactment to issue every fiscal year 2024 and 2025 SRS payment — a fixed deliverable placed inside the retroactive-payment offset rules.
underreported.why_unreported: The 45-day Treasury deadline sits inside a subsection captioned "Special Rule for Fiscal Year 2024 and 2025 Payments," whose text is otherwise devoted to double-payment offsets — the operational deliverable is not surfaced in the section heading.

underreported.section: Section 3 — Resource Advisory Committee Pilot Program Extension
underreported.summary: Along with extending the pilot, the section strikes paragraph (6) of 16 U.S.C. 7125(g) entirely — a removal, not just an extension.
underreported.why_unreported: The section label describes only the extension; the removal of paragraph (6) is not signaled in the section title.

gaps: The bill extends SRS payments through fiscal year 2026 but does not appropriate a specific dollar amount — the payment formula in 16 U.S.C. 7111 relies on the "full funding amount" defined elsewhere in the underlying Act, and no new authorization figure is stated.

The bill provides retroactive fiscal year 2024 and 2025 payments but does not address whether counties owe interest, penalty offsets, or reconciliation for spending decisions already made on the assumption no payment would arrive.
The bill extends Title II special-projects authority to fiscal year 2028 but does not add or modify criteria for which projects a Resource Advisory Committee may recommend.
The bill relies on the existing 25-percent and 50-percent revenue-sharing baselines but does not adjust those percentages to reflect current federal-land receipt levels.

The bill covers Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management counties but does not extend SRS eligibility to counties containing other categories of federal land (e.g., National Park Service, Bureau of Indian Affairs, military installations).

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Salinas
featured_quotes.text: In central and southern Oregon, my district, the Federal Government owns over 3 million acres of forestland that pays no taxes to our local government. Generations of families built their lives and livelihood around Federal timber harvest, and counties relied on revenue shares from those sales to fund public services. When the timber industry collapsed, the revenue shares also disappeared. Congress made a commitment to support rural communities and the critical infrastructure to make sure they did not get left behind.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Lamalfa
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate being able to get this over the line here soon, as we both know too much about wildfires in our respective States, as well. This will go a long way toward helping that issue.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bentz
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, in 1990, the spotted owl was listed under the Endangered Species Act as a threatened species. Almost immediately, timber production from Federal forests in the Western United States plummeted by 80 percent. The economic and societal costs of timber-dependent States and their timber-reliant counties was appalling. Demand for SNAP and Medicaid shot up. Alcoholism and meth addictions became routine. County tax revenues were decimated.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, with such a large percentage of Wyoming's resources historically locked up in Federal lands, including national forests, communities across my State have long weathered challenges associated with reduced flexibility and a decreased tax base. While a percentage of revenue from timber sales previously alleviated tax shortfalls, shifting land management priorities in Washington, D.C., have led to significant declines in timber harvest.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: This bill is vital to restoring critical funding, preventing further school closures, and ensuring rural students have access to quality education that can compete with urban communities. However, this is not just an education issue. This is about investing in the future of rural America and supporting communities surrounded by Federal forests.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Actively managing our national forests is critical for both forest health and the economic health of our rural communities. Congress has long recognized that responsible timber harvesting is essential for encouraging that stewardship. Since many communities throughout the United States, including Pennsylvania's 15th Congressional District, are located within national forest lands, declining timber harvests can lead to chronic underfunding of local schools, emergency services, and other projects that rely on a strong tax base.

bills.title: Save Our Seas 2.0 Amendments Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act to improve the administration of the Marine Debris Foundation, to amend the Marine Debris Act to improve the administration of the Marine Debris Program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Signed into law December 26, 2025 as Public Law 119-65. Sponsored by Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) with one cosponsor; passed the Senate May 20, 2025 and the House December 15, 2025 on the strength of a favorable Commerce Committee report (S. Rept. 119-12). The bill is largely structural and administrative — restructuring an existing NOAA program and its associated congressionally chartered foundation — rather than authorizing new dollars, which is the profile that typically clears both chambers by voice or unanimous consent.
bills.summary: The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Marine Debris Program identifies, prevents, and removes marine debris (including lost and discarded fishing gear) to protect the U.S. economy, marine environment, and navigation safety; the Marine Debris Foundation is the congressionally chartered nonprofit that raises private funds and runs grant programs alongside it. This bill restructures both — reorganizing the Marine Debris Act into subtitles, giving the NOAA Marine Debris Program authority to use "other agreements" and in-kind contributions, tightening Foundation governance (Board recommendations, Secretary of Commerce approval, a chief executive officer role, and location in the National Capital Region or a coastal shoreline community), adding Indian Tribe / Tribal Government engagement provisions, and reauthorizing the underlying Marine Debris Act through fiscal year 2029 with an additional $2M for fiscal year 2025.
bills.brief: Restructures NOAA's Marine Debris Program and the Marine Debris Foundation, adds Tribal engagement and outreach requirements, and reauthorizes the underlying Marine Debris Act through fiscal year 2029.

top_lines.headline: What the Program & Foundation Do
subs: NOAA Marine Debris Program identifies, prevents, and removes marine debris nationwide
Runs national/regional coordination with states, Tribes, and regional organizations
Marine Debris Foundation raises private funds and awards grants alongside the program

top_lines.headline: Program Modernization
subs: Adds "other agreements" to NOAA Marine Debris Program contracting authority
Lets the Under Secretary contribute in-kind for non-grant, non-cooperative-agreement projects
Reorganizes the Marine Debris Act into Subtitles A (NOAA/Coast Guard), B (Foundation), C (transferred), and D (Administration)

top_lines.headline: Foundation Governance Overhaul
subs: Board must recommend candidates before Under Secretary appoints
Director appointments now require Secretary of Commerce approval
6-year terms for appointed Directors
Adds USAID Administrator to the Board's ex officio membership
Foundation must locate its principal office in the National Capital Region or a coastal shoreline community

top_lines.headline: New CEO Role
subs: Board appoints, reviews, and may remove the Foundation's chief executive officer
Chief executive officer, in turn, appoints and reviews all Foundation officers and employees

top_lines.headline: Tribal Engagement Added
subs: Foundation must develop best practices for outreach to Indian Tribes and Tribal Governments
Includes technical assistance, capacity building, and awareness of grants
Adds Indian Tribes, Tribal organizations, regional organizations, and foreign governments to the list of authorized grant recipients
Rule of construction: nothing satisfies government-to-government consultation or affects treaty rights

top_lines.headline: Money & Reauthorization
subs: Adds $2M for fiscal year 2025 to the Marine Debris Foundation authorization
Reauthorizes the underlying Marine Debris Act appropriations through fiscal year 2029

sections.label: Section 2 — Modifications to the Marine Debris Program of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration

items.main: Reorganizes the Marine Debris Act by inserting a new "Subtitle A — NOAA and Coast Guard Programs" heading and redesignating sections 3 through 6 (33 U.S.C. 1952-1955) as sections 101 through 104.
items.detail: The renumbering is structural — no substantive change to the underlying program authorities — and sets up the transfers of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act's Foundation and cross-cutting provisions into the Marine Debris Act as Subtitle B and Subtitle C, respectively.

items.main: Expands the NOAA Marine Debris Program's contracting authority under Section 101(d) (33 U.S.C. 1952(d)) to include "other agreements" and adds a new in-kind contribution mechanism.
items.detail: The subsection heading and text are amended to add "other agreements" alongside the existing grants, cooperative agreements, and contracts. A new paragraph (7) allows the Under Secretary to contribute in-kind — up to the amount of the benefit NOAA derives from the project — for projects funded through a contract or other agreement that is not a cooperative agreement or a grant.

sections.label: Section 3 — Modifications to the Marine Debris Foundation

items.main: Transfers Subtitle B of title I of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act (Public Law 116-224) into the Marine Debris Act after new Section 104, so the Marine Debris Foundation provisions now live in the Marine Debris Act at 33 U.S.C. 1961-1969.
items.detail: The transfer places the Foundation charter, Board of Directors, Powers, and related provisions inside the Marine Debris Act framework. Section 111(a) is amended to describe the Foundation as a "corporation" rather than an "organization", and Section 111(b) adds "Indian Tribes" to the purposes reference alongside "Tribal governments".

items.main: Overhauls the Board of Directors selection under Section 112(b): the Board must recommend candidates before the Under Secretary appoints, appointments now require Secretary of Commerce approval, and appointed Directors serve 6-year terms.
items.detail: New paragraph (1) requires the Board to submit candidate recommendations to the Under Secretary. Amendments to paragraphs (2) and (4)(A) each insert "with the approval of the Secretary of Commerce" after "the Board", extending Commerce Department sign-off to the Board actions those paragraphs govern. Paragraph (3) is rewritten to set Director terms at 6 years. Paragraph (6) adds the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development to the ex officio membership and requires Secretary of Commerce approval alongside the EPA Administrator.

items.main: Creates a chief executive officer role for the Foundation with hire, review, and removal authority over all other Foundation officers and employees.
items.detail: A new Section 112(h) provides that the Board shall appoint and review the performance of, and may remove, the chief executive officer of the Foundation. The chief executive officer, in turn, may appoint, remove, and review the performance of any officer or employee of the Foundation. Conforming amendments in Section 112(g) shift the earlier reference from "officers and employees" to "the initial officers and employees" and swap "its chief operating officer" for "the chief executive officer of the Foundation."

items.main: Requires the Foundation's principal office to be located in the National Capital Region — as defined in 10 U.S.C. 2674(f)(2) — or a coastal shoreline community, and adds best-practices requirements for Tribal outreach.
items.detail: A new Section 113(g) sets the principal-office location. A new Section 113(h) requires the Foundation to develop and implement best practices for outreach to Indian Tribes and Tribal Governments, including a process to support technical assistance and capacity building and to promote awareness of programs and grants. A new Section 113(i) is a rule of construction: nothing in the Act satisfies government-to-government consultation with Tribal Governments or affects or modifies any treaty right of any Tribal Government.

items.main: Amends Section 118(a) — the Foundation authorization — to add $2M for fiscal year 2025 and to broaden the list of authorized grant recipients.
items.detail: Paragraph (1) inserts the fiscal year 2025 amount after the existing "through 2024" authorization language. Paragraph (2) replaces "and State and local government agencies" with ", State and local government agencies, regional organizations, Indian Tribes, Tribal organizations, and foreign governments" — extending grant eligibility beyond the prior State/local baseline.

items.main: Reauthorizes Section 9(a) of the Marine Debris Act — the underlying appropriations authorization — through fiscal year 2029.
items.detail: The prior authorization language is replaced with "for each of fiscal years 2018 through 2029 for carrying out" — extending the appropriations window that funds the NOAA Marine Debris Program and related activities.

items.main: Transfers Subtitle C of title I of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act (33 U.S.C. 1971-1977) into the Marine Debris Act after Section 119, and moves sections 7, 8, 9 (as amended), and 10 of the Marine Debris Act (33 U.S.C. 1981-1984) to appear after Section 127 as new Sections 131, 132, 133, and 134.
items.detail: A new heading "Subtitle D — Administration" is inserted before Section 131. The transfers put the definitions, authorization, and general-provisions sections all inside a single reorganized Marine Debris Act.

items.main: Rewrites the definitions section (new Section 131 / 33 U.S.C. 1981) — striking one paragraph, renumbering the remaining paragraphs, and inserting nine new terms.
items.detail: New defined terms include "circular economy," "coastal shoreline community" (city or county directly adjacent to the open ocean, major estuaries, or the Great Lakes), "EPA Administrator," "Indian Tribe" (with the meaning given in 25 U.S.C. 5304 — Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act), "nonprofit organization," "post-consumer materials management," "Tribal Government" (with reference to 25 U.S.C. 5131), "Tribal organization," and "Under Secretary." Section 2(7) of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act is transferred into Section 131 and redesignated as paragraph (8), and Section 2 of the Save Our Seas 2.0 Act is renumbered accordingly. Existing paragraph (13) is amended to add "Indian Tribe" alongside the other listed entities.

items.main: Replaces "Administrator" with "Under Secretary" throughout the Marine Debris Act's operative sections (33 U.S.C. 1951 and note, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1983) and makes matching conforming changes to cross-references and terminology.
items.detail: Section 103 of the Marine Debris Act replaces "Administrator of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration" with "Under Secretary" and "Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency" with "EPA Administrator," and updates a cross-reference from "section 3" to "section 101." Section 123 changes "title I" to "subtitle B." Section 133 updates cross-references from "sections 3, 5, and 6" to "sections 101, 103, and 104." Section 134 uses "EPA Administrator" in place of the full agency name. Subtitle A changes lowercase "tribal government" to capitalized "Tribal Government" throughout.

underreported.summary: The bill adds the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development to the Marine Debris Foundation's Board ex officio membership.
underreported.why_unreported: The section heading is titled "Board of Directors" (appointment / vacancies / removal) but this specific provision inserts a new federal agency head into the Board — a governance change not signaled by the section label or the bill's short title.

underreported.summary: The Foundation must locate its principal office either in the National Capital Region or in a coastal shoreline community.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill title describes administrative improvements; a mandated headquarters siting rule limiting the Foundation's principal-office location is a distinct operational constraint not visible in the title.

underreported.summary: The bill states that nothing in the Act satisfies any requirement for government-to-government consultation with Tribal Governments or affects any treaty right.
underreported.why_unreported: The section captioned "Best Practices; Rule of Construction" places a substantive limit on Tribal consultation obligations alongside a best-practices requirement — the limitation is bundled inside a section otherwise focused on outreach.

gaps: The bill reauthorizes the Marine Debris Act appropriations through fiscal year 2029 but sets no annual dollar amount for the NOAA Marine Debris Program itself — only $2M for fiscal year 2025 for the Foundation authorization.
The bill mandates that the Foundation develop best practices for Tribal outreach but does not set a deadline for adopting those practices or reporting on them.

The bill adds Indian Tribes, Tribal organizations, regional organizations, and foreign governments to the list of authorized grant recipients but does not set aside or reserve any minimum share of funds for those recipients.

The bill requires the Foundation's principal office to be in the National Capital Region or a coastal shoreline community but does not address whether existing office arrangements must relocate or the timeline for compliance.

The bill restructures the Marine Debris Foundation Board with Secretary of Commerce approval requirements but does not set a deadline for filling vacancies or a maximum period during which appointments may remain unapproved.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Bonamici
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, as the co-chair of the bipartisan Oceans Caucus, I rise enthusiastically today in support of S. 216, the Senate companion to my bipartisan legislation, the Save Our Seas 2.0 Amendments Act. Marine debris does not stay in one place. A plastic bottle tossed inland can end up hundreds of miles away, wrapped around a propeller, tangled in fishing gear, or broken down into microplastics that end up in the food we eat. Across the country, communities see the damage every day.

bills.title: Continuing Appropriations Act, 2027
bills.official_title: Making continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Tom Cole (R-OK-4), Chair of the House Appropriations Committee — the committee of referral — and cleared by the House per the latest recorded action. Short-term continuing resolutions with a hard December 4, 2026 expiration date are the standard vehicle Congress uses to avoid a shutdown when full-year appropriations are not enacted by October 1, and they typically clear both chambers under time pressure. The Indian Health Service anomaly amounts, District of Columbia local-spending authority, and survivor payments to the widow and heirs of two deceased members of Congress are the most likely points of pushback in Senate negotiations, though not enough to defeat a shutdown-avoidance measure.
bills.summary: A short-term continuing resolution that keeps the federal government funded at fiscal year 2026 rates and under fiscal year 2026 authorities from October 1, 2026 through December 4, 2026 for all twelve regular appropriations areas, buying Congress time to finish full-year fiscal year 2027 appropriations. It also carries a small set of program-specific anomalies, extends the National Flood Insurance Program authority, and blocks the automatic Member of Congress cost-of-living adjustment during the covered period.
bills.brief: Funds the federal government at fiscal year 2026 levels through December 4, 2026 and extends a handful of expiring authorities including the National Flood Insurance Program.

top_lines.headline: Continuing Resolution Basics
subs: Continues fiscal year 2026 rates and authorities into fiscal year 2027
Covers all 12 regular appropriations areas (Ag, CJS, DoD, E&W, FSGG, DHS, Interior, Labor-HHS-Ed, Legislative, Milcon-VA, State, T-HUD)
Expires on December 4, 2026 or upon enactment of the underlying full-year Act, whichever comes first

top_lines.headline: Defense Restrictions
subs: No new production of items not funded for production in fiscal year 2026
No production-rate increases above those sustained with fiscal year 2026 funds
No new multi-year procurements using advance procurement funding for economic order quantity

Additional $8.30M for Indian Health Service — Indian Health Facilities staffing
WIC apportioned up to the rate necessary to maintain participation
SBA business loan program apportioned up to the rate necessary for increased demand
FEMA Disaster Relief Fund apportioned up to the rate necessary for response and recovery

Livestock Mandatory Reporting Act and Agricultural Marketing Act (7 U.S.C. 1636i, 1635 note) extended through December 4, 2026
TANF and Section 1108(b) of the Social Security Act continued through December 4, 2026

top_lines.headline: District of Columbia Local Funds
subs: DC may expend local funds at the rate set in the Fiscal Year 2027 Local Budget Act of 2026 (Bill 26-0659)
Rate is modified as of the date of enactment of this Act

items.main: Continues fiscal year 2026 appropriations rates and authorities for continuing projects across the 12 regular appropriations acts through December 4, 2026.
items.detail: Section 101 lists the 12 anchor appropriations acts (Ag, CJS, DoD, E&W, FSGG, DHS, Interior, Labor-HHS-Ed, Legislative, Milcon-VA, State, T-HUD) and continues each at fiscal year 2026 rates. Section 106 sets the expiration to whichever of three events occurs first: enactment of the applicable full-year fiscal year 2027 Act, enactment of a full-year Act without a provision for the covered activity, or December 4, 2026. Section 110 requires that only the most limited funding action permitted be used to continue projects.

items.main: Prohibits new starts, production increases, and new multi-year procurements at the Department of Defense during the continuing resolution period.
items.detail: Section 102 bars using continuing-resolution funds for production not funded in fiscal year 2026, production-rate increases above fiscal year 2026 levels, or initiation of projects not previously funded. It also bars new multi-year procurement using advance procurement funding for economic order quantity procurement unless specifically appropriated later.

sections.label: Sections 111-125 — Anomalies and Expiring Authority Extensions

items.main: Provides IHS staffing anomalies of $75.77M for Indian Health Services and $8.30M for Indian Health Facilities to staff and operate facilities opened, renovated, or expanded in fiscal years 2022, 2026, and 2027.
items.detail: Section 123(a) provides an additional rate for operations of $75.77M for the Indian Health Service — Indian Health Services account. Section 123(b) provides an additional $8.30M for the Indian Health Service — Indian Health Facilities account. Both amounts are apportioned up to the rate for operations necessary to staff and operate the covered facilities.

items.main: Extends the National Flood Insurance Program's authority through December 4, 2026 by substituting that date for the September 30, 2026 statutory expiration.
items.detail: Section 121 applies sections 1309(a) and 1319 of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968 (42 U.S.C. 4016(a) and 4026) by substituting the date specified in section 106(3) — December 4, 2026 — for "September 30, 2026". A retroactive-application clause treats the substitution as if it had been in effect on September 30, 2026 if this Act is enacted after that date.

items.main: Continues Small Business Administration general business loan programs, FEMA Disaster Relief Fund response and recovery activities, and Wildland Fire Management wildfire suppression at the rates necessary to meet demand.
items.detail: Section 118 permits the SBA Business Loans Program Account to be apportioned up to the rate for operations necessary to accommodate increased demand for 7(a), 5(g), 503, and 303(b) commitments. Section 122 permits the FEMA Disaster Relief Fund to be apportioned up to the rate necessary to carry out Stafford Act response and recovery activities. Section 125 permits Interior and Forest Service Wildland Fire Management accounts to be apportioned up to the rate necessary for wildfire suppression activities.

sections.label: Sections 126-128 — Mandatory Payments, Survivor Payments, and Member COLA

items.main: Continues TANF and Section 1108(b) of the Social Security Act through December 4, 2026 out of any money in the Treasury not otherwise appropriated.
items.detail: Section 126 continues activities authorized by part A of title IV (other than under section 403(c) or 418) and section 1108(b) of the Social Security Act at fiscal year 2026 authority and manner through the date specified in section 106(3), appropriating such sums as may be necessary.

items.main: Appropriates $174,000 each to survivors of two deceased Members of Congress and blocks the Member of Congress automatic cost-of-living adjustment during the continuing resolution period.
items.detail: Section 127 appropriates $174,000 for payment to Alfredia Scott, widow of David A. Scott, late a Representative from Georgia, and $174,000 for payment to the heirs at law of Lindsey O. Graham, late a Senator from South Carolina. Section 128 blocks any adjustment under section 601(a) of the Legislative Reorganization Act of 1946 (2 U.S.C. 4501) relating to cost of living adjustments for Members of Congress during the covered period.

underreported.summary: The bill re-designates each amount previously designated as an emergency or disaster-relief requirement under prior Balanced Budget and Emergency Deficit Control Act triggers as an emergency requirement under the fiscal year 2022 budget resolution and fiscal year 2027 House budget enforcement, and treats prior disaster-relief designations as continuing.
underreported.why_unreported: Section is captioned to continue "emergency" and "disaster-relief" treatment of amounts referenced elsewhere, but the operative effect is to attach the fiscal year 2027 House budget enforcement designation to those amounts — a scorekeeping choice not visible from the section label.

underreported.summary: The bill permits rescissions and cancellations of discretionary budget authority that were previously scheduled to continue by reducing the rate for operations otherwise provided by section 101 for the current applicable Treasury Appropriations Fund Symbol, capped at the lesser of the prior-Act amount or the balances available as of October 1, 2026.
underreported.why_unreported: Section title reads "Rescissions or cancellations of discretionary budget authority that continue pursuant to section 101" but the mechanical effect is to allow OMB to reduce operating rates for programs receiving current appropriations to absorb previously-scheduled rescissions, with an OMB report to Appropriations Committees due November 20, 2026.

underreported.section: Section 120 — Substitutions in Section 747 of Division E of Public Law 119-75
underreported.summary: The bill substitutes the years 2026 for 2025, 2027 for 2026, and 2028 for 2027 in Section 747 of title VII of division E of the FY2026 Financial Services and General Government Appropriations Act, and updates the underlying statutory reference.
underreported.why_unreported: The section number and mechanical language mask what the substitution does — it advances the year references in the underlying provision by one year, but the plain text of the CR does not restate the underlying provision, so a reader cannot tell what activity the year shift affects.

gaps: The bill covers only 65 days (October 1 through December 4, 2026) and does not address what happens if full-year appropriations are not enacted by December 4, 2026.

The bill anomalies specifically fund the Indian Health Service for staffing new facilities but do not include a similar anomaly for staffing at other federal health facilities opened during the same period.
The bill extends the National Flood Insurance Program authority via Section 121 but leaves the underlying program's transactional ceilings and borrowing authority unchanged.
The bill continues TANF and mandatory payments through December 4, 2026 but does not address the treatment of monthly obligations due for periods after that date if the CR lapses.

The bill blocks the Member of Congress cost-of-living adjustment during the covered period but does not address civilian federal employee pay adjustments that would otherwise take effect in January 2027.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Womack
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, I rise to support H.R. 9770, the Continuing Appropriations Act of 2027, in hopes that it is not necessary. If we were to complete our work as the Framers had intended and outlined for us, we wouldn't be standing here today. This is an insurance policy. This ensures that, assuming we don't finish our work by the end of September, by the end of this fiscal year, our government will be held harmless. Who could argue an insurance policy that holds a government harmless when we begin a new fiscal year?
