bills.title: Stop Secret Spending Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 to ensure that other transaction agreements are reported to USAspending.gov, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Barry Moore (R-AL-1) with 3 cosponsors including Rep. Panetta (D-CA) and Rep. Goodlander (D-NH), and referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. The House-passed measure now moves to the Senate per the latest recorded action. Transparency additions to USAspending.gov that pull "other transaction agreements" — a Defense Department and civilian-agency contracting vehicle used heavily by innovation programs — into public disclosure tend to draw industry pushback from OTA recipients and agencies that use OTAs to move quickly, but the cross-aisle sponsor mix and the multi-year phase-in soften Senate opposition.

referencedSources.label: 31 U.S.C. 6101 (Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act note)

bills.summary: USAspending.gov is the public federal spending database created by the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 (FFATA), where federal agencies must post grants, contracts, and other awards. This bill expands the definition of covered federal awards to include "other transaction agreements" — a contracting vehicle used by the Defense Department and other agencies that is not currently required to be reported — and requires the Treasury Secretary to automatically transmit those data to USAspending.gov within 3 years of enactment, publish an annual report identifying federal spending not posted to the site and the reasons why, and produce a list of the Federal agencies required to post information.
bills.brief: Pulls "other transaction agreements" — a contracting vehicle used heavily by the Defense Department for innovation programs — into USAspending.gov's public reporting requirement.

top_lines.headline: OTAs Added to USAspending.gov
subs: Adds "other transaction agreements" to the FFATA definition of covered Federal award
Treasury must ensure OTA data is automatically transmitted to the website within 3 years of enactment
A centralized view of OTA data must be available on the website

top_lines.headline: Annual Report on Unreported Federal Spending
subs: Treasury (with OMB) must post annually to USAspending.gov the total federal spending on awards not posted
Report must include the reason each item was not posted
Categories: national-security or classified, legislative or judicial branch awards, subawards below a primary subaward

top_lines.headline: Data Quality and Agency List
subs: Treasury + OMB must establish requirements to ensure posted information is complete and accurate
Agency heads responsible for ensuring their posted data is complete and accurate
Treasury and OMB may verify the accuracy of data posted
Treasury must publish a list of Federal agencies and components required to post information

top_lines.headline: Inspector General Reports
subs: IG reports required from CFO Act agencies (paragraphs (1) and (2) of 31 U.S.C. 901(b))
Initial IG report due within 1 year of enactment
Subsequent reports at least every 2 years for 10 years

top_lines.headline: GAO Study on FAR
subs: GAO must recommend within 1 year updates to FAR clause 52.204-10 to reflect FFATA reporting

items.main: Expands the FFATA definition of covered "Federal award" to include other transaction agreements, and directs Treasury to automatically transmit OTA data to USAspending.gov within 3 years of enactment with a centralized view of the data.
items.detail: Amends section 2(a)(4)(A) of the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 (31 U.S.C. 6101 note) to add "(iii) includes other transaction agreements" and technical cross-reference fixes. Amends section 4 to require Treasury to ensure that within 3 years of enactment OTA data is automatically transmitted to the website established under FFATA section 2 (or its successor) and that a centralized view is available.

items.main: Requires Treasury (in consultation with OMB) to post an annual report to USAspending.gov identifying total federal spending on awards not posted and the reasons why.
items.detail: Adds a new FFATA subsection (h) requiring, within 1 year of enactment and annually thereafter, a report listing the total federal spending on federal awards not posted and the reason data has not been posted — including whether the spending was national-security-related or classified, awarded by a legislative or judicial branch agency, or a subaward below a primary subaward.

items.main: Adds a two-step implementation plan requiring an initial detailed OTA compilation within 1 year and a plan to Congress within 2 years if OTA data is not yet flowing to USAspending.gov.
items.detail: If Treasury has not yet complied with the new OTA subsection (e) by the 1-year mark, Treasury must publish on USAspending.gov a report listing and describing in detail all OTAs entered into by relevant agencies in the preceding fiscal year. If Treasury has not complied by the 2-year mark, Treasury must submit to Congress a plan describing the current status and the actions underway and planned to ensure full incorporation of OTA data by the 3-year mark.

items.main: Restructures FFATA Inspector General reporting to run from the CFO Act agencies described in paragraphs (1) and (2) of 31 U.S.C. 901(b), on a schedule tied to enactment.
items.detail: Strikes the prior FFATA paragraph (2) and inserts a new one requiring IGs of each covered agency to submit to Congress and publicly release an initial report within 1 year of enactment and not less than once every 2 years thereafter for 10 years, on the date of submission of the agency financial report required under 31 U.S.C. 3521(f) or 9105(a)(3).

items.main: Requires Treasury and OMB to establish quality-of-information requirements, verify accuracy, and publish a list of Federal agencies and components required to post information under FFATA.
items.detail: Adds new FFATA subsections (c) through (e). Subsection (c) requires Treasury and OMB, in consultation with agency heads, to establish requirements for complete and accurate information; makes agency heads responsible for accuracy; and gives Treasury and OMB verification authority. Subsection (d) requires agencies to comply with display standards. Subsection (e) requires Treasury, in coordination with OMB, to determine within 1 year of enactment (and biennially thereafter) which Federal agencies and components must post information; publish the list on the FFATA website; and notify each covered head and IG.

items.main: Directs the Comptroller General to make, within 1 year of enactment, recommendations for updates to FAR clause 52.204-10 that incorporate FFATA reporting requirements.
items.detail: The Comptroller General shall make recommendations for any updates the Comptroller General determines advisable to clause 52.204.10 of the Federal Acquisition Regulation with respect to incorporating requirements under the Federal Funding Accountability and Transparency Act of 2006 (31 U.S.C. 6101 note).

underreported.section: Section 3(b) — Full Disclosure of Federal Funds
underreported.summary: The bill scopes FFATA reporting to agencies and components identified on a list Treasury must publish, with the amendments to the underlying disclosure rules taking effect only when the first list is published.
underreported.why_unreported: The section heading reads "Full Disclosure of Federal Funds" but the mechanical effect narrows the immediate universe of covered posters to those on the published list — an agency not yet on the list does not have the new complete-and-accurate posting obligations.

underreported.summary: The Inspector General reporting requirement runs until the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment.
underreported.why_unreported: Section 3 is captioned "Other Amendments" but embedded in the IG paragraph is a 10-year sunset on the recurring IG report — a structural time limit that is not signaled by the section heading.

gaps: The bill mandates OTA data flow to USAspending.gov but does not define "other transaction agreement" or specify which OTA-issuing agencies must comply beyond "agencies that have the authority to enter into an other transaction agreement, as determined by the Director" of OMB.

The bill requires an annual report on unreported federal spending with three exception categories (national-security/classified, legislative/judicial, sub-awards) but does not require any breakdown by dollar amount within those categories.
The bill requires agency IG reports every 2 years for 10 years but does not identify a lead agency to consolidate the reports or synthesize government-wide findings.
The bill requires Treasury to publish a list of covered agencies but does not set a process for an agency (or the public) to appeal inclusion or exclusion from the list.
The bill directs the Comptroller General to recommend updates to FAR clause 52.204-10 but does not require the FAR Council to adopt the recommendations or set a deadline for consideration.

added: New FFATA section 2(a)(4)(A)(iii) — "includes other transaction agreements" added to the definition of a Federal award
New FFATA subsection 4(e) — Treasury must ensure OTA data is automatically transmitted to USAspending.gov and a centralized view is available
New FFATA subsection 2(h) — annual report on total Federal spending not posted, with reasons
New FFATA subsection 3(c) — Treasury and OMB requirements for complete and accurate posted information
New FFATA subsection 3(d) — Treasury display standards for posted information
New FFATA subsection 3(e) — Treasury agency reporting determination and published list of covered agencies
New two-step implementation plan (initial OTA compilation at 1 year, Congress plan at 2 years) tied to the 3-year OTA-transmission deadline
New GAO study within 1 year on updates to FAR clause 52.204-10
modified: FFATA section 6(a) (Inspector General reports) — scope narrowed to CFO Act agencies (paragraphs (1) and (2) of 31 U.S.C. 901(b)); IG reports required within 1 year of enactment and not less than every 2 years for 10 years
FFATA section 3(b) — posting duty tied to agencies and components on the published list
removed: Prior FFATA section 6(a)(2) — replaced with a new deadline structure tied to enactment of this Act

bills.title: Kay Hagan Tick Act Reauthorization
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Kay Hagan Tick Act, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Christopher H. Smith (R-NJ-4) with 36 cosponsors, and passed the House per the latest recorded action after referral to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce. The measure is a short window-shift reauthorization of two Public Health Service Act authorities that expired at the end of fiscal year 2025 — the kind of bipartisan public-health reauthorization that typically clears the Senate. The introduced-clause change replacing the specific reference to the "Tick-Borne Disease Working Group" with "appropriate individuals" removes a statutorily named consultation body and could draw questions in the Senate HELP Committee, though not enough to derail a broadly cosponsored measure.
bills.summary: Section 317U of the Public Health Service Act authorizes a national strategy and regional Centers of Excellence in Vector-Borne Disease at CDC to identify, report, prevent, and respond to vector-borne diseases including tick-borne illnesses; section 2822 authorizes enhanced support to help state and local health departments address vector-borne diseases. Both authorizations lapsed at the end of fiscal year 2025 — this bill reauthorizes them for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, and also replaces the requirement that CDC consult with the statutorily named "Tick-Borne Disease Working Group" with a broader requirement to consult with "appropriate individuals", and adds language requiring the national strategy to address the underlying capacity of state and local health departments to identify, report, prevent, and respond to such diseases.
bills.brief: Reauthorizes both authorities of the Kay Hagan Tick Act — the CDC-led National Strategy and Regional Centers of Excellence in Vector-Borne Disease, and enhanced support to health departments — for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.

top_lines.headline: Vector-Borne Disease Authorities Reauthorized
subs: Section 317U of the Public Health Service Act reauthorized through FY2030
Section 2822 (enhanced support for health departments) reauthorized through FY2030
Prior authorization window: FY2021-FY2025

top_lines.headline: Consultation Language Change
subs: "Tick-Borne Disease Working Group" reference struck
Replaced with "appropriate individuals"
Broadens the pool CDC must consult in developing the national strategy

top_lines.headline: Strategy Scope Clarified
subs: National strategy must address increasing capacity to identify, report, prevent, and respond to vector-borne diseases
Language inserted into the existing "activities of the Centers" list

items.main: Reauthorizes Section 317U of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 247b-23) — the National Strategy and Regional Centers of Excellence in Vector-Borne Disease — for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
items.detail: Amends subsection (f) of Section 317U by striking "2021 through 2025" and inserting "2026 through 2030". Amends subsection (b) by striking the reference to the "Tick-Borne Disease Working Group established under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act (42 U.S.C. 284s) and other individuals, as appropriate" and inserting "appropriate individuals". Amends subsection (c)(4) by inserting ", including by increasing capacity to identify, report, prevent, and respond to such diseases" before the period at the end.

items.main: Reauthorizes Section 2822 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 300hh-32) — Enhanced Support To Assist Health Departments in Addressing Vector-Borne Diseases — for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
items.detail: Amends Section 2822(c) by striking "2021 through 2025" and inserting "2026 through 2030". No dollar figure is changed; the authorization window is shifted forward by five fiscal years.

underreported.summary: The bill strikes the specific reference to the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group (established under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act, 42 U.S.C. 284s) from the CDC consultation requirement and replaces it with the general phrase "appropriate individuals".
underreported.why_unreported: The section is captioned "Reauthorization of Programs" but this operative change removes a statutorily named consultation body — a substantive policy change unrelated to the reauthorization window.

gaps: The bill reauthorizes both PHS Act authorities for FY2026-FY2030 but does not set any dollar amount — reauthorization sets an authorization ceiling only in years where a subsequent appropriations act names one.

The bill strikes the requirement to consult the Tick-Borne Disease Working Group but does not address whether that Working Group itself continues to be authorized under section 2062 of the 21st Century Cures Act.

The bill adds "increasing capacity to identify, report, prevent, and respond to such diseases" to the CDC national strategy activities but does not specify performance metrics or reporting requirements for that capacity-building.
The bill reauthorizes enhanced support to health departments but does not specify a set-aside for tribal health departments alongside state and local departments.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, at a May 29th press conference in New Hampshire, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., who has been a tremendous leader in the war on Lyme disease, announced a ``sweeping plan to combat Lyme disease and to advance treatment.'' Secretary Kennedy said: ``Millions of Americans battling Lyme disease and other tick-borne illnesses have spent years searching for answers, treatment, and support.

bills.title: EARLY Act Reauthorization of 2025
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz (D-FL-25) with 20 cosponsors and a cross-party original cosponsor group including Reps. Miller-Meeks (R-IA), Fitzpatrick (R-PA), Harshbarger (R-TN), Castor (D-FL), and Dingell (D-MI). The House-passed measure was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and now moves to the Senate. Short reauthorizations of expiring CDC public-health authorizations that shift the year window without changing dollars are the profile that typically clears the Senate by unanimous consent or voice.

referencedSources.label: 42 U.S.C. 280m (Section 399NN of the Public Health Service Act — EARLY Act)

bills.summary: The Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009 (Section 399NN of the Public Health Service Act, 42 U.S.C. 280m) directs CDC to run a national evidence-based public education campaign and a health-care-professional education campaign on breast health, symptoms, early detection, and support for young women (defined as women 15 to 44) diagnosed with breast cancer; the Act also funds prevention research and grants to organizations serving young women with breast cancer. This bill extends the program's authorization of appropriations by striking the current "2026" end year in subsection (h) and inserting "2031", extending $9M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031.
bills.brief: Extends the CDC-run EARLY Act young women's breast health and support program's $9M-per-year authorization through fiscal year 2031.

top_lines.headline: What the EARLY Act Does
subs: CDC national public education campaign on breast health and early detection
Health-care-professional education campaign on symptoms, family history, referrals
Prevention research on breast cancer in younger women
Grants to organizations providing information and support to young women diagnosed with breast cancer
"Young women" defined as women 15 to 44 years of age

top_lines.headline: What This Bill Changes
subs: Strikes "2026" in Section 399NN(h) and inserts "2031"
Extends the $9M-per-year authorization from FY2022-2026 through FY2031
No changes to the underlying program activities or eligibility

sections.label: Section 2 — Reauthorization of the Young Women's Breast Health Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young Act of 2009

items.main: Extends the EARLY Act authorization of appropriations by striking "2026" and inserting "2031" in Section 399NN(h) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 280m(h)).
items.detail: The referenced statute currently authorizes $9M for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to carry out subsections (a) (public education campaign), (b) (health-care-professional education), (c)(1) (CDC prevention research), and (d) (support for young women diagnosed with breast cancer). This bill's one operative amendment shifts the end year of that authorization from 2026 to 2031 without changing the dollar figure or the scope of the covered activities.

gaps: The bill extends the authorization through FY2031 but does not adjust the $9M-per-year dollar figure — the amount has been held flat since the 2020 amendment (Public Law 116-260) and is not indexed for inflation.

The bill continues the "young women" statutory definition of women 15 to 44 but does not address whether the CDC campaign and research should specifically account for higher-risk populations flagged in the underlying statute (Ashkenazi Jewish populations, racial and ethnic minority groups).
The bill does not modify the Advisory Committee established under Section 399NN(a)(4) — including its membership or its reporting obligations to Congress.
The bill continues the every-3-year impact measurement requirement under Section 399NN(f) but does not require CDC to make its measurement data publicly available.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzpatrick
featured_quotes.text: I am proud to co-lead this critical legislation, Mr. Speaker, to reauthorize the Breast Cancer Education and Awareness Requires Learning Young, or EARLY Act, a proven lifesaving initiative that promotes early detection and education for young and high-risk women. Breast cancer remains the most common cancer among women, with over 300,000 new cases and 42,000 projected deaths in 2025. I have seen the power of early detection up close, Mr. Speaker. Both my mom and my sister are breast cancer survivors. This is a very, very personal issue.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Guthrie
featured_quotes.text: I commend my colleague. I know he talked about his mom and his sister, but as we all know, those of us who have been here a little bit of time, his brother was our colleague and had cancer as well. We miss him. May God bless his family.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Wasserman Schultz
featured_quotes.text: To my colleague from Pennsylvania (Mr. Fitzpatrick), I was proud to be elected in the same class as his late brother, Mike. He was a good and decent man, someone who always reached across the aisle. I was really fortunate to be able to serve with him and with the current Congressman Fitzpatrick. First, I thank Chairman Guthrie and Ranking Member Pallone for their strong support of this legislation, because one in eight American women, as you have heard, will get breast cancer, and 42,000 are expected to lose their life from it this year.

bills.title: FDA Modernization Act 3.0
bills.official_title: To require the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, to publish a final rule relating to nonclinical testing methods.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Earl L. "Buddy" Carter (R-GA-1) with 41 cosponsors and a cross-party original cosponsor group including Reps. Barragan (D-CA), Buchanan (R-FL), DeLauro (D-CT), Harshbarger (R-TN), and Carter (R-LA). The House-passed measure directs FDA to issue an interim final rule implementing changes Congress already enacted in section 3209(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 — a narrow rulemaking-forcing mechanism that is the standard vehicle for accelerating overdue regulatory alignment and typically clears the Senate on the same bipartisan footing.

referencedSources.label: 21 U.S.C. 355 (Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act §505)

bills.summary: Section 3209(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (Public Law 117-328) amended Section 505(i) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355) to replace "preclinical tests (including tests on animals)" with "nonclinical tests" and added a statutory definition of "nonclinical test" — a test conducted in vitro, in silico, or in chemico, or a nonhuman in vivo test occurring before or during clinical trials — but FDA regulations in title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations still refer to "animal" tests. This bill requires the HHS Secretary, acting through the FDA Commissioner, to publish within 1 year an interim final rule replacing "animal" references in a listed set of 21 CFR sections with "nonclinical" and adding the statutory "nonclinical test" definition to CFR sections 312.3, 314.3, 315.2, and 601.31. The interim final rule takes effect immediately without requiring FDA to demonstrate good cause.
bills.brief: Requires FDA to publish within 1 year an interim final rule that replaces "animal" references in listed drug and biologic regulations with "nonclinical" to conform them to the 2023 statutory change enabling in vitro, in silico, and in chemico testing methods.

top_lines.headline: Rulemaking Mandate
subs: FDA must publish an interim final rule within 1 year of enactment
Rule takes effect immediately without demonstrating good cause
Rule implements 2023 statutory changes to FFDCA Section 505(i)

top_lines.headline: Terminology Update in 21 CFR
subs: Replaces references to "animal" tests, data, studies, models, and research with "nonclinical"
Applies to 21 specifically listed CFR sections across 21 CFR parts 312, 314, 315, 330, and 601
Plus "any other section necessary to ensure regulatory consistency"

top_lines.headline: Statutory Definition Ported to CFR
subs: Adds "nonclinical test" definition to 21 CFR 312.3, 314.3, 315.2, and 601.31
Definition from FFDCA Section 505(z): tests conducted in vitro, in silico, or in chemico, or a nonhuman in vivo test
Test may occur before or during the clinical trial phase

top_lines.headline: Technical Amendment
subs: Redesignates the second Section 505(z) — clinical trial diversity action plans, added by section 3601(a) of division FF of Public Law 117-328 — as subsection (aa)
Resolves duplicate-subsection numbering in Section 505

sections.label: Section 2 — Regulations on Nonclinical Testing Methods

items.main: Requires FDA to publish an interim final rule within 1 year of enactment to conform 21 CFR references to "animal" tests, data, studies, models, and research to "nonclinical" terminology, implementing the changes to FFDCA Section 505(i) made by section 3209(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 (Public Law 117-328; 136 Stat. 5821).
items.detail: The interim final rule must amend 21 listed CFR sections — 312.22(c); 312.23(a)(3)(iv), (a)(5)(ii), (a)(5)(iii), (a)(8), (a)(8)(i), (a)(8)(ii), (a)(10)(i), (a)(10)(ii); 312.33(b)(6); 312.82(a); 312.88; 314.50(d)(2), (d)(2)(iv), (d)(5)(i), (d)(5)(vi)(a), (d)(5)(vi)(b); 314.93(e)(2); 315.6(d); 330.10(a)(2); 601.35(d) — and any other section necessary to ensure regulatory consistency with the 2023 statutory change.

items.main: Requires FDA to add the statutory definition of "nonclinical test" from FFDCA Section 505(z) to 21 CFR 312.3, 314.3, 315.2, and 601.31, and provides that the interim final rule becomes immediately effective without requiring FDA to demonstrate good cause.
items.detail: The referenced statutory definition in 21 U.S.C. 355(z) defines a "nonclinical test" as "a test conducted in vitro, in silico, or in chemico, or a nonhuman in vivo test, that occurs before or during the clinical trial phase of the investigation of the safety and effectiveness of a drug." Notwithstanding 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the interim final rule takes effect immediately as an interim final rule without FDA having to make the traditional "good cause" showing.

items.main: Redesignates the second subsection (z) of Section 505 — the clinical trial diversity action plans provision added by section 3601(a) of division FF of Public Law 117-328 — as subsection (aa).
items.detail: The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 inadvertently created two subsection (z)s in FFDCA Section 505 — one defining "nonclinical test" and another requiring clinical trial diversity action plans. This bill's technical amendment redesignates the second (z) as (aa) so both provisions can be cited unambiguously.

underreported.section: Section 2(a)(3) — Immediate Effectiveness of Interim Final Rule
underreported.summary: The interim final rule becomes immediately effective without requiring FDA to demonstrate good cause, notwithstanding 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B).
underreported.why_unreported: The section is titled "Regulations on Nonclinical Testing Methods" but this paragraph waives the Administrative Procedure Act's "good cause" showing that normally accompanies bypassing notice-and-comment — a procedural choice not signaled by the section label.

underreported.summary: The rule must amend "any other section necessary to ensure regulatory consistency with the amendments to section 505(i) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. 355(i)) made by section 3209(a) of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023".
underreported.why_unreported: The section lists 21 specific CFR sections but this catch-all clause gives FDA authority to amend additional unspecified sections — a scope-expansion mechanism embedded in an otherwise-precise list.

gaps: The bill sets a 1-year deadline for the interim final rule but does not require FDA to issue a subsequent final rule that would follow the ordinary notice-and-comment process.

The bill lists 21 CFR sections and a catch-all but does not address whether FDA's biologics-specific regulations at 21 CFR Part 600 (beyond 601.31 and 601.35(d)) or animal-drug regulations should be similarly updated.
The bill implements the 2023 statutory change but does not address the parallel FFDCA Section 351 (biologics licensing) which references similar preclinical/animal terminology.

The bill adds the "nonclinical test" definition to four CFR sections but does not require FDA to develop guidance for sponsors on which nonclinical methods (in vitro, in silico, in chemico, nonhuman in vivo) are appropriate for which drug categories.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Carter
featured_quotes.text: Many of our families would feel incomplete without the pets and animals that bring unconditional love into our lives. Yet every year, millions of animals, including dogs, man's best friend, are still subjected to testing in the development of new medicines. As policymakers, we have a responsibility to protect those who cannot protect themselves. That responsibility includes embracing scientific innovation that can reduce unnecessary animal suffering while continuing to deliver safe and effective treatments to patients.

added: New interim final rule requirement: FDA must publish within 1 year to conform 21 listed CFR sections to "nonclinical" terminology
"Nonclinical test" definition (from 21 U.S.C. 355(z)) must be added to 21 CFR 312.3, 314.3, 315.2, and 601.31
Waiver of 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) "good cause" showing for the interim final rule
modified: 21 CFR references to "animal" tests, data, studies, models, and research replaced with "nonclinical" in the 21 listed CFR sections
21 U.S.C. 355 — second subsection (z) (clinical trial diversity action plans, added by section 3601(a) of division FF of Public Law 117-328) redesignated as subsection (aa)

bills.title: Expanding Whistleblower Protections for Contractors Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To ensure that whistleblowers, including contractors, are protected from retaliation when a Federal employee orders a reprisal, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA-42) with one cosponsor — Rep. James Comer (R-KY-1), Chair of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (the bill's committee of referral). That cross-aisle pairing of the Democratic sponsor with the Republican committee chair drove the House-passed measure per the latest recorded action. The bill extends contractor whistleblower coverage to intelligence community elements within DoD, to state, tribal, and territorial governments acting as contractors, and to personal-services contractors — the intelligence-community pieces and the anti-arbitration waiver clause are the most likely points of Senate pushback, but the sponsor-committee-chair pairing gives the measure a plausible path.
bills.summary: 10 U.S.C. 4701 protects Department of Defense and NASA contractor employees from being fired, demoted, or discriminated against for disclosing evidence of wrongdoing in defense contracts; 41 U.S.C. 4712 does the same for non-defense federal contractors. This bill rewrites both statutes to swap "employee" for a new defined term "protected individual" — which explicitly covers state, tribal, territorial, and personal-services contractors and intelligence-community elements within DoD — expands the covered protected activities to include refusing to obey unlawful orders and disclosing gross mismanagement or gross waste, prohibits executive branch officials from requesting a reprisal, authorizes disciplinary action against officials who do, and bars waiver of the rights, forum, and remedies by any agreement including predispute arbitration.
bills.brief: Rewrites the defense and non-defense federal contractor whistleblower statutes to cover a broader "protected individual" class including intelligence community elements within DoD and state, tribal, and territorial contractors, protects refusal to obey unlawful orders, bars retaliation ordered by executive branch officials, and bans predispute arbitration waiver of the statutory remedies.

top_lines.headline: New "Protected Individual" Class
subs: Replaces "employee" throughout 10 U.S.C. 4701 and 41 U.S.C. 4712 with "protected individual"
Covers contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and subgrantees of DoD, NASA, and (in §4712) the Federal Government
Covers state, DC, tribal, Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa, Virgin Islands, N. Mariana Islands, and other territorial governments
Covers political subdivisions, agencies, and instrumentalities of those governments
Covers intelligence community elements within DoD (§4701) and generally (§4712) — defined by 50 U.S.C. 3003
Covers employees, former employees, and personal-services contractors of the above

top_lines.headline: Expanded Protected Activities
subs: Refusing to obey an order that would require violating a law, rule, or regulation
Disclosing gross mismanagement of a DoD or NASA (or Federal) contract or grant
Disclosing gross waste of Department funds or a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety
Disclosing abuse of authority or violation of law related to any contract, subcontract, grant, or subgrant

top_lines.headline: Executive Branch Reprisal-Request Ban
subs: Executive branch officials may not request that a contractor, subcontractor, grantee, or subgrantee engage in a prohibited reprisal
Agencies may propose appropriate disciplinary action against any executive branch official who does
Applies to both DoD/NASA (§4701) and non-defense (§4712) programs

top_lines.headline: Non-Waivable Rights and Anti-Arbitration
subs: Rights, forum, and remedies may not be waived by any public or private agreement
Includes any policy, form, or condition of employment
Explicitly bars predispute arbitration agreements as a waiver mechanism

sections.label: Section 2 — Defense Contractor Employees: Protection From Reprisal (10 U.S.C. 4701)

items.main: Rewrites 10 U.S.C. 4701(a)(1) so a "protected individual" — rather than an "employee" — may not be discharged, demoted, or discriminated against for refusing to obey an unlawful order or disclosing evidence of gross mismanagement, gross waste, abuse of authority, or violation of law related to DoD or NASA contracts, subcontracts, grants, or subgrants, or a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety.
items.detail: The rewrite lists three distinct protected activities: (A) refusing to obey an order that would require the protected individual to violate a law, rule, or regulation related to any contract, subcontract, grant, or subgrant; (B) disclosing to a person or body described in paragraph (2) information the protected individual reasonably believes is evidence of gross mismanagement, gross waste, abuse of authority, or violation of law related to (i) DoD contracts or (ii) NASA contracts; and (iii) a substantial and specific danger to public health or safety.

items.main: Adds a new definition of "protected individual" that includes contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and subgrantees of DoD and NASA — including state, DC, tribal, Puerto Rico, Guam, American Samoa, Virgin Islands, N. Mariana Islands, and other territorial governments, political subdivisions of those governments, and elements of the intelligence community (as defined in 50 U.S.C. 3003) within DoD.
items.detail: The definition also covers employees and former employees of those contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and subgrantees (where the protected activity occurred before termination), and persons performing personal services for DoD or NASA under contractual agreement.

items.main: Prohibits executive branch officials from requesting a reprisal against a contractor, subcontractor, grantee, or subgrantee, and authorizes the head of an executive agency to propose appropriate disciplinary action against any executive branch official who does.
items.detail: Amends 10 U.S.C. 4701(a)(3)(B) to add that it "shall not be within the authority of an executive branch official to request" a prohibited reprisal, and adds new 10 U.S.C. 4701(c)(1)(E) authorizing agency-head disciplinary action against such an official. Also bars waiver of the rights, forum, and remedies by any public or private agreement, policy, form, or condition of employment — including any predispute arbitration agreement.

sections.label: Section 3 — Enhancement of Non-Defense Contractor Protection From Reprisal (41 U.S.C. 4712)

items.main: Applies the same "protected individual" definition, protected activities, executive-branch reprisal-request ban, disciplinary-action authority, and anti-arbitration waiver rule to the non-defense federal contractor whistleblower statute at 41 U.S.C. 4712.
items.detail: The Section 3 amendments parallel Section 2's changes to 10 U.S.C. 4701, applying them to all Federal Government contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and subgrantees (not limited to DoD and NASA). The intelligence-community-element coverage under this section is defined by reference to Section 3 of the National Security Act of 1947 (50 U.S.C. 3003) without the DoD-only limitation that appears in the Section 2 amendments to 10 U.S.C. 4701.

underreported.section: Section 2(3) — Repeal of 10 U.S.C. 4701(e) and Section 3(4) — Repeal of 41 U.S.C. 4712(f)
underreported.summary: The bill strikes subsection (e) of 10 U.S.C. 4701 and subsection (f) of 41 U.S.C. 4712 and redesignates the following subsections accordingly.
underreported.why_unreported: The section headings describe rewrites of the reprisal-protection rules, but this operative deletion removes an existing subsection of each statute — the text of the deleted subsections is not restated in this bill, so the plain reading of this Act does not show what those subsections previously required.

underreported.summary: The non-defense "protected individual" definition in the amended 41 U.S.C. 4712 covers intelligence-community elements without the "within the Department of Defense" limitation applied in the amended 10 U.S.C. 4701.
underreported.why_unreported: Both sections are captioned as protection-from-reprisal rewrites, but the intelligence-community coverage under Section 3 is broader than under Section 2 — a scope difference not visible from the section labels.

gaps: The bill bars waiver of the rights, forum, and remedies by any predispute arbitration agreement but does not address the enforceability of post-dispute arbitration or settlement agreements that release these claims.

The bill covers intelligence-community elements within DoD (in the amended 10 U.S.C. 4701) but does not address protections for intelligence-community civil employees separately covered by 50 U.S.C. 3234.

The bill authorizes agency heads to propose disciplinary action against executive branch officials who request reprisals but does not require agencies to report the number of such disciplinary proposals or their outcomes.
The bill's rewrites do not address the statute of limitations or the burden-of-proof standard for a protected individual's retaliation claim under the amended sections.

added: "Protected individual" defined in both 10 U.S.C. 4701 and 41 U.S.C. 4712 to include contractors, subcontractors, grantees, subgrantees, state/tribal/territorial governments, political subdivisions, intelligence-community elements, employees and former employees, and personal-services contractors
New protected activity: refusing to obey an order that would require the protected individual to violate a law, rule, or regulation related to any contract, subcontract, grant, or subgrant
New 10 U.S.C. 4701(c)(1)(E) and 41 U.S.C. 4712(c)(1)(E) authority: propose appropriate disciplinary action against any executive branch official who requests a prohibited reprisal
Anti-waiver rule barring public or private agreement (including predispute arbitration) from waiving the rights, forum, and remedies
modified: 10 U.S.C. 4701(a)(1) — rewritten to cover "protected individual" and to list three protected activities (unlawful-order refusal, disclosure of DoD/NASA wrongdoing, disclosure of substantial and specific public health/safety danger)
10 U.S.C. 4701(a)(3)(B) — clarified that executive branch officials have no authority to request a prohibited reprisal
41 U.S.C. 4712(a)(1) — rewritten in parallel to cover Federal Government contracts and "protected individual"
41 U.S.C. 4712(a)(3)(B) — parallel executive-branch reprisal-request ban
10 U.S.C. 4701(f) and 41 U.S.C. 4712(f) — as redesignated, add the "protected individual" definitional paragraph
removed: 10 U.S.C. 4701(e) — struck; remaining subsections redesignated
41 U.S.C. 4712(f) — struck; remaining subsections redesignated

bills.title: Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Reauthorization Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To reauthorize the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Christopher H. Smith (R-NJ-4) with 21 cosponsors and a cross-party original cosponsor group including Reps. Matsui (D-CA), Bilirakis (R-FL), Pingree (D-ME), Tenney (R-NY), and Mfume (D-MD). The House-passed measure now moves to the Senate. Short reauthorizations of the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program have historically cleared both chambers by voice or unanimous consent — the most recent prior reauthorization (Public Law 117-15) advanced on that pattern — and the modest $2M-per-year increase in the primary authorization matches the profile that typically clears the Senate.

referencedSources.label: 42 U.S.C. 274m (Section 379B of PHS Act — C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program authorization of appropriations)
42 U.S.C. 274k (Section 379 of PHS Act — C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program) and 274k note (Cord Blood Inventory, from Section 2 of Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005)

bills.summary: The C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program is a federally administered system, run by the Health Resources and Services Administration, that identifies, matches, and distributes bone marrow and cord blood units for transplantation for patients without a matched biologically related donor; the National Cord Blood Inventory (Section 2 of the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005) contracts with qualified cord blood banks to build and maintain an inventory goal of at least 150,000 units of high-quality cord blood. This bill adds $33.009M of appropriations authorization for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program on top of the existing $31.009M for FY2022 through FY2026, and extends the National Cord Blood Inventory authorization by striking "2026" and inserting "2031".
bills.brief: Extends the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program appropriations authorization at $33.009M per year through FY2031 and extends the National Cord Blood Inventory authorization through FY2031.

top_lines.headline: What the Program Does
subs: Identifies, matches, and distributes bone marrow and cord blood units for transplantation
Runs a national single point of access for transplant physicians and patients
Runs a patient advocacy and case management office
Recruits bone marrow and cord blood donors, with priority to underrepresented populations
Contracts with qualified cord blood banks to build the National Cord Blood Inventory (goal: at least 150,000 high-quality units)

top_lines.headline: Program Authorization Increased
subs: Existing $31.009M-per-year authorization for FY2022 through FY2026 preserved
Adds $33.009M for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031
Effectively a $2M-per-year increase over the FY2022-2026 authorization

top_lines.headline: Cord Blood Inventory Extended
subs: Amends Section 2(g) of the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005
Strikes "2026" and inserts "2031"
Extends existing $23M-per-year National Cord Blood Inventory authorization through FY2031

sections.label: Section 2 — Reauthorization of the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program

items.main: Adds a new authorization of $33.009M for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 to Section 379B of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 274m), on top of the existing $31.009M-per-year authorization for fiscal years 2022 through 2026.
items.detail: The amendment restructures Section 379B by turning the existing single-figure authorization into paragraph (1) and adding a new paragraph (2) authorizing $33.009M for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031. This is the appropriations authorization used to fund the HRSA-administered C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program described in Section 379 of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 274k) — a $2M-per-year increase over the fiscal year 2022-2026 authorization.

items.main: Extends the National Cord Blood Inventory authorization by striking "2026" and inserting "2031" in Section 2(g) of the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C. 274k note).
items.detail: The referenced Cord Blood Inventory note currently authorizes $23M for each of fiscal years 2022 through 2026 to build and maintain an inventory goal of at least 150,000 units of high-quality cord blood through contracts with qualified cord blood banks. This bill's one operative amendment to Section 3 shifts the end year of that authorization from 2026 to 2031 without changing the dollar figure or the underlying contract, recordkeeping, or standard-of-care requirements.

gaps: The bill increases the C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Program authorization by $2M per year but does not adjust the $23M-per-year National Cord Blood Inventory authorization for FY2027-2031, holding it flat.

The bill extends both authorizations through FY2031 but does not modify the 150,000-unit inventory goal set in Section 2(a) of the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005, despite the intervening 20+ years of program operation.

The bill preserves the existing every-2-year state-of-the-science review under 42 U.S.C. 274k(o) but does not require any new report to Congress on new-cell-therapy inclusion tied to the FY2027-2031 authorization window.
The bill raises the annual authorization but does not address the number of qualified cord blood banks or contract-structure changes required to absorb the higher funding level.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Each year over 3.6 million babies are born in the United States. In the past, virtually every placenta and umbilical cord was tossed as medical waste. Today, doctors have turned this medical waste into medical miracles. Not only has God, in his infinite wisdom and goodness, created a placenta and an umbilical cord to nurture and protect the precious life of an unborn child, but now we know another gift awaits immediately after birth. Something very special is left behind: umbilical cord blood that is teeming with life-saving stem cells.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Bilirakis
featured_quotes.text: Every year, thousands of Americans battling leukemia, lymphoma, sickle cell disease, and other blood disorders rely on the C.W. Bill Young program to help find a compatible donor. For many patients, that match is their only chance at survival, Mr. Speaker. This legislation reauthorizes the program, modernizes the National Cord Blood Inventory, and strengthens our Nation's transplant system to help ensure patients continue to have access to these lifesaving transplants.

added: New Section 379B paragraph (2) of the Public Health Service Act (42 U.S.C. 274m) — $33.009M authorized for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031
modified: 42 U.S.C. 274m — existing appropriation clause redesignated as paragraph (1) to accommodate the new paragraph (2)

Section 2(g) of the Stem Cell Therapeutic and Research Act of 2005 (42 U.S.C. 274k note) — authorization end year shifted from "2026" to "2031", extending the $23M-per-year National Cord Blood Inventory authorization through FY2031

C.W. Bill Young Cell Transplantation Pro.note: Authorization added by Section 2 for each of fiscal years 2027 through 2031 (in addition to existing $31,009,000 authorization for FY2022-2026)

bills.title: Smithsonian American Women's History Museum Act
bills.official_title: To permit the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum to be located within the Reserve of the National Mall, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The underlying museum-site designation had 231 cosponsors, but the provisions limiting the museum to biological women, barring depiction of any biological male as a female, and mandating political-viewpoint representation drew enough opposition to block the bill in the House. Advancing a version would require dropping or softening those provisions.
bills.summary: This bill sets the location of the future Smithsonian American Women's History Museum at a site on the National Mall and clears the way for the Smithsonian to build there. It also limits the museum's subject to the history of biological women and requires its exhibits to represent a range of political viewpoints.
bills.brief: Designates a National Mall site for the Smithsonian American Women's History Museum and limits its mission to the history of biological women.

top_lines.headline: National Mall Site Designation
subs: Designates the South Monument site on the National Mall
President may choose an alternative site within 180 days
Transfers the land's jurisdiction to the Smithsonian

top_lines.headline: Museum Mission Scope
subs: Limits the museum to the history of biological women
Bars depicting any biological male as a female

top_lines.headline: Exhibit Content and Reporting
subs: Requires equal representation of diverse political viewpoints
Reports to Congress within 120 days, then every 2 years

items.main: Designates the South Monument site on the National Mall as the museum's location, with the President able to designate an alternative site within 180 days.
items.detail: The site is bordered by 14th Street Southwest, Jefferson Drive Southwest, Raoul Wallenberg Place Southwest, and Independence Avenue Southwest. The provision authorizes siting the museum within the Reserve of the National Mall by striking a prior exception clause in Section 107(d) of division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021.

items.main: Requires the federal agency holding the land to transfer administrative jurisdiction to the Smithsonian Institution and allows construction of a museum building.
items.detail: The Board of Regents may plan, design, and construct the building with approval from the Commission of Fine Arts, the National Capital Planning Commission, and the National Capital Memorial Advisory Commission. The Smithsonian must reimburse the land-holding agency within 60 days for costs from the approval process.

items.main: Sets the museum's mission scope to the history, achievements, and lived experiences of biological women, and prohibits depicting any biological male as a female.
items.detail: The provision adds a 'Scope of Mission' subsection to Section 103 of division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021. It states the museum may not identify, present, describe, or otherwise depict any biological male as a female.

items.main: Requires the museum's Council to ensure exhibits and programs reflect equal representation of diverse political viewpoints among women.
items.detail: The Council must seek guidance from a 'broad array' of knowledgeable and respected sources reflecting varied political ideologies, cultures, and lived experiences. The Secretary of the Smithsonian must report to seven House and Senate committees within 120 days of enactment and every 2 years thereafter on compliance.

underreported.summary: Restricts the museum's subject matter to biological women and prohibits it from depicting any biological male as a female.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title and headline concern permitting the museum's location on the National Mall, but this subsection defines the museum's mission content rather than its site.

underreported.section: Section 2(e) - Ensuring Diversity of Political Viewpoints
underreported.summary: Requires the Council to ensure exhibits and programs give equal representation to the diversity of political viewpoints held by women.
underreported.why_unreported: This imposes an ongoing content requirement on the museum's exhibits, an effect not implied by a bill framed around the museum's physical location.

criticisms.why: I stand proudly to support H.R. 1329, the bipartisan Smithsonian American Women's History Museum Act, as an original cosponsor. For 30 years, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have worked together to establish a space that carries on the legacy of the American women who fought tirelessly for our rights. It is absolutely unacceptable that any Member would oppose this bill because they want a biological male, a man, to be honored in the space designed for women, biological women.

gaps: The bill designates the South Monument site and authorizes constructing a building but does not identify a funding source or construction cost for the museum.
The bill prohibits depicting any biological male as a female but does not define 'biological male' or 'biological female.'
The bill requires exhibits to give equal representation to diverse political viewpoints but does not define how equal representation is measured.
The bill mandates biennial compliance reports to Congress but specifies no consequence if the museum does not comply.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. De La Cruz
featured_quotes.text: I stand proudly to support H.R. 1329, the bipartisan Smithsonian American Women's History Museum Act, as an original cosponsor. For 30 years, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have worked together to establish a space that carries on the legacy of the American women who fought tirelessly for our rights. It is absolutely unacceptable that any Member would oppose this bill because they want a biological male, a man, to be honored in the space designed for women, biological women.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Cammack
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate my colleague from the great State of Wisconsin for his leadership on this issue. As you can see, I have my daughter, Augusta Dair, here with me today because I wanted her to be a witness to this incredible moment in our Nation's history where we stood up for all of the women who have helped build this country and told their stories. That is what this museum is. It is not a political statement. It is a promise, a promise that the women who came before us will not be erased, will not be minimized, and will not be forgotten.

added: A 'Scope of Mission' limiting the museum to the history of biological women and barring depiction of any biological male as a female
A requirement that exhibits reflect equal representation of diverse political viewpoints among women
Reports to Congress within 120 days of enactment and every 2 years thereafter
modified: The museum's designated site is set to the South Monument site on the National Mall (Section 107(a) of division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021)
removed: An exception clause in Section 107(d) of division T of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 that had limited siting the museum within the Reserve of the National Mall

bills.title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To amend the Clean Air Act with respect to the ethanol waiver for Reid Vapor Pressure under that Act, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, the bill has 55 cosponsors, and it passed the House. The year-round E15 change has support tied to ethanol production, while the provisions cutting small refining companies' renewable-fuel obligations by 75 percent and barring reallocation of those volumes may draw opposition from biofuel producers, and Senate passage would require 60 votes.
bills.summary: This bill lets gasoline blended with 10 to 15 percent ethanol (E15) be sold year-round by extending the Clean Air Act's vapor-pressure waiver to those blends. It also cuts renewable-fuel compliance obligations for small refining companies and changes how their exemption petitions are handled.
bills.brief: Allows year-round sale of 10 to 15 percent ethanol gasoline and reduces small refining companies' renewable-fuel obligations by 75 percent.

top_lines.headline: Year-Round E15 Ethanol Blends
subs: Extends the Reid Vapor Pressure waiver to 10 to 15 percent ethanol blends
EPA must update E15 pump labels and storage-tank rules within 18 months

top_lines.headline: Small Refining Company Obligations
subs: Defines 'small refining company' as under 75,000 barrels per day in 2025
Cuts their renewable-fuel compliance requirements 75 percent from 2028
Bars reallocating those obligations to other refiners

top_lines.headline: Small Refinery Exemptions
subs: Ends exemption-extension petitions for years after 2027
New closure-risk exemption capped at 150 million gallons for 2028
Returns retired credits for 2016 to 2018 compliance years

items.main: Extends the Clean Air Act's Reid Vapor Pressure treatment from 10 percent to 10 to 15 percent ethanol blends, allowing E15 to be sold during the high-ozone summer season.
items.detail: Amends Sections 211(f)(4) and 211(h) of the Clean Air Act so that a fuel meeting the vapor-pressure conditions can be introduced into commerce. For any State whose Governor submitted a notification after January 1, 2022, the paragraph (4) vapor-pressure limit applies to gasoline blends containing 10 to 15 percent denatured anhydrous ethanol.

items.main: Requires the EPA to finalize a rule within 18 months modifying E15 fuel-dispenser labeling and underground storage-tank regulations.
items.detail: The rule, issued after notice and public comment, must address compatibility of gasoline-ethanol blends greater than 10 and up to 15 volume percent ethanol under the Clean Air Act and the Solid Waste Disposal Act.

items.main: Creates a 'small refining company' category for producers whose 2025 daily average obligated-fuel production did not exceed 75,000 barrels per day, including affiliated entities.
items.detail: The definition reaches groups of affiliated entities linked through subsidiaries, parent companies, joint ventures, holding companies, or spin-offs. Beginning in 2028, the Administrator must reduce each small refining company's compliance requirements by 75 percent, subject to losing eligibility if production later exceeds the limit.

items.main: Ends the small refinery exemption-extension petition process after compliance year 2027 and bars reallocating reduced obligations to other refiners.
items.detail: No small refinery may petition for an extension for any calendar year after 2027, no petition submitted after July 1, 2028 may be considered, and outstanding petitions must be acted on by October 1, 2028. For 2028 and later, the Administrator may not reallocate a small refining company's reduced renewable-fuel obligation to other persons.

sections.label: Section 1(d)-(g) - Small Refinery Credits and At-Risk Exemptions

items.main: Returns retired renewable-fuel credits to certain small refineries for the 2016 through 2018 compliance years.
items.detail: Eligible credits are returned and deemed eligible for future compliance years or applied in the refinery's EPA Moderated Transaction System account. Eligibility depends on having submitted petitions that remained outstanding as of December 1, 2022, among other conditions.

items.main: Creates a new exemption for at-risk qualifying small refineries facing imminent closure, capped at 150 million gallons of biofuel-equivalent volume for 2028.
items.detail: A qualifying small refinery may petition by December 31 if it is at imminent risk of closure, permanent idling, or conversion solely due to compliance costs; the Administrator must act within 90 days. Petitions are not treated as confidential business information and must be made public within 30 days.

underreported.section: Section 1(c) - Adjusted Compliance Requirements for Small Refining Companies
underreported.summary: Reduces the renewable-fuel compliance requirements of each small refining company by 75 percent beginning in 2028 and bars reallocating the reduced volumes to other refiners.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title concerns the ethanol vapor-pressure waiver, but this provision cuts renewable-fuel obligations for a class of refiners defined broadly to include affiliated corporate groups.

underreported.section: Section 1(g)(iii) - Public Disclosure of Exemption Petitions
underreported.summary: Bars at-risk small refinery exemption petitions from confidential-business-information treatment and requires public release within 30 days of submission.
underreported.why_unreported: This makes ordinarily confidential refinery compliance filings public, an effect not implied by a bill about the ethanol waiver.

criticisms.why: I rise to express my strong opposition to H.R. 1346. This bill is disastrous for Wyoming refiners and independent petroleum producers, leading to a direct loss of at least 750 jobs in my home State. Just to correct the record, it isn't the farmers who produce ethanol or E15. It is the refiners, and this bill threatens to put them out of business. In fact, it is interesting that anyone who supports this bill has not yet mentioned the fact that it is the refiners that will be forced, mandated, to meet the E15 requirement.

I appreciate my colleagues on both sides of this debate and where they are coming from. I understand my friends who come from States that want support for farming. We all want to make sure that we are figuring that out. We worked through the farm bill. I just think we ought to be going about this a different way. If we need to do something to support farmers, let's have a direct conversation about it. Expanding E15 is just the wrong direction to go. It is going to harm refiners. It is going to drive up the cost of gas.

gaps: The bill enables year-round sale of blends up to 15 percent ethanol but does not address blends above 15 percent ethanol.

The bill cuts small refining companies' compliance requirements by 75 percent and bars reallocation of those volumes but does not state how the resulting shortfall in obligated renewable fuel is absorbed.
The bill caps 2028 at-risk exemptions at 150 million gallons of biofuel-equivalent volume but does not specify how the Administrator prioritizes competing petitions if they exceed the cap.
The bill requires EPA to modify E15 labeling and storage-tank rules within 18 months but sets no date by which the modified rule must take effect.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: I rise to express my strong opposition to H.R. 1346. This bill is disastrous for Wyoming refiners and independent petroleum producers, leading to a direct loss of at least 750 jobs in my home State. Just to correct the record, it isn't the farmers who produce ethanol or E15. It is the refiners, and this bill threatens to put them out of business. In fact, it is interesting that anyone who supports this bill has not yet mentioned the fact that it is the refiners that will be forced, mandated, to meet the E15 requirement.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Roy
featured_quotes.text: I appreciate my colleagues on both sides of this debate and where they are coming from. I understand my friends who come from States that want support for farming. We all want to make sure that we are figuring that out. We worked through the farm bill. I just think we ought to be going about this a different way. If we need to do something to support farmers, let's have a direct conversation about it. Expanding E15 is just the wrong direction to go. It is going to harm refiners. It is going to drive up the cost of gas.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Budzinski
featured_quotes.text: As a lead Democrat on this bill, I have been proud to work with Congressman Adrian Smith on this issue. We both understand, like many other Members, that year-round E15 is bigger than politics. This is about American farmers. It is about American consumers, and it is about American energy. E15 is truly one of those rare issues where everyone wins. Here is why: American farmers win because it creates strong and stable markets for homegrown corn. American consumers win because E15 helps to lower prices at the pump.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Miller-Meeks
featured_quotes.text: Every single year since 2011, the EPA has issued an emergency waiver to allow E15 to be sold during the Speaker, I yield 2 minutes to the gentlewoman from Iowa (Mrs. Miller-Meeks), a valued member of the Energy and Commerce Committee.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Finstad
featured_quotes.text: As a fourth-generation corn and soybean farmer from southern Minnesota raising that fifth generation and representing 21 counties in southern Minnesota, a very strong egg-producing district, I have had many conversations with my neighbor farmers. I know by hearing what they are telling me and firsthand in my own experience as a farmer that we are facing uncertainty in our input costs and uncertainty in the global markets. We need a new domestic opportunity for our corn. E15 delivers on that.

added: A 'small refining company' category for producers under 75,000 barrels per day in 2025
A closure-risk exemption for at-risk qualifying small refineries, capped at 150 million gallons of biofuel-equivalent volume for 2028
A requirement that EPA modify E15 dispenser labeling and underground storage-tank rules within 18 months
modified: The Reid Vapor Pressure ethanol threshold changed from 10 percent to 10 to 15 percent in Section 211(h) of the Clean Air Act
Small refining companies' renewable-fuel compliance requirements reduced by 75 percent beginning in 2028
removed: Small refinery exemption-extension petitions ended for calendar years after 2027, with no petitions considered after July 1, 2028
The Administrator barred from reallocating reduced small refining company obligations to other refiners for 2028 and later

bills.title: Deploying American Blockchains Act of 2025
bills.official_title: To direct the Secretary of Commerce to take actions necessary and appropriate to promote the competitiveness of the United States related to the deployment, use, application, and competitiveness of blockchain technology or other distributed ledger technology, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House and the bill passed the House, and its rules of construction impose no obligation on private entities, limiting opposition. It carries only one cosponsor and now sits with the Senate Commerce Committee, so Senate floor time is uncertain.
bills.summary: This bill makes the Secretary of Commerce the federal government's lead advisor on blockchain and distributed-ledger technology and sets up a Blockchain Deployment Program to promote its use. The program develops voluntary best practices, convenes advisory committees, and reports to Congress, but requires nothing of private companies.
bills.brief: Directs the Commerce Department to lead a voluntary federal program promoting blockchain and distributed-ledger technology.

top_lines.headline: Commerce Department Blockchain Role
subs: Names the Commerce Secretary as the President's principal blockchain advisor
Creates a Blockchain Deployment Program in the Commerce Department
The program sunsets 7 years after enactment

top_lines.headline: Blockchain Advisory Committees
subs: Advisory committees must be established within 180 days
Membership spans industry, academia, cybersecurity, and rural stakeholders

top_lines.headline: Best Practices and Reporting
subs: Commerce develops and shares voluntary blockchain best practices
Public report to Congress within 2 years, then annually

sections.label: Section 3 - Department of Commerce Leadership on Blockchain

items.main: Designates the Secretary of Commerce as the President's principal advisor on blockchain and distributed-ledger technology and creates a Blockchain Deployment Program.
items.detail: The Secretary must develop policies on issues including decentralized identity, cybersecurity, key storage, artificial intelligence, fraud reduction, and supply-chain resiliency, and examine how federal agencies use and could adopt the technology. The Blockchain Deployment Program terminates 7 years after enactment.

items.main: Requires the Secretary to establish blockchain advisory committees within 180 days, with broad governmental and nongovernmental membership.
items.detail: Members include federal agency representatives and nongovernmental stakeholders such as infrastructure operators, application developers, small to large businesses, think tanks and academia, cybersecurity experts, rural stakeholders, and artists and content creators. The Secretary also develops and disseminates voluntary best practices on an ongoing basis.

items.main: States that nothing in the section requires a private entity to share information, seek assistance, implement recommendations, or adopt the best practices.
items.detail: The rules of construction make participation and adoption voluntary for private entities. In carrying out the section the Secretary must consult stakeholders, develop standardized terminology, and support open-source infrastructure.

items.main: Requires a public report to Congress within 2 years of enactment and annually thereafter on the program's activities.
items.detail: The Secretary must post the report on the Commerce Department website and submit it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. It must describe the Secretary's activities, any recommendations for additional legislation, and emerging risks and long-term trends.

underreported.summary: Bars construing the section to require any private entity to share information, request assistance, implement a recommendation, or adopt the best practices.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill is titled around deploying blockchain, but its operative effect on the private sector is entirely voluntary rather than a mandate.

gaps: The bill directs Commerce to lead on blockchain competitiveness but authorizes no funding for the Blockchain Deployment Program or advisory committees.
The bill establishes advisory committees but sets no limit on their number, size, or members' terms.
The bill directs examination of federal agencies' blockchain use but sets no standards or requirements for that use.
The bill requires development of standardized terminology but does not say who resolves disputes over definitions.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. Cammack
featured_quotes.text: This bill is about far more than emerging technology. It is about securing America's future, economically, strategically, and technologically, in an increasingly digital world. Blockchain technology is not a passing trend. It is a foundational innovation that is reshaping how we think about security, identity, data integrity, and commerce. From supply chains and finance to healthcare and identity management, blockchain is transforming the way our systems function. Mr. Speaker, we are at a crossroads.

added: The Secretary of Commerce as the President's principal advisor on blockchain and distributed-ledger technology
A Blockchain Deployment Program in the Commerce Department that sunsets 7 years after enactment
Blockchain advisory committees, to be established within 180 days
A public report to Congress within 2 years of enactment and annually thereafter

bills.title: CLEAN Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970 to increase the frequency of lease sales, to require replacement sales, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House and the bill passed the House. The provisions forcing annual lease sales and mandatory parcel offerings, and compressing permit timelines around environmental review, may draw opposition from members favoring more agency discretion, and the bill now sits with a Senate committee where 60 votes would be needed.
bills.summary: This bill speeds up federal geothermal energy leasing by requiring lease sales every year instead of every 2 years and forcing the Interior Department to offer most eligible parcels for lease. It also sets short deadlines for the government to act on geothermal drilling permit applications.
bills.brief: Requires annual federal geothermal lease sales, mandatory parcel offerings, and deadlines for geothermal drilling permits.

top_lines.headline: Annual Geothermal Lease Sales
subs: Requires geothermal lease sales every year instead of every 2 years
Canceled or delayed sales must be replaced within the same year

top_lines.headline: Mandatory Parcel Offerings
subs: Interior must offer 75 percent of nominated eligible parcels for lease
The remaining 25 percent required unless a written justification is given

top_lines.headline: Drilling Permit Deadlines
subs: 30-day notice on whether a permit application is complete
30-day deadline to issue or defer the permit
10-day decision once deferred conditions are met

sections.label: Section 2(a) - Annual Leasing and Parcel Offerings

items.main: Changes the required interval between federal geothermal lease sales from every 2 years to every year and requires replacement sales for any canceled or delayed sale.
items.detail: Amends Section 4(b) of the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970. If a lease sale for a year is canceled or delayed, the Secretary of the Interior must conduct a replacement sale during the same year.

items.main: Requires the Secretary to offer for lease 75 percent of nominated parcels eligible for geothermal development, plus the remaining 25 percent unless a written justification is provided.
items.detail: Eligibility is based on the parcels identified under the resource management plan in effect for the State. The remaining 25 percent may be withheld only if the Secretary provides a written justification identifying a statutory, environmental, or administrative basis that prevents offering them.

items.main: Adds deadlines for the Secretary to act on geothermal drilling permit applications.
items.detail: Within 30 days of receiving an application, the Secretary must notify the applicant whether it is complete. Within 30 days of a completeness notice, the Secretary must issue the permit if National Environmental Policy Act and other requirements are met, or defer with a list of steps and agency actions whose timelines may not exceed the deadlines in Section 107(g) of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969. A deferred decision must issue within 10 days after the conditions are met.

underreported.section: Section 2(a) - Parcel Offering Requirement (25 percent exception)
underreported.summary: Allows the Secretary to withhold the remaining 25 percent of nominated parcels by providing a written justification identifying a statutory, environmental, or administrative basis.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title emphasizes committing leases, but this exception lets the Secretary withhold a quarter of nominated parcels on an administrative basis, which the bill does not define.

gaps: The bill requires offering 75 percent of nominated parcels but does not define how parcels are nominated or who nominates them.
The bill compresses permit decision deadlines around National Environmental Policy Act review but does not change the underlying environmental review timelines it references.
The bill requires annual and replacement lease sales but specifies no consequence if the Secretary fails to hold a required sale.
The bill permits withholding parcels for a 'statutory, environmental, or administrative basis' but does not define an administrative basis.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Westerman
featured_quotes.text: Most of America's geothermal resources lie beneath Federal lands, and interest in leasing those areas continues to grow. It is imperative that we increase the frequency of geothermal lease sales from every 2 years to annually and further streamline the permitting process. Doing so will help keep energy costs low and keep America's lights on.

added: A requirement to hold a replacement geothermal lease sale within the same year for any canceled or delayed sale
Mandatory parcel-offering levels of 75 percent, plus the remaining 25 percent absent written justification
Deadlines for acting on geothermal drilling permit applications (30-day completeness notice, 30-day issue-or-defer, 10-day decision after conditions are met)
modified: The interval between federal geothermal lease sales changed from every 2 years to every year (Section 4(b) of the Geothermal Steam Act of 1970)

bills.title: Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Federal Reserve Act to prohibit the Federal reserve banks from offering certain products or services directly to an individual, to prohibit the use of central bank digital currency for monetary policy, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House and the bill drew 135 cosponsors and passed the House. Because the prohibition on Federal Reserve digital-currency work is generally opposed by members who favor preserving Fed flexibility, and Senate passage would require 60 votes, its path in the Senate is uncertain.
bills.summary: This bill amends the Federal Reserve Act to bar the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency (CBDC) or offering banking products and accounts directly to individuals. It also bars the Board of Governors from testing, developing, or using a CBDC and preserves privately issued, cash-like digital dollars.
bills.brief: Prohibits the Federal Reserve from creating or issuing a central bank digital currency or providing retail banking directly to individuals.

top_lines.headline: Federal Reserve Retail Banking Ban
subs: Bars Federal Reserve banks from offering products or services directly to individuals
Bars maintaining accounts on behalf of individuals

top_lines.headline: Central Bank Digital Currency Ban
subs: Bars the Fed from issuing a CBDC directly or indirectly through intermediaries
Bars the Board from testing, studying, developing, or implementing a CBDC
Bars using a CBDC to implement monetary policy

top_lines.headline: Privacy Exception and Sense of Congress
subs: Preserves open, permissionless, private dollar currency with cash-like privacy
States the Fed lacks CBDC authority unless Congress grants it

items.main: Bars Federal Reserve banks from offering financial products or services directly to individuals, maintaining individual accounts, or issuing a CBDC.
items.detail: Section 2 adds paragraph (18) to Section 16 of the Federal Reserve Act barring direct retail financial services, individual accounts, and issuance of a CBDC or substantially similar digital asset. Section 3 adds paragraph (19) barring a Federal reserve bank from offering a CBDC indirectly to an individual through a financial institution or other intermediary.

sections.label: Section 4 - Central Bank Digital Currency Prohibition
