items.main: Bars the Board of Governors from testing, studying, developing, creating, or implementing a CBDC, and bars the Board and the Federal Open Market Committee from using one for monetary policy.
items.detail: Adds paragraph (11) to Section 10 of the Federal Reserve Act. An exception preserves any dollar-denominated currency that is open, permissionless, and private and fully preserves the privacy protections of physical U.S. currency. A CBDC is defined as digital money denominated in the national unit of account, a direct liability of the Federal Reserve System, and widely available to the general public.

items.main: States the sense of Congress that the Board of Governors does not currently have authority to issue a CBDC.
items.detail: It further states the Board will not have such authority unless Congress grants it under its Article I, Section 8 powers. A sense of Congress carries no binding legal effect.

underreported.section: Section 2 - Prohibition on Direct Retail Services and Accounts
underreported.summary: Bars Federal Reserve banks from offering any financial products or services directly to individuals and from maintaining individual accounts, beyond the digital-currency prohibitions.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill's title concerns a central bank digital currency, but this provision more broadly bars the Fed from all direct retail banking with individuals.

underreported.summary: Preserves any dollar-denominated currency that is open, permissionless, and private and preserves cash-like privacy protections.
underreported.why_unreported: This carve-out leaves room for privately issued digital dollars, an effect not apparent from a bill described as banning digital currency.

gaps: The bill bars a CBDC or any 'substantially similar' digital asset but does not define what makes an asset substantially similar, which sets the ban's scope.
The bill's exception preserves 'open, permissionless, and private' dollar currency but does not identify who determines whether a currency meets those criteria.
The bill bars the Board from studying a CBDC but does not address the disposition of any digital-currency research already underway.
The Sense of Congress asserts the Fed lacks CBDC authority but has no binding legal effect on that question.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Steil
featured_quotes.text: He was actually one of the first in Congress to raise the alarm. Since then, the case has only grown stronger about the risks posed by U.S. CBDC. Mr. Speaker, the global economy is at a crossroads when it comes to digital payments. Jurisdictions around the world are upgrading their payment systems to be faster, to be cheaper, and cross-border. The private sector is leading the way, including payment stablecoins to enhance the payment rails. As the United States grapples with modernizing our own payment systems, we are confronted with a choice.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Lynch
featured_quotes.text: At the expense of U.S. global economic leadership, this misguided legislation would prevent the Federal Reserve from issuing a central bank digital currency, also known as a CBDC. Unfortunately, the facts surrounding the development of CBDC have been obscured by disinformation, conspiracy theories, and extreme political ideology. Republicans and the crypto industry have made unfounded claims that a CBDC will be used as a surveillance tool by the Federal Government. Let's be clear about what a CBDC is.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Meuser
featured_quotes.text: This bill is about defending our Constitution and protecting the privacy of the American people. The Constitution is unambiguous in Article I, Section 8, which grants only Congress exclusive authority to coin money, regulate the value thereof, and of foreign coin. This is a clear provision of the United States Constitution. It is a foundational element of our constitutional Republic designed to keep such important authority over our Nation's currency issuance within the hands of the people's Representatives.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Rose
featured_quotes.text: Among the many rights that we enjoy as Americans, privacy is among the most fundamental. Establishing a central bank digital currency would not only usurp consumers' privacy and individual freedoms, but it would also hinder free market innovation. Digital assets are here to stay. I agree strongly with President Trump that the United States should be a leader in this space. However, the last administration held a very different view.

added: A prohibition on Federal Reserve banks offering products, services, or accounts directly to individuals (Section 16(18))
Prohibitions on issuing a CBDC directly (Section 16(18)) and indirectly through intermediaries (Section 16(19))
A prohibition on the Board testing, developing, or implementing a CBDC or using one for monetary policy (Section 10(11))
An exception for open, permissionless, private dollar currency and a definition of 'central bank digital currency'

bills.title: Law-Enforcement Innovate to De-Escalate Act
bills.official_title: To modernize Federal firearms laws to account for advancements in technology and less-than-lethal weapons, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, the bill drew 95 cosponsors, and it passed the House. The exemptions loosening firearms-tax and National Firearms Act treatment for a device class may draw opposition from members concerned about firearm-law carve-outs, and Senate passage would require 60 votes.
bills.summary: This bill creates a federal definition of 'less-than-lethal projectile device' and exempts qualifying devices from federal firearms restrictions, the National Firearms Act, and the federal firearms and ammunition excise tax. Qualifying devices are those whose projectiles do not exceed 500 feet per second and are designed not to cause death or serious injury.
bills.brief: Exempts qualifying less-than-lethal projectile devices from federal firearms restrictions, the National Firearms Act, and the firearms excise tax.

top_lines.headline: Less-Than-Lethal Device Definition
subs: Defines a 'less-than-lethal projectile device' with a 500 feet-per-second projectile cap
Attorney General must rule on classification requests within 90 days

top_lines.headline: Firearms Law Exemptions
subs: Exempts qualifying devices from Title 18 firearm restrictions
Exempts them from the National Firearms Act

top_lines.headline: Firearms Excise Tax Exemption
subs: Exempts qualifying devices from the federal firearms and ammunition excise tax
Treasury publishes and annually updates a list of qualifying devices
Annual report to the Ways and Means and Finance committees

sections.label: Title I - Firearms Law Definition and Exemption (Section 102)

items.main: Adds a definition of 'less-than-lethal projectile device' to Section 921(a) of Title 18 and treats such devices as outside the Title 18 firearm restrictions.
items.detail: A qualifying device is one not designed or readily convertible to discharge handgun, rifle, or shotgun ammunition or any projectile exceeding 500 feet per second, is intended for use unlikely to cause death or serious bodily injury, and cannot readily accept ammunition feeding devices loaded through a pistol grip or used in semiautomatic firearms. On request, the Attorney General must determine whether a device qualifies within 90 days of receiving it.

sections.label: Title II - Firearms and Ammunition Excise Tax Exemption (Section 202)

items.main: Exempts less-than-lethal projectile devices, listed devices, and their shells or cartridges from the firearms and ammunition excise tax imposed by Section 4181 of the Internal Revenue Code.
items.detail: Adds subsection (d) to Section 4182 using the same device definition. On request from a manufacturer, producer, or importer, the Secretary of the Treasury must determine eligibility within 90 days. The Secretary must publish and annually update a list of qualifying devices, and separately publish and report to the Ways and Means and Finance committees a list of non-lethal devices whose projectiles exceed 500 feet per second.

sections.label: Title II - National Firearms Act Exemption (Section 203)

items.main: Amends the National Firearms Act firearm definition to exclude less-than-lethal projectile devices.
items.detail: Section 5845(a) of the Internal Revenue Code is amended by adding less-than-lethal projectile devices (as defined in Section 4182(d)(2)) and listed devices to the items, such as antique firearms, excluded from the definition.

underreported.section: Section 202 - List of Non-Lethal Devices Exceeding 500 Feet Per Second
underreported.summary: Directs Treasury to publish and annually report to Congress a list of non-lethal devices that would qualify except that their projectiles exceed 500 feet per second.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond exempting qualifying devices, this creates an ongoing federal tracking and reporting process for higher-velocity non-lethal devices, which the bill's tax-exemption purpose does not signal.

criticisms.why: Mr. Speaker, this bill would rip a dangerous new loophole in the Gun Control Act by changing the definition of firearm throughout the entire criminal code to exclude from coverage certain less-than-lethal but still highly dangerous weapons, such as tasers, which have been identified as a contributing factor in more than 500 deaths throughout the United States of America. Mr. Speaker, this bill would exempt these weapons, which are currently classified as firearms, from all regulations under all Federal firearm laws.

Police already have access to less-than-lethal weapons like tasers. They don't need a change in the law. That is not an excuse for changing the law. This bill expands access to dangerous, prohibited individuals by stripping away Federal safeguards. Tasers may not shoot bullets, but they are still dangerous in the wrong hands. This bill would mean that anyone can buy them without a background check including people convicted of serious violent crimes and domestic abusers with restraining orders against them.

Let's get honest about what this bill does and doesn't do. It does not require training. It does not set standards. It does not improve accountability, and it does not apply only to law enforcement. It does carve out a sweeping exemption in our Federal firearms laws and makes it easier for dangerous people to access dangerous weapons with fewer safeguards. Supporters keep saying that this bill is about helping law enforcement, but if that were true, the bill would mention law enforcement. It doesn't.

gaps: The bill defines qualifying devices by a 500 feet-per-second projectile cap but does not exempt devices above that speed, only adds them to a monitoring list.
The bill sets up separate 90-day determinations by the Attorney General under Title I and the Secretary of the Treasury under Title II but does not require the two determinations to be consistent.
The bill requires an annually updated public list of qualifying devices but sets no deadline for the first list.
The bill exempts shells or cartridges designed for qualifying devices but does not address ammunition that fits both a qualifying device and a conventional firearm.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Raskin
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, this bill would rip a dangerous new loophole in the Gun Control Act by changing the definition of firearm throughout the entire criminal code to exclude from coverage certain less-than-lethal but still highly dangerous weapons, such as tasers, which have been identified as a contributing factor in more than 500 deaths throughout the United States of America. Mr. Speaker, this bill would exempt these weapons, which are currently classified as firearms, from all regulations under all Federal firearm laws.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Johnson
featured_quotes.text: Police already have access to less-than-lethal weapons like tasers. They don't need a change in the law. That is not an excuse for changing the law. This bill expands access to dangerous, prohibited individuals by stripping away Federal safeguards. Tasers may not shoot bullets, but they are still dangerous in the wrong hands. This bill would mean that anyone can buy them without a background check including people convicted of serious violent crimes and domestic abusers with restraining orders against them.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Kamlager-Dove
featured_quotes.text: Let's get honest about what this bill does and doesn't do. It does not require training. It does not set standards. It does not improve accountability, and it does not apply only to law enforcement. It does carve out a sweeping exemption in our Federal firearms laws and makes it easier for dangerous people to access dangerous weapons with fewer safeguards. Supporters keep saying that this bill is about helping law enforcement, but if that were true, the bill would mention law enforcement. It doesn't.

featured_quotes.name: Mrs. McBath
featured_quotes.text: Democrats will continue to support law enforcement innovation and the adoption of tools that keep everyone safer, but we must oppose this misguided legislation that does not promote innovation or de-escalation and will only put our law enforcement, those experiencing domestic abuse, and others in danger.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Frost
featured_quotes.text: When I first heard about this bill, I thought it was very interesting that my Republican colleagues had this newfound conviction in helping to prevent law enforcement doing bad things to people and working to de-escalate law enforcement. I am someone who has been a victim of the abuse of law enforcement, and I just haven't heard my colleagues ever talk about it. I came at this bill skeptically when I looked at it. It turns out the bill itself was pretty much written by a corporation, Axon, that wants to sell a new type of taser.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fitzgerald
featured_quotes.text: I will spend the time I have remaining responding to a few points made by my colleagues. First of all, the U.S. States and territories already criminalize the misuse of less-lethal devices through existing assault and battery laws, and 34 States also restrict possession by violent felons and domestic abusers. Let me repeat that. It is illegal for violent felons and domestic abusers to own or misuse less-lethal devices. Mr. Speaker, our bill does not change that.

added: A federal definition of 'less-than-lethal projectile device' (Title 18 Section 921(a) and Internal Revenue Code Section 4182(d))
An exemption from the firearms and ammunition excise tax under Section 4181 for qualifying devices, shells, and cartridges
Separate 90-day classification determinations by the Attorney General and the Secretary of the Treasury
An annual public list of qualifying devices and an annual list and report to Congress of non-lethal devices exceeding 500 feet per second
modified: The Title 18 Section 921(a) firearm definition amended to reference less-than-lethal projectile devices
The National Firearms Act firearm definition (Section 5845(a)) amended to exclude less-than-lethal projectile devices

bills.title: Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
bills.official_title: To amend the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 to exclude from gross income any damages, other than punitive damages, received on account of any sexual acts or sexual contact.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, and the bill carries 3 cosponsors. The exclusion for non-punitive damages received on account of sexual acts or contact has cross-ideological appeal that limits opposition, though Senate passage would require 60 votes.
bills.summary: This bill lets people exclude from their taxable income money awarded for sexual acts or sexual contact, other than punitive damages, whether or not there are medical records or visible injuries. It also makes a written statement in a court decision or settlement enough to shift the burden of proof to the IRS and directs Treasury to publicize the tax break.
bills.brief: Excludes non-punitive damages received on account of sexual acts or sexual contact from federal taxable income.

top_lines.headline: Tax Exclusion for Abuse Damages
subs: Excludes non-punitive damages for sexual acts or sexual contact from gross income
Applies whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries

top_lines.headline: Burden of Proof Shift
subs: A decision or agreement stating damages are for sexual acts counts as credible evidence
Treats the taxpayer as meeting the burden-of-proof requirements of Section 7491(a)

top_lines.headline: Public Awareness Program
subs: Treasury must run a program to publicize the exclusion
Coordinated with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women

items.main: Amends Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code to exclude from gross income damages received on account of a sexual act or sexual contact.
items.detail: The exclusion covers damages other than punitive damages and applies whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries. 'Sexual act' and 'sexual contact' are defined by reference to Section 2246 of Title 18, United States Code, as in effect on enactment.

items.main: Provides that a decision or agreement stating that damages are on account of a sexual act or sexual contact is treated as credible evidence of that fact.
items.detail: For purposes of Section 7491(a), such a statement is treated as credible evidence and the taxpayer is treated as having met the requirements of Section 7491(a)(2) on whether the damages are on account of the act or contact.

sections.label: Section 2(d)-(e) - No Inference and Public Awareness

items.main: Bars drawing inferences about the physical-injury exclusion and directs Treasury to promote public awareness of the new exclusion.
items.detail: No inference may be drawn from the amendment about whether 'personal physical injuries or physical sickness' includes injuries without medical records or observable injuries. The Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women, must conduct a program to promote public awareness of the exclusion.

underreported.summary: Treats a decision or agreement's statement that damages are on account of a sexual act or contact as credible evidence and deems the taxpayer to have met the Section 7491(a)(2) burden-of-proof requirements.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond creating a tax exclusion, this changes the evidentiary burden in tax disputes over whether damages qualify, an effect not signaled by the exclusion itself.

gaps: The bill applies the exclusion only to decisions made and agreements entered after enactment and does not address claims or agreements predating enactment.
The bill treats a decision or agreement's characterization as credible evidence but does not address damages where the decision or agreement does not state their basis.
The bill directs Treasury to run a public-awareness program but sets no timeline or funding for it.
The bill excludes non-punitive damages for sexual acts or contact but does not specify how awards covering both sexual and non-sexual claims are allocated.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smith
featured_quotes.text: Survivors of sexual assault face a long road to recovery without having to battle with the IRS over keeping the compensatory damages or settlements that they receive. Unfortunately, right now, the burden of proof that a sexual assault survivor would have to provide to the IRS, including medical records to prove that they deserve to have their settlement funds excluded from gross income for tax purposes, ignores the fact that such victims often do not have the same observable physical injuries that other victims of assault might have.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Smucker
featured_quotes.text: I think the chairman and Ms. Moore both have described it really well. The core problem here, first of all, we believe our current law already says that any victim of physical abuse and any victim of sexual abuse who receives a settlement does not owe tax on that settlement, which makes complete sense.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Moore
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, we hear all the time about the high-profile civil cases involving sexual abuse. I am thinking about the accounts of trusted gymnast physicians abusing star athletes and the victims of Jeffrey Epstein and many of his associates. We even hear about sexual assault that occurs within our own body, and we have to address that problem. Let's just take a moment to acknowledge that all sexual abuse does not make the headlines.

added: An income-tax exclusion for non-punitive damages received on account of a sexual act or sexual contact
A burden-of-proof rule treating a decision or agreement's characterization as credible evidence under Section 7491(a)
A Treasury public-awareness program conducted with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women
modified: Section 104(a)(2) of the Internal Revenue Code amended to exclude damages for sexual acts or contact, whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries

bills.title: Ukraine Support Act
bills.official_title: To authorize support for Ukraine, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Democrat in the Republican-majority House and the bill carries 43 cosponsors. Its expanded Russia sanctions, 500 percent tariffs, and additional Ukraine funding face uncertain support in the Senate, where 60 votes would be required, and the broad presidential waiver and termination authority over the sanctions may further shape its path.
bills.summary: This bill expands U.S. support for Ukraine through diplomacy, military assistance, and a broad sanctions regime against Russia. It extends Lend-Lease and loan authority, creates a Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund, and requires the President to impose sanctions, 500 percent tariffs, and a 100 percent tax on blocked Russian and Belarusian sovereign-asset income once Russia is found to be waging war or refusing peace.
bills.brief: Expands U.S. security assistance for Ukraine and requires mandatory sanctions, tariffs, and asset taxes against Russia upon a presidential determination.

top_lines.headline: Security Assistance for Ukraine
subs: Extends Ukraine Lend-Lease authority through fiscal year 2028
Raises the Ukraine and NATO direct-loan ceiling to $8B
Adds $300M for the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative in 2026 and 2027

top_lines.headline: Sanctions and Tariffs on Russia
subs: President must decide every 90 days whether Russia is waging war or refusing peace
Triggers mandatory sanctions on 13 named Russian banks and oil, gas, and mining firms
Raises duties on all Russian imports to at least 500 percent

top_lines.headline: Reconstruction and Diplomacy
subs: Creates a Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund in the Treasury
100 percent tax on blocked Russian and Belarusian sovereign-asset income
Authorizes $250M for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty for 2026

sections.label: Title I - Diplomacy and Support for Ukraine

items.main: Establishes a Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund in the Treasury for rebuilding, humanitarian aid, economic growth, and governance in Ukraine.
items.detail: Added as Section 9512 of the Internal Revenue Code, the fund receives revenues from the tax imposed under new section 892A and is available to the Secretary of State subject to Foreign Assistance Act requirements. The bill also creates an Insurance for Ukraine Initiative in the State Department and codifies a Special Coordinator for Ukrainian Reconstruction.

items.main: Authorizes $250M for Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty for fiscal year 2026 and $30M for each of fiscal years 2025 through 2029 for U.S.-European nuclear energy cooperation.
items.detail: It directs a strategy to counter Russian influence in Europe's nuclear energy sector and extends federal war-risk insurance eligibility for vessels trading with Ukraine for 5 years. It also directs use of the Countering Russian Influence Fund to help Ukraine combat disinformation.

items.main: Extends Ukraine Lend-Lease authority through fiscal year 2028 and raises the direct-loan ceiling for Ukraine and NATO allies to $8B.
items.detail: Amends the Ukraine Democracy Defense Lend-Lease Act of 2022 from fiscal years 2022 and 2023 to fiscal years 2022 through 2028. Through fiscal year 2026, direct loans under Section 23 of the Arms Export Control Act may be made available with gross obligations not to exceed $8B, raised from $4B, and adds recovery-and-return reporting.

items.main: Extends the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative with $300M for fiscal year 2026 and $300M for fiscal year 2027, and authorizes support for Baltic countries.
items.detail: Amends Section 1250 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2016, extending its authority from December 31, 2026 to December 31, 2027. It authorizes $30M in Foreign Military Financing grants and $4M in nonproliferation and anti-terrorism programs per Baltic country for each of fiscal years 2026 through 2028.

sections.label: Title III - Sanctions and Export Controls

items.main: Requires the President to determine within 15 days, and at least every 90 days, whether Russia is waging a war of aggression or refusing to negotiate or honor a peace agreement, triggering mandatory sanctions.
items.detail: Upon an affirmative determination, the President must within 15 days sanction 3 or more of 13 named financial institutions, including the Central Bank of the Russian Federation, and all Russian oil, gas, coal, and mineral companies, and specified Russian officials.

items.main: Raises duties on all Russian imports to at least 500 percent, bans energy products refined from Russian crude, and imposes a 100 percent tax on blocked Russian and Belarusian sovereign-asset income.
items.detail: The 500 percent ad valorem duty and import ban apply after an affirmative determination. The 100 percent tax falls on interest and dividends from Russian and Belarusian assets blocked under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act and applies without regard to any U.S. treaty obligation.

items.main: Sets a congressional review process for lifting Russia sanctions and a termination-and-reimposition mechanism.
items.detail: The President may terminate sanctions, duties, and export controls on certifying that Russia has ceased its war or peace-agreement violations, and must immediately reimpose them if Russia restarts. The President may also waive individual sanctions on determining a waiver is vital to national security, with 15 days' notice to Congress.

underreported.summary: Applies the 100 percent tax on blocked Russian and Belarusian sovereign-asset income without regard to any U.S. treaty obligation.
underreported.why_unreported: This overrides existing U.S. tax-treaty obligations, an effect beyond the sanctions and support purposes stated in the bill's titles.

underreported.summary: Lets the President waive any Title III sanction on determining the waiver is vital to national security, with 15 days' notice to Congress.
underreported.why_unreported: The sanctions are described as mandatory upon a determination, but this provision preserves broad presidential discretion to waive them case by case.

underreported.summary: Deems NATO-, Ukraine-, or designated-country-owned vessels trading with Ukraine eligible for federal war-risk insurance for 5 years.
underreported.why_unreported: This extends federal war-risk insurance exposure to foreign-owned commercial vessels, a financial commitment not apparent from the bill's support framing.

gaps: The bill establishes a Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund funded by a tax on blocked sovereign-asset income but does not estimate how much revenue that tax will raise.
The bill authorizes appropriations for Radio Free Europe, nuclear cooperation, and Baltic support but does not itself appropriate those funds.

The bill makes sanctions mandatory upon a determination but lets the President waive any of them for national security and terminate them all on a certification, without specifying limits on that discretion.
The bill raises duties on Russian imports to at least 500 percent but, apart from the oil-refinery ban, does not address transshipment of Russian goods through third countries.
The bill raises the direct-loan ceiling for Ukraine and NATO allies to $8B but does not set repayment or recovery terms beyond those in existing law.

added: A Ukraine Reconstruction Trust Fund in the Treasury (Internal Revenue Code Section 9512)
An Insurance for Ukraine Initiative and a Special Coordinator for Ukrainian Reconstruction in the State Department
A sanctions-trigger regime requiring mandatory sanctions on Russian banks, energy and mining firms, and officials upon a presidential determination
A 500 percent duty on Russian imports, a ban on energy products refined from Russian crude, and a 100 percent tax on blocked Russian and Belarusian sovereign-asset income
modified: Ukraine Lend-Lease authority extended from fiscal years 2022 and 2023 to fiscal years 2022 through 2028
The Ukraine and NATO direct-loan ceiling raised from $4B to $8B
The Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative extended with $300M for fiscal years 2026 and 2027 and authority through December 31, 2027 (from December 31, 2026)

bills.title: Main Street Capital Access Act
bills.official_title: To make improvements to the Federal banking laws, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House, the bill carries 33 cosponsors, and it passed the House. The exemption of most sub-$10B bank mergers from antitrust review and the limits on guidance enforcement are likely to draw Democratic opposition in the Senate, where 60 votes would be required.
bills.summary: This bill rewrites a broad range of federal banking laws to ease regulation of smaller banks, speed up new-bank formation, and limit how agencies use supervisory guidance. It raises several size thresholds, exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review, and orders studies of bank-fintech partnerships.
bills.brief: Eases federal banking regulation for smaller institutions and exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review.

top_lines.headline: Community Bank Regulatory Relief
subs: Raises the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B
Tailors capital and reporting rules for banks under $6B in assets
Indexes enhanced-regulation thresholds every 5 years

top_lines.headline: Bank Merger and Competition Changes
subs: Exempts most bank mergers under $10B from antitrust review
Adds merger-approval clarity and process reviews

top_lines.headline: Supervision and Guidance Limits
subs: Requires agencies to state their guidance is not legally binding
Shortens the regulatory-review cycle from 10 to 8 years
Cuts the new-bank de novo review period from 180 to 90 days

sections.label: Titles I-II - New Bank Formation and Regulatory Tailoring

items.main: Speeds new-bank formation and directs banking regulators to tailor rules to institutions' size and risk, raising the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B.
items.detail: Cuts a new-bank de novo review period from 180 to 90 days and makes related pilot authorities permanent unless regulators find adverse safety effects in a 2031 review window. Regulators must publish annual charter-application data, and the Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement asset threshold is raised to $6B. A new Section 177 of the Financial Stability Act indexes enhanced-regulation thresholds every 5 years.

items.main: Extends and adjusts the Community Development Financial Institutions bond-guarantee program.
items.detail: Sets the minimum guarantee at $25M with a $1B annual cap, changes the fee to between 10 and 15 basis points, and extends the program's authority to December 31, 2028. It also requires annual Treasury testimony on the Community Development Financial Institutions Fund.

sections.label: Titles III-IV - Bank Supervision and Guidance Accountability

items.main: Limits how financial agencies use supervisory guidance and adds supervision-process and accountability requirements.
items.detail: Requires nine financial agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Department of Housing and Urban Development, to prominently state on any guidance that it does not have the force of law and does not bind regulated parties. It also adds fair-audit and appeals provisions for examinations and Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation board accountability requirements, and shortens a regulatory review cycle from every 10 years to every 8 years.

sections.label: Titles V-VI - Local Bank Funding and Merger Clarity

items.main: Modernizes Federal Reserve discount-window access, promotes keeping deposits local, and eases bank merger review.
items.detail: For merger transactions resulting in an institution with less than $10B in assets that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area, the responsible agency may not consider whether the merger would create a monopoly or lessen competition. It also adds merger-approval timelines and a study of merger review procedures.

sections.label: Titles VII-VIII - Bank Resolution and Innovation

items.main: Changes bank-failure resolution rules and eases limits on merchant banking and bank-fintech partnerships.
items.detail: Sets the general holding period for merchant banking investments at no less than 15 years and orders studies of bank-fintech and credit-union-fintech partnerships. It also reduces the Federal Reserve's discretionary surplus fund by $425M effective September 1, 2036.

underreported.summary: Bars the responsible agency from considering monopoly or competition effects for bank and holding-company mergers resulting in institutions under $10B that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area.
underreported.why_unreported: The title is captioned as promoting competition and merger clarity, but this provision removes antitrust review for a class of mergers.

underreported.summary: Requires nine financial agencies to state on all guidance that it is not legally binding and that noncompliance does not establish a violation.
underreported.why_unreported: This reaches beyond banks to agencies such as the Securities and Exchange Commission and Housing and Urban Development, limiting how each enforces expectations set through guidance.

underreported.summary: Reduces the Federal Reserve's discretionary surplus fund amount by $425M, effective September 1, 2036.
underreported.why_unreported: This distant-dated reduction to the Federal Reserve surplus is a budget offset unrelated to the bill's stated banking-access purpose.

gaps: The bill aims to promote new bank formation but sets no target or deadline for reducing charter-application processing times, only requiring the agencies to report them.
The bill exempts most sub-$10B mergers from antitrust review but does not address the cumulative effect of successive exempt mergers on local competition.
The bill raises the Small Bank Holding Company threshold to $6B but, unlike the enhanced-regulation thresholds it indexes, does not index that threshold for future growth.
The bill orders studies of bank-fintech and credit-union-fintech partnerships but makes no change to the rules governing those partnerships.
The bill reduces the Federal Reserve discretionary surplus fund by $425M in 2036 but does not state how the resulting funds are used.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Loudermilk
featured_quotes.text: I obviously rise in support of H.R. 6955 not only because it is a good bill, but also because I recognize the need to rightsize Federal regulations and gain more transparency into the financial regulatory process. For too long, Federal financial regulators have taken this one-size- fits-all approach. If we applied that same status to ourselves, then let's just issue every Member of Congress one suit of clothes so that we all wear the same suit of clothes.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Velazquez
featured_quotes.text: Community banks and credit unions are the foundations of our financial system. As ranking member of the House Small Business Committee, I understand better than most the role they play in our communities, offering small business loans, farm loans, and mortgages. They are critical lifelines to our rural and underserved communities that have been left behind by our biggest banks.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Huizenga
featured_quotes.text: As a small business owner, I have seen it. I have lived it. When community banks disappear, families and small businesses lose the local lenders who know their communities and their customers best. Less competition means fewer financing options, higher borrowing costs, and less investment on Main Street, not Wall Street, as some of my colleagues are trying to assert. This bill lowers unnecessary regulatory costs for community and midsize banks, not those big business center banks on Wall Street and in New York and around the world.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Garcia
featured_quotes.text: I rise against H.R. 6955. Instead of the Main Street Act, this bill, Mr. Speaker, should be called the Wall Street wins Main Street loses act. It does not help end the affordability crisis, feed hardworking Americans, or keep a roof over their heads. Instead, this bill sneaks in deregulatory measures, further weakens the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and weakens community reinvestment and anti- discrimination safeguards. For this reason, at the appropriate time, I will offer a motion to recommit this bill back to committee.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moylan
featured_quotes.text: When the people of Guam set out to enterprise new business ventures, we turn to our community banks to raise capital. However, much of America's financial system is not designed with small businesses in mind. While big banks have the resources to cut through red tape, small community ventures often struggle to comply with a regulatory regime that never had them in mind.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Knott
featured_quotes.text: For the vast majority of our Nation's history, community banks were the primary artery into progress for all Americans. That reality is being threatened today by sloppy and ineffective policies that originate right here in Washington, D.C. Whether it is the Dodd-Frank regulatory structure or the millions of rules and regulations that are in existence today, community banks have been choked out by these all-encompassing regulations. With administrative costs rising every year, local banks simply cannot afford to operate.

added: A requirement that nine financial agencies mark their guidance as non-binding (Section 402)
Annual charter- and deposit-insurance-application transparency reports by the banking regulators (Section 102)
Periodic indexing of enhanced-regulation thresholds (Section 177 of the Financial Stability Act)
A minimum 15-year merchant banking investment holding period and bank-fintech partnership studies (Sections 801-802)
modified: The Small Bank Holding Company Policy Statement asset threshold raised to $6B (Section 202)
The new-bank de novo review period cut from 180 days to 90 days (Section 101)
The Community Development Financial Institutions bond-guarantee minimum set at $25M with a $1B annual cap and authority extended to December 31, 2028 (Section 104)
The Federal Reserve discretionary surplus fund reduced by $425M effective September 1, 2036 (Section 803)
removed: Antitrust and competition review for bank and holding-company mergers resulting in institutions under $10B that would not leave only one bank in a metropolitan area (Section 601)

bills.title: National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs Appropriations Act, 2027
bills.official_title: Making appropriations for national security, Department of State, and related programs for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
bills.likelihoodReason: The sponsor is a Republican in the Republican-majority House and the bill passed the House with no cosponsors, as is typical for an appropriations measure. Standalone appropriations bills are generally reconciled with a Senate version or folded into a broader package before enactment, and Senate passage would require 60 votes.
bills.summary: This bill provides fiscal year 2027 funding for the Department of State, foreign assistance, and related international programs. It sets specific amounts for diplomacy, global health, humanitarian aid, and security assistance, and attaches policy conditions to many of those funds.
bills.brief: Funds the Department of State and U.S. foreign operations for fiscal year 2027.

top_lines.headline: Diplomacy and State Operations
subs: $9.76B for Diplomatic Programs
Funds embassy operations, worldwide security, and consular activities

top_lines.headline: Global Health and Humanitarian Aid
subs: $3.35B for global health and $5.53B for HIV/AIDS programs
$1.25B contribution to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria
$5B for international humanitarian and refugee assistance

top_lines.headline: Security and Economic Assistance
subs: $6.75B for Foreign Military Financing grants
$6.89B for National Security Investment Programs
$1.66B for international narcotics control and law enforcement

sections.label: Title I - Department of State Operations

items.main: Provides $9.76B for Diplomatic Programs, the Department of State's main operating account.
items.detail: Of that amount, up to $4.16B remains available until expended for overseas operations and $738.6M is for Worldwide Security Protection. The title also funds embassy security and construction, the Harry S Truman Building, and educational and cultural exchange programs.

items.main: Provides $3.35B for global health programs and an additional $5.53B for HIV/AIDS, including a $1.25B U.S. contribution to the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
items.detail: The global health funds carry conditions barring money to organizations that support coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization and restricting family-planning assistance. The title also provides $5B for international humanitarian assistance, of which not less than $2.75B is for disaster relief.

items.main: Provides $6.89B for National Security Investment Programs and funds several development agencies.
items.detail: At least 15 percent of the National Security Investment Programs funds must go to programs in Africa. The title also provides $830M for the Millennium Challenge Corporation, $410.5M for the Peace Corps, and $205.2M for the Democracy Fund.

items.main: Provides $6.75B for the Foreign Military Financing program of nonrepayable grants for defense articles and services.
items.detail: NATO members and major non-NATO allies may use the funds for procurement not sold through the U.S. government. The title also provides $1.66B for international narcotics control and law enforcement, $870M for nonproliferation, anti-terrorism, and demining, and $119.2M for international military education and training.

sections.label: Titles V-VII - Multilateral Assistance and General Provisions

items.main: Funds multilateral assistance and export programs and sets government-wide policy conditions and rescissions.
items.detail: Title V funds international financial institutions and Title VI funds export and investment assistance. Title VII carries the bill's general provisions, including reporting and notification requirements, policy restrictions, and rescissions of portions of prior-year unobligated balances.

underreported.section: Title III - Global Health Programs (family-planning provisos)
underreported.summary: Bars global health funds to any organization the President determines supports or manages coercive abortion or involuntary sterilization, and sets detailed conditions on voluntary family-planning projects.
underreported.why_unreported: These are substantive abortion-related policy conditions attached to a health appropriations line, beyond the funding amounts themselves.

underreported.section: Title III - International Humanitarian Assistance (Israel earmark)
underreported.summary: Earmarks not less than $6.5M of the $5B humanitarian account for refugees resettling in Israel.
underreported.why_unreported: A specific country earmark sits within a general humanitarian and refugee account.

underreported.summary: Rescinds portions of prior-year unobligated balances alongside the new appropriations.
underreported.why_unreported: The bill claws back previously appropriated funds in addition to setting fiscal year 2027 amounts, offsetting part of the new spending.

criticisms.why: Mr. Chair, the State Department funding bill that we are considering here fails to meet this critical, historic moment. Our Nation is at a dangerous crossroads. We are at war, a war that Congress never voted to authorize, a war so recklessly managed that our allies increasingly see us as a threat rather than a reliable partner. Yet, amid this global chaos, Republicans have abandoned investments to make the world a safer, healthier place. Their callous neglect has caused hundreds of thousands of needless deaths along the way.

Last year, the Trump administration illegally dismantled USAID and fired over 1,300 State Department employees. It rescinded $13 billion for critical humanitarian and development programs, and now House Republicans want to approve legislation that amounts to a 20 percent cut from 2025 enacted levels, locking in those dangerous Trump cuts. It isn't penny-wise, and it certainly is pound-foolish. Case in point: When the administration cut funding for global health, it ended key disease outbreak surveillance and prevention programs.

gaps: The bill provides $6.75B in Foreign Military Financing grants but does not set country allocations in the text, leaving them to notification procedures.
The bill provides $5B for international humanitarian assistance but earmarks only disaster relief and Israel refugees, leaving allocation of the balance unspecified in the text.
The bill funds a National Security Investment Programs account but does not define that program beyond the Foreign Assistance Act authorities it cites.
The bill rescinds portions of prior-year balances but does not identify in the summary which programs those balances were originally appropriated for.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Wasserman Schultz
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Chair, the State Department funding bill that we are considering here fails to meet this critical, historic moment. Our Nation is at a dangerous crossroads. We are at war, a war that Congress never voted to authorize, a war so recklessly managed that our allies increasingly see us as a threat rather than a reliable partner. Yet, amid this global chaos, Republicans have abandoned investments to make the world a safer, healthier place. Their callous neglect has caused hundreds of thousands of needless deaths along the way.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Meeks
featured_quotes.text: Last year, the Trump administration illegally dismantled USAID and fired over 1,300 State Department employees. It rescinded $13 billion for critical humanitarian and development programs, and now House Republicans want to approve legislation that amounts to a 20 percent cut from 2025 enacted levels, locking in those dangerous Trump cuts. It isn't penny-wise, and it certainly is pound-foolish. Case in point: When the administration cut funding for global health, it ended key disease outbreak surveillance and prevention programs.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Diaz-Balart
featured_quotes.text: I am pleased to present the fiscal year 2027 National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs appropriations bill to the House for consideration and for approval. Now, let me start by noting the untimely, sad passing of our friend and colleague, Senator Lindsey Graham. As chairman of the State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Subcommittee in the Senate, he was my counterpart. We worked together closely on our top priority, the national security of the United States.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Hageman
featured_quotes.text: I commend Chairman Diaz-Balart for his bold leadership to reform U.S. foreign aid over the last several funding cycles. Today, we have a bill before us with additional important reforms. This bill puts forward a second consecutive year of spending cuts, counters the global climate lunacy agenda, and holds rogue U.N. agencies accountable. Specifically, this bill delivers real solutions on issues I have prioritized over the last several years.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Amo
featured_quotes.text: This disastrous bill doesn't just turn America's back on the world. It makes Americans less safe and more vulnerable to disease. An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda has taken more than 700 lives and infected more than 1,900 people. American citizens have already been infected, and the outbreak will spread if we fail to contain it. Republicans' solution? Ban the United States from supporting the World Health Organization, the group coordinating the response to the Ebola outbreak.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Green
featured_quotes.text: I respectfully request that funding for Israel's military be considered through a standalone bill, allowing Members to vote separately on question. I first made this request in December 2025, when I opposed legislation linking funding for our military with funding for Israel's military. My position has not changed. Today, I again respectfully request that funding for the Department of State and related programs not be linked to funding for Israel's military.

removed: Rescinds portions of prior-year unobligated balances (Title VII)

bills.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act
bills.official_title: To provide for reconciliation pursuant to title II of H. Con. Res. 14.
bills.likelihoodReason: This bill was enacted as Public Law 119-21. It moved through the budget reconciliation process referenced in its title, which allowed Senate passage by a simple majority rather than the usual 60 votes.
bills.summary: This is a 2025 budget reconciliation law that makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, adds new temporary deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors, and restricts Medicaid and SNAP. It also appropriates tens of billions for border enforcement and defense, expands energy leasing, and raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion.
bills.brief: A budget reconciliation law that makes the 2017 tax cuts permanent, restricts Medicaid and SNAP, funds border enforcement, and raises the debt limit by $5 trillion.

top_lines.headline: Permanent Individual Tax Changes
subs: Makes the 2017 individual tax rates and standard deduction permanent
Raises the child tax credit to $2,200 per child
Raises the state and local tax (SALT) deduction cap to $40,000 through 2029

top_lines.headline: New Temporary Deductions
subs: No tax on up to $25,000 of tips through 2028
No tax on up to $12,500 of overtime ($25,000 joint) through 2028
New $6,000 senior deduction and a car-loan interest deduction, both through 2028

top_lines.headline: Medicaid and SNAP Restrictions
subs: Requires states to impose Medicaid community-engagement (work) requirements
Expands SNAP work requirements and shifts benefit costs to states
Restricts Medicaid and SNAP eligibility for certain noncitizens

top_lines.headline: Border and Immigration Enforcement
subs: $46.55B for border wall and infrastructure
$45B for immigration detention capacity
New immigration application, asylum, and parole fees

top_lines.headline: Energy, Defense, and Debt Limit
subs: Expands onshore, offshore, Alaska, and coal leasing and repeals clean-energy provisions
Adds Department of Defense resources for shipbuilding, munitions, and missile defense
Raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion

sections.label: Title I - Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry

items.main: Expands SNAP work requirements for able-bodied adults and requires states to pay a share of benefit costs based on their payment error rate.
items.detail: States with a payment error rate under 6 percent keep a 100 percent federal share, while higher error rates lower the federal share to as little as 85 percent, raising the state share to 15 percent. The title also restricts SNAP eligibility for certain noncitizens and updates commodity reference prices, crop insurance, and dairy and sugar programs.

items.main: Provides additional Department of Defense resources across shipbuilding, munitions, nuclear forces, air and missile defense, and border support.
items.detail: Separate sections fund enhancements to the defense industrial base, low-cost weapons, air superiority, nuclear forces, and Department of Defense border support and counter-narcotics activities, along with authorized military construction projects.

sections.label: Titles III-IV - Banking, Housing, Commerce, and Transportation

items.main: Caps Consumer Financial Protection Bureau funding, rescinds certain program funds, and funds transportation and space programs.
items.detail: Title III caps the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's funding and rescinds green retrofit program funds. Title IV funds Coast Guard readiness, air traffic control improvements, spectrum auctions, and Mars and Artemis missions, and rescinds certain other amounts.

sections.label: Titles V-VI - Energy, Natural Resources, and Environment

items.main: Expands federal oil, gas, and coal leasing and repeals or rescinds clean-energy and environmental provisions.
items.detail: The energy title reinstates and expands onshore, offshore, Alaska, and National Petroleum Reserve leasing, restarts coal leasing, addresses the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and creates an Energy Dominance Financing program. It also repeals and rescinds a range of prior clean-energy and environmental appropriations.

sections.label: Title VII - Finance (Tax, Health, and Debt Limit)

items.main: Makes the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent, adds temporary deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors, and raises the SALT cap to $40,000.
items.detail: The permanent changes include the reduced rates, increased standard deduction, and a $2,200 child tax credit. The tips ($25,000 cap), overtime ($12,500, or $25,000 joint), car-loan interest ($10,000 cap), and senior ($6,000) deductions all end after December 31, 2028, and the SALT cap reverts to $10,000 after 2029.

items.main: Restricts Medicaid and Affordable Care Act (ACA) subsidies and raises the federal debt limit by $5 trillion.
items.detail: The health subtitle requires states to establish Medicaid community-engagement requirements, limits provider taxes and state directed payments, restricts eligibility for certain noncitizens, tightens ACA premium tax credit eligibility, and creates a Rural Health Transformation Program. A separate subtitle increases the public debt limit by $5 trillion.

sections.label: Title VIII - Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (Student Aid)

items.main: Overhauls federal student loan limits, repayment, and Pell Grants and adds accountability based on earnings outcomes.
items.detail: The title changes student loan borrowing limits and repayment terms, modifies Pell Grant rules, and makes programs ineligible for aid based on low earning outcomes of graduates.

sections.label: Titles IX-X - Border Enforcement, Immigration, and Judiciary

items.main: Appropriates $46.55B for the border wall and infrastructure and $45B for immigration detention, and creates new immigration fees.
items.detail: It also funds additional U.S. Customs and Border Protection personnel and technology and appropriates funds for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Department of Homeland Security, and the Department of Justice. New fees apply to asylum, parole, employment authorization, and other immigration applications, and a separate subtitle extends and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program.

underreported.summary: The new deductions for tips, overtime, car-loan interest, and seniors all terminate after December 31, 2028, while the reduced rates and standard deduction are made permanent.
underreported.why_unreported: The most-publicized new deductions are temporary through 2028, a distinction not apparent from the headline tax-relief framing.

underreported.section: Title X, Subtitle A - Immigration Fees
underreported.summary: Creates a broad set of new fees on immigration applications, including asylum, parole, employment authorization, temporary protected status, and visa integrity fees.
underreported.why_unreported: Beyond enforcement spending, the law imposes a wide new fee regime across immigration applications.

underreported.section: Title X, Subtitle C - Radiation Exposure Compensation
underreported.summary: Extends and expands the Radiation Exposure Compensation program to cover atmospheric testing, uranium mining, and Manhattan Project waste claims.
underreported.why_unreported: A radiation-victim compensation program is carried within the judiciary title of a budget reconciliation law.

gaps: The law makes the 2017 rate cuts permanent but lets its new tips, overtime, car-loan, and senior deductions expire after 2028 without specifying what follows.
The law raises the SALT cap to $40,000 for 2025, then reverts it to $10,000 after 2029, leaving the later cliff unaddressed.
The law requires states to establish Medicaid community-engagement requirements but leaves the timing, exemptions, and verification largely to the states and the Secretary.
The law appropriates $46.55B for border infrastructure and $45B for detention but does not tie those amounts to staffing or capacity targets in its own terms.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Foxx
featured_quotes.text: The question before the House is: Should the House now consider House Resolution 566? Though the resolution waives all points of order against consideration of the motion to concur in the Senate amendment to H.R. 1, the Committee on Rules is not aware of any violation of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act, nor has the Congressional Budget Office identified any violation of the act. The reason for this motion is plain and obvious.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. McGovern
featured_quotes.text: We have a letter from the Congressional Budget Office confirming that there are unfunded mandates in this bill.

featured_quotes.name: Ms. Brown
featured_quotes.text: For the first time in history, this bill would force States to pay for part of SNAP benefits, and it would require States to increase their share of administrative costs. This is an unfunded mandate, plain and simple. Let's be clear. The costs are staggering, the consequences are devastating, and the cruelty is deeply disturbing. This policy punishes those who can least afford it: seniors on a fixed income, veterans, and families already forced to choose between gas and groceries. States will be stuck in a corner.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Langworthy
featured_quotes.text: The stakes for the American people could not be higher. We are rapidly approaching a fiscal cliff. If we do nothing, the Trump tax cuts, the most progrowth tax reforms in generations, will expire. That means higher taxes on nearly every American. That means a gutted child tax credit. That means small businesses will lose the tools they need to survive and to thrive. That means less take-home pay for working families that have already been crushed by the Biden-era inflation. This isn't some hypothetical scenario.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Thompson
featured_quotes.text: Mr. Speaker, Republicans are openly bragging about how the bill kicks children and the elderly off Medicaid, nutritional assistance, and more, all to pay for another tax break for wealthy Republican donors. My Republican colleagues are not talking about the trillions and trillions of dollars their political giveaway is going to cost. In fact, Mr. Speaker, Vice President Vance has said historic levels of Homeland Security funding in the bill sweetens the deal for the devil.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Alford
featured_quotes.text: Today, Mr. Speaker, we face a watershed moment for the American people. This Republican majority was given a clear mandate by the American people, which is the America First agenda. This bill is our opportunity to deliver on that agenda. H.R. 1 stops the largest tax increase in U.S. history, while providing the largest tax cut for working-and middle-class families ever, with no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, and tax breaks for seniors.

added: Temporary deductions for tips ($25,000), overtime ($12,500 or $25,000 joint), car-loan interest ($10,000), and seniors ($6,000), all ending after 2028
A Medicaid community-engagement (work) requirement and a Rural Health Transformation Program
$46.55B for border wall and infrastructure and $45B for immigration detention
New immigration application, asylum, and parole fees
modified: The 2017 individual tax rates and increased standard deduction made permanent
The child tax credit raised to $2,200 per child
The SALT deduction cap raised to $40,000 for 2025, reverting to $10,000 after 2029
SNAP work requirements expanded, with benefit-cost sharing shifted to states by payment error rate
removed: Repeals and rescissions of prior clean-energy and environmental provisions across several titles
A cap on Consumer Financial Protection Bureau funding
